title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Ansible ships with thousands of modules. A beginner does not know where to start, so they write everything with shell:. Then every run reports changed, --check cannot predict anything, and handlers fire every time.
For the Lemonade Stand you need perhaps thirty modules: write files, install nginx, start services, create a user, call the health endpoint. This lesson is the map.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Ansible ships with thousands of modules. A beginner does not know where to start, so they write everything with shell:. Then every run reports changed, --check cannot predict anything, and handlers fire every time.
For the Lemonade Stand you need perhaps thirty modules: write files, install nginx, start services, create a user, call the health endpoint. This lesson is the map.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipA box of LEGO pieces



A module is one LEGO piece with a single job. A wheel rolls. A hinge bends. A window lets light in. You don’t carve a wheel out of a plain brick. You pick the wheel piece, because it already works.
shell is the plain brick: you can build anything with it, but you have to shape it yourself, and it never tells you whether anything changed. Grab the special piece first: copy for files, package for software, service for programs that keep running. Use the plain brick only when no special piece exists.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
The concept, precisely

A module is a small program with parameters (its inputs) and return values (a JSON result).
Every module returns at least changed (true or false) and failed. Many add more, such as rc and stdout for command, or stat.exists for stat.
Save the result with register: and use it in later tasks (lesson 6).
Write the fully qualified collection name (FQCN): namespace.collection.module. All modules below live in ansible.builtin, which ships with ansible-core.
Most modules are declarative and idempotent. The exceptions, marked ⚠, always run.

Find modules and read their documentation without leaving the terminal:








Command
What it does
Example




ansible-doc -l
List every installed module.
ansible-doc -l ansible.builtin (71 modules in 2.21)


ansible-doc NAME
Full documentation: parameters, return values, examples.
ansible-doc ansible.builtin.copy


ansible-doc -s NAME
A short task snippet with every parameter.
ansible-doc -s ansible.builtin.lineinfile


ansible-doc -t TYPE -l
List other plugin types.
ansible-doc -t lookup -l

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Checking and talking










Module
What it does
Key parameters
Returns
Example




ping
Checks Ansible can log in and run Python.
none
ping: pong
ansible.builtin.ping:


debug
Prints a message or a variable.
msg, var, verbosity
msg
debug: { var: menu.status }


assert
Fails unless every condition is true.
that (list), fail_msg, success_msg
msg
assert: { that: [lemonade_app_port > 1024] }


fail
Stops the host with a message.
msg

fail: { msg: "No menu defined" }


pause
Waits, or asks the operator to press Enter.
seconds, minutes, prompt
user_input
pause: { seconds: 10 }


set_fact
Creates a variable for the rest of the play.
key: value pairs, cacheable

set_fact: { menu_size: "{{ lemonade_menu \| length }}" }

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Running programs ⚠










Module
What it does
Key parameters
Returns
Example




command
Runs a program without a shell. The default for ad hoc.
cmd or argv, chdir, creates, removes
rc, stdout, stdout_lines, stderr
command: { cmd: nginx -t }


shell
Runs a line through /bin/sh: pipes, >, $VAR.
cmd, chdir, creates, executable
same as command
shell: "ps aux \| grep -c nginx"


raw
Sends a bare SSH command. Needs no Python on the host.
free text
rc, stdout
raw: apt-get install -y python3


script
Copies a local script to the host and runs it.
free text, creates, chdir
rc, stdout
script: scripts/seed_menu.sh



creates: PATH skips the command when PATH already exists. removes: PATH skips it when PATH does not exist. Those two parameters make a command idempotent.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Files and folders










Module
What it does
Key parameters
Returns
Example




copy
Puts a local file, or inline text, on the host.
src or content, dest, mode, owner, backup, force, validate
dest, checksum
copy: { src: logo.png, dest: /srv/lemonade/site/ }


template
Renders a Jinja2 template, then copies it.
src (a .j2 file), dest, mode, validate
same as copy
template: { src: nginx.conf.j2, dest: /etc/nginx/conf.d/lemonade.conf }


file
Makes a folder, link or empty file, sets owner and mode, or deletes.
path, state (directory, file, touch, link, hard, absent), mode, owner, recurse
path, state
file: { path: /srv/lemonade, state: directory, mode: "0755" }


lineinfile
Makes sure one line is in a file, or replaces the line matching a regex.
path, line, regexp, state, create, insertafter
msg
lineinfile: { path: /etc/lemonade.env, regexp: "^PORT=", line: "PORT=8080" }


blockinfile
Makes sure a block of lines sits between two marker comments.
path, block, marker, state
msg
blockinfile: { path: /etc/hosts, block: "192.0.2.21 db1" }


replace
Replaces every match of a regex in a file.
path, regexp, replace
msg
replace: { path: menu.txt, regexp: "2\\.50", replace: "2.75" }


stat
Looks at a file without changing it.
path, get_checksum
stat.exists, stat.size, stat.mode, stat.isdir
stat: { path: /srv/lemonade/site/index.html }


get_url
Downloads a file from a URL.
url, dest, checksum, mode
dest, checksum_src
get_url: { url: https://example.com/app.tgz, dest: /tmp/, checksum: "sha256:..." }


unarchive
Unpacks a .tar.gz or .zip.
src, dest, remote_src, creates
dest
unarchive: { src: /tmp/app.tgz, dest: /srv/lemonade, remote_src: true }



Where src is searched: copy and unarchive look in a role’s files/ folder, and template looks in templates/. validate: "nginx -t -c %s" checks the new file before it replaces the old one, so a typo never reaches nginx.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Packages and services









Module
What it does
Key parameters
Example




package
Installs or removes packages with whatever manager the OS uses.
name (string or list), state (present, absent, latest; documented as required, so always write it)
package: { name: nginx, state: present }


apt
Debian and Ubuntu packages.
name, state, update_cache, cache_valid_time
apt: { name: nginx, update_cache: true, cache_valid_time: 3600 }


dnf
Fedora, RHEL and Rocky packages.
name, state, enablerepo
dnf: { name: nginx, state: latest }


service
Starts, stops or enables a service with any init system.
name, state (started, stopped, restarted, reloaded), enabled
service: { name: nginx, state: started, enabled: true }


systemd_service
The same, with systemd extras.
name, state, enabled, daemon_reload, masked
systemd_service: { name: lemonade, daemon_reload: true, state: restarted }



started is idempotent: it does nothing when the service is already running. restarted and reloaded act every time, so use them in handlers.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Users and groups









Module
What it does
Key parameters
Example




group
Makes sure a Unix group exists.
name, gid, state, system
group: { name: lemonade, system: true }


user
Makes sure a Unix user exists.
name, group, groups, append, shell, system, create_home, state
user: { name: lemonade, group: lemonade, system: true, shell: /usr/sbin/nologin }



groups replaces the user’s extra groups unless you also set append: true.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Code, web and waiting










Module
What it does
Key parameters
Returns
Example




git
Clones or updates a repository.
repo, dest, version (default HEAD), depth
before, after (commit IDs)
git: { repo: https://github.com/acme/lemonade.git, dest: /srv/lemonade/app, version: v1.1.0 }


uri
Makes an HTTP request and checks the status.
url, method, status_code (default [200]), body, return_content
status, content, json
uri: { url: "http://web1:8080/health" }


wait_for
Waits for a port, a file or a text in a file.
port, host, path, search_regex, state, timeout (default 300)
elapsed
wait_for: { port: 8080, timeout: 30 }


cron
Manages one cron job, found again by its name.
name, job, minute, hour, weekday, state

cron: { name: nightly-report, hour: "2", minute: "0", job: /srv/lemonade/report.sh }




Beyond ansible.builtin
Many useful modules live in collections that you install separately (lesson 9):

ansible.posix.authorized_key adds an SSH public key to a user.
ansible.posix.firewalld and community.general.ufw manage firewalls.
community.postgresql.postgresql_db creates databases.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Worked examples
A web server from nothing: the four steps that every web role has. Packages and services need root, so the play sets become: true.
- name: Install nginx
  ansible.builtin.package: { name: nginx, state: present }

- name: Write the Lemonade site
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/conf.d/lemonade.conf
    validate: nginx -t -c %s
  notify: Reload nginx

- name: Keep nginx running after reboots
  ansible.builtin.service: { name: nginx, state: started, enabled: true }
A health check that reads the page. Run against a local copy of the menu page:
- name: Ask the menu page for a 200
  ansible.builtin.uri:
    url: http://127.0.0.1:18080/index.html
    return_content: true
  register: menu

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ menu.status }} {{ 'Pink Lemonade' in menu.content }}"
ok: [localhost] =>
    msg: 200 True
Asking for a page that does not exist fails, because 404 is not in status_code:
fatal: [localhost]: FAILED! =>
    msg: 'Status code was 404 and not [200]: HTTP Error 404: File not found'
    status: 404
Two modules fighting over one file. Each task below is idempotent on its own:
- ansible.builtin.copy:
    dest: prices.conf
    content: "classic = 2.50\n"      # add "force: false" to fix the fight
- ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
    path: prices.conf
    line: "pink = 3.00"
Three runs in a row report changed=2, changed=2, changed=2. copy resets the file to one line, and then lineinfile adds the second line back. With force: false, copy only creates the file when it is missing, and the runs report changed=0.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Rules and conventions

Pick the most specific module. package over shell: apt-get, copy over shell: echo >.
Always write the FQCN, so readers and ansible-lint know where the module comes from.
One owner per file. Either template manages the whole file, or lineinfile/blockinfile manage parts of it. Never both.
Quote file modes: mode: "0644" (lesson 4).
Validate config files with validate: before they go live.
Make command and shell honest with creates, removes or changed_when.
Read ansible-doc for the return values before you write register:.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




shell: systemctl restart nginx in normal tasks
Restarts on every run; changed every time.
service with state: started in tasks, state: restarted in a handler.


copy and lineinfile on one file
The playbook is never changed=0.
Give the file one owner, or use force: false on copy.


user: { groups: www-data } without append
The user loses its other groups, such as sudo.
Add append: true.


apt without update_cache on a new server
No package matching 'nginx' is available.
update_cache: true and cache_valid_time: 3600.


package without state
Behaviour depends on the OS package manager behind it; the docs mark state as required.
Always write state: present.


Host has no Python
Every module fails.
Bootstrap with raw: apt-get install -y python3.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
A playbook runs its tasks one after another. As functions on the server state, that is a composition:
\[
R = t_n \circ \cdots \circ t_2 \circ t_1
\]
where:

\(t_1, t_2, \dots, t_n\) are the tasks in order; each is a function from states to states (lesson 1);
\(\circ\) means “do the right-hand function first, then the left-hand one”, so \((t_2 \circ t_1)(s) = t_2(t_1(s))\);
\(R\) is the whole run.

Example. The fight above has \(n = 2\) tasks: \(t_1\) is copy and \(t_2\) is lineinfile, so \(R = t_2 \circ t_1\) and \(R(s) = t_2(t_1(s))\). Starting from an empty folder \(s\): \(t_1(s)\) is a file with the one line classic = 2.50, and \(t_2\) of that adds pink = 3.00. So \(R(s)\) is the two-line file.
Even when every \(t_i\) is idempotent, \(R\) can still report changes on every run. Ansible reports task \(i\) as changed when it altered the state it was given:
\[
C = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \big[\, t_i(s_{i-1}) \neq s_{i-1} \,\big], \qquad s_i = t_i(s_{i-1})
\]
where:

\(s_0\) is the state before the run, and \(s_i\) is the state after task \(i\);
\([\,P\,]\) is 1 when the statement \(P\) is true and 0 when it is false;
\(C\) is the changed= count for this host.

Example, the fight above. Let \(s^\ast\) be the finished file with two lines, classic = 2.50 and pink = 3.00. Start the second run from \(s_0 = s^\ast\):

\(t_1\) = copy with force: true: \(t_1(s^\ast)\) is the one-line file, which is different from \(s^\ast\). That counts 1.
\(t_2\) = lineinfile: it adds pink = 3.00 back, which is different from the one-line file. That counts 1.
\(C = 1 + 1 = 2\), and the final state is \(s^\ast\) again.

So \(R(R(s)) = R(s)\): the file ends the same. But \(C = 2\) on every run, so a handler would fire every time. With force: false, \(t_1(s^\ast) = s^\ast\) and \(t_2(s^\ast) = s^\ast\), so \(C = 0 + 0 = 0\). A playbook is only truly idempotent when both the state and the change count settle.

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
The Lemonade web servers are almost identical, but not quite:

web1 is a bigger machine and should run 4 nginx workers. web2 should use the normal 1.
Every web server serves the same menu.
During a test you want to try 8 workers once, without editing any file.

If the same playbook must produce slightly different results, the differences go into variables. Then the question is: when a value is set in several places, which one wins?

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
The Lemonade web servers are almost identical, but not quite:

web1 is a bigger machine and should run 4 nginx workers. web2 should use the normal 1.
Every web server serves the same menu.
During a test you want to try 8 workers once, without editing any file.

If the same playbook must produce slightly different results, the differences go into variables. Then the question is: when a value is set in several places, which one wins?

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipSchool rules and the loudspeaker



At school there are rules at different levels:

The school rule: “Lunch is at 12:00.”
Your class rule: “Class 4B has lunch at 12:30.”
A note just for you: “Maya, you have lunch at 11:45 because of your dentist visit.”
The head teacher’s loudspeaker announcement: “Today everyone has lunch at 13:00!”

When rules disagree, the more specific one wins: your note beats the class rule, and the class rule beats the school rule. The loudspeaker beats everything.
Ansible variables work the same way. Role defaults are the school rule, group_vars is the class rule, host_vars is the note just for you, and -e on the command line is the loudspeaker.

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
The concept, precisely

A variable is a name with a value. Use it in Jinja as { lemonade_app_port }.
Values can be strings, numbers, booleans, lists or dictionaries. Read inside a dictionary with menu.price or menu['price'].
Facts are variables Ansible discovers on each host: its OS, IP addresses, memory and so on.
Magic variables are variables Ansible sets itself, such as inventory_hostname.
Registered variables hold the result of a task (register:).


Naming rules



Rule
Valid
Invalid




Letters, digits and underscores only
lemonade_app_port
lemonade-app-port, app port, app.port


Start with a letter or _
web_port
8080_port


Not a Python keyword or playbook keyword
menu_items
class, async, environment, hosts


Prefix role variables with the role name
lemonade_menu
menu (too easy to clash)


Prefix secrets with vault_
vault_db_password
(lesson 10)

title: 6. Variables and Facts
section: Every place a variable can come from
text:
Every place a variable can come from









Source
Where it lives
Rule / convention
Example




Role defaults
roles/x/defaults/main.yml
Lowest precedence. Put every tunable value here.
lemonade_nginx_workers: 1


Inventory
vars: in inventory.yml
Prefer group_vars/ files.
all: vars: { ansible_connection: local }


group_vars/
next to inventory or playbook
One file or folder per group.
group_vars/web.yml


host_vars/
next to inventory or playbook
One file or folder per host.
host_vars/web1.yml


Facts
gathered by setup
Read with ansible_facts['…'].
ansible_facts['distribution']


Play vars
in the play
For values that belong to this playbook only.
vars: { lemonade_version: "1.1.0" }


vars_files
listed in the play
Usually secrets.
vars_files: [secrets/vault.yml]


vars_prompt
in the play
Asks a person; blocks automation.
vars_prompt: [{ name: release }]


Role vars
roles/x/vars/main.yml
High precedence. For constants users must not change.
lemonade_folders: [nginx, site]


Block and task vars
on a block or task
Only visible there.
vars: { greeting: hi }


include_vars
a task
Loads a file at run time.
include_vars: { file: "{{ ansible_facts['os_family'] }}.yml" }


set_fact / register
a task
Created while the play runs.
register: menu_check


Role parameters
roles: [{ role: x, var: 1 }]
For one use of a role.
- { role: lemonade_web, lemonade_app_port: 9090 }


Extra vars
-e on the command line
Always wins.
-e lemonade_nginx_workers=8




The precedence ladder
The official documentation lists 22 levels. From lowest (1) to highest (22):

command-line values such as -u deploy (these are not variables)
role defaults
inventory file or script group vars
inventory group_vars/all
playbook group_vars/all
inventory group_vars/*
playbook group_vars/*
inventory file or script host vars
inventory host_vars/*
playbook host_vars/*
host facts and cached set_fact
play vars
play vars_prompt
play vars_files
role vars (vars/main.yml)
block vars
task vars
include_vars
set_fact and registered vars
role (and include_role) parameters
include parameters
extra vars (-e)

You rarely need all 22. Remember the short version: defaults < group < host < play < role vars < task < set_fact < -e.
Two more rules matter:

Dictionaries and lists are replaced, not merged. The lab’s role default menu has one drink and group_vars/web.yml has three. The web servers get exactly three, not four. Merge on purpose with the combine filter (lesson 7).
Variables are per host. web1 and web2 each have their own lemonade_nginx_workers.

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
Facts
With gather_facts: true (the default), each play starts with a hidden setup task that fills ansible_facts.









Keyword or setting
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




gather_facts
Run setup at the start of the play.
Turn off when you don’t read facts.
gather_facts: false


gather_subset
Collect only some facts.
min is fast; !hardware skips one area.
gather_subset: [min, network]


ansible_facts['x']
Read a fact.
The preferred form. The key has no ansible_ prefix.
ansible_facts['distribution']


ansible_x
Old top-level form.
Deprecated: 2.21 warns, and the default changes in 2.24.
ansible_distribution


setup filter
Show only matching facts.
Ad hoc exploration.
-a "filter=ansible_python_version"


/etc/ansible/facts.d/*.fact
Custom facts on the host.
JSON or INI files, read into ansible_local.
ansible_local['lemonade']['version']


fact_caching (ansible.cfg)
Remember facts between runs.
jsonfile or redis; fact_caching_timeout is in seconds.
fact_caching = jsonfile

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
Magic variables








Variable
Value
Example value in the lab




inventory_hostname
The host’s name in the inventory.
web1


inventory_hostname_short
The name up to the first dot.
web1


hostvars
Every host’s variables, by name.
hostvars['db1']['ansible_host'] → 192.0.2.21


groups
Every group and its hosts.
groups['web'] → ['web1', 'web2']


group_names
Groups the current host is in.
['prod', 'web']


ansible_play_hosts
Hosts still active in this play.
['web1', 'web2']


ansible_play_batch
Hosts in the current serial batch.
['web1']


playbook_dir
Folder of the playbook.
.../examples


role_path
Folder of the running role.
.../roles/lemonade_web


inventory_dir
Folder of the inventory file.
.../examples


ansible_check_mode
true during --check.
false


ansible_version
Ansible’s version as a dictionary.
ansible_version.full → 2.21.6


omit
Leaves a module parameter out entirely.
mode: "{{ file_mode \| default(omit) }}"

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
Registered results
register: name stores a task’s JSON result. For command and shell:








Key
Meaning
Example




rc
Exit code. 0 means success.
0


stdout / stdout_lines
Output as one string, or as a list of lines.
Classic Lemonade / ['Classic Lemonade']


stderr / stderr_lines
Error output.
''


changed
Did the task change something?
false


failed
Did the task fail?
false


skipped
Was the task skipped by when?
present only when skipped


results
With loop: one result per item.
menu.results[0].stdout



- name: Read the first drink
  ansible.builtin.command: head -n 1 /srv/lemonade/menu.txt
  register: first_drink
  changed_when: false        # reading never changes anything

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "First drink is {{ first_drink.stdout }}"

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
Worked example: who wins?
lemonade_nginx_workers is set in two files:
# roles/lemonade_web/defaults/main.yml   (level 2)
lemonade_nginx_workers: 1
# host_vars/web1.yml                     (level 9)
lemonade_nginx_workers: 4
web1 gets 4 and web2 falls back to 1. Now add the loudspeaker for one dry run:
ansible-playbook site.yml --limit web --check --diff -e lemonade_nginx_workers=8
TASK [lemonade_web : Render the nginx config] **********************************
-worker_processes 4;
+worker_processes 8;
changed: [web1]
-worker_processes 1;
+worker_processes 8;
changed: [web2]
Read another host’s variables through hostvars, for example so a web server can find the database:
ansible web1 -m ansible.builtin.debug -a "msg='{{ hostvars[\"db1\"].ansible_host }}:{{ hostvars[\"db1\"].db_port }}'"
web1 | SUCCESS =>
    msg: 192.0.2.21:5432
Read one fact:
ansible db1 -m ansible.builtin.setup -a "filter=ansible_python_version"
db1 | SUCCESS =>
    ansible_facts:
        ansible_python_version: 3.15.2

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
Rules and conventions

Put every knob in role defaults, with a sensible value. Override in group_vars or host_vars.
Keep -e for one-off runs and CI pipelines, not for values that belong in Git.
Define each variable in as few places as possible. Two definitions are a choice; five are a puzzle.
Use ansible_facts['name'], not the deprecated ansible_name.
Turn off facts (gather_facts: false) when no task needs them.
Check the merged result with ansible-inventory --host web1, or with a debug: var=... task.

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




A variable name with a dash
'lemonade' is undefined, because Jinja reads lemonade-port as subtraction.
Use underscores.


Expecting lists or dictionaries to merge
Drinks from the role default vanish.
Merge explicitly with combine, or define the full list in one place.


Setting a value in role vars/ and overriding it in group_vars
The override is ignored, because role vars are level 15.
Move it to defaults/.


Using ansible_distribution
Deprecation warning: top-level facts will not be injected after the change in 2.24.
ansible_facts['distribution'].


register inside a loop, then .stdout
object of type 'dict' has no attribute 'stdout'
Use .results[i].stdout, or loop over .results.

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
It is a hot Saturday and the Lemonade Stand is busy. You need quick answers and quick fixes, and writing a playbook for each one would be overkill:

Which version is each web server running right now?
Put a “Closed for lunch” notice on both web servers.
Restart nginx on web2 only.

An ad hoc command runs one module on many hosts from a single line in the terminal.

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
It is a hot Saturday and the Lemonade Stand is busy. You need quick answers and quick fixes, and writing a playbook for each one would be overkill:

Which version is each web server running right now?
Put a “Closed for lunch” notice on both web servers.
Restart nginx on web2 only.

An ad hoc command runs one module on many hosts from a single line in the terminal.

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipSimon says



In the game Simon says, one person calls out an instruction and everybody does it at once: “Simon says touch your nose!” Nobody writes anything down first. It is a single instruction, for right now.
An ad hoc command is “Simon says” for servers. ansible web -a "uptime" means “Simon says: every web server, tell me your uptime.” When you want the same instructions every week, write them into a playbook instead. That is the recipe card you keep.

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
The concept, precisely
The shape of every ad hoc command:
ansible <pattern> -m <module> -a "<arguments>" [flags]

<pattern> chooses the hosts (lesson 2).
-m names the module. When you leave it out, Ansible uses ansible.builtin.command.
-a gives the module’s arguments, either as key=value key=value or as JSON.
Arguments are Jinja templates, so { inventory_hostname } becomes each host’s own name.

Ansible runs the module on every matched host in parallel, up to forks hosts at a time (default 5).

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
command or shell?
Both run a program. The difference is whether a shell (/bin/sh) reads your line first.









ansible.builtin.command
ansible.builtin.shell




Pipes \|, redirects >
No
Yes


$HOME, *.txt, &&
No
Yes


Safe with odd input
Yes: arguments are never re-parsed
Take care: a ; in a variable runs a second command


Idempotent
No, unless you add creates= or removes=
Same


Use it when
You run one program with arguments
You truly need shell features



Rule: use command by default, and use shell only for pipes, redirects or shell variables. Before both, look for a real module. copy is better than shell: echo > file.

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
Worked examples
All from devops/ansible/examples/. Paths in the output are shown with the default lab_root.
Which version does each web server serve?
ansible web -a "grep -o 'version .*<' {{ lab_root }}/{{ inventory_hostname }}/site/index.html"
web1 | CHANGED | rc=0 >>
version 1.1.0<
web2 | CHANGED | rc=0 >>
version 1.1.0<
CHANGED here does not mean anything changed. command cannot tell, so it always says CHANGED. rc=0 is the exit code.
A pipe needs shell. With command, ls receives |, wc and -l as file names:
ansible db1 -a "ls {{ lab_root }}/db1 | wc -l"                      # FAILED rc=1: ls: |: No such file
ansible db1 -m ansible.builtin.shell -a "ls {{ lab_root }}/db1 | wc -l"   # CHANGED rc=0 >> 2
A real module is idempotent. Run this twice:
ansible web -m ansible.builtin.copy \
  -a "content='Closed for lunch' dest={{ lab_root }}/{{ inventory_hostname }}/site/notice.txt"
web1 | CHANGED =>        # first run
    changed: true
web1 | SUCCESS =>        # second run
    changed: false
creates= makes command idempotent. It skips the command when the file already exists:
ansible db1 -a "touch {{ lab_root }}/db1/seeded creates={{ lab_root }}/db1/seeded"
db1 | CHANGED | rc=0 >>                                   # first run
db1 | SUCCESS | rc=0 >>                                   # second run
skipped, since /tmp/lemonade-lab/db1/seeded exists
On real servers, with sudo:
ansible web -b -m ansible.builtin.package -a "name=nginx state=present"
ansible web2 -b -m ansible.builtin.service -a "name=nginx state=restarted"
ansible db1 -m ansible.builtin.setup -a "filter=ansible_distribution*"

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
Rules and conventions

Ad hoc for questions and emergencies, playbooks for anything you repeat. If you type the same ad hoc command twice, put it in a playbook.
Look at the hosts first: add --list-hosts before any command that changes things.
Prefer a module over command/shell. Modules report changed honestly and support --check.
Quote the -a string, and use single quotes inside it.
Restarting services is not idempotent by design. state=restarted always restarts. Use state=started to only make sure a service is running.

Common mistakes



Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Pipe or > with the default module

Use -m ansible.builtin.shell.


Forgetting -b for packages
This command has to be run under the root user.
Add -b, and -K if sudo asks for a password.

Works, but $ inside is expanded by your local shell.
Use single quotes outside, or escape $.

Using -o in scripts
Deprecation warning; it breaks in ansible-core 2.23.
Configure the oneline callback, or use a playbook.

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Ansible starts at most \(f\) hosts at the same time. If every host takes about the same time per task, the hosts run in waves:
\[
w = \left\lceil \frac{n}{f} \right\rceil
\]
where:

\(n\) is the number of hosts the pattern matched (a count, \(n \ge 1\));
\(f\) is the number of forks, set by -f or forks in ansible.cfg (default 5);
\(\lceil x \rceil\) (“ceiling”) rounds \(x\) up to the next whole number;
\(w\) is the number of waves.

Example. The lab has \(n = 3\) hosts.

With \(f = 5\): \(w = \lceil 3/5 \rceil = \lceil 0.6 \rceil = 1\) wave. All three run together.
With \(f = 1\): \(w = \lceil 3/1 \rceil = 3\) waves. One host at a time.

The time for one task is then roughly:
\[
T \approx w \cdot t + c
\]
where:

\(T\) is the total time in seconds;
\(t\) is the time one host needs for the task, in seconds;
\(c\) is Ansible’s fixed start-up cost, in seconds (reading the inventory, starting Python);
\(w\) is the number of waves from the formula above.

Example. In the lab, ansible all -a "sleep 1" has \(t = 1\) s. Measured on a laptop:

-f 1: \(w = 3\), so \(T \approx 3 \cdot 1 + c\). Measured: 4.3 s, which gives \(c \approx 1.3\) s.
-f 3: \(w = 1\), so \(T \approx 1 \cdot 1 + c\). Measured: 1.8 s, which gives \(c \approx 0.8\) s.

For a summer fleet of \(n = 12\) web servers with \(t = 4\) s, the default \(f = 5\) gives \(w = \lceil 12/5 \rceil = \lceil 2.4 \rceil = 3\) waves, so \(T \approx 3 \cdot 4 = 12\) s plus start-up. Raising \(f\) to 12 gives one wave, about 4 s. The formula is an approximation: real hosts take different times, and Ansible starts a new host as soon as a fork is free.

title: 4. Playbooks
4. Playbooks
4. Playbooks
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipThe team’s playbook and the pilot’s checklist



A football coach keeps a playbook. Each play says which players do what: “defenders, stay back; strikers, run left”. Ansible borrowed the name. A play says which hosts (players) run which tasks (moves).
Pilots and surgeons use checklists too. In The Checklist Manifesto (2009), the surgeon Atul Gawande tells how a simple 19-item checklist, tested in eight hospitals around the world, cut deaths after surgery from 1.5% to 0.8%. People are not bad at their jobs. They just forget steps when they are busy. A checklist never forgets.
A playbook is a checklist for computers. Computers follow it perfectly, every single time.

title: 4. Playbooks
text:
The concept, precisely

A playbook is a YAML file that holds a list of plays.
A play maps a set of hosts (hosts:) to an ordered list of tasks.
A task calls one module with arguments.
Ansible runs task by task: task 1 on all hosts, then task 2 on all hosts, and so on. This is the default linear strategy.

The first play of the lab’s site.yml:
- name: Configure the web servers   # play name, shown in the output
  hosts: web                        # which hosts (a pattern)
  gather_facts: false               # skip collecting system facts (faster)
  roles:
    - lemonade_web                  # the tasks come from this role
A play with tasks written directly in it:
- name: Configure the database server
  hosts: db
  tasks:
    - name: Write the database settings          # task name
      ansible.builtin.copy:                      # module (FQCN)
        content: "port = {{ db_port }}\n"        # module arguments
        dest: "{{ lab_root }}/db1/db.conf"

title: 4. Playbooks
text:
YAML rules that matter
Ansible files are YAML. Most beginner errors are YAML errors, not Ansible errors.









Rule
Right
Wrong
Why




Indent with spaces, never tabs
··hosts: web
⇥hosts: web
YAML forbids tabs for indentation. Two spaces is the convention.


A list item starts with -
- name: Render
-name: Render
The space after - is required.


A map entry is key: value
state: directory
state:directory
The space after : is required.


Quote a value that starts with {{
dest: "{{ path }}"
dest: {{ path }}
Unquoted { starts a YAML dictionary.


Quote a value that contains :
msg: "Price: 2.50"
msg: Price: 2.50
: would start a second key.


Write booleans as true / false
become: true
become: yes
yes, no, on, off are booleans in YAML 1.1 too, but they confuse readers. A country code NO silently becomes false.


Quote file modes
mode: "0644"
mode: 644
Unquoted 644 is the decimal number 644, which is the wrong permission. See the maths below.


\| keeps line breaks
content: \|

For files and scripts.


> folds lines into one
msg: >

For long sentences.


--- at the top is optional
---

It marks the start of a YAML document.


# starts a comment
# why we do this

Explain why, not what.

text:
Every play keyword



Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example

Label printed as PLAY [...].
Always set it.

Which hosts the play targets.
A pattern (lesson 2). Required.

Set on the play or on single tasks.

Default true. Turn off when you don’t use facts.

Smaller is faster.

Variables for this play.

Run after pre_tasks, before tasks.

The main task list.

title: 4. Playbooks
text:
Worked example
Look before you leap. From devops/ansible/examples/:
ansible-playbook site.yml --list-tasks
  play #1 (web): Configure the web servers  TAGS: []
      lemonade_web : Create the nginx and site folders  TAGS: []
      lemonade_web : Render the nginx config    TAGS: []
      lemonade_web : Render the menu page   TAGS: []
  play #2 (db): Configure the database server   TAGS: []
      Create the database folder    TAGS: []
      Write the database settings   TAGS: []
Preview a port change on web1 without touching anything:
ansible-playbook site.yml --limit web1 --check --diff -e lemonade_app_port=9090
TASK [lemonade_web : Render the nginx config] **********************************
-    location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; }
+    location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:9090; }
changed: [web1]

PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
web1   : ok=4    changed=1    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
The file on disk still says 8080. --check only predicted the change.

title: 4. Playbooks
text:
Reading PLAY RECAP








Counter
Meaning
Good or bad?




ok
Tasks that succeeded, including the changed ones.
Expected.


changed
Tasks that modified the host.
Expected on the first run; should be 0 on the second.


unreachable
Ansible could not connect. The host is dropped from the rest of the play.
Check SSH, DNS and the firewall.


failed
A task failed. The host stops running further tasks.
Read the error above the recap.


skipped
A when was false, or a module could not run in check mode.
Usually fine.


rescued
A failure handled by a rescue: section.
Fine. The recovery worked.


ignored
A failure hidden by ignore_errors: true.
Look at it. Something did fail.



The exit code tells scripts and CI what happened: 0 all good, 1 general error, 2 at least one host failed, 4 a host was unreachable (or the playbook could not be parsed), 5 bad command-line options, 99 you pressed Ctrl-C.

title: 4. Playbooks
text:
Rules and conventions

One playbook per purpose: site.yml builds everything; rolling-update.yml upgrades; small task files live in roles.
Name every play and task. The names are your log.
Use FQCNs: ansible.builtin.copy, not copy.
Put tasks in roles once a play has more than a handful of tasks (lesson 9).
Run --syntax-check, then --check --diff, then the real run.
Set gather_facts: false when no task uses facts. It saves one task per host.

title: 4. Playbooks
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Unquoted { } at the start of a value
YAML parsing failed: This may be an issue with missing quotes around a template block.
Quote it: dest: "{{ path }}".


msg: Price: 2.50
YAML parsing failed: Colons in unquoted values must be followed by a non-space character.
Quote the whole value.


mode: 644
Files get odd permissions (--w----r-T).
mode: "0644".


Tabs in the file
YAML parsing failed: Tabs are usually invalid in YAML.
Set your editor to insert spaces.


Expecting --check to run command tasks
Tasks show skipped.
Add check_mode: false to read-only commands.


when: "{{ x }}"
Deprecation warning: conditionals should not be surrounded by { }; this stops working in ansible-core 2.23.
Write when: x.

title: 7. Jinja2 Templates
text:
Each Lemonade web server needs its own nginx config. web1 has 4 workers and web2 has 1. Both forward to port 8080. The menu page must list every drink with its price.
Keeping two hand-written copies means editing two files for every price change, and one day they will differ. Instead we want one file with blanks, and Ansible fills the blanks for each host.

title: 7. Jinja2 Templates
text:
Each Lemonade web server needs its own nginx config. web1 has 4 workers and web2 has 1. Both forward to port 8080. The menu page must list every drink with its price.
Keeping two hand-written copies means editing two files for every price change, and one day they will differ. Instead we want one file with blanks, and Ansible fills the blanks for each host.

title: 7. Jinja2 Templates
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipMad Libs



Mad Libs is a word game invented by Roger Price and Leonard Stern in the 1950s. You get a story with blanks: “Today I drank a (adjective) lemonade that cost (number) dollars.” Your friends call out words, you write them into the blanks, and you read out a funny story.
A Jinja2 template is a Mad Libs page for computers. worker_processes {{ lemonade_nginx_workers }}; has one blank. For web1 Ansible writes 4 into it; for web2 it writes 1. Templates can do one trick that Mad Libs can’t: “repeat this line for every drink on the menu”.

title: 7. Jinja2 Templates
text:
The concept, precisely

Jinja2 is a template language for Python. Ansible uses it everywhere: in playbook values, in when: conditions, and in template files.
Templating happens on the control node, before anything is sent to the host.
The ansible.builtin.template module renders a .j2 file with the host’s variables and copies the result to the host. It is copy with blanks filled in.
A filter transforms a value: { name | upper }. A test asks a yes/no question: { port is defined }. A lookup fetches data from outside, on the control node.

title: 7. Jinja2 Templates
7. Jinja2 Templates
text:
Filters you will use
All results below are real outputs from ansible-core 2.21. In the examples, ports is {http: 80, app: 8080} and the menu holds Classic Lemonade (2.50, in stock), Pink Lemonade (3.00, out of stock) and Iced Tea (2.00, in stock).









Filter
What it does
Rule / convention
Example → result




default(v)
Uses v when the variable is undefined.
default(v, true) also replaces empty strings.
missing \| default('none') → none


mandatory
Fails with a clear error when undefined.
For values that have no sensible default.
x \| mandatory → Mandatory variable 'x' not defined.


upper, lower
Changes the case.

'Sunny' \| upper → SUNNY


replace(a, b)
Replaces text.
Plain text, not a regex.
'Sunny Stand' \| replace('Sunny','Rainy') → Rainy Stand


join(sep)
List → string.

['web1','web2'] \| join(', ') → web1, web2


split(sep)
String → list.

'web1,web2' \| split(',') → ['web1', 'web2']


int, float
Text → number.
Needed before maths on strings.
'4' \| int + 1 → 5


bool
Text → true/false.
'yes', 'true', '1' → True.
'yes' \| bool → True


length
Number of items or characters.

menu \| length → 3


sum
Adds up a list of numbers.

menu \| map(attribute='price') \| sum → 7.5


map(attribute=a)
Takes one field from each dictionary.
Follow with list to see a list.
menu \| map(attribute='name') \| list


selectattr(a)
Keeps the items whose field is true, or passes a test.
selectattr('price', '>', 2) also works.
menu \| selectattr('in_stock') \| map(attribute='name') \| list → ['Classic Lemonade', 'Iced Tea']


unique, sort
Removes duplicates; sorts.

['web','prod','web'] \| unique → ['web', 'prod']


combine(d)
Merges dictionaries; the right side wins.
recursive=true merges nested ones.
ports \| combine({'app': 9090}) → {http: 80, app: 9090}


dict2items
Dictionary → list of {key, value}.
For looping over a dictionary.
ports \| dict2items → [{key: http, value: 80}, …]


items2dict
The reverse.

… \| items2dict → {http: 80, app: 8080}


to_json, to_nice_json
Data → JSON text.

ports \| to_json → {"http": 80, "app": 8080}


to_yaml, to_nice_yaml
Data → YAML text.
Indent with indent=2.
ports \| to_nice_yaml → app: 8080…


from_json, from_yaml
Text → data.
Parse command output.
'{"a": 1}' \| from_json → {a: 1}


regex_replace(p, r)
Regex replace.
Back-references are \\1.
'web-01' \| regex_replace('^web-(\\d+)$', 'server \\1') → server 01


ternary(a, b)
a if true, b if false.

(8080 > 1024) \| ternary('unprivileged','privileged') → unprivileged


format(...)
printf-style formatting.

'%.2f' \| format(2.5) → 2.50

is defined / is undefined
Does the variable exist?
missing is defined → False

null_var is none → True


is version(v, op)
Compare version strings correctly.
'2.21.6' is version('2.17', '>=') → True

'web1' is match('web') → True

'prod-web1' is search('web') → True

result is changed

Lookup
What it reads
Example

An environment variable.

The template module









Parameter
What it does
Rule / convention
Example

The .j2 file.
Searched in the role’s templates/ folder.
src: nginx.conf.j2

Path on the host.

dest: /etc/nginx/conf.d/lemonade.conf

File permissions.

title: 7. Jinja2 Templates
7. Jinja2 Templates
text:
Rules and conventions

Quote any YAML value that starts with {{: dest: "{{ path }}".
No { } inside when:. Conditions are already Jinja: when: lemonade_app_port != 80.
Keep logic out of templates. Compute values in variables, and keep templates to blanks, simple ifs and loops.
Use FQCN for lookups: lookup('ansible.builtin.env', 'HOME').
Use default() for optional values and mandatory for required ones. Make the choice visible.
Name templates after their target, plus .j2: nginx.conf.j2.

title: 7. Jinja2 Templates
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




dest: {{ path }}
YAML parsing failed: This may be an issue with missing quotes around a template block.
dest: "{{ path }}".


'4' + 1
can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
'4' \| int + 1.


lookup('file', ...) expecting a file on the host
Unable to access the file 'motd.txt': File not found.
Lookups read the control node. Use slurp or command: cat for host files.


{ menu \| map(attribute='name') } in a sentence
Prints ['Classic Lemonade', 'Pink Lemonade', …] with brackets and quotes.
End with \| join(', ') for human text.


Editing a rendered file on the server
The next run silently overwrites your edit.
Change the template; trust the Ansible managed header.

title: 7. Jinja2 Templates
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Rendering a template is a function of the template text and the host’s variables:
\[
\operatorname{render}(T, V_h) = F_h
\]
where:

\(T\) is the template text, such as nginx.conf.j2;
\(V_h\) is the set of variables of host \(h\) after precedence (lesson 6);
\(F_h\) is the resulting file for host \(h\).

The same \(T\) with different \(V_h\) gives different files. That is the whole point.
Example. \(T\) = nginx.conf.j2. With \(V_{\texttt{web1}}\) containing workers = 4, \(F_{\texttt{web1}}\) has worker_processes 4;. With \(V_{\texttt{web2}}\) containing workers = 1, \(F_{\texttt{web2}}\) has worker_processes 1;.
The default filter is a piecewise function:
\[
\operatorname{default}(x, d) =
\begin{cases}
x & \text{if } x \text{ is defined} \\
d & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
where \(x\) is the variable being read and \(d\) is the fallback value.
Example. missing | default('none'): missing is undefined, so the second case applies and the result is none. lemonade_app_port | default(80) on a web host: the variable is defined as 8080, so the first case applies and the result is 8080.
The menu total combines map and sum:
\[
P = \sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i
\]
where:

\(n\) is the number of drinks in lemonade_menu;
\(p_i\) is the price of drink \(i\), in dollars;
\(P\) is the total, which is what lemonade_menu | map(attribute='price') | sum returns.

Example. \(n = 3\), with \(p_1 = 2.50\), \(p_2 = 3.00\) and \(p_3 = 2.00\), so \(P = 2.50 + 3.00 + 2.00 = 7.50\). Ansible printed 7.5. To show it as money, use '%.2f' | format(P), which gives 7.50.
selectattr is set-builder notation:
\[
S = \lbrace\, d \in M : \operatorname{inStock}(d) \,\rbrace
\]
where \(M\) is the set of drinks on the menu, \(\operatorname{inStock}(d)\) is true when drink \(d\) has in_stock: true, and \(S\) is the drinks that pass.
Example. \(M\) = {Classic, Pink, Iced Tea}, and only Pink is out of stock, so \(S\) = {Classic, Iced Tea}. That matches the filter table above.

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Every command in this book has been run from devops/ansible/examples/, and nobody typed -i inventory.yml. Why? Because a file called ansible.cfg sits in that folder and says where the inventory is.
On a team this matters even more. If Alice has forks = 50 in her home folder and Bob has the default 5, the same playbook behaves differently for each of them. You want one project config in Git, and you want to know which settings are actually in force.

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Every command in this book has been run from devops/ansible/examples/, and nobody typed -i inventory.yml. Why? Because a file called ansible.cfg sits in that folder and says where the inventory is.
On a team this matters even more. If Alice has forks = 50 in her home folder and Bob has the default 5, the same playbook behaves differently for each of them. You want one project config in Git, and you want to know which settings are actually in force.

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipThe rule book on the top of the pile



Imagine several board-game rule books stacked in a pile: one from the game box, one your family wrote, and one your class made. The house rule is simple: read only the book on the top of the pile, and ignore the others completely. You never mix page 3 from one book with page 5 from another.
Ansible looks for ansible.cfg in the same way. It checks a fixed list of places, uses the first file it finds, and ignores the rest.
There is also a referee. Whatever the rule book says, if the referee calls out a rule during the game (“this round, everyone gets two turns!”), the referee wins. Environment variables and command-line flags are the referee.

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Where ansible.cfg is found
Ansible checks these places in order and uses the first one that exists:








Order
Location
Rule / convention




1
The file named in the ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable
For CI, or to test another config.


2
./ansible.cfg in the current folder
The usual choice: one per project, in Git.


3
~/.ansible.cfg in your home folder
Personal defaults. Keep it small.


4
/etc/ansible/ansible.cfg
System-wide, often installed by a package manager.



The files are not merged. If ./ansible.cfg exists, ~/.ansible.cfg is ignored completely.
The world-writable caveat. If the current folder can be written by every user (mode 777), Ansible refuses to read ./ansible.cfg from it. Another user could otherwise plant a config that runs their code. Real output:
[WARNING]: Ansible is being run in a world writable directory (.../ww), ignoring it as an ansible.cfg source.
  config file = None
Fix it with chmod 755 ., or point ANSIBLE_CONFIG at the file explicitly.

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
The settings that matter
The lab’s ansible.cfg is three lines:
[defaults]
inventory = inventory.yml
callback_result_format = yaml
A fuller project config:
[defaults]
inventory = inventories/prod
remote_user = deploy
forks = 20
roles_path = roles
collections_path = collections
interpreter_python = auto_silent

[ssh_connection]
pipelining = true










Setting (section)
What it does
Default
Environment variable
Example




inventory (defaults)
Inventory file or folder.
/etc/ansible/hosts
ANSIBLE_INVENTORY
inventory = inventory.yml


remote_user (defaults)
SSH login user.
your local user
ANSIBLE_REMOTE_USER
remote_user = deploy


forks (defaults)
Hosts handled in parallel.
5
ANSIBLE_FORKS
forks = 20


host_key_checking (defaults)
Refuse unknown SSH host keys.
True
ANSIBLE_HOST_KEY_CHECKING
keep True in production


timeout (defaults)
SSH connection timeout, in seconds.
10
ANSIBLE_TIMEOUT
timeout = 30


roles_path (defaults)
Where to find roles.
~/.ansible/roles:/usr/share/ansible/roles:/etc/ansible/roles
ANSIBLE_ROLES_PATH
roles_path = roles


collections_path (defaults)
Where to find collections.
~/.ansible/collections:/usr/share/ansible/collections
ANSIBLE_COLLECTIONS_PATH
collections_path = collections


stdout_callback (defaults)
The output plugin.
default
ANSIBLE_STDOUT_CALLBACK
stdout_callback = default


callback_result_format (defaults)
Results as json or readable yaml.
json
ANSIBLE_CALLBACK_RESULT_FORMAT
callback_result_format = yaml


gathering (defaults)
When to gather facts: implicit, explicit, smart.
implicit
ANSIBLE_GATHERING
gathering = smart

Where to keep facts between runs.

ANSIBLE_CACHE_PLUGIN

interpreter_python (defaults)
Python on the hosts.
auto
ANSIBLE_PYTHON_INTERPRETER
interpreter_python = auto_silent


vault_password_file (defaults)

log_path (defaults)

none

retry_files_enabled (defaults)

False
ANSIBLE_RETRY_FILES_ENABLED

become (privilege_escalation)
Use sudo by default.
False
ANSIBLE_BECOME

become_method (privilege_escalation)
How to escalate.
sudo
ANSIBLE_BECOME_METHOD

become_user (privilege_escalation)

root
ANSIBLE_BECOME_USER

pipelining (ssh_connection or connection)

False
ANSIBLE_PIPELINING

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
section: Who wins: config, environment, flags, playbook
text:
Who wins: config, environment, flags, playbook
The same setting can come from several places. From weakest to strongest:

ansible.cfg
environment variables, such as ANSIBLE_FORKS
command-line options, such as -f
playbook keywords, such as remote_user: in a play
variables, such as ansible_user in inventory, or -e

text:
Every ansible-config subcommand








Command
What it does
Example output

DEFAULT_FORKS(env: ANSIBLE_FORKS) = 10

long YAML

Writes a full commented example config.
;action_warnings=True …

ansible-lint in practice
ansible-lint is a separate package (pipx install ansible-lint). It reports rule names you can look up, for example:








Rule
What it catches
Example it would flag

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Worked example
From devops/ansible/examples/, see where every non-default setting came from:
ANSIBLE_FORKS=10 ansible-config dump --only-changed
CONFIG_FILE() = <lab>/ansible.cfg
DEFAULT_FORKS(env: ANSIBLE_FORKS) = 10
DEFAULT_HOST_LIST(<lab>/ansible.cfg) = ['<lab>/inventory.yml']

DEFAULT_HOST_LIST came from the lab’s ansible.cfg.
DEFAULT_FORKS came from the environment variable, which beats any forks = line in the file.
Add -f 20 to a real command, and 20 beats both.

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Rules and conventions

One ansible.cfg per project, in Git, next to the playbooks. Then everyone runs with the same settings.
Keep ~/.ansible.cfg minimal. It is ignored whenever a project file is found, so anything you rely on there silently disappears inside projects.
Leave host_key_checking = True for real servers. Turning it off hides man-in-the-middle attacks.
Turn on pipelining once sudo works without requiretty. It cuts SSH round trips.
Run ansible --version when confused. The config file = line says which file won.
Run ansible-lint and --syntax-check in CI (CI/CD part).

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Running from another folder
No inventory was parsed; roles not found.
cd into the project, or set ANSIBLE_CONFIG.


Expecting settings from two files to merge
A setting in ~/.ansible.cfg “does nothing”.
Only the first file found is used. Put everything in the project file.


Project folder is world-writable
ignoring it as an ansible.cfg source.
chmod 755 .


Writing pipelining under an unrelated section such as [privilege_escalation]
No speed-up.
Put it under [defaults], [connection] or [ssh_connection].


Using ansible-config validate without -t all
False error about callback_result_format.
ansible-config validate -t all.

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Which config file. Let \(L = (\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3, \ell_4)\) be the list of locations above, in order. Ansible uses
\[
\operatorname{cfg} = \ell_{k}, \qquad k = \min \lbrace\, i : \ell_i \text{ exists and is allowed} \,\rbrace
\]
where:

\(\ell_1\) is the path in ANSIBLE_CONFIG, \(\ell_2\) is ./ansible.cfg, \(\ell_3\) is ~/.ansible.cfg, and \(\ell_4\) is /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg;
“allowed” excludes \(\ell_2\) when the current folder is world-writable;
\(\min\) picks the smallest index \(i\) that qualifies, so \(k\) is the position of the first usable file;
if no location qualifies, there is no config file and every setting has its default.

Example 1, the lab: ANSIBLE_CONFIG is not set, so \(\ell_1\) does not exist. ./ansible.cfg exists and the folder is not world-writable, so the set contains 2 (and maybe 3 and 4), and \(k = 2\). The lab file wins. ansible --version confirms it on its config file = line.
Example 2, the same folder after chmod 777 .: \(\ell_2\) is no longer allowed. If neither \(\ell_3\) nor \(\ell_4\) exists, the set is empty, and the real output above shows config file = None.
Which value for one setting. For a setting \(x\), each layer \(j\) may give a value \(v_j(x)\):
\[
\operatorname{value}(x) = v_{j^\ast}(x), \qquad j^\ast = \max \lbrace\, j : v_j(x) \text{ is set} \,\rbrace
\]
where:

\(j \in \lbrace 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \rbrace\) numbers the layers config file, environment, command line, playbook keyword and variable, from weakest to strongest;
\(v_j(x)\) is the value that layer \(j\) gives, if any;
\(j^\ast\) is the strongest layer that sets \(x\).

Example, forks: ansible.cfg says forks = 5 (\(v_1 = 5\)), the environment has ANSIBLE_FORKS=10 (\(v_2 = 10\)), and the command has -f 20 (\(v_3 = 20\)). Then \(j^\ast = \max \lbrace 1, 2, 3 \rbrace = 3\), so Ansible uses 20 forks. Remove -f 20 and \(j^\ast = 2\): 10, which is what dump --only-changed printed. With lesson 3’s wave formula, 12 hosts then need \(\lceil 12/10 \rceil = 2\) waves instead of \(\lceil 12/5 \rceil = 3\).

title: DevOps: A Hands-On Book
text:
This book teaches the tools that take a small web application from a laptop to servers that stay up:
Each lesson starts with a real problem, then explains the idea the way you would explain it to a ten-year-old, and then gives the exact rules. Every keyword, command and convention appears in a table with a short example. Each lesson ends with a small piece of mathematics. Every symbol in it is defined and every formula is worked through with real numbers.

title: DevOps: A Hands-On Book
section: The running example: the Lemonade Stand
text:
The running example: the Lemonade Stand
Every chapter uses the same tiny business, so you never have to learn a new scenario.

The Lemonade Stand is a web page that shows a lemonade menu and its prices. Customers open it in a browser. The owner wants it to stay online, to change prices without breaking anything, and to add new drinks every week.








Piece
Value used throughout the book




Application
lemonade-stand, an HTTP server on port 8080 with a /health endpoint


Servers
web1 (192.0.2.11) and web2 (192.0.2.12) in group web, db1 (192.0.2.21) in group db


Cluster
namespace lemonade, Deployment and Service lemonade-web, label app: lemonade


Container image
lemonade-stand:<git-sha>, built by the pipeline


AWS
region eu-west-2, VPC 10.0.0.0/16


Google Cloud
project lemonade-stand-dev, region europe-west2



The server IP addresses come from 192.0.2.0/24, a range reserved for documentation (RFC 5737), so they can never clash with a real machine.

title: DevOps: A Hands-On Book
text:
How the parts fit together
 developer pushes a commit
             │
             ▼
 ┌────────────────────────┐  Part 3: CI/CD
 │  test → build image    │  tests every change, builds a container image
 └───────────┬────────────┘
             │ image: lemonade-stand:<git-sha>
             ▼
 ┌────────────────────────┐  Part 2: k3s   (or ECS / Cloud Run in Parts 4–5)
 │  run the containers    │  keeps copies alive, replaces crashed ones, rolls out versions
 └───────────┬────────────┘
             │ runs on
             ▼
 ┌────────────────────────┐  Part 1: Ansible
 │  configured machines   │  installs packages, writes config files, installs k3s
 └───────────┬────────────┘
             │ created by
             ▼
 ┌────────────────────────┐  Part 6: Terraform
 │  cloud infrastructure  │  networks, VMs, buckets, databases on AWS (Part 4) or Google Cloud (Part 5)
 └────────────────────────┘
Read the parts in order the first time. Parts 1–3 work entirely on your laptop. Parts 4–5 show the same ideas as rented cloud services, done by hand so you can see each piece. Part 6 then automates Parts 4–5.

title: DevOps: A Hands-On Book
text:
The parts


Part 1: Ansible
Inventories, ad-hoc commands, playbooks, modules, variables and facts, Jinja2 templates, loops and handlers, roles, Vault and rolling deployments. The lab pretends your laptop is three servers.


Part 2: k3s
Containers, the k3s architecture explained as a school, kubectl, Pods, labels, Deployments and rolling updates, Services, Traefik ingress, ConfigMaps and Secrets, storage, health checks and scheduling, Jobs, and Helm. Every example ran on a real single-binary cluster.


Part 3: CI/CD
What CI, continuous delivery and continuous deployment mean, GitHub Actions syntax, testing, artifacts, secrets and approvals, deployment strategies, DORA metrics, and an end-to-end pipeline that ships the Lemonade Stand to k3s.


Part 4: AWS
Regions and availability zones, IAM and the AWS CLI, VPC networking, EC2, S3, load balancers and auto scaling, RDS and DynamoDB, containers on ECR and ECS, Lambda, and CloudWatch with a cost estimate for the whole stand. The lab runs against LocalStack, so it costs nothing.


Part 5: Google Cloud
Projects and the resource hierarchy, the gcloud CLI, IAM and service accounts, Compute Engine and VPC firewalls, Cloud Storage, Cloud Run (the stall that folds away when nobody is buying), Artifact Registry and GKE, Cloud SQL and Firestore, and SRE-style monitoring with error budgets.


Part 6: Terraform
Infrastructure as code, HCL, the init → plan → apply loop, providers and resources, variables, loops and functions, state and backends, modules, the same stand on AWS and Google Cloud, and Terraform in a pipeline. The lab starts real Lemonade containers through Docker, so it needs no cloud account.

title: DevOps: A Hands-On Book
text:
Why k3s instead of “full” Kubernetes
Kubernetes is powerful, but a production installation has many separate pieces to install, secure and upgrade. k3s is a CNCF-certified Kubernetes distribution packaged as one binary. It bundles a container runtime, networking, DNS, an ingress controller, a load balancer and local storage. It is the same Kubernetes API, so every manifest and kubectl command in Part 2 also works on a large cluster later. You just have much less to set up while you learn.

title: DevOps: A Hands-On Book
section: How to read the math in this book
text:
How to read the math in this book
The mathematics here is small. It turns a rule into one exact line, such as “how many batches will a rolling update take?”. Every lesson defines its symbols again where they are used, but this table collects them in one place.









Symbol
Read it as
Meaning
Example




\(x \in S\)
“\(x\) is in \(S\)”
\(x\) is a member of the set \(S\)
\(\texttt{web1} \in \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2} \rbrace\)


\(x \notin S\)
“\(x\) is not in \(S\)”
\(x\) is not a member of \(S\)
\(\texttt{db1} \notin \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2} \rbrace\)


\(A \cup B\)
“\(A\) union \(B\)”
everything in \(A\) or \(B\)
\(\lbrace 1, 2 \rbrace \cup \lbrace 2, 3 \rbrace = \lbrace 1, 2, 3 \rbrace\)


\(A \cap B\)
“\(A\) intersect \(B\)”
only what is in both \(A\) and \(B\)
\(\lbrace 1, 2 \rbrace \cap \lbrace 2, 3 \rbrace = \lbrace 2 \rbrace\)


\(A \setminus B\)
“\(A\) minus \(B\)”
what is in \(A\) but not in \(B\)
\(\lbrace 1, 2 \rbrace \setminus \lbrace 2, 3 \rbrace = \lbrace 1 \rbrace\)


\(A \subseteq B\)
“\(A\) is a subset of \(B\)”
every member of \(A\) is also in \(B\)
\(\lbrace 1 \rbrace \subseteq \lbrace 1, 2 \rbrace\)


\(\lvert S \rvert\)
“size of \(S\)”
how many members \(S\) has
\(\lvert \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2}, \texttt{db1} \rbrace \rvert = 3\)


\(\emptyset\)
“the empty set”
a set with no members
\(\lbrace 1 \rbrace \cap \lbrace 2 \rbrace = \emptyset\)


\(\lceil x \rceil\)
“ceiling of \(x\)”
the smallest whole number \(\ge x\) (round up)
\(\lceil 2.5 \rceil = 3\), \(\lceil 3 \rceil = 3\)


\(\lfloor x \rfloor\)
“floor of \(x\)”
the largest whole number \(\le x\) (round down)
\(\lfloor 2.5 \rfloor = 2\)


\(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i\)
“sum of \(a_i\) for \(i\) from 1 to \(n\)”
\(a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n\)
\(\sum_{i=1}^{3} i = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6\)


\(x^n\)
“\(x\) to the power \(n\)”
\(x\) multiplied by itself \(n\) times
\(2^{8} = 256\)


\(\max(a, b)\)
“maximum of \(a\) and \(b\)”
the larger value
\(\max(4, 7) = 7\)


\(\min(a, b)\)
“minimum of \(a\) and \(b\)”
the smaller value
\(\min(4, 7) = 4\)


\(f(x)\)
“\(f\) of \(x\)”
apply the rule \(f\) to the input \(x\)
if \(f(x) = 2x\) then \(f(3) = 6\)


\(f(f(s)) = f(s)\)
“doing it twice equals doing it once”
idempotent: repeating the action changes nothing more
“make sure the light is on”, done twice, leaves it on


\(P \Rightarrow Q\)
“if \(P\) then \(Q\)”
whenever \(P\) is true, \(Q\) must be true
“a test fails” \(\Rightarrow\) “the deploy stops”


\(P \land Q\)
“\(P\) and \(Q\)”
both are true
two conditions in an Ansible when: list


\(P \lor Q\)
“\(P\) or \(Q\)”
at least one is true
web:db selects hosts in web or db


\(\neg P\)
“not \(P\)”
\(P\) is false
!db excludes the db group


\(a \le b\)
“\(a\) is at most \(b\)”
\(a\) is smaller than or equal to \(b\)
requested CPU \(\le\) available CPU


\(\approx\)
“is about”
an approximate value
\(1/3 \approx 0.33\)



A worked example combines several of these symbols. Ansible runs a task on at most \(f\) hosts at a time. With \(n\) hosts it therefore needs
\[
w = \left\lceil \frac{n}{f} \right\rceil
\]
where:

\(w\) is the number of waves (rounds) needed, a whole number;
\(n\) is the number of target hosts;
\(f\) is the forks setting, the largest number of hosts Ansible works on at once;
\(\lceil \cdot \rceil\) rounds the division up, because a half-full wave still takes a whole round.

Example: the Lemonade fleet has \(n = 3\) hosts. With the default \(f = 5\), \(w = \lceil 3/5 \rceil = \lceil 0.6 \rceil = 1\) wave. With \(f = 2\), \(w = \lceil 3/2 \rceil = \lceil 1.5 \rceil = 2\) waves: web1 and web2 first, then db1.

title: What CI and CD Mean
text:
Three friends work on the Lemonade Stand code:

Ana adds a new drink, mint lemonade.
Ben changes how prices are rounded.
Caro adds the bulk discount: 10% off from the tenth cup.

Each of them works alone on a private branch for three weeks. On release day they merge everything. Ben’s rounding change breaks Caro’s discount, Ana’s new drink has no price in Ben’s new format, and nobody remembers which of the 60 commits caused which bug. The release slips by a week.
Nothing here was hard to write. It was hard to combine. The longer changes wait apart, the more painful it is to put them together. CI/CD is the set of habits and tools that keeps that pain small.






TipExplain it like I’m ten



Continuous integration is like a class writing one storybook together. If every child writes a whole chapter alone for a month and then glues all the chapters together, the dog is called Rex in chapter 2 and Max in chapter 3, and the story falls apart. If instead everyone adds a page every day and the teacher reads the whole book each afternoon, mistakes are tiny and found at once. Martin Fowler’s famous article on Continuous Integration makes this same point: integrate often so each integration is small.
Continuous delivery means the lemonade is always bottled, labelled and ready in the fridge. Opening the stand is just a decision (“let’s sell now!”), not a week of work. Jez Humble and David Farley wrote the book on this, Continuous Delivery (2010).
Continuous deployment goes one step further: every bottle that passes the taste test goes straight onto the counter, with nobody pressing a button.
The stop cord. In Toyota’s car factories, any worker can pull a cord, the andon, when they see a problem. A light shows where, and help comes at once, so the problem is fixed before more cars are built with it. In CI, a red build is our andon: the team stops and fixes it before adding new work on top.
“If it hurts, do it more often.” Martin Fowler calls this one of his favourite sayings in Frequency Reduces Difficulty. Merging once a month hurts, so merge every day. Releasing is scary, so release so often that it becomes boring.
Ten releases a day. In 2009, John Allspaw and Paul Hammond showed in their talk 10+ Deploys per Day: Dev and Ops Cooperation at Flickr that a large website could release many small changes every day, safely, because developers and operations people shared tools, information and responsibility. The talk inspired the first DevOpsDays conference.

The concepts, precisely









Term
Plain definition
What triggers it

A green CI build
The pipeline itself

—
—

—
—

A pipeline step

section: The practices that make CI work
text:
The practices that make CI work
These are the habits Fowler lists in his article, rewritten for the Lemonade Stand:








Practice
What it means
Lemonade example




One source repository
All code, tests, Dockerfile and pipeline files live in one place
server.mjs, server.test.mjs, Dockerfile and .github/workflows/ in one repo


Automate the build
One command builds and checks everything
npm test; docker build .


Make the build self-testing
The build fails if a test fails
node --test exits with code 1 on any failure


Commit to mainline every day
No branch lives for weeks
Ana merges “mint lemonade, hidden behind a flag” on day 1

Not “works on my laptop”
GitHub Actions runner ubuntu-latest


Fix a broken build immediately
Red build = stop the line
Ben reverts his rounding commit within 10 minutes


Keep the build fast
Feedback in minutes, not hours

workflows/deploy.yml

title: What CI and CD Mean
section: A worked example: the same three weeks, done with CI
text:
A worked example: the same three weeks, done with CI
Here is what Ana, Ben and Caro do instead.
Day 1. Ana opens a small pull request that adds mint lemonade to the menu. The pipeline runs npm test on a fresh machine:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml (core of it)
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 26
      - run: npm test
The check is green, she merges. Total change: 1 line in MENU plus 1 test.
Day 2. Ben tidies the pricing code and, without noticing, writes cups > 10 where Caro’s rule needs cups >= 10. His pull request turns red, because Caro’s discount test (merged that morning) now fails. This is the real output of that bug:
✖ gives 10% off from the tenth cup
  AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: Expected values to be strictly deep-equal:
  + actual - expected
    {
      cups: 10,
  +   totalCents: 2900
  -   totalCents: 2610
    }
ℹ tests 4
ℹ pass 3
ℹ fail 1
Ten cups cost 2900 cents instead of the discounted 2610. The failure points at one small change made today, so Ben fixes it in minutes. Without CI, the same bug would have surfaced on release day, buried among 60 commits.
Day 3 onward. Every merge to main produces a tested container image (continuous delivery). The team chooses to let the pipeline deploy each image automatically after a reviewer approves production (still continuous delivery, because a human presses the button). If they removed the approval, it would become continuous deployment.
Run the real tests yourself:
cd devops/ci-cd/examples/lemonade-stand
npm test
✔ adds up the price of every cup
✔ gives 10% off from the tenth cup
✔ rejects unknown drinks and bad quantities
✔ serves health, prices and 404 over HTTP
ℹ tests 4
ℹ pass 4
ℹ fail 0

title: What CI and CD Mean
text:
Rules and conventions

Merge into main at least once a day. A branch older than two days is a warning sign.
Every change goes through the same pipeline; there is no “quick fix straight to the server”.
A red main is the team’s top priority. Fix it or revert it; do not pile new commits on top.
Keep commits small enough that a failure points at one idea.
Hide unfinished features behind flags instead of hiding them on long branches.
The pipeline definition lives in the repository and is reviewed like code.
“Done” means merged, tested and deployable, not “works on my machine”.

title: What CI and CD Mean
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Calling a build server “CI” while branches live for weeks
Painful merges, “merge day”
Merge to main daily; use feature flags


Ignoring a red build
New failures hide behind the old one; people stop trusting the pipeline
Stop the line: revert or fix before anything else


Tests only run on a developer’s laptop
“It worked for me” bugs
Run every check on a clean runner


Confusing delivery with deployment
Arguments about whether “we do CD”
Ask one question: does a human press the release button?


Huge releases “to be safe”
Big, scary, slow releases that are hard to debug
Smaller batches; release more often

title: The End-to-End Lemonade Pipeline
text:
Each earlier lesson built one piece. Now the Lemonade team wants the whole journey to happen without anyone typing a deploy command:

A pull request runs the tests.
A merge to main builds one image and pushes it to GHCR.
That exact image rolls out to the staging k3s cluster.
A reviewer approves.
The same image rolls out to the production k3s cluster, pod by pod, and rolls back by itself if it does not become healthy.

This lesson connects the two workflow files in the lab, shows what must be set up once by hand (and where Ansible from Part 1 does it), and then reads this website’s real pipeline line by line.






TipExplain it like I’m ten



Think of a relay race. The first runner tests the recipe, the second bottles it, the third gives it to the practice table, and the last one carries it to the real party. The important rule of a relay is that the same baton goes all the way round. If a runner drops the baton and grabs a different one, the race does not count. In our pipeline, the baton is the image digest: sha256:... built once and handed from job to job.
When John Allspaw and Paul Hammond explained how Flickr deployed more than ten times a day in their 2009 talk, “one-step build and deploy” was the first tool on their list: the whole relay starts with one push of a button, or here, with one merge.

title: The End-to-End Lemonade Pipeline
text:
The pipeline, piece by piece






flowchart LR
  PR[Pull request] --> T1[test]
  M[Merge to main] --> T2[test] --> I[image: build and push once]
  I -->|digest| S[staging: deploy.yml]
  S --> A{Reviewer approves production?}
  A -->|yes| P[production: deploy.yml]
  P -->|rollout fails| U[kubectl rollout undo]









Job
File
Runs when
What it does
Lesson




test
ci.yml
Every push and pull request
npm test on Node 26
4


image
ci.yml
Push to main, after test
Build once, push :<sha>, output repo@sha256:...
5


staging
ci.yml → deploy.yml
After image
Apply manifests with the digest, wait for the rollout
7

ci.yml → deploy.yml

deploy.yml
“Run workflow” button
Redeploy or roll back to any earlier digest

Step 1: the handover from build to deploy
The end of ci.yml calls the reusable deploy workflow twice, passing the digest from the image job:
staging:
  needs: image
  uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy.yml
  with: { environment: staging, image: "${{ needs.image.outputs.ref }}" }
  secrets: inherit

production:
  needs: [image, staging]
  uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy.yml
  with: { environment: production, image: "${{ needs.image.outputs.ref }}" }
  secrets: inherit
Both calls receive the same needs.image.outputs.ref, so staging and production cannot drift apart. production needs staging, so a failed staging rollout stops the release.


Step 2: the deploy itself
The core of deploy.yml, after the kubeconfig is written:
- name: Apply and wait for the rolling update
  env:
    IMAGE: ${{ inputs.image }}
  run: |
    sed "s|__IMAGE__|$IMAGE|g" k8s/deployment.yaml | kubectl apply -f -
    kubectl -n lemonade rollout status deployment/lemonade-web --timeout=180s
- name: Roll back
  if: failure()
  run: kubectl -n lemonade rollout undo deployment/lemonade-web
sed puts the digest into the manifest from Part 2, kubectl apply hands it to k3s, and rollout status waits until all three pods are new and ready. The readiness probe on /health is the smoke test: a pod that cannot answer never receives traffic. If the rollout does not finish in 180 seconds, the job fails and if: failure() runs rollout undo.
The job also carries environment: ${{ inputs.environment }} and concurrency: deploy-${{ inputs.environment }}, so the production job waits for its reviewer and two deploys to one cluster never overlap.

Two honest warnings:

Network. GitHub-hosted runners are on the internet, so the k3s API (port 6443) must be reachable from there. Many teams do not want that. Two common answers: a self-hosted runner inside the shop’s network (runs-on: [self-hosted, lemonade]), or a pull-based tool such as Argo CD or Flux that runs inside the cluster and pulls the new image reference from git.
Privilege. k3s.yaml is a cluster-admin key. The lab uses it for simplicity. In production, an admin creates the lemonade namespace once, and CI gets a ServiceAccount bound to the built-in edit role in that namespace only (then the Namespace object is removed from the manifest, because CI may no longer create namespaces).

section: A second real pipeline: this website
text:
A second real pipeline: this website
This book is published by .github/workflows/pages.yml. It is a good contrast: a static site instead of a container, GitHub Pages instead of k3s. Its skeleton:
name: Publish Knowledge Library
on:

  workflow_dispatch:

  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  build:   # checkout, setup-node, many test steps, quarto render, upload-pages-artifact
  deploy:
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    needs: build

      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5

title: The End-to-End Lemonade Pipeline
text:
Rules and conventions

One pipeline from commit to production; no side doors.
Build the image once and pass the digest; every environment runs the same bytes.
Staging must succeed before production can start (needs).
Production waits for a human (environment reviewers) until the team trusts the pipeline enough for continuous deployment.
Every deploy waits for health (rollout status plus a readiness probe) and rolls back automatically on failure.
Keep a manual path (workflow_dispatch) to redeploy any earlier digest.
Give CI the least access that works: namespaced credentials, environment-scoped secrets, read-only tokens by default.

title: The End-to-End Lemonade Pipeline
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

1. One baton for every environment
Let \(E\) be the set of environments and \(d\) the digest the image job produced for commit \(c\). The pipeline guarantees
\[
\forall e \in E:\ \operatorname{digest}_e(c) = d
\]
where

\(E = \lbrace \text{staging}, \text{production} \rbrace\) for the Lemonade Stand;
\(\operatorname{digest}_e(c)\) is the digest that environment \(e\) runs for commit \(c\);
\(\forall e \in E\) reads “for every environment \(e\)”.

Example. Commit 3f2c1ab produces \(d = \texttt{sha256:7aaa...}\). Staging runs \(\texttt{sha256:7aaa...}\) and production runs \(\texttt{sha256:7aaa...}\), so the property holds for both elements of \(E\). If production rebuilt the image, it could get \(\texttt{sha256:9b10...}\) and the property would be false: production would run bytes that staging never tested.


2. Where the lead time goes
The change lead time from Lesson 8 splits into machine time and waiting time:
\[
L = \sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i + w
\]
where

\(k\) is the number of jobs on the path from merge to production;
\(t_i\) is the duration of job \(i\) in minutes;
\(w\) is the time spent waiting for the reviewer, in minutes;
\(L\) is the time from merge to production, in minutes (code review before the merge adds to the full lead time, but is left out here).

Example. test 1 minute, image 2 minutes, staging 2 minutes, production 2 minutes, so \(k = 4\) and \(\sum t_i = 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7\) minutes. The reviewer approves after \(w = 23\) minutes. Then
\[
L = 7 + 23 = 30 \text{ minutes,}
\]
and \(\frac{23}{30} \approx 77\%\) of it is waiting for a person. Making the jobs twice as fast would save only 3.5 minutes; a faster approval habit, or trusting the pipeline enough to drop the approval (continuous deployment), saves far more. Measuring where time goes stops a team from optimising the wrong part.

Jez Humble and David Farley, Continuous Delivery (2010), chapter 5, “Anatomy of the Deployment Pipeline”.
