title: 5. Cloud Storage
section: Worked example: a public menu and a private report
text:
Worked example: a public menu and a private report
# The public menu bucket.
gcloud storage buckets create gs://lemonade-stand-dev-menu \
  --location=europe-west2 --uniform-bucket-level-access
gcloud storage cp examples/index.html gs://lemonade-stand-dev-menu/ \
  --cache-control="public, max-age=60"
gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://lemonade-stand-dev-menu \
  --member=allUsers --role=roles/storage.objectViewer
gcloud storage buckets update gs://lemonade-stand-dev-menu --lifecycle-file=examples/lifecycle.json

# The private reports bucket and a same-day link for the accountant.
gcloud storage buckets create gs://lemonade-stand-dev-reports \
  --location=europe-west2 --uniform-bucket-level-access --public-access-prevention
gcloud storage sign-url gs://lemonade-stand-dev-reports/2026-11-25.csv --duration=8h \
  --impersonate-service-account=reports@lemonade-stand-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com
Illustrative output:
$ curl -s https://storage.googleapis.com/lemonade-stand-dev-menu/index.html | grep h1
<h1>Lemonade Stand</h1>

$ gcloud storage sign-url gs://lemonade-stand-dev-reports/2026-11-25.csv --duration=8h ...
---
expiration: '2026-11-25 17:00:00'
http_verb: GET
resource: gs://lemonade-stand-dev-reports/2026-11-25.csv
signed_url: https://storage.googleapis.com/lemonade-stand-dev-reports/2026-11-25.csv?x-goog-signature=...

title: 5. Cloud Storage
text:
Rules and conventions

One bucket per purpose and audience: public menu, private reports. Never mix public and private files in one bucket.
Always use uniform bucket-level access. Turn on public access prevention for every bucket that is not meant to be public.
Put the bucket in the same region as the service that reads it, to avoid cross-region transfer charges and latency.
Set Cache-Control explicitly on files that change. Use long max-age only for files whose name changes with their content (such as app.3f9c2ab.js).
Use lifecycle rules instead of clean-up scripts.
Only move objects to a colder class if they will stay longer than its minimum duration.
Share private files with signed URLs that live as briefly as the task needs, not by making them public “for a minute”.

an XML listing or an error, not the menu

gcloud storage rm -r gs://bucket to “empty” it
the bucket itself is gone too
use gcloud storage rm gs://bucket/** to keep the bucket

title: 5. Cloud Storage
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Monthly storage cost is size times price per class.
\[
C = \sum_{c} s_c \times p_c
\]
where:

\(c\) runs over the storage classes you use (Standard, Nearline, …);
\(s_c\) is how much data sits in class \(c\), in GB, averaged over the month;
\(p_c\) is the price of class \(c\) in your location, in dollars per GB per month;
\(C\) is the storage part of the bill in dollars (operations and network transfer are billed separately).

Example: at the time of writing, London (europe-west2) lists Standard at \(p = 0.023\) and Nearline at \(p = 0.013\) dollars per GB-month (check the pricing page for today’s numbers). The menu is \(s = 0.001\) GB in Standard and the photo archive is \(40\) GB in Nearline. Then \(C = 0.001 \times 0.023 + 40 \times 0.013 = 0.000023 + 0.52 \approx 0.52\) dollars per month. Keeping the photos in Standard would cost \(40 \times 0.023 = 0.92\) dollars, so Nearline saves \(0.92 - 0.52 = 0.40\) dollars a month.
The minimum storage duration means you pay for at least that many days.
\[
d_{\text{billed}} = \max(d, d_{\min})
\]
where:

\(d\) is the number of days the object actually stayed in the class;
\(d_{\min}\) is the class’s minimum duration (Nearline 30, Coldline 90, Archive 365, Standard 0);
\(\max\) picks the larger of the two;
\(d_{\text{billed}}\) is the number of days you are charged for.

Example: a photo moved to Nearline and deleted 10 days later gives \(d_{\text{billed}} = \max(10, 30) = 30\) days, so you pay for 20 days of storage you did not use. Our lifecycle rule keeps photos in Nearline from day 30 to day 365, so \(d = 335\) and \(d_{\text{billed}} = \max(335, 30) = 335\): no penalty.
Durability says how many objects you should expect to lose.
\[
\mathbb{E}[L] = N \times (1 - a)
\]
where:

\(N\) is the number of objects stored for one year;
\(a\) is the annual durability, \(0.99999999999\) (eleven nines);
\(1 - a = 10^{-11}\) is the chance that one particular object is lost in a year;
\(\mathbb{E}[L]\) is the expected number of objects lost that year (an average over many years, not a promise for any one year).

Example: the Lemonade Stand keeps \(N = 10{,}000{,}000\) files. Then \(\mathbb{E}[L] = 10^{7} \times 10^{-11} = 10^{-4}\) objects per year. Put another way, on average one object every \(1 / 10^{-4} = 10{,}000\) years. Durability protects against hardware failure, not against you deleting the file: for that, turn on object versioning or soft delete.

title: 8. Cloud SQL and Firestore
text: Cloud Run instances come and go, so the Lemonade Stand needs somewhere permanent to keep its data. Google Cloud offers many databases. This lesson covers the two a small app is most likely to need: Cloud SQL, a managed PostgreSQL server, and Firestore, a document database with no server at all.

title: 8. Cloud SQL and Firestore
text:
The problem

Orders have a fixed shape (who, which drink, how many, when) and must never be lost or double-counted. They belong in a relational database with transactions.
“Cups sold today” is one number, updated on every sale and read on every page view. A full SQL server is overkill for that.
The owner does not want to install Postgres, patch it, or remember to take backups.

title: 8. Cloud SQL and Firestore
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






Tip



Cloud SQL is a tidy filing cabinet. Every drawer is a table, and every sheet in it is filled in on the same form: name, drink, cups, time. A twin cabinet in another building copies every sheet the moment it is written. If the first building has a fire, the twin takes over. Every night, someone photocopies the whole cabinet: that is a backup.
The idea of keeping data in neat tables of rows comes from Edgar F. Codd, who described the relational model in 1970 in “A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks” (Communications of the ACM). Postgres, MySQL and Cloud SQL all follow his idea.
Firestore is a box of index cards. Each card (a document) can have whatever you write on it, such as cups: 42. Cards are grouped into folders (collections). There is no cabinet to look after: Google keeps the box.

title: 8. Cloud SQL and Firestore
text:
The idea, precisely

Cloud SQL








Concept
Meaning
Lemonade value




Instance
one managed database server
lemonade-db


Edition
enterprise or enterprise-plus (faster, bigger, higher SLA)
enterprise


Tier
machine size
db-custom-1-3840 (1 vCPU, 3.75 GB)


Database
a named database inside the instance
orders


Connection name
PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE
lemonade-stand-dev:europe-west2:lemonade-db


Availability type
ZONAL (one zone) or REGIONAL (primary plus standby in another zone)
REGIONAL in prod



High availability (--availability-type=REGIONAL) keeps a standby in a second zone, with every write copied to it before it is confirmed. If the primary’s zone fails, Cloud SQL switches over automatically, usually within about a minute. Google’s SLA for the Enterprise edition is 99.95% a month.
Backups. Automated backups run daily in a window you choose (--backup-start-time), and by default the last 7 are kept. Point-in-time recovery (--enable-point-in-time-recovery) also keeps the write-ahead log, so you can restore to any moment inside the log-retention window, not only to last night.
Connecting from Cloud Run. Add --add-cloudsql-instances=<connection name> to gcloud run deploy. Cloud Run then opens a Unix socket at /cloudsql/<connection name>, and the app connects to that path as its host. The service account needs roles/cloudsql.client (lesson 3). No public IP and no firewall rule are involved.
import pg from 'pg';

export const pool = new pg.Pool({
  host: `/cloudsql/${process.env.INSTANCE_CONNECTION_NAME}`,
  database: 'orders',
  user: 'lemonade',
  password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD,
  max: 5, // at most 5 connections per Cloud Run instance
});


Firestore








Concept
Meaning
Lemonade value




Database
one per project to start, named (default), in one location
europe-west2


Collection
a group of documents
daily


Document
up to 1 MiB of fields, addressed by a path
daily/2026-11-25


Field
a typed value
cups: 42



Firestore needs no instance size. It scales by itself, and you pay per document read, write and delete, plus storage. The Standard edition has a daily free allowance of 50,000 reads, 20,000 writes and 20,000 deletes, and 1 GiB of storage (at the time of writing).
Counting a sale is one atomic write:
import { Firestore, FieldValue } from '@google-cloud/firestore';

const db = new Firestore();
await db.doc('daily/2026-11-25').set({ cups: FieldValue.increment(1) }, { merge: true });
FieldValue.increment adds 1 on the server, so two sales at the same moment both count.


Which one?







Need
Choose




Joins, transactions across tables, SQL reports
Cloud SQL


Simple documents and counters, no server to size, scale to zero
Firestore


Both
both: they are not rivals

title: 8. Cloud SQL and Firestore
text:
Rules and conventions

Keep the database in the same region as Cloud Run (europe-west2).
Connect from Cloud Run through --add-cloudsql-instances (or the Cloud SQL connectors), never through a public IP opened to 0.0.0.0/0.
Size the connection pool from the formula below, and always set Cloud Run’s --max-instances.
Production: --availability-type=REGIONAL, daily backups and point-in-time recovery. Dev: ZONAL, to save money.
Take an on-demand backup before every schema migration.
Firestore: model documents around how the page reads them. Keep hot counters in their own small documents.
Choose locations carefully. The Firestore location cannot be changed, and moving Cloud SQL means a migration.

title: 6. Cloud Run
text: Cloud Run runs a container and gives it an HTTPS URL. Google starts more copies when traffic grows, stops them when traffic stops, and bills you only while requests are being handled. For a small web app like the Lemonade Stand, it is usually the best home on Google Cloud.

title: 6. Cloud Run
6. Cloud Run
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






Tip



Cloud Run is a magic pop-up lemonade stall.

When no customers are around, the stall folds itself away, and nobody pays a helper to stand there. That is scale to zero.
When the first customer arrives, a helper unfolds the stall in a moment. That moment is a cold start.
Each helper can serve up to 80 customers at the same time (they are quick at pouring). That number is the concurrency.
When the queue grows, more helpers and stalls pop up by themselves. That is autoscaling.
When you invent a new recipe, you can serve it to 1 customer in 10 first and watch their faces. That is a canary.

Google announced Cloud Run in April 2019, built on the open-source Knative project. Its product lead Steren Giannini summed it up as running any stateless, request-driven container in a fully managed environment (Cloud Run, bringing serverless to containers). Researchers at Berkeley explained why this style (“serverless”) matters in Cloud Programming Simplified (Jonas et al., 2019): you stop renting machines and pay per use, a bit like taking a taxi instead of owning a car.

title: 6. Cloud Run
text:
The idea, precisely

Services and revisions

A service (lemonade-web) has a stable URL, such as https://lemonade-web-123456789012.europe-west2.run.app.
Every deploy, and every settings change, creates a new revision, for example lemonade-web-00002-k4d. A revision is immutable: image plus settings, frozen.
The service’s traffic setting says which revisions get what share of requests.



The container contract

Listen for HTTP on the port in the PORT environment variable (default 8080, matching the Lemonade app).
Be stateless: anything written to local disk lives in memory and disappears with the instance. Use Cloud Storage or Cloud SQL for data.
Start quickly. A slow start makes every cold start slow.
Be built for linux/amd64. An image built on an Apple-silicon laptop without --platform=linux/amd64 fails to start.



Concurrency, instances and scaling








Setting
Default
Meaning




--concurrency
80 (maximum 1000)
the most requests one instance handles at the same time


--min-instances
0
instances kept warm even with no traffic (no cold starts, but you pay)


--max-instances
100
a hard-ish cap on instances, which protects your bill and your database


--cpu, --memory
1 vCPU, 512 MiB
resources per instance


--timeout
300 s
the longest one request may take





Who can call it
--allow-unauthenticated grants roles/run.invoker to allUsers, which makes the service public. Without it, callers need an identity token from an account that has run.invoker, which is right for internal services.


Billing modes

Request-based (the default): CPU is only allocated while a request is being processed. You pay for instance time while at least one request is in flight, rounded up to 100 ms, plus a small fee per request.
Instance-based (--no-cpu-throttling): you pay for the whole life of each instance at a lower rate, and there is no per-request fee. Use it for background work between requests.

text:
Command reference









Command or flag
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




gcloud run deploy
creates or updates a service
one service per app
gcloud run deploy lemonade-web --image=IMAGE --region=europe-west2


--image
deploys an existing image
pin a tag or a digest, never latest in prod
--image=europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev/lemonade-stand-dev/lemonade/lemonade-stand:v1


--source
builds from source (Cloud Build), then deploys
uses your Dockerfile, or buildpacks if none
gcloud run deploy lemonade-web --source=. --region=europe-west2


--port
the container’s listening port
must match the app
--port=8080


--concurrency, --min-instances, --max-instances
scaling limits
set max to protect the database
--concurrency=80 --max-instances=10


--cpu, --memory
per-instance resources
memory in Mi or Gi
--cpu=1 --memory=512Mi


--allow-unauthenticated
makes the service public
omit it for internal services
--allow-unauthenticated


--service-account
the identity the code runs as
a dedicated account (lesson 3)
--service-account=lemonade-run@lemonade-stand-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com


--set-env-vars

secrets belong in Secret Manager
--set-env-vars=NODE_ENV=production


--no-traffic
deploys a revision that gets 0%
the first step of a canary
--no-traffic


--tag
gives a revision its own URL
test it before sending users
--tag=canary


gcloud run services update-traffic
changes the traffic split
percentages add up to 100
gcloud run services update-traffic lemonade-web --to-tags=canary=10


--to-revisions, --to-latest
split by revision name, or send all to the newest
--to-latest is the “promote” button
--to-revisions=lemonade-web-00001-x7k=100


gcloud run services describe
shows URL, traffic and settings
--format="value(status.url)" for scripts
gcloud run services describe lemonade-web --region=europe-west2


gcloud run revisions list
lists revisions

gcloud run revisions list --service=lemonade-web --region=europe-west2


gcloud run services logs read
prints recent logs

gcloud run services logs read lemonade-web --region=europe-west2 --limit=20


gcloud run services delete
deletes the service and its revisions

gcloud run services delete lemonade-web --region=europe-west2

title: 6. Cloud Run
section: Worked example: deploy, then a 10% canary
text:
Worked example: deploy, then a 10% canary
The lab script examples/deploy-cloud-run.sh wraps these steps. The core is three commands:
# v1 for everyone.
gcloud run deploy lemonade-web --image="$REGISTRY/lemonade-stand:v1" --region=europe-west2 \
  --port=8080 --concurrency=80 --max-instances=10 --allow-unauthenticated

# v2 deployed but hidden, reachable only at its tag URL.
gcloud run deploy lemonade-web --image="$REGISTRY/lemonade-stand:v2" --region=europe-west2 \
  --no-traffic --tag=canary

# Send 10% of real customers to v2.
gcloud run services update-traffic lemonade-web --region=europe-west2 --to-tags=canary=10
Here REGISTRY=europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev/lemonade-stand-dev/lemonade (lesson 7). Illustrative output of the first deploy:
Deploying container to Cloud Run service [lemonade-web] in project [lemonade-stand-dev] region [europe-west2]
✓ Deploying new service... Done.
  ✓ Creating Revision...
  ✓ Routing traffic...
  ✓ Setting IAM Policy...
Done.
Service [lemonade-web] revision [lemonade-web-00001-x7k] has been deployed and is serving 100 percent of traffic.
Service URL: https://lemonade-web-123456789012.europe-west2.run.app
After the canary step, describe shows the split:
Traffic:
  90% lemonade-web-00001-x7k
  10% lemonade-web-00002-k4d
        canary: https://canary---lemonade-web-123456789012.europe-west2.run.app
If v2 behaves, promote it with update-traffic --to-latest. If not, roll back instantly with --to-revisions=lemonade-web-00001-x7k=100. The old revision is still there, so a rollback needs no rebuild and no redeploy.

title: 6. Cloud Run
text:
Rules and conventions

Deploy immutable images by tag or digest (lemonade-stand:3f9c2ab), produced by CI. Never deploy latest to production.
Always set --max-instances. It caps cost during a traffic spike or attack, and it stops 1,000 instances from opening 1,000 database connections.
Use --min-instances=1 only when cold starts really hurt users; it costs money around the clock.
New versions go out as --no-traffic --tag=canary, then 10%, then 100%.
Give each service its own service account with the smallest roles (lesson 3).
Keep services stateless. Store files in Cloud Storage and rows in Cloud SQL or Firestore.
Read config from environment variables, and secrets from Secret Manager, never from the image.

title: 6. Cloud Run
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




The app listens on a fixed port, not on PORT
The user-provided container failed to start and listen on the port defined provided by the PORT=8080 environment variable
read process.env.PORT, or set --port to the app’s port


Image built on Apple silicon
the same “failed to start” error, or exec format error in the logs
docker build --platform=linux/amd64 …


Forgetting --allow-unauthenticated for a public site
browsers get 403 Forbidden
redeploy with the flag, or grant run.invoker to allUsers


No --max-instances
a surprise bill, or the database runs out of connections
--max-instances=10


Writing uploads to local disk
files vanish when instances restart; memory fills up
write to Cloud Storage


Deploying v2 straight to 100%
a bad release reaches every customer
--no-traffic --tag=canary, then shift gradually

title: 9. Monitoring, Logging and SRE
text: A service you cannot see is a service you cannot fix. This lesson gives the Lemonade Stand eyes (logs and metrics), an alarm (uptime checks and alerts), a reliability target (an SLO with an error budget), and a spending alarm (a billing budget).

title: 9. Monitoring, Logging and SRE
9. Monitoring, Logging and SRE
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






Tip



Logs are the app’s diary: “10:02 sold one pink lemonade”, “10:03 oops, the till did not open”.
Metrics are the scoreboard: how many cups an hour, how long each customer waited.
An uptime check is a friend who knocks on the door every minute from different cities and shouts if nobody answers.
An error budget is a jar of oops tokens. Promise “the stand works 999 times out of 1,000”, and you get 1 oops token for every 1,000 customers. Trying a new recipe might spend a few tokens; that is fine. When the jar is empty, you stop inventing recipes and fix the stand until the jar refills next month.
This idea comes from Google’s own Site Reliability Engineering team. In the free book Site Reliability Engineering (Beyer, Jones, Petoff and Murphy, 2016), the chapter “Embracing Risk” explains that aiming for 100% reliability is a mistake: users cannot tell 99.99% from 100%, and chasing the last bit stops all progress. Pick a target, measure it, and let the leftover budget pay for change.

title: 9. Monitoring, Logging and SRE
text:
The idea, precisely

Cloud Logging

Anything a Cloud Run container prints to stdout or stderr becomes a log entry. Cloud Run also writes one request log per HTTP request.
Print one JSON object per line and Logging understands it: the severity field sets the level, and message becomes the text.

console.log(JSON.stringify({ severity: 'ERROR', message: 'till did not open', orderId: 'o-1042' }));

Find entries with the Logging query language: field="value" comparisons joined with AND / OR, and severity>=ERROR.
Logs in the _Default bucket are kept for 30 days by default.



Cloud Monitoring

Google Cloud records metrics for every product automatically. For Cloud Run: run.googleapis.com/request_count (labelled by response code class such as 5xx), request_latencies and container/instance_count.
An uptime check sends a request to a URL from several regions around the world, every 1, 5, 10 or 15 minutes.
An alerting policy watches a metric, or an uptime check, and notifies a channel (email, SMS, Slack, PagerDuty) when a condition holds for long enough.



SLIs, SLOs and error budgets








Term
Meaning
Lemonade value




SLI (indicator)
a measured ratio: good events ÷ valid events
successful (non-5xx) requests ÷ all requests


SLO (objective)
the target for the SLI over a window
99.9% over 30 days


Error budget
how much failure the SLO allows
0.1% of requests


Burn rate
how fast the budget is being spent, compared with “evenly over the window”
1 means “exactly on budget”



In Cloud Monitoring, you define a service, attach an SLO to it in the console or the API, and create alerts on its burn rate.


Billing budgets
A budget watches spending on a billing account and emails you at thresholds you choose. It does not stop spending. To cap cost, use --max-instances, quotas, or an automated action triggered by the budget’s Pub/Sub notifications.

title: 9. Monitoring, Logging and SRE
text:
Command reference









Command or flag
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




gcloud logging read
prints log entries matching a query
quote the query in single quotes
gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND severity>=ERROR' --limit=10


--freshness
how far back to look
default 1d
--freshness=2h


--format
output shape
json for scripts
--format="value(timestamp,jsonPayload.message)"


gcloud logging logs list
lists log names in the project

gcloud logging logs list


gcloud run services logs read
recent logs of one service
the quickest look
gcloud run services logs read lemonade-web --region=europe-west2 --limit=20


gcloud monitoring uptime create
creates an uptime check
check /health, not /
see the worked example


--resource-type, --resource-labels
what to check
uptime-url needs host and project_id
--resource-type=uptime-url --resource-labels=host=…,project_id=lemonade-stand-dev


--path, --protocol, --period
request path, http/https/tcp, minutes between checks
period is 1, 5, 10 or 15
--path=/health --protocol=https --period=1


gcloud monitoring uptime list-configs
lists uptime checks

gcloud monitoring uptime list-configs


gcloud monitoring policies create
creates an alerting policy from a file
keep policies in Git
gcloud monitoring policies create --policy-from-file=alert-5xx.yaml


gcloud beta monitoring channels create
creates a notification channel
beta only at the time of writing
gcloud beta monitoring channels create --channel-content-from-file=email.yaml


gcloud billing budgets create
creates a budget with alert thresholds
percent is a fraction: 0.5 = 50%
gcloud billing budgets create --billing-account=01A2B3-C4D5E6-F7A8B9 --display-name="Lemonade monthly" --budget-amount=20USD --threshold-rule=percent=0.5


gcloud billing budgets list
lists budgets

gcloud billing budgets list --billing-account=01A2B3-C4D5E6-F7A8B9

title: 9. Monitoring, Logging and SRE
section: Worked example: eyes, an alarm and a spending alarm
text:
Worked example: eyes, an alarm and a spending alarm
# Eyes: what went wrong in the last two hours?
gcloud logging read \
  'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND resource.labels.service_name="lemonade-web" AND severity>=ERROR' \
  --freshness=2h --limit=5 --format="value(timestamp,jsonPayload.message)"

# Alarm: knock on /health every minute from several regions.
gcloud monitoring uptime create lemonade-health \
  --resource-type=uptime-url \
  --resource-labels=host=lemonade-web-123456789012.europe-west2.run.app,project_id=lemonade-stand-dev \
  --path=/health --protocol=https --period=1

# Spending alarm: emails at 50%, 90% and 100% of $20.
gcloud billing budgets create --billing-account=01A2B3-C4D5E6-F7A8B9 \
  --display-name="Lemonade monthly" --budget-amount=20USD \
  --threshold-rule=percent=0.5 --threshold-rule=percent=0.9 --threshold-rule=percent=1.0
Illustrative output of the log query:
2026-11-22T12:14:03.118Z  till did not open
2026-11-22T12:13:58.402Z  till did not open
2026-11-22T12:13:41.977Z  database connection refused
Three lines are enough to show the database went first and the till errors followed. Finally, add an alerting policy on the uptime check so a failure notifies your email channel. Keep the policy file in Git, next to the code.

title: 9. Monitoring, Logging and SRE
text:
Rules and conventions

Log one JSON object per line with a severity. Never log passwords, tokens or full card numbers.
Check /health with an uptime check; it should answer fast and touch only what really matters.
Alert on symptoms users feel (errors, slowness, the uptime check) rather than on causes (CPU at 80%).
Page a human only when the error budget is burning fast. Send slow burns to a ticket or an email.
Choose an SLO a little below what you achieve today, then tighten it once you can keep it.
When the error budget is spent, freeze feature releases and work on reliability until it recovers.
Create a billing budget on day one, and remember that it warns but never stops spending.

title: 9. Monitoring, Logging and SRE
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Printing plain text such as ERROR: …
every entry shows as DEFAULT severity, and the severity>=ERROR filter finds nothing
print JSON with a severity field


Alerting on every single failed request
the owner is woken at night and starts ignoring alerts
alert on burn rate, or on the uptime check failing for several minutes


Uptime check on / (the full menu with database calls)
alerts when only the specials box is slow
check /health


An SLO of 100%
any one failure “breaks the SLO”, and nobody dares to deploy
pick 99.9% and use the budget


Thinking a budget caps spending
the bill keeps growing after the 100% email
set --max-instances, quotas, or automate on the budget notification


percent=50 in --threshold-rule
the request is rejected: percent must be between 0.0 and 1.0
use a fraction: percent=0.5

title: 7. Artifact Registry and GKE
text: Cloud Run and GKE both pull images from a registry. On Google Cloud, that registry is Artifact Registry. This lesson stores the Lemonade image there, then shows what changes, and what stays the same, when you run the Part 2 manifests on Google’s managed Kubernetes.

title: 7. Artifact Registry and GKE
text:
The problem

CI builds lemonade-stand on every commit. The image needs a private home in London, next to Cloud Run, so deploys are fast and nobody outside can download it.
One day the shop may need more than Cloud Run offers, such as background workers, a queue and a database in one cluster. The owner already knows k3s from Part 2. Must they learn everything again?

title: 7. Artifact Registry and GKE
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






Tip



Artifact Registry is a library for lunchboxes. Each lunchbox is a container image.

A tag is a sticker on the lunchbox, such as v1. Stickers can be peeled off and stuck on a different box.
A digest is the box’s fingerprint. It is calculated from what is inside, so it can never move to another box.
Lunchboxes are packed in layers: bread, filling, fruit. If ten lunchboxes use the same bread, the library keeps one loaf.

GKE Autopilot is like a hotel instead of a house. With k3s you own the house: you fix the plumbing and buy new beds. With Autopilot you only book rooms (pods), say how big each room must be (resource requests), and the hotel builds and cleans the floors (nodes) for you.
Google ran its own services in containers on a system called Borg for about a decade before it open-sourced Kubernetes in 2014. The Borg paper by Abhishek Verma and colleagues (EuroSys 2015) explains the ideas Kubernetes, and therefore GKE, grew from: declare what you want and let the system pack the work onto machines.

title: 7. Artifact Registry and GKE
text:
The idea, precisely

Repositories and image names
An Artifact Registry Docker repository lives in one location. A full image reference has five parts:
europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev / lemonade-stand-dev / lemonade / lemonade-stand : v1
└──── registry host ───────┘  └── project ID ───┘  └ repo ─┘  └── image ────┘   └ tag








Part
Lemonade value
Rule




Host
europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev
<location>-docker.pkg.dev


Project
lemonade-stand-dev
the project ID


Repository
lemonade
created once with gcloud artifacts repositories create


Image
lemonade-stand
the app name


Tag or digest
:v1 or @sha256:…
tags can move; digests cannot



The older Container Registry (gcr.io) is deprecated; new work uses Artifact Registry.


Tags and digests
A digest is the SHA-256 hash of the image manifest. Change one byte of the image and the digest changes completely. A tag is just a name that points at a digest, and docker push can move it. So “v1 yesterday” and “v1 today” might be different images, but @sha256:… always means the same bytes.


Access

roles/artifactregistry.reader: may pull. Give it to the Cloud Run or GKE service account.
roles/artifactregistry.writer: may push. Give it to the CI service account.
gcloud auth configure-docker europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev teaches your local Docker to log in with your gcloud credentials.



GKE Autopilot in one page
GKE is Google’s managed Kubernetes. In Autopilot mode, Google also runs the nodes: you deploy pods, and GKE creates, sizes, patches and removes the machines underneath. You pay for the CPU and memory your pods request, plus a small hourly cluster fee.
Everything from Part 2 that talks to the Kubernetes API works unchanged: kubectl, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Jobs, probes and resource requests. What changes is the plumbing that k3s bundled:








In k3s (Part 2)
In GKE Autopilot
What you do




k3s server (control plane)
run by Google
nothing


k3s agents (nodes)
created automatically from pod requests
always set resources.requests


Flannel networking
GKE Dataplane V2
nothing


Traefik Ingress
GKE Ingress (Google Cloud load balancer) or Gateway API
replace Traefik-specific settings


ServiceLB for type: LoadBalancer
a Google Cloud network load balancer
nothing: you get a real external IP


local-path provisioner
Persistent Disk CSI, StorageClass standard-rwo
change storageClassName, or omit it


/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml
gcloud container clusters get-credentials
one command

title: 7. Artifact Registry and GKE
section: Worked example: push once, run anywhere
text:
Worked example: push once, run anywhere
REGISTRY=europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev/lemonade-stand-dev/lemonade

gcloud artifacts repositories create lemonade --repository-format=docker --location=europe-west2
gcloud auth configure-docker europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev

docker build --platform=linux/amd64 -t "$REGISTRY/lemonade-stand:v1" ../ci-cd/examples/lemonade-stand
docker push "$REGISTRY/lemonade-stand:v1"
Illustrative output of the push and the tag list:
v1: digest: sha256:4c1e0b9f2d7a…e83a size: 1573

$ gcloud artifacts docker tags list $REGISTRY/lemonade-stand
TAG  IMAGE                                                                       DIGEST
v1   europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev/lemonade-stand-dev/lemonade/lemonade-stand      sha256:4c1e0b9f2d7a…e83a
The same image now runs in both places:
# Cloud Run (lesson 6)
gcloud run deploy lemonade-web --image="$REGISTRY/lemonade-stand:v1" --region=europe-west2

# GKE Autopilot, reusing the Part 2 manifests
gcloud container clusters create-auto lemonade-auto --region=europe-west2
gcloud container clusters get-credentials lemonade-auto --region=europe-west2
kubectl set image deployment/lemonade-web -n lemonade web="$REGISTRY/lemonade-stand:v1"
The last line assumes the Deployment from Part 2 is already applied with kubectl apply, and that its container is named web. Everything you learned there works on this cluster.

title: 7. Artifact Registry and GKE
text:
Rules and conventions

One repository per application, or per team, in the same region as the services that pull from it.
CI pushes images tagged with the Git commit SHA (lemonade-stand:3f9c2ab). Humans may add friendly tags such as v1.2.0.
Production deploys pin the digest (@sha256:…) or an immutable SHA tag, so a moved tag cannot change what runs.
Grant artifactregistry.writer only to CI, and artifactregistry.reader to runtimes.
Add a cleanup policy so old images do not pile up on the bill forever.
On Autopilot, always set CPU and memory requests: they are both the bill and the scheduling input.
Pick GKE only when you need Kubernetes features. For one stateless web app, Cloud Run is simpler and cheaper.

title: 7. Artifact Registry and GKE
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Skipping configure-docker
denied: Unauthenticated request on docker push
gcloud auth configure-docker europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev


Pushing to a repository that does not exist
name unknown: Repository "lemonade" not found
create it first


Wrong host name, such as europe-west2.pkg.dev
no such host
the host is <location>-docker.pkg.dev


Deploying :latest
a rollback brings back the “wrong” latest
deploy a SHA tag or a digest


No resource requests on Autopilot
pods get Autopilot’s default size and the bill is higher than expected
set resources.requests on every container


Keeping the Traefik-only parts of a k3s Ingress
the Ingress gets no address on GKE
use GKE Ingress or the Gateway API


Forgetting the test cluster
a fee every hour, every day
gcloud container clusters delete lemonade-auto --region=europe-west2

title: 7. Artifact Registry and GKE
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
A digest is a hash of the content.
\[
d = H(m)
\]
where:

\(m\) is the image manifest, the small JSON file that lists the image’s layers;
\(H\) is SHA-256, a function that turns any input into a 64-hex-digit fingerprint;
\(d\) is the digest, written sha256:<64 hex digits>.

Example (real output of printf '…' | shasum -a 256 on two tiny inputs):

\(H(\texttt{"lemonade v1"}) = \texttt{c8c38131…add94d27e}\)
\(H(\texttt{"lemonade v2"}) = \texttt{b02aa2a9…ba222f491}\)

One character changed, and the fingerprint changed completely. That is why a digest can never point at the wrong image, while a tag is only a movable label \(\tau(\texttt{v1}) = d\) that a new push can repoint.
Shared layers are stored once. A registry keeps each layer once per repository, keyed by its digest.
\[
S = \sum_{\ell \,\in\, L_1 \cup L_2 \cup \cdots \cup L_k} \operatorname{size}(\ell)
\]
where:

\(k\) is the number of image versions in the repository;
\(L_i\) is the set of layers in version \(i\);
\(L_1 \cup \cdots \cup L_k\) is the set of distinct layers, so a shared layer is counted only once;
\(\operatorname{size}(\ell)\) is the compressed size of layer \(\ell\) in MB;
\(S\) is the storage used.

Example: every Lemonade version shares the same Node.js base layers, about 50 MB in total, plus its own app layer of about 2 MB. With \(k = 10\) versions, the distinct layers are the base (50 MB) and ten app layers (\(10 \times 2 = 20\) MB), so \(S = 50 + 20 = 70\) MB. Counting each image separately would give \(10 \times 52 = 520\) MB. This idealised model assumes the base layers really are identical. Upgrading the base image adds a new 50 MB set.
On Autopilot you pay for what pods request.
\[
R_{\text{cpu}} = \sum_{p \in P} r_{\text{cpu}}(p), \qquad R_{\text{mem}} = \sum_{p \in P} r_{\text{mem}}(p)
\]
where:

\(P\) is the set of running pods;
\(r_{\text{cpu}}(p)\) is pod \(p\)’s CPU request in vCPU (250m = \(0.25\)), and \(r_{\text{mem}}(p)\) its memory request in GiB;
\(R_{\text{cpu}}\) and \(R_{\text{mem}}\) are the totals that GKE bills per hour, at its per-vCPU and per-GiB rates.

Example: the Lemonade Deployment runs 3 replicas, each requesting 250m CPU and 512Mi memory. Then \(R_{\text{cpu}} = 3 \times 0.25 = 0.75\) vCPU and \(R_{\text{mem}} = 3 \times 0.5 = 1.5\) GiB. Over a 730-hour month, that is \(0.75 \times 730 = 547.5\) vCPU-hours and \(1.5 \times 730 = 1095\) GiB-hours, whatever size the hidden nodes are. Doubling the replicas to 6 doubles both numbers. On k3s on your own VM, by contrast, you pay for the whole VM even when it is half empty.

title: 1. What Google Cloud Is
text: Before the Lemonade Stand can rent a single computer from Google, you need three answers. Where will its things live? Who pays for them? Which city are they in? This lesson answers all three.

title: 1. What Google Cloud Is
text:
The problem
The Lemonade Stand runs on two laptops in the back room. When one laptop overheats on a hot day, the menu page disappears and customers walk away. The owner wants to rent Google’s computers instead.
The first time they open the Google Cloud console, they meet unfamiliar words: organization, project ID, billing account, region, zone. Every later lesson creates things inside these containers, so we learn them first.

title: 1. What Google Cloud Is
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






Tip



Think of Google Cloud as a huge school.

The organization is the whole school.
Folders are the wings of the school, such as “Year 5” or “Science wing”.
A project is one classroom. Each classroom has its own door key, its own supply cupboard and its own bill for pencils. Whatever you build for the Lemonade Stand goes into the classroom called lemonade-stand-dev.
Resources are the desks, books and computers inside the classroom.
The billing account is the parent who pays for the pencils. One parent can pay for several classrooms.

The school has buildings in many cities. A region is a city, such as London. A zone is one separate building in that city, with its own power and cooling. If one building has a power cut, the other buildings in the same city keep working.
Luiz André Barroso and Urs Hölzle, two of the engineers who designed Google’s datacenters, wrote a famous book called The Datacenter as a Computer (first edition 2009). Their big idea: a whole warehouse full of machines behaves like one giant computer. When you use Google Cloud, you rent a tiny slice of that giant computer.

title: 1. What Google Cloud Is
text:
The idea, precisely

The resource hierarchy
Everything in Google Cloud sits in a tree:
Organization  example.com                      (optional: needs Google Workspace or Cloud Identity)
└── Folder    shop                             (optional: folders can nest up to 10 levels)
    └── Project  lemonade-stand-dev            (required: every resource belongs to exactly one project)
        ├── Cloud Run service   lemonade-web
        ├── Storage bucket      lemonade-stand-dev-menu
        └── VM                  web1

An organization is the root. It exists only if you have a company domain managed by Google Workspace or Cloud Identity. A personal Gmail account has no organization, so its projects have no parent, and that is fine for learning.
A folder groups projects, for example by team or by environment (dev, prod).
A project is the basic container. APIs, billing, permissions and quotas are all switched on per project.
A resource is a real thing you create: a VM, a bucket, a database.

Permissions set high in the tree flow down to everything below. Lesson 3 uses this.


A project has three names










Field
Example
Who chooses it
Unique?
Can change?




Project name
Lemonade Stand Dev
you
no
yes


Project ID
lemonade-stand-dev
you, at creation
yes, across all of Google Cloud
never


Project number
123456789012
Google
yes
never



Project ID rules: 6 to 30 characters, made of lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. It must start with a letter and must not end with a hyphen. Once a project is deleted, its ID can never be used again. Commands almost always want the project ID.


Billing accounts
A billing account holds a payment method. You link a project to it. A project with no billing account can only use free things. A project can link to at most one billing account, but one billing account can pay for many projects.


Regions and zones








Term
Example
Meaning




Region
europe-west2
a geographic place (London) with several zones


Zone
europe-west2-a
one isolated deployment area inside a region: its own power, cooling and network



Naming convention: a region is <area>-<direction><number>, and a zone is the region plus - and a letter. europe-west2 has the zones europe-west2-a, europe-west2-b and europe-west2-c.


Global, regional and zonal resources
Every resource has a scope. The scope tells you which outage can take it down.








Scope
Lives in
Lemonade examples




Zonal
one zone
a VM (web1), a zonal persistent disk


Regional
all zones of one region
a subnet, a Cloud Run service, a high-availability Cloud SQL instance


Global
everywhere
a VPC network, firewall rules, VM images



The rule “a zonal resource dies with its zone” can be written in one line.
\[
\operatorname{up}(x, z) \iff Z(x) \setminus \lbrace z \rbrace \neq \emptyset
\]
where:

\(x\) is one resource, such as the VM web1;
\(z\) is the zone that has an outage;
\(Z(x)\) is the set of zones the resource runs in;
\(\setminus\) means “remove”, so \(Z(x) \setminus \lbrace z \rbrace\) is the set of zones still working for \(x\);
\(\emptyset\) is the empty set, so “\(\neq \emptyset\)” means “at least one zone is left”;
\(\iff\) means “exactly when”;
\(\operatorname{up}(x, z)\) is true when \(x\) keeps working during the outage of \(z\).

Example: the zone europe-west2-a goes down.

web1 is zonal: \(Z(\texttt{web1}) = \lbrace a \rbrace\). Then \(\lbrace a \rbrace \setminus \lbrace a \rbrace = \emptyset\), so \(\operatorname{up}\) is false. The menu VM is down.
The Cloud Run service is regional: \(Z(\texttt{lemonade-web}) = \lbrace a, b, c \rbrace\). Then \(\lbrace a, b, c \rbrace \setminus \lbrace a \rbrace = \lbrace b, c \rbrace \neq \emptyset\), so \(\operatorname{up}\) is true. Customers still see the menu.

The model assumes that a regional service moves its work to the healthy zones by itself. Google-managed regional services such as Cloud Run do this. For your own VMs, you must place copies in two zones yourself.


APIs must be switched on
Each Google Cloud product is an API with a service name, such as run.googleapis.com. A new project has most APIs off. If you call an API that is off, you get an error that names the service and says it “has not been used in project … or it is disabled”. Enable it once per project.

title: 1. What Google Cloud Is
text:
Rules and conventions

One project per environment: lemonade-stand-dev, lemonade-stand-prod. Deleting a project is the cleanest way to clean up.
Put the environment at the end of the project ID, because the ID is permanent and globally unique.
Pick one region near your customers and keep it everywhere. This book uses europe-west2 (London).
Treat zones as failure domains. Anything that must survive a zone outage needs two zones or a regional service.
Enable only the APIs you use. Each enabled API is something else that can be called in the project.
Link a billing account and create a budget alert (lesson 9) before creating paid resources.

title: 4. Compute Engine and VPC
text: Cloud Run (lesson 6) will be our main home for the Lemonade Stand. But underneath every cloud product there are virtual machines and networks. Building one VM by hand shows what the managed products do for you.

title: 4. Compute Engine and VPC
4. Compute Engine and VPC
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






Tip



A VM (virtual machine) is a pretend computer made from a slice of a real one. It is like renting one locker in a huge locker room: it feels like your own locker, but it sits in a row with thousands of others.
The VPC network is the fence and paths around your lockers. A subnet is one row of lockers in one city, and each locker in the row gets a house number (an IP address).
Firewall rules are the guard at the gate with a list of instructions. The guard reads the most important instruction first: rule 900 beats rule 1000. If two instructions are equally important and one says “stop”, the guard says “stop”.
A startup script is the note you leave inside the locker: “When you wake up, put the menu on the wall.”

title: 4. Compute Engine and VPC
text:
The idea, precisely

Virtual machines








Part
Meaning
Lemonade value




Machine type
how many vCPUs and how much memory
e2-micro


Image
the operating system to start from
newest image in family debian-12 from project debian-cloud


Boot disk
a persistent disk holding the OS; it lives in the VM’s zone
10 GB, the default


Zone
where the VM physically runs
europe-west2-a


Network tags
labels that firewall rules can target
web


Metadata
key–value notes the VM can read at metadata.google.internal
startup-script, menu



Machine type names follow <family>-<shape>-<vCPUs>. In the E2 family:








Shape
Memory per vCPU
Examples




micro, small, medium
fixed sizes on shared cores
e2-micro = 2 shared vCPUs, 1 GB


standard
4 GB
e2-standard-2, e2-standard-4


highmem
8 GB
e2-highmem-2


highcpu
1 GB
e2-highcpu-4



\[
M = n \times k
\]
where:

\(M\) is the machine’s memory in GB;
\(n\) is the number of vCPUs, the last number in the name;
\(k\) is the memory per vCPU for the shape, in GB (standard \(4\), highmem \(8\), highcpu \(1\)).

Example: e2-standard-4 has \(n = 4\) and \(k = 4\), so \(M = 4 \times 4 = 16\) GB. e2-highcpu-4 has the same 4 vCPUs but \(k = 1\), so \(M = 4 \times 1 = 4\) GB, which suits CPU-heavy work. The shared-core sizes (micro, small, medium) do not follow the formula; read their sizes from the table.
A startup script is stored in the metadata key startup-script. It runs as root on every boot, so write it to be safe to run twice. Its output goes to the system journal: sudo journalctl -u google-startup-scripts.service.


VPC networks and subnets

A VPC network is global: one network can have subnets in many regions.
A subnet is regional and owns an IP range written in CIDR notation, such as 10.10.0.0/24.
New projects get a default network in auto mode, with one subnet in every region. For anything real, create a custom-mode network and choose your own ranges.
In each subnet’s primary range, Google keeps 4 addresses: the first (network address), the second (default gateway), the second-to-last (reserved for future use) and the last (broadcast).



Firewall rules
VPC firewall rules are stateful: if a request is allowed in, its reply is allowed out automatically.








Field
Meaning
Lemonade value




Direction
INGRESS (coming in) or EGRESS (going out)
INGRESS


Action
ALLOW or DENY
ALLOW for port 80


Rules
protocol and ports
tcp:80


Source ranges
which senders match (ingress)
0.0.0.0/0 (everyone)


Target tags
which VMs the rule protects
web


Priority
0 to 65535; lower number wins; default 1000
1000



Every network also has two implied rules at the lowest priority, 65535: deny all ingress and allow all egress. So anything you do not allow in is blocked.


External IPs and Cloud NAT

By default a VM gets an ephemeral external IP, which changes if the VM stops. Reserve a static one with gcloud compute addresses create.
--no-address gives the VM only an internal IP. That is safer, but the VM then cannot download updates by itself.
Cloud NAT fixes that: it lets internal-only VMs make outbound connections. Nobody on the internet can connect in through it. It needs a Cloud Router.
For SSH without an external IP, use IAP TCP forwarding: allow port 22 from Google’s IAP range 35.235.240.0/20 and connect with gcloud compute ssh --tunnel-through-iap.

one router and NAT per region

title: 4. Compute Engine and VPC
section: Worked example: web1 behind a guarded gate
text:
Worked example: web1 behind a guarded gate
The startup script (examples/startup-script.sh) installs nginx and copies the menu from metadata into the web root:
#!/bin/bash
# Compute Engine runs this as root on every boot of the VM.
apt-get update
apt-get install -y nginx
curl -s -H "Metadata-Flavor: Google" \
  "http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/attributes/menu" \
  > /var/www/html/index.html
The network, three firewall rules and the VM:
gcloud compute networks create lemonade-net --subnet-mode=custom
gcloud compute networks subnets create lemonade-london \
  --network=lemonade-net --region=europe-west2 --range=10.10.0.0/24

gcloud compute firewall-rules create lemonade-allow-http --network=lemonade-net \
  --allow=tcp:80 --source-ranges=0.0.0.0/0 --target-tags=web --priority=1000
gcloud compute firewall-rules create lemonade-deny-spammers --network=lemonade-net \
  --action=DENY --rules=tcp:80 --source-ranges=203.0.113.0/24 --target-tags=web --priority=900
gcloud compute firewall-rules create lemonade-allow-iap-ssh --network=lemonade-net \
  --allow=tcp:22 --source-ranges=35.235.240.0/20 --target-tags=web

gcloud compute instances create web1 --zone=europe-west2-a \
  --machine-type=e2-micro --image-family=debian-12 --image-project=debian-cloud \
  --subnet=lemonade-london --tags=web \
  --metadata-from-file=startup-script=examples/startup-script.sh,menu=examples/index.html
Illustrative output:
Created [https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/lemonade-stand-dev/zones/europe-west2-a/instances/web1].
NAME  ZONE            MACHINE_TYPE  PREEMPTIBLE  INTERNAL_IP  EXTERNAL_IP  STATUS
web1  europe-west2-a  e2-micro                   10.10.0.2    192.0.2.80   RUNNING

$ curl http://192.0.2.80/
<h1>Lemonade Stand</h1>
The internal IP is 10.10.0.2 because .0 is the network address and .1 is the gateway, so the first VM gets the next free address.






Note



Cost note. The always-free e2-micro allowance applies only in us-west1, us-central1 and us-east1 (at the time of writing). In London, this VM is billed. Delete it when you finish: gcloud compute instances delete web1 --zone=europe-west2-a.

title: 4. Compute Engine and VPC
text:
Rules and conventions

Create a custom-mode network with planned, non-overlapping ranges. Plan them so a future office VPN or a second region never clashes.
Target firewall rules with network tags (or service accounts), never “all instances”, so a new VM is closed until you tag it.
Name rules <network>-<allow|deny>-<purpose> and leave gaps in priorities (900, 1000, 1100) so you can insert rules later.
Never open SSH (22) or RDP (3389) to 0.0.0.0/0. Use IAP tunnelling.
Prefer internal-only VMs plus Cloud NAT for servers that do not serve the public directly.
Make startup scripts idempotent: they run on every boot.
Use image families, not fixed image names, so new VMs get security patches.
Treat a single VM as zonal: for availability, use a managed instance group across zones, or a regional service such as Cloud Run.

title: 4. Compute Engine and VPC
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Firewall rule created without --target-tags, or the VM has no tag
curl to port 80 times out
add --tags=web to the VM (gcloud compute instances add-tags web1 --tags=web)


Adding an allow rule at 1000 to unblock a range denied at 900
the range is still blocked
the lower number wins: give the allow rule a smaller number (800), or delete the deny


--no-address with no Cloud NAT
apt-get update hangs in the startup script
create a Cloud Router and Cloud NAT, or allow an external IP


Overlapping subnet ranges
The IP range … conflicts with …
choose a range that does not overlap, e.g. 10.20.0.0/24


Expecting the external IP to survive a stop
the menu URL changes after a restart
reserve a static address


Debugging the startup script blind
nginx is missing and you do not know why
read sudo journalctl -u google-startup-scripts.service

title: Google Cloud
text:
Parts 1 to 3 ran the Lemonade Stand on machines you look after yourself. In this part, Google looks after the machines. You rent exactly what you need, pay by the second, and let managed products handle patching, scaling and backups.
Google Cloud has hundreds of products. A small web app needs about eight of them, and this part teaches only those eight. The main path is Cloud Run, which runs the Lemonade container with no servers to manage. A virtual machine appears once (lesson 4), so you can see what Cloud Run does for you.

title: Google Cloud
section: The Lemonade Stand on Google Cloud
text:
The Lemonade Stand on Google Cloud
                       customer's browser
                               │ HTTPS
          ┌────────────────────┴─────────────────────┐
          ▼                                          ▼
 Cloud Storage bucket                     Cloud Run service  lemonade-web
 lemonade-stand-dev-menu                  europe-west2, 0 to 10 instances
 (static menu, photos)                    runs image from Artifact Registry
                                                     │ Unix socket /cloudsql/…

                          (orders)                             (cups sold today)

 Everything lives in project lemonade-stand-dev, region europe-west2 (London),
 and is watched by Cloud Logging, Cloud Monitoring and a billing budget.

title: Google Cloud
text:
Follow along safely
Real cloud resources cost real money. Four habits keep the bill near zero:

Use the free trial. New customers get free credit ($300 for 90 days at the time of writing), and several products have an always-free tier.
Create a billing budget first (lesson 9). It emails you at 50%, 90% and 100% of an amount you choose.
Use one project per experiment, such as lemonade-stand-dev.
Delete the project when you are done. gcloud projects delete lemonade-stand-dev removes everything inside it in one step.

Every command in this part was checked against gcloud 594.0.1 with --help in Google’s official google-cloud-cli Docker image. Outputs that needed a real account are marked illustrative: they show the real format with example values.

What comes next

title: 2. The gcloud CLI
text: Everything you can click in the Google Cloud console, you can also type. The gcloud command-line tool is how scripts, CI pipelines and this book talk to Google Cloud.

title: 2. The gcloud CLI
2. The gcloud CLI
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






Tip



gcloud is a universal remote control for Google’s giant computer.
Every button press is a short sentence in a fixed order: which room, which thing, what to do. “Living room, lights, turn on” becomes gcloud compute instances start.
A configuration is a save slot in a video game. Slot 1 remembers you were in the “dev” world in London. Slot 2 remembers the “prod” world. Loading a slot puts you back exactly where you were.
The remote can also print its answers as plain words that other programs can read. Unix pioneer Doug McIlroy taught the idea that small programs should work together and pass plain text to each other (Unix philosophy). gcloud --format="value(...)" follows that idea: it prints only the value you asked for, ready for the next command.

title: 2. The gcloud CLI
text:
The idea, precisely

Install and log in
Install the Google Cloud CLI from the official installer, or run it without installing anything through Google’s Docker image:
docker run --rm gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:slim gcloud version
Google Cloud SDK 594.0.1
Then run gcloud init once. It logs you in, asks for a default project and region, and saves the answers.
There are two different logins, and beginners mix them up:








Command
Who uses the credentials
Typical use




gcloud auth login
the gcloud tool itself
you typing gcloud run deploy


gcloud auth application-default login
your programs (client libraries, Terraform) through Application Default Credentials
a Node.js script that reads Firestore from your laptop





The command grammar
Every command has the same shape:
gcloud [release-level] <group> [<subgroup>] <command> [POSITIONAL] [--flags]
gcloud                  compute  instances    create    web1         --zone=europe-west2-a

Release level is optional: nothing means GA (stable), or beta / alpha for newer commands that may change.
Group is the product: compute, run, storage, sql, iam.
Subgroup is the kind of thing: instances, firewall-rules, services.
Command is the verb: create, list, describe, update, delete.
Positional is usually the name of the thing.
Flags start with -- and look like --name=value.

Add --help to any command to see its full manual.


Properties and configurations
gcloud remembers settings called properties, written as section/name. The core section is the default, so project means core/project.








Property
Meaning
Example value




core/project
the default project
lemonade-stand-dev


core/account
the logged-in account
owner@example.com


compute/region
the default region for Compute Engine
europe-west2


compute/zone
the default zone
europe-west2-a


run/region
the default region for Cloud Run
europe-west2



A configuration is a named set of properties. Only one is active at a time.

Command or flag
What it does
Rule / convention
Example

interactive first-time setup
run once per machine
gcloud init

logs gcloud in as you
opens a browser
gcloud auth login

gives your code credentials
separate from auth login
gcloud auth application-default login


gcloud auth list
shows accounts, marks the active one

gcloud auth list


gcloud config set
sets a property in the active configuration

gcloud config get

gcloud config get project


gcloud config list

gcloud config list

it activates it unless --no-activate

the safest way to touch prod

per project

title: 2. The gcloud CLI
section: Worked example: one save slot per environment
text:
Worked example: one save slot per environment
These commands ran for real in the google-cloud-cli:slim container, version 594.0.1, with no account logged in.
gcloud config configurations create lemonade-dev
gcloud config set project lemonade-stand-dev
gcloud config set run/region europe-west2
gcloud config configurations create lemonade-prod --no-activate
gcloud config configurations list
Created [lemonade-dev].
Activated [lemonade-dev].
Updated property [core/project].
Updated property [run/region].
Created [lemonade-prod].
NAME           IS_ACTIVE  ACCOUNT  PROJECT             COMPUTE_DEFAULT_ZONE  COMPUTE_DEFAULT_REGION
default        False
lemonade-dev   True                lemonade-stand-dev
lemonade-prod  False
Notice that prod is not active. A careless delete runs against dev.
One real surprise: gcloud config set compute/region europe-west2 failed in this container with You do not currently have an active account selected. gcloud checks Compute regions against the API, so it needs a login. run/region has no such check.

Which project wins?
The same property can come from three places. A real run shows the order:
gcloud config get project
CLOUDSDK_CORE_PROJECT=lemonade-stand-test gcloud config get project
CLOUDSDK_CORE_PROJECT=lemonade-stand-test gcloud config get project --project=lemonade-stand-prod
lemonade-stand-dev
lemonade-stand-test
lemonade-stand-prod
The flag beats the environment variable, and the environment variable beats the configuration. Environment variables are named CLOUDSDK_<SECTION>_<PROPERTY>.
\[
v(k) = \operatorname{first}\big( F(k),\ E(k),\ C(k) \big)
\]
where:

\(k\) is a property name, such as core/project;
\(F(k)\) is the value given by a command-line flag (--project), or “undefined” if no flag was typed;
\(E(k)\) is the value of the environment variable (CLOUDSDK_CORE_PROJECT), or undefined;
\(C(k)\) is the value stored in the active configuration, or undefined;
\(\operatorname{first}(\dots)\) returns the first value in the list that is defined;
\(v(k)\) is the value gcloud actually uses.

Example: in the third command, \(F = \texttt{lemonade-stand-prod}\), \(E = \texttt{lemonade-stand-test}\), \(C = \texttt{lemonade-stand-dev}\). The first defined value is \(F\), so \(v = \texttt{lemonade-stand-prod}\). In the second command no flag was typed, so \(F\) is undefined and \(v = E = \texttt{lemonade-stand-test}\). In the first, only \(C\) is defined, so \(v = \texttt{lemonade-stand-dev}\).


--format and --filter in a script
gcloud config configurations list --filter="is_active=true" --format="value(name)"
lemonade-dev
--filter chose the rows; --format="value(name)" printed only the name, with no header, so a script can store it in a variable.

title: 2. The gcloud CLI
text:
Rules and conventions

Create one configuration per environment and name it after the project: lemonade-dev, lemonade-prod.
Leave the dev configuration active by default. Reach prod with an explicit --project=lemonade-stand-prod or --configuration=lemonade-prod, so every prod command is visible in your history.
In scripts, always pass --project and --region explicitly. Never rely on whoever ran gcloud config set last.
In scripts, use --format="value(...)" or --format=json. Never parse the default table: its columns can change.
Use --quiet only in scripts, and never together with delete on prod unless a human approved it.
Use gcloud auth application-default login for your code and gcloud auth login for the CLI. On servers, use a service account instead of either (lesson 3).
Prefer GA commands. Use beta and alpha only when no GA command exists, and expect them to change.

the script breaks after a gcloud update

the filter returns nothing

You cannot perform this action because the Google Cloud CLI component manager is disabled

title: 3. IAM and Service Accounts
text: IAM (Identity and Access Management) answers one question for every request: may this principal use this permission on this resource? This lesson shows how Google Cloud decides, and how to give the Lemonade Stand’s programs exactly the access they need.

title: 3. IAM and Service Accounts
text:
The problem
Three things need access in lemonade-stand-dev:

The owner manages everything.
The Cloud Run app must connect to the orders database, and nothing more.
Every customer on the internet must be able to open the menu, but must not change anything.

Giving everyone “Owner” would work for a day, until a bug in the app deletes the database. We need precise, small grants.

title: 3. IAM and Service Accounts
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






Tip



IAM works like a library card.

Who you are is written on the card: a person, or a robot helper. In IAM this is the principal.
What the card lets you do is a bundle of stamps: “borrow books”, “renew books”. One stamp is a permission; a bundle of stamps is a role.
Where the card works is the branch or shelf it was issued for: the resource.

A card issued by the city library works in every branch in the city. A card issued by one branch works only there. That is inheritance: grants made higher in the tree count everywhere below.
At the front desk there is also a short “not allowed” list. If your name is on it for “borrow”, no card can help you. That is a deny rule, and it is checked first.
The robot that carries books between branches has its own card, with only the stamps it needs. That is a service account.
The rule “give each helper only the stamps it needs” is very old. Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder wrote it down in 1975 in The Protection of Information in Computer Systems, where it is called the principle of least privilege.

title: 3. IAM and Service Accounts
text:
The idea, precisely

Principals
A principal is an identity that can be granted access. In commands it is written with a type prefix:








Prefix
Who
Example




user:
a Google account
user:owner@example.com


group:
a Google group
group:lemonade-staff@example.com


serviceAccount:
a program’s identity
serviceAccount:lemonade-run@lemonade-stand-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com


domain:
everyone in a Workspace domain
domain:example.com


allUsers
anyone on the internet, even without logging in
used for a public menu


allAuthenticatedUsers
anyone with any Google account
almost never what you want





Permissions and roles
A permission has the shape service.resource.verb, for example run.services.get or cloudsql.instances.connect. You never grant a permission directly. You grant a role, which is a named set of permissions.








Kind
Example
When to use




Basic
roles/owner, roles/editor, roles/viewer
personal sandboxes only: each holds thousands of permissions


Predefined
roles/run.invoker, roles/cloudsql.client, roles/storage.objectViewer
the normal choice, maintained by Google


Custom
projects/lemonade-stand-dev/roles/lemonadeRunViewer
when no predefined role is small enough





Allow policies
Each resource can have one allow policy: a list of bindings. A binding says “these members get this role”.
bindings:
- role: roles/cloudsql.client
  members:
  - serviceAccount:lemonade-run@lemonade-stand-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com
- role: roles/owner
  members:
  - user:owner@example.com
etag: BwYb3x0KxY8=
version: 1
The etag protects against two people editing the policy at the same time: gcloud sends it back, and the update fails if someone changed the policy in between.


Inheritance and deny
The policy that really applies to a resource is the union of its own bindings and the bindings of every ancestor in the hierarchy. Inheritance only adds access. You cannot take away, on a project, a role that was granted on its folder.
To take access away, Google Cloud has separate deny policies, attached to an organization, folder or project. IAM checks deny rules before allow rules. If a deny rule matches, the request fails, whatever roles the principal holds.


Service accounts
A service account is an identity for a program, not a person. Its email has the shape NAME@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com.

Attach it to a workload, for example gcloud run deploy --service-account=…. The program then gets short-lived tokens automatically, with no password and no key file.
Impersonation lets a person act as a service account for a while, with --impersonate-service-account. It needs the role roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator on that account.
Avoid key files. A downloaded JSON key works until someone deletes it, and keys leak through laptops and Git repositories.
Workload Identity Federation lets something outside Google Cloud, such as a GitHub Actions job, swap its own signed token for short-lived Google credentials. CI/CD can then deploy with no stored key at all (see Part 3).

title: 3. IAM and Service Accounts
text:
Command reference









Command or flag
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




gcloud iam service-accounts create
creates a robot identity
name: 6 to 30 chars, lowercase, digits, hyphens
gcloud iam service-accounts create lemonade-run --display-name="Lemonade Cloud Run"


gcloud iam service-accounts list
lists service accounts in the project

gcloud iam service-accounts list


gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding
adds one binding to the project policy
--member needs its prefix
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding lemonade-stand-dev --member="serviceAccount:lemonade-run@lemonade-stand-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com" --role="roles/cloudsql.client"


gcloud projects remove-iam-policy-binding
removes one binding
exact same member and role
… remove-iam-policy-binding lemonade-stand-dev --member="user:old@example.com" --role="roles/editor"


gcloud projects get-iam-policy
prints the project policy
flatten to one row per member
gcloud projects get-iam-policy lemonade-stand-dev --flatten="bindings[].members" --format="table(bindings.role,bindings.members)"


gcloud run services add-iam-policy-binding
grants a role on one Cloud Run service
the smallest scope
gcloud run services add-iam-policy-binding lemonade-web --region=europe-west2 --member=allUsers --role=roles/run.invoker


gcloud iam roles describe
lists the permissions inside a role

gcloud iam roles describe roles/run.invoker


gcloud iam roles create
creates a custom role from YAML
role ID uses letters, digits, _, .
gcloud iam roles create lemonadeRunViewer --project=lemonade-stand-dev --file=lemonade-role.yaml


gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding
grants a role on a service account
used to allow impersonation
… add-iam-policy-binding deployer@lemonade-stand-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com --member="user:owner@example.com" --role="roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator"


--impersonate-service-account
runs any command as that account
short-lived token, no key
gcloud run services list --impersonate-service-account=deployer@lemonade-stand-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com


gcloud iam service-accounts keys create
downloads a long-lived key
avoid; prefer impersonation or federation
(avoid)


gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create
creates a pool for outside identities
then add an OIDC provider
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create github --location=global

title: 3. IAM and Service Accounts
text:
Worked example: three small grants
# 1. A robot identity for the app, allowed to connect to Cloud SQL and nothing else.
gcloud iam service-accounts create lemonade-run --display-name="Lemonade Cloud Run"
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding lemonade-stand-dev \
  --member="serviceAccount:lemonade-run@lemonade-stand-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
  --role="roles/cloudsql.client"

# 2. Everyone may call (view) this one service: the menu is public.
gcloud run services add-iam-policy-binding lemonade-web --region=europe-west2 \
  --member=allUsers --role=roles/run.invoker

# 3. A read-only role for a status-page robot, built from the lab file.
gcloud iam roles create lemonadeRunViewer --project=lemonade-stand-dev \
  --file=examples/lemonade-role.yaml
The custom role file is four permissions long (examples/lemonade-role.yaml):
title: Lemonade Run Viewer
description: See the Lemonade Cloud Run service and its revisions. Nothing else.
stage: GA
includedPermissions:
  - run.services.get
  - run.services.list
  - run.revisions.get
  - run.revisions.list
Check the result (illustrative output):
$ gcloud projects get-iam-policy lemonade-stand-dev \
    --flatten="bindings[].members" --format="table(bindings.role,bindings.members)"
ROLE                   MEMBERS
roles/cloudsql.client  serviceAccount:lemonade-run@lemonade-stand-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com
roles/owner            user:owner@example.com
The allUsers grant does not appear here, because it lives on the service, not on the project. Smaller scope, smaller blast radius.

title: 3. IAM and Service Accounts
text:
Rules and conventions

Grant roles to groups, not to individual people. Then joining or leaving the team is one group change.
Grant at the smallest scope that works: service, then bucket, then project. Use the organization or folder only for rules that apply to everything.
Use predefined roles first, custom roles when the predefined ones are too big, and basic roles only in a personal sandbox.
Give each workload its own service account (lemonade-run, lemonade-deployer). Do not run apps as the default Compute Engine service account, which in older projects often holds the very broad Editor role.
Never download service account keys when impersonation or Workload Identity Federation can do the job.
Expect a short delay: a new grant usually takes effect within a couple of minutes, occasionally longer.
Review grants regularly. Remove allUsers everywhere except the things that really are public.

title: 3. IAM and Service Accounts
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Forgetting the prefix in --member
the command fails with an INVALID_ARGUMENT error about the member
write user:, serviceAccount:, group:


Granting roles/editor to the app
it works, until a bug or an attacker deletes data
grant roles/cloudsql.client (or a custom role) only


Trying to remove an inherited role on the project
remove-iam-policy-binding says the binding does not exist
remove it where it was granted (folder or organization), or use a deny policy


Deploying with --service-account but lacking permission to use it
Permission 'iam.serviceaccounts.actAs' denied
grant yourself roles/iam.serviceAccountUser on that service account


Testing straight after a grant
403 PERMISSION_DENIED for a minute or two
wait and retry; grants take time to spread


Committing a key file to Git
a security alert, or a surprise bill from someone else’s crypto miner
delete the key now (gcloud iam service-accounts keys delete) and use impersonation

title: 3. IAM and Service Accounts
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Inheritance is a union over the resource’s path. Let \(B(a)\) be the set of (principal, role) pairs granted directly on node \(a\).
\[
E(r) = \bigcup_{a \in \operatorname{path}(r)} B(a)
\]
where:

\(r\) is the resource being accessed;
\(\operatorname{path}(r)\) is \(r\) together with all its ancestors (project, folders, organization), as defined in lesson 1;
\(B(a)\) is the set of pairs \((u, \rho)\), meaning “principal \(u\) has role \(\rho\)”, written in the allow policy of node \(a\);
\(\bigcup\) (“big union”) collects the pairs from every node on the path into one set;
\(E(r)\) is the effective set of grants for \(r\).

Example: \(\operatorname{path}(\texttt{lemonade-web}) = (\texttt{lemonade-web}, \texttt{lemonade-stand-dev}, \texttt{shop}, \texttt{example.com})\).

\(B(\texttt{example.com}) = \lbrace (\texttt{alice}, \texttt{viewer}) \rbrace\)
\(B(\texttt{shop}) = \emptyset\)
\(B(\texttt{lemonade-stand-dev}) = \lbrace (\texttt{alice}, \texttt{run.developer}) \rbrace\)
\(B(\texttt{lemonade-web}) = \lbrace (\texttt{allUsers}, \texttt{run.invoker}) \rbrace\)

So \(E(\texttt{lemonade-web}) = \lbrace (\texttt{alice}, \texttt{viewer}), (\texttt{alice}, \texttt{run.developer}), (\texttt{allUsers}, \texttt{run.invoker}) \rbrace\), which has \(1 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 3\) pairs.
The decision checks deny first, then looks for any role that contains the permission.
\[
\operatorname{allowed}(u, \pi, r) \iff \neg\, D(u, \pi, r) \;\land\; \exists\, (u, \rho) \in E(r) : \pi \in \operatorname{perms}(\rho)
\]
where:

\(u\) is the principal making the request and \(\pi\) (“pi”) is the permission it needs;
\(D(u, \pi, r)\) is true when a deny rule on any node of \(\operatorname{path}(r)\) matches \(u\) and \(\pi\);
\(\neg\) means “not” and \(\land\) means “and”;
\(\exists\) means “there is at least one”;
\(\operatorname{perms}(\rho)\) is the set of permissions inside role \(\rho\).

Example: Alice runs gcloud run deploy, which needs \(\pi = \texttt{run.services.update}\). No deny rule matches, so \(\neg D\) is true. The pair \((\texttt{alice}, \texttt{run.developer})\) is in \(E\), and \(\texttt{run.services.update} \in \operatorname{perms}(\texttt{run.developer})\). Both sides are true, so the deploy is allowed. Now the organization adds a deny rule for deleting Cloud Run services. Alice runs gcloud run services delete lemonade-web: \(D\) is true, so \(\neg D\) is false, and the request is denied, even though run.developer contains the delete permission.
Least privilege is a set difference that should be empty.
\[
X = G \setminus N, \qquad \text{goal: } \lvert X \rvert = 0
\]
where:

\(N\) is the set of permissions the workload really needs;
\(G\) is the set of permissions its roles grant;
\(G \setminus N\) is everything granted but not needed: the extra power an attacker would get;
\(\lvert X \rvert\) is how many extra permissions there are.

Example: the status-page robot needs \(N = \lbrace \texttt{run.services.get}, \texttt{run.services.list} \rbrace\). The custom role grants \(G = \lbrace \texttt{run.services.get}, \texttt{run.services.list}, \texttt{run.revisions.get}, \texttt{run.revisions.list} \rbrace\). Then \(X = \lbrace \texttt{run.revisions.get}, \texttt{run.revisions.list} \rbrace\) and \(\lvert X \rvert = 4 - 2 = 2\): two harmless read permissions, a fair trade for one simple role. Granting roles/viewer instead would make \(\lvert X \rvert\) run into the thousands.
