title: 9. Serverless: Lambda
text:
Every evening the owner wants one answer: how many orders today, and how much money? The job takes a fraction of a second. Keeping a server running 24 hours a day for it wastes money, and someone still has to patch that server.
We want to hand AWS a small piece of code that runs only when needed and costs nothing in between.

title: 9. Serverless: Lambda
text:
Every evening the owner wants one answer: how many orders today, and how much money? The job takes a fraction of a second. Keeping a server running 24 hours a day for it wastes money, and someone still has to patch that server.
We want to hand AWS a small piece of code that runs only when needed and costs nothing in between.

title: 9. Serverless: Lambda
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipA robot that wakes up when the bell rings



Imagine a little robot asleep in a cupboard. When someone rings the bell (an event), it wakes up, does one job, gives back the answer and goes back to sleep. You pay only for the seconds it is awake.
The first ring after a long sleep takes a moment longer, because the robot has to wake up and put its shoes on (a cold start). If ten people ring at the same time, ten robots wake up (concurrency). Each robot works in its own tiny room, so they never bump into each other.
Those tiny rooms are real. AWS engineers, including Marc Brooker, described them in the paper Firecracker: Lightweight Virtualization for Serverless Applications (NSDI 2020). Each Lambda function gets its own very small virtual machine that starts in a fraction of a second (USENIX).

title: 9. Serverless: Lambda
text:
The concept, precisely

A function is your code plus its settings: runtime, memory, timeout, role and environment variables.
The handler is the entry point, written file.function. count_orders.handler means “the function handler in count_orders.py”.
An event is the JSON input, for example a list of orders. The context object tells the code how much time is left.
The runtime is the language environment, for example python3.13 or nodejs22.x.
Memory runs from 128 MB to 10,240 MB. CPU power grows with memory. The timeout can be up to 900 seconds (15 minutes).
The execution role is the function’s IAM role (lesson 2). Its logs go to CloudWatch (lesson 10).
Triggers start the function: an HTTP request, a new file in S3, a message in a queue, or a schedule.
A function URL gives one function its own HTTPS address, which is simplest. API Gateway adds routes, authentication, throttling and usage plans for real APIs.
A cold start happens when Lambda must create a new execution environment. Warm environments are reused for later requests.
Concurrency is the number of requests being handled at the same moment. Each region has an account limit (by default 1,000). Reserved concurrency sets aside part of it for one function.
Versions freeze code and settings. An alias (live) points to a version, so you can switch back quickly.










Command or setting
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




aws lambda create-function
creates the function
needs a zip (or image) and a role
--function-name count-orders --runtime python3.13


--handler
entry point
file.function
--handler count_orders.handler


--zip-file
the code
fileb:// for binary files
--zip-file fileb://count_orders.zip


--role
execution role ARN
minimal permissions plus logging
--role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/lemonade-lambda


--memory-size
memory in MB
128–10,240; more memory is also more CPU
--memory-size 128


--timeout
maximum run time in seconds
1–900; keep it short
--timeout 10


--environment
settings for the code
not for secrets; use Secrets Manager
Variables={TABLE=lemonade-orders}


aws lambda invoke
runs it once
--cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out for a JSON payload
--payload '{"orders":[]}' result.json


aws lambda update-function-code
uploads new code
then publish a version
--zip-file fileb://count_orders.zip


aws lambda create-function-url-config
gives it an HTTPS address
--auth-type AWS_IAM unless it is truly public
--auth-type NONE


aws lambda put-function-concurrency
reserves concurrency
protects other functions and the database
--reserved-concurrent-executions 5


aws scheduler create-schedule
runs it on a timetable
AWS cron has 6 fields and a ?
--schedule-expression "cron(0 18 * * ? *)"

title: 9. Serverless: Lambda
section: Worked example: the evening order count
text:
Worked example: the evening order count
The whole function, examples/count_orders.py:
"""Lambda handler: count today's Lemonade orders and add up the money."""


def handler(event, context):
    orders = event.get("orders", [])
    return {
        "orders": len(orders),
        "revenue": round(sum(order["price"] * order["cups"] for order in orders), 2),
    }
Package it, create it and call it with two orders (2 cups at $2.50 and 1 cup at $3.00):
python3 -m zipfile -c count_orders.zip count_orders.py
aws lambda create-function --function-name count-orders --runtime python3.13 \
  --handler count_orders.handler --zip-file fileb://count_orders.zip \
  --role arn:aws:iam::000000000000:role/lemonade-lambda
aws lambda invoke --function-name count-orders --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out \
  --payload '{"orders":[{"price":2.5,"cups":2},{"price":3.0,"cups":1}]}' result.json
cat result.json
Output of cat result.json (LocalStack, which runs the real Python runtime in Docker):
{"orders": 2, "revenue": 8.0}
Check: \(2 \times 2.50 + 1 \times 3.00 = 8.00\). Finally, ring the bell every evening at 18:00 London time:
aws scheduler create-schedule --name lemonade-daily-count \
  --schedule-expression "cron(0 18 * * ? *)" --schedule-expression-timezone Europe/London \
  --flexible-time-window Mode=OFF \
  --target '{"Arn":"<function ARN>","RoleArn":"<scheduler role ARN>"}'
aws scheduler get-schedule --name lemonade-daily-count \
  --query '[Name,ScheduleExpression,ScheduleExpressionTimezone,State]' --output text
Output of the last command (LocalStack):
lemonade-daily-count    cron(0 18 * * ? *)  Europe/London   ENABLED
AWS cron reads minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week year: minute 0, hour 18, every day of every month. The ? means “any day of the week”, because you may not fix both day fields at once.

title: 9. Serverless: Lambda
text:
Rules and conventions

One function, one job. count-orders counts orders. It does not also send emails.
Keep handlers pure where you can: logic in plain functions you can test without AWS, as above.
Short timeouts (seconds, not minutes) and reserved concurrency so a flood of events cannot overwhelm the orders database.
Make handlers safe to run twice. Many triggers deliver an event at least once, so the same order may arrive again.
No state between calls. Anything you need tomorrow goes to S3 or DynamoDB, not to a local file.
Function URL for one simple endpoint, API Gateway for a real API.

title: 9. Serverless: Lambda
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Handler name does not match the file
Runtime.ImportModuleError
--handler count_orders.handler for count_orders.py


JSON payload sent without the binary-format flag
Invalid base64 error from the CLI
add --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out


Timeout left at a few seconds for a slow job
Task timed out after 3.00 seconds
measure, then raise --timeout


Role without CloudWatch Logs permission
the function runs but no logs appear
attach AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole


Recursive trigger: the function writes to the bucket that triggers it
thousands of invocations and a bill
write to a different bucket or prefix

text: The network from lesson 3 is ready, but it is empty. The Lemonade Stand needs two web servers, web1 in eu-west-2a and web2 in eu-west-2b. Each runs nginx in front of the app on port 8080. They should set themselves up without anyone logging in, and cost nothing on days we switch them off.

title: 4. EC2: Virtual Servers
4. EC2: Virtual Servers
text:
The concept, precisely

An instance is a virtual server running on AWS hardware.
An AMI (Amazon Machine Image) is the starting disk: an operating system plus anything pre-installed. The Lemonade servers use Amazon Linux 2023. AWS publishes the newest AMI ID as a public parameter, so you never need to copy IDs by hand.
The instance type sets the CPU and memory. Its name reads family, generation, extra letters, dot, size:



Name
Family
Generation
Extra letters
Size




t3.micro
t: burstable general purpose
3
none
micro


t4g.micro
t
4
g: AWS Graviton (ARM)
micro


m7i.large
m: general purpose
7
i: Intel
large



Other family letters: c for compute-heavy work, r for lots of memory, g for GPUs. Burstable (t) instances run at a low baseline and can burst higher for short periods, which suits a small web page.
A key pair lets you log in with SSH. The private key is downloaded once, and AWS keeps only the public half. Session Manager (part of AWS Systems Manager) lets you open a shell without SSH or open ports.
User data is a script that cloud-init runs once, as root, on the first boot.
EBS (Elastic Block Store) volumes are network disks. The root volume survives stop and start. By default it is deleted on terminate.
An Elastic IP is a public IPv4 address that stays the same across stop and start. Every public IPv4 address costs $0.005 per hour.
An instance profile attaches an IAM role (lesson 2) to the server, so programs on it get temporary credentials instead of stored keys.
Instance states: pending → running → stopping → stopped → pending …; terminate goes shutting-down → terminated and cannot be undone.










Command or option
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




aws ec2 run-instances
starts new instances
the five essentials below
run-instances --count 2 ...


--image-id
which AMI
look it up, do not hard-code
--image-id resolve:ssm:/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64


--instance-type
size
start small; resize later
--instance-type t3.micro


--subnet-id
which subnet, and therefore which AZ
private subnet for web servers
--subnet-id subnet-...


--security-group-ids
which door guards
one or more SG IDs
--security-group-ids sg-...


--user-data
first-boot script
file:// reads a local file; 16 KB limit
--user-data file://user-data.sh


--key-name
SSH key pair
optional if you use Session Manager
--key-name lemonade-key


--iam-instance-profile
role for programs on the server
never store access keys on a server
--iam-instance-profile Name=lemonade-web


--tag-specifications
name and tags at launch
always set Name and Project
'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=lemonade-web}]'


--metadata-options
instance metadata settings
require IMDSv2 tokens
HttpTokens=required


aws ec2 describe-instances
lists instances
filter by tag
--filters Name=tag:Name,Values=lemonade-web


aws ec2 stop-instances / start-instances
sleep / wake
stopped: no compute charge, disk still billed
--instance-ids i-...


aws ec2 terminate-instances
delete forever
check the ID twice
--instance-ids i-...


aws ec2 create-key-pair
makes an SSH key
save the private key with chmod 400
--key-name lemonade-key --query KeyMaterial


aws ec2 allocate-address / associate-address
Elastic IP
release it when no longer needed
--instance-id i-... --allocation-id eipalloc-...

title: 4. EC2: Virtual Servers
section: Worked example: two web servers that set themselves up
text:
Worked example: two web servers that set themselves up
The first-boot note, examples/user-data.sh:
#!/bin/bash
# Runs once, as root, on the first boot of a Lemonade web server (Amazon Linux 2023).
dnf install -y nginx
echo '<h1>Lemonade Stand</h1><p>Classic lemonade: $2.50</p>' > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
systemctl enable --now nginx
Launch two servers with it, then list them:
aws ec2 run-instances --count 2 --instance-type t3.micro \
  --image-id resolve:ssm:/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 \
  --subnet-id "$PRIV" --security-group-ids "$SG" --user-data file://user-data.sh \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=lemonade-web}]' \
  --query 'Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType,State.Name,PrivateIpAddress]' --output text
Output (LocalStack; LocalStack takes a plain AMI ID instead of resolve:ssm:):
i-e309deca737f6ef78 t3.micro    pending 10.0.11.4
i-cf3da684e71a54fd7 t3.micro    pending 10.0.11.5
Both start as pending and get private addresses from the subnet 10.0.11.0/24. A real launch puts web2 in the second private subnet, 10.0.12.0/24, so the two servers sit in different AZs. Put them to sleep, then give them back:
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-e309deca737f6ef78 i-cf3da684e71a54fd7
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-e309deca737f6ef78 i-cf3da684e71a54fd7
Output (LocalStack, filtered):
i-e309deca737f6ef78 running stopping
i-cf3da684e71a54fd7 running stopping
i-e309deca737f6ef78 shutting-down
i-cf3da684e71a54fd7 shutting-down

title: 4. EC2: Virtual Servers
text:
Rules and conventions

Servers are cattle, not pets. Anything you set up by hand will be lost when the server is replaced. Put it in user data, or later in Ansible (Part 1) or Terraform (Part 6).
Look AMIs up by parameter (resolve:ssm:...), because AMI IDs differ per region and change with every update.
Use Session Manager instead of opening port 22. If you must use SSH, allow only your own IP.
Give servers a role, never access keys.
Require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) so a bug in the web app cannot easily leak the server’s credentials.
Stop what you will need again; terminate what you will not. Release unused Elastic IPs.

title: 4. EC2: Virtual Servers
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




User data without #!/bin/bash on the first line
nothing gets installed
the shebang tells cloud-init how to run it; check /var/log/cloud-init-output.log


Expecting user data to run on every boot
changes made in user data never re-apply
it runs once; build a new instance or use a configuration tool


Lost the private key file
cannot SSH in
AWS cannot recover it; use Session Manager or replace the instance


Data written to the root disk, then terminate
the data is gone
keep data in RDS or S3, or set DeleteOnTermination=false on a data volume


Stopped instance “costs nothing”
small charges continue
EBS disks and Elastic IPs are billed while stopped

title: 2. IAM and the AWS CLI
text:
Several people and programs touch the Lemonade account: the owner, a friend who edits the menu, the web servers that read files from S3, and the CI/CD pipeline from Part 3 that deploys new versions. If they all share the owner’s password, one leaked key can delete everything, and nobody can tell who did what.
Each person and each program needs its own identity, allowed to do only its own job.

title: 2. IAM and the AWS CLI
text:
Several people and programs touch the Lemonade account: the owner, a friend who edits the menu, the web servers that read files from S3, and the CI/CD pipeline from Part 3 that deploys new versions. If they all share the owner’s password, one leaked key can delete everything, and nobody can tell who did what.
Each person and each program needs its own identity, allowed to do only its own job.

title: 2. IAM and the AWS CLI
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipHotel key cards



In a hotel, every guest gets a key card. Your card opens your room and the swimming pool, and only during your stay. It does not open the kitchen. The manager’s master key opens everything, so it stays locked in the safe.
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the hotel front desk. It hands out key cards (identities), and each card has a list printed on it (a policy): “opens room 12 and the pool”. The door follows two simple rules:

If any list says “no” for this door, it stays shut.
If no list says “yes”, it also stays shut.

In 1975 Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder wrote down the rule hotels already follow. Every program and every user should work with the smallest set of permissions needed to do the job, so that a mistake can only do a little damage. They called it least privilege (The Protection of Information in Computer Systems). Werner Vogels lists the same idea among his ten AWS lessons: build security in from the ground up (2016).

title: 2. IAM and the AWS CLI
text:
The concept, precisely
Identities (who is asking):

The root user is the email address that created the account. It can do everything, including closing the account. Protect it with MFA, create no access keys for it, and use it only for the few tasks that require it.
An IAM user is a long-term identity with a password (for the console) and/or access keys (for the CLI). Use one per person or program, never a shared one.
An IAM group is a set of users. Attach permissions to the group, not to each user.
An IAM role is an identity with permissions but no long-term password or keys. Someone or something assumes it and receives temporary credentials from AWS STS (Security Token Service). EC2 servers, Lambda functions and GitHub Actions (Part 3, via OIDC) should use roles.
IAM Identity Center is the recommended way for people to sign in. You create users once, they sign in through a portal, and they get short-lived credentials for the accounts and roles they may use (aws configure sso). Small personal accounts can start with IAM users. Teams should use Identity Center.
MFA (multi-factor authentication) asks for a second proof, such as a code from an app or a security key, besides the password.

Policies (what is allowed) are JSON documents. An identity-based policy is attached to a user, group or role. A resource-based policy is attached to a resource, such as an S3 bucket policy (lesson 5), and names a Principal.









Field
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




Version
the policy language version
always "2012-10-17", the current one, not today’s date
"Version": "2012-10-17"


Statement
a list of rules
one or more statements
"Statement": [ { ... } ]


Sid
a name for one statement
optional; describe the intent
"Sid": "EditTheMenuOnly"


Effect
allow or deny
exactly "Allow" or "Deny"
"Effect": "Allow"


Action
which API calls
service:Operation; * wildcards allowed but avoid them
"s3:PutObject"


Resource
which things, by ARN
as narrow as possible
"arn:aws:s3:::lemonade-menu-7f3a/index.html"


Condition
extra requirements
{"operator": {"key": "value"}}
{"Bool": {"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true"}}


Principal
who (resource-based policies only)
not used in identity-based policies
"Principal": "*"



Our menu editor needs to read and replace one file and nothing else:
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "EditTheMenuOnly",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::lemonade-menu-7f3a/index.html"
    }
  ]
}
This is examples/menu-editor-policy.json.

title: 2. IAM and the AWS CLI
text:
The AWS CLI
Every AWS CLI command has the same shape:
aws <service> <operation> [--parameters] [--global-options]
aws  s3api     list-buckets                --output table









Command or option
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




aws configure
saves access keys, region and output format
keys go to ~/.aws/credentials, settings to ~/.aws/config
aws configure --profile lemonade


aws configure sso
signs in through IAM Identity Center
preferred for people: no long-term keys on disk
aws configure sso


aws configure list
shows which values are in use and where they came from
run it when something looks wrong
aws configure list


--profile / AWS_PROFILE
picks a named set of settings
one profile per account or role
export AWS_PROFILE=lemonade


--region / AWS_REGION
picks the region
set a default once; override per command
--region eu-west-2


--output
json, text, table, yaml
text for scripts, table for eyes
--output text


--query
filters the response (JMESPath)
[] flattens lists, . picks fields
--query 'Users[].UserName'


aws sts get-caller-identity
“who am I?”
run it before anything destructive
aws sts get-caller-identity


aws iam create-user / create-group
creates identities
names are case-insensitive and unique in the account
aws iam create-user --user-name menu-editor


aws iam add-user-to-group
puts a user in a group
grant via groups
--user-name menu-editor --group-name lemonade-editors


aws iam create-policy
stores a policy
file:// reads a local file
--policy-document file://menu-editor-policy.json


aws iam attach-group-policy
gives a group a policy
attach to groups and roles
--group-name lemonade-editors --policy-arn <arn>


aws iam simulate-principal-policy
tests a decision without doing it
great for checking least privilege
--action-names s3:DeleteObject


aws <service> help
the built-in manual
every operation has one
aws iam create-role help

title: 2. IAM and the AWS CLI
section: Worked example: a menu editor with one job
text:
Worked example: a menu editor with one job
Create the user, a group and the policy, then attach the policy to the group:
aws iam create-user --user-name menu-editor
aws iam create-group --group-name lemonade-editors
aws iam add-user-to-group --user-name menu-editor --group-name lemonade-editors
POLICY_ARN=$(aws iam create-policy --policy-name lemonade-menu-editor \
  --policy-document file://menu-editor-policy.json --query Policy.Arn --output text)
aws iam attach-group-policy --group-name lemonade-editors --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN"
aws iam list-groups-for-user --user-name menu-editor --query 'Groups[].GroupName' --output text
Output of the last line (LocalStack; the create-* commands also print JSON, skipped here). $POLICY_ARN holds arn:aws:iam::000000000000:policy/lemonade-menu-editor:
lemonade-editors
Now ask AWS what the menu editor may do, without doing it:
aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
  --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/menu-editor \
  --action-names s3:PutObject s3:DeleteObject \
  --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::lemonade-menu-7f3a/index.html \
  --query 'EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]' --output text
Illustrative output (LocalStack’s free edition does not implement the simulator):
s3:PutObject    allowed
s3:DeleteObject implicitDeny
implicitDeny means “no statement said yes”. The editor can replace the menu but cannot delete it.

title: 2. IAM and the AWS CLI
text:
Rules and conventions

Lock the root user away: turn on MFA, delete any root access keys, and sign in as root only for account-level tasks.
Humans use Identity Center or MFA-protected users; machines use roles. Long-term access keys are the easiest secret to leak.
Grant through groups and roles, never by attaching policies to single users.
Start from nothing and add. Write the narrowest Action and Resource that work, test them with the simulator, and widen only when something legitimately fails.
Prefer AWS-managed policies only as a starting point. AdministratorAccess and AmazonS3FullAccess are convenient and far too wide for a menu editor.
Run aws sts get-caller-identity before any command that deletes things. The most common accident is the right command in the wrong account.

title: 2. IAM and the AWS CLI
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Daily work as root
one stolen password owns everything
create an admin identity with MFA, then stop using root


Access keys committed to git
surprise EC2 servers mining cryptocurrency
delete the key at once, rotate, use roles or aws configure sso


"Action": "*" to “make it work”
anything can delete anything
find the exact action in the error message and allow only that


Wrong ARN form for S3
AccessDenied although the action looks right
the bucket is arn:aws:s3:::name; the objects are arn:aws:s3:::name/*


AWS_REGION left set in the shell
commands hit the wrong region
aws configure list shows where each value comes from

title: 3. VPC and Networking
text:
Customers must reach the Lemonade web servers. The orders database must never be reachable from the internet. The web servers still need to download software updates. All of this must work in two availability zones.
We need our own private network with a public part, a private part, and clear rules about who may talk to whom.

title: 3. VPC and Networking
text:
Customers must reach the Lemonade web servers. The orders database must never be reachable from the internet. The web servers still need to download software updates. All of this must work in two availability zones.
We need our own private network with a public part, a private part, and clear rules about who may talk to whom.

title: 3. VPC and Networking
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipA gated town



A VPC is your own gated town. Every house has a number, and all numbers start with 10.0.
The town has neighbourhoods (subnets). Each neighbourhood is in exactly one part of the city (one availability zone). The town gate (internet gateway) leads to the outside world. Street signs (route tables) tell each neighbourhood where to go: “anything outside the town? Use the gate.”
The public neighbourhood has a sign to the gate. The private neighbourhood has no sign to the gate, so strangers cannot walk in. Its residents still send letters through the post office (NAT gateway), which can post letters out and bring the replies back.
Each house also has a door guard (security group). The guard remembers who you visited, so the reply is always let back in. Each neighbourhood can have a checkpoint (network ACL) that checks everyone in both directions against a numbered list and remembers nobody.
Werner Vogels counts the network among the ten big AWS lessons: it is the part every service depends on, so it must be designed, not left to chance (2016).

title: 3. VPC and Networking
text:
The concept, precisely

A VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is an isolated network in one region, defined by a CIDR block such as 10.0.0.0/16. Every region also has a ready-made default VPC (172.31.0.0/16), which is fine for experiments.
CIDR notation a.b.c.d/p means “all addresses whose first \(p\) bits equal those of a.b.c.d”. A smaller \(p\) means a bigger block.
A subnet is a slice of the VPC’s block that lives in one AZ.
A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway. A private subnet does not. Nothing else makes a subnet public.
An internet gateway (IGW) connects the VPC to the internet in both directions, for resources with public IP addresses.
A route table is a list of destination → target rules attached to subnets. Each one contains an automatic local route for the VPC’s own block.
A NAT gateway sits in a public subnet and lets private resources make outgoing connections (for updates), while nothing from the internet can start a connection inward.
A security group (SG) is a stateful firewall on each network interface. It has allow rules only, and replies to allowed traffic are always allowed back. A rule may name another security group as its source.
A network ACL (NACL) is a stateless firewall on a subnet. It has numbered allow and deny rules, checked from the lowest number up, and replies must be allowed explicitly.

The Lemonade network:
VPC 10.0.0.0/16 (eu-west-2)
├── public  10.0.1.0/24  (eu-west-2a)  ALB, NAT gateway   route 0.0.0.0/0 → internet gateway
├── public  10.0.2.0/24  (eu-west-2b)  ALB
├── private 10.0.11.0/24 (eu-west-2a)  web1, database     route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT gateway
└── private 10.0.12.0/24 (eu-west-2b)  web2, (standby)    route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT gateway









Command or field
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




aws ec2 create-vpc
creates the network
/16 to /28; use a private range (10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x)
--cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16


aws ec2 create-subnet
creates a slice in one AZ
must fit inside the VPC; must not overlap other subnets
--cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --availability-zone eu-west-2a


aws ec2 create-internet-gateway
creates the gate
one per VPC; attach it afterwards
create-internet-gateway


aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway
connects the gate to the VPC
does nothing until a route uses it
--internet-gateway-id igw-... --vpc-id vpc-...


aws ec2 create-route-table
creates a list of routes
one public table, one private table per AZ
--vpc-id vpc-...


aws ec2 create-route
adds destination → target
0.0.0.0/0 means “everything else”
--destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id igw-...


aws ec2 associate-route-table
attaches a table to a subnet
a subnet without one uses the main table
--subnet-id subnet-...


aws ec2 create-nat-gateway
outbound internet for private subnets
lives in a public subnet; one per AZ for resilience
--subnet-id <public> --allocation-id eipalloc-...


aws ec2 create-security-group
creates a door guard
--description is required
--group-name lemonade-web


aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress
adds an inbound allow rule
allow only the ports you serve
--protocol tcp --port 8080 --source-group sg-alb


aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry
adds a numbered NACL rule
leave gaps (100, 200) to insert rules later
--rule-number 100 --rule-action allow


aws ec2 describe-subnets
shows subnets and free addresses
AvailableIpAddressCount shows what is left
--filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-...

title: 3. VPC and Networking
section: Worked example: a public subnet for the stand
text:
Worked example: a public subnet for the stand
Create the VPC, one public subnet, the gate and its route:
VPC=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 --query Vpc.VpcId --output text)
PUB=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id "$VPC" --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 \
  --availability-zone eu-west-2a --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text)
IGW=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --query InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId --output text)
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --internet-gateway-id "$IGW" --vpc-id "$VPC"
RT=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id "$VPC" --query RouteTable.RouteTableId --output text)
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id "$RT" --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id "$IGW"
aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id "$RT" --subnet-id "$PUB"
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --route-table-ids "$RT" \
  --query 'RouteTables[].Routes[].[DestinationCidrBlock,GatewayId]' --output text
Output of the last command (LocalStack):
10.0.0.0/16 local
0.0.0.0/0   igw-b2f14496bcda0770e
The local route was added automatically. The second route makes the subnet public. Now let the web servers’ door guard accept the app port from inside the VPC only:
SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name lemonade-web \
  --description "Lemonade web servers" --vpc-id "$VPC" --query GroupId --output text)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id "$SG" \
  --protocol tcp --port 8080 --cidr 10.0.0.0/16
Output (LocalStack, filtered with --query):
tcp 8080    8080    10.0.0.0/16
Clean up in reverse order: delete-security-group, disassociate-route-table, delete-route-table, detach-internet-gateway, delete-internet-gateway, delete-subnet, delete-vpc.

title: 3. VPC and Networking
text:
Rules and conventions

Plan the addresses once. Use a /16 for the VPC and /24 subnets. Do not overlap with other networks you may connect later, such as your office or another VPC.
One public and one private subnet per AZ, and at least two AZs.
Only load balancers and NAT gateways live in public subnets. Servers and databases go in private subnets.
Reference security groups, not addresses. “Web servers accept 8080 from the ALB’s group” stays correct when IPs change.
Security groups are the everyday tool. Keep NACLs at their default (allow all) unless you need a subnet-wide deny.
Name and tag everything, for example Name=lemonade-public-a.

title: 3. VPC and Networking
text:
Common mistakes



Mistake
Symptom
Fix




IGW attached but no 0.0.0.0/0 route
the “public” server cannot be reached
add the route and associate the table with the subnet


Server in a public subnet without a public IP
still unreachable from the internet
use a load balancer, or assign a public IP or Elastic IP


SSH (port 22) open to 0.0.0.0/0
constant login attempts from bots
use Session Manager, or allow only your own IP /32


NACL allows inbound but not the reply ports
connections hang
NACLs are stateless: allow outbound ephemeral ports 1024–65535


Forgotten NAT gateway in a test account
about $37 a month for nothing
delete it after the lesson; Corey Quinn has written for years about the cost of managed NAT

title: 6. Load Balancers and Auto Scaling
text:
We have two web servers in two AZs, so customers would need to know two addresses. If web1 crashes, its customers see an error. On a hot Saturday two servers are too few; at 3 a.m. two are too many.
We want one address for customers, broken servers taken out automatically, and the number of servers to follow the queue.

title: 6. Load Balancers and Auto Scaling
text:
We have two web servers in two AZs, so customers would need to know two addresses. If web1 crashes, its customers see an error. On a hot Saturday two servers are too few; at 3 a.m. two are too many.
We want one address for customers, broken servers taken out automatically, and the number of servers to follow the queue.

title: 6. Load Balancers and Auto Scaling
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipOne window, many helpers



A busy lemonade stand has one serving window (the load balancer) and several helpers behind it. The window sends each customer to a helper who is free.
Every 30 seconds the manager asks each helper, “Are you OK?” (a health check on /health). A helper who does not answer twice in a row gets no more customers. When they answer again five times in a row, they come back.
The head of staffing (the Auto Scaling group) keeps between 2 and 6 helpers. When the queue is long, they call another helper. When it is quiet, they send one home. A card on the wall (the launch template) says how every new helper must be dressed and what they must know.
Amazon’s David Yanacek explains in the Builders’ Library that health checks must be careful: a check that also fails when a shared database is slow can send every helper home at once and close the whole stand (Implementing health checks).

title: 6. Load Balancers and Auto Scaling
text:
The concept, precisely

Elastic Load Balancing has three types. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) understands HTTP and HTTPS and can route by path or host name. A Network Load Balancer handles plain TCP and UDP. A Gateway Load Balancer is for network appliances. The Lemonade Stand uses an ALB.
A listener waits on a port and protocol (for example HTTP on 80) and forwards requests by its rules.
A target group is a set of targets (instances, IP addresses or Lambda functions), the port to send to (8080), and a health check.
An ALB must sit in at least two subnets in different AZs. It spreads requests over healthy targets in all of them.
A launch template stores how to build one server: AMI, instance type, security group, user data, instance profile.
An Auto Scaling group (ASG) keeps the number of running servers between a minimum and a maximum, aiming at the desired capacity. It replaces unhealthy instances and spreads them over the subnets you give it.
A target tracking policy changes the desired capacity to keep one metric near a target, for example average CPU at 50%.
An instance refresh replaces old instances with new ones a few at a time, which is the rolling update you know from k3s (Part 2).

customers → ALB :80 (public subnets a, b) → listener → target group lemonade-web :8080
                                                          ├── web1 (healthy)    AZ a
                                                          └── web2 (healthy)    AZ b
                                     ASG lemonade-web: min 2, desired 2, max 6, CPU target 50%









Command or field
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




aws elbv2 create-load-balancer
creates the ALB
two or more public subnets in different AZs
--name lemonade-alb --subnets subnet-a subnet-b --security-groups sg-alb


aws elbv2 create-target-group
the set of servers and their health check
port of the app, not of the ALB
--name lemonade-web --protocol HTTP --port 8080 --vpc-id vpc-...


--health-check-path
URL the ALB checks
a cheap endpoint that tests only this server
--health-check-path /health


--health-check-interval-seconds
time between checks, \(i\)
default 30 s for HTTP
--health-check-interval-seconds 10


--unhealthy-threshold-count
failures in a row before removal, \(u\)
default 2
--unhealthy-threshold-count 2


--healthy-threshold-count
successes in a row before return, \(k\)
default 5
--healthy-threshold-count 3


--health-check-timeout-seconds
how long to wait for an answer
default 6 s for HTTP; must be shorter than the interval
--health-check-timeout-seconds 5


aws elbv2 create-listener
opens a port on the ALB
HTTP 80 for practice, HTTPS 443 with a certificate for real customers
--protocol HTTP --port 80 --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=<arn>


aws elbv2 describe-target-health
shows each target’s health
first place to look when the site is down
--target-group-arn <arn>


aws ec2 create-launch-template
the “how to build a server” card
new versions instead of edits
--launch-template-name lemonade-web --launch-template-data file://lt.json


aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group
keeps \(m \le d \le M\) servers
private subnets in two AZs; attach the target group
--min-size 2 --max-size 6 --desired-capacity 2


--health-check-type ELB
uses the ALB’s health check to replace servers
add a grace period for slow starts
--health-check-grace-period 120


aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy
adds a scaling rule
target tracking is the simplest
--policy-type TargetTrackingScaling


aws autoscaling start-instance-refresh
rolling replacement after a template change
keep a minimum healthy percentage
--preferences MinHealthyPercentage=50

title: 6. Load Balancers and Auto Scaling
section: Worked example: the front door and the staffing rule
text:
Worked example: the front door and the staffing rule
aws elbv2 create-target-group --name lemonade-web --protocol HTTP --port 8080 \
  --vpc-id "$VPC" --health-check-path /health
aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name lemonade-web \
  --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=lemonade-web --min-size 2 --max-size 6 \
  --desired-capacity 2 --vpc-zone-identifier "$PRIV_A,$PRIV_B" \
  --target-group-arns "$TG_ARN" --health-check-type ELB --health-check-grace-period 120
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --auto-scaling-group-name lemonade-web \
  --policy-name cpu-50 --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-configuration '{"PredefinedMetricSpecification":{"PredefinedMetricType":"ASGAverageCPUUtilization"},"TargetValue":50}'
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn "$TG_ARN" \
  --query 'TargetHealthDescriptions[].[Target.Id,TargetHealth.State]' --output text
Illustrative output of the last command (ELB and Auto Scaling are not in LocalStack’s free edition):
i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718 healthy
i-0f9e8d7c6b5a43210 healthy
Stop nginx on one server and ask again about a minute later. Its state becomes unhealthy, the ALB stops sending it customers, and the ASG replaces it.

title: 6. Load Balancers and Auto Scaling
text:
Rules and conventions

Keep /health shallow. It should check this server (is the app answering?), not shared dependencies like the database. Otherwise one slow database marks every server unhealthy at once.
Minimum 2, in 2 AZs. One server is a single point of failure even with a load balancer.
Servers accept traffic only from the ALB’s security group, never from the internet directly.
Change servers by changing the launch template, then run an instance refresh. Never fix one server by hand.
Give new servers a grace period long enough for user data to finish, or the ASG will kill them while they are still installing.
Use HTTPS for real customers: a free certificate from AWS Certificate Manager on a 443 listener, and redirect 80 → 443.

title: 6. Load Balancers and Auto Scaling
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Target group on port 80, app on 8080
all targets unhealthy
the target group port is the app port


Health check path returns 302 or 404
targets flap or stay unhealthy
point it at /health, which returns 200


Server security group does not allow the ALB
health checks time out
allow port 8080 from the ALB’s security group


Grace period shorter than setup time
endless replace-and-launch loop
raise --health-check-grace-period


Max size equal to min size
no scaling on busy days
set a real maximum, such as 6

title: 5. S3: Storing Files
text: The Lemonade menu is one HTML file and a few photos. Running a server just to hand out a file is overkill. We also want to keep last week’s menu when someone overwrites it by mistake, keep old photos cheaply, and share a private price list with a supplier for five minutes only.

title: 5. S3: Storing Files
text: The Lemonade menu is one HTML file and a few photos. Running a server just to hand out a file is overkill. We also want to keep last week’s menu when someone overwrites it by mistake, keep old photos cheaply, and share a private price list with a supplier for five minutes only.

title: 5. S3: Storing Files
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipA coat check that never loses a coat



At a theatre you hand your coat to the coat check and get a ticket with a label. S3 is a giant coat check for files.

The coat check room is a bucket. Its name must be unique in the whole world, like lemonade-menu-7f3a.
Your coat is an object, and its ticket label is the key, like archive/2026-11-menu.html. The / is just part of the label: there are no real folders.
The coat check keeps your coat in several buildings at once, so it practically never loses one.
With versioning it keeps every coat you ever hung on the same hook, so a mistake can be undone.
A presigned link is a ticket you give a friend so they can collect one coat, and it stops working after five minutes.

S3 opened on 14 March 2006, the day AWS counts as its birthday (Werner Vogels, 2016). Andy Warfield, an S3 engineer, explains that it runs on millions of hard disks. Every change that could affect durability gets its own human “durability review”, on top of the statistical model (Building and operating a pretty big storage system called S3, 2023).

title: 5. S3: Storing Files
text:
The concept, precisely

A bucket is a container in one region. Its name is 3–63 characters of lowercase letters, numbers, dots and hyphens, unique across all AWS accounts.
An object is data (up to 5 TB) plus metadata such as Content-Type. It is addressed by its key. Keys that share a beginning, like archive/, share a prefix.
Storage classes trade price against access speed:








Class
For
API name




Standard
files read often (the menu)
STANDARD


Intelligent-Tiering
unknown access patterns; S3 moves objects for you
INTELLIGENT_TIERING


Standard-IA
read rarely, needed quickly
STANDARD_IA


Glacier Flexible Retrieval
archives; minutes to hours to read back
GLACIER


Glacier Deep Archive
archives read perhaps once a year
DEEP_ARCHIVE



Durability (will the file survive?) is designed for 99.999999999% (“eleven nines”) a year. Availability (can I read it right now?) is 99.99% for Standard. Those are two different promises.
Reads are strongly consistent: after a successful write, the next read sees it.
Versioning keeps every version of every key. A delete adds a delete marker instead of destroying data.
Block Public Access is on by default for new buckets and blocks every public policy. New objects are encrypted at rest by default.
A bucket policy is a resource-based IAM policy (lesson 2) with a Principal.
Static website hosting serves a bucket over HTTP at http://<bucket>.s3-website.<region>.amazonaws.com. For HTTPS and a custom domain, put CloudFront in front and keep the bucket private.
A presigned URL carries a signature and an expiry, so anyone holding it can do exactly one thing for a limited time.
Lifecycle rules move or delete objects automatically after some days.










Command
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




aws s3 mb / rb
make / remove a bucket
rb --force empties it first
aws s3 mb s3://lemonade-menu-7f3a


aws s3 cp
copy a file up or down
set --content-type for web files
aws s3 cp index.html s3://lemonade-menu-7f3a/


aws s3 ls
list buckets or objects
--recursive --human-readable --summarize
aws s3 ls s3://lemonade-menu-7f3a


aws s3 sync
make a bucket match a folder
--delete also removes extra files
aws s3 sync site/ s3://lemonade-menu-7f3a/


aws s3 website
turn on website hosting
index and error documents
--index-document index.html


aws s3 presign
create a time-limited link
--expires-in in seconds, at most 7 days
--expires-in 300


aws s3api put-public-access-block
Block Public Access settings
keep all four true unless the bucket is a public website
--public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicPolicy=false,...


aws s3api put-bucket-policy
attach the bucket policy
public read only for public content
--policy file://menu-bucket-policy.json


aws s3api put-bucket-versioning
turn on versioning
cannot be turned fully off later, only suspended
--versioning-configuration Status=Enabled


aws s3api list-object-versions
see old versions
restore by copying an old version back
--prefix index.html


aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration
automatic transitions and expiry
filter by prefix or tag
--lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json


aws s3api head-object
metadata without downloading
check ContentType
--bucket lemonade-menu-7f3a --key index.html



aws s3 holds friendly, file-like commands. aws s3api is a one-to-one copy of the S3 API, covering every setting.

title: 5. S3: Storing Files
section: Worked example: the menu as a website
text:
Worked example: the menu as a website
Create the bucket, upload the menu, allow public reads and switch on website hosting:
aws s3 mb s3://lemonade-menu-7f3a
aws s3 cp index.html s3://lemonade-menu-7f3a/index.html --content-type text/html
aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket lemonade-menu-7f3a --policy file://menu-bucket-policy.json
aws s3 website s3://lemonade-menu-7f3a --index-document index.html
curl -i http://lemonade-menu-7f3a.s3-website.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/
On real AWS, first allow a public policy on this one bucket with put-public-access-block (set BlockPublicPolicy and RestrictPublicBuckets to false), and use the address http://lemonade-menu-7f3a.s3-website.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com. The policy, examples/menu-bucket-policy.json, lets anyone read objects and nothing else:
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "AnyoneCanReadTheMenu",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": "*",
    "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::lemonade-menu-7f3a/*"
  }]
}
Output of curl (LocalStack, trimmed):
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Lemonade Stand</title></head>
Turn on versioning, upload the menu again, and look at the versions:
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket lemonade-menu-7f3a --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
aws s3 cp index.html s3://lemonade-menu-7f3a/index.html --content-type text/html
aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket lemonade-menu-7f3a --prefix index.html \
  --query 'Versions[].[Key,IsLatest,Size]' --output text
Output (LocalStack):
index.html  True    233
index.html  False   233
Both versions are kept. The older one can always be copied back. Archive old photos after 30 days with a lifecycle rule:
{"Rules": [{"ID": "old-photos-to-glacier", "Status": "Enabled",
  "Filter": {"Prefix": "photos/archive/"},
  "Transitions": [{"Days": 30, "StorageClass": "GLACIER"}]}]}
By default S3 does not move objects smaller than 128 KB to another class, because the move would cost more than it saves. That is why the rule targets photos, not tiny HTML menus.
Finally, give the supplier a five-minute link:
aws s3 presign s3://lemonade-menu-7f3a/index.html --expires-in 300
Output (LocalStack; the host is the lab’s LocalStack container, and the signature is shortened):
http://aws-lab-localstack:4566/lemonade-menu-7f3a/index.html?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Credential=test%2F20261125%2Feu-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20261125T142332Z&X-Amz-Expires=300&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&X-Amz-Signature=4d5b5a...

title: 5. S3: Storing Files
text:
Rules and conventions

Keep buckets private by default. Make a bucket public only when everything in it is meant for the whole world, like the menu. Better still, use CloudFront.
One bucket per purpose (lemonade-menu-…, lemonade-backups-…), with a random suffix for uniqueness.
Turn on versioning for anything you would be sad to lose, and add a lifecycle rule that expires old versions.
Set Content-Type on web files, or browsers will download the page instead of showing it.
Use presigned URLs to share private files. Never make a bucket public “for a minute”.
Use aws s3 sync to publish a whole folder in one command.

title: 5. S3: Storing Files
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Website endpoint with Block Public Access still on
403 Forbidden
adjust Block Public Access for that bucket, or use CloudFront with origin access control


Policy Resource is the bucket ARN, not bucket/*
403 on every object
objects are arn:aws:s3:::lemonade-menu-7f3a/*


Bucket name already taken
BucketAlreadyExists
names are global: add a suffix


Uploading the page without Content-Type
the browser downloads index.html
--content-type text/html


Versioning on, no lifecycle rule
the bill slowly grows with every overwrite
expire noncurrent versions after 30 days

title: 1. What the Cloud Is
text:
The Lemonade Stand needs two web servers and one database server. Buying three computers costs money before a single cup is sold. The computers sit in one cupboard, so a flood or a power cut takes the whole stand down. On a sunny Saturday two web servers are not enough. On a rainy Tuesday in November even one is too many.
We want computers that we can get in a minute, pay for only while we use them, and place in more than one building.

title: 1. What the Cloud Is
text:
The Lemonade Stand needs two web servers and one database server. Buying three computers costs money before a single cup is sold. The computers sit in one cupboard, so a flood or a power cut takes the whole stand down. On a sunny Saturday two web servers are not enough. On a rainy Tuesday in November even one is too many.
We want computers that we can get in a minute, pay for only while we use them, and place in more than one building.

title: 1. What the Cloud Is
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipRenting bikes instead of buying them



Imagine you want to ride a bike on Saturdays. You could buy a bike: it costs a lot today, it sits in the garage all week, and you must fix the flat tyres yourself. Or you could rent one from a bike shop: you pay only for the hours you ride, and the shop fixes the brakes.
AWS is a giant bike-rental shop for computers. It has shops in many cities (regions). Each city has several shops in different neighbourhoods with their own electricity (availability zones). If the lights go out in one neighbourhood, the other shops keep renting bikes.
In 2006 Jeff Bezos called the boring work of running servers “undifferentiated heavy lifting”. Every company has to do it, but doing it well does not make anyone’s lemonade taste better (AWS blog, 2006). AWS does the heavy lifting, so you can spend your time on the lemonade.
Amazon’s CTO Werner Vogels adds a warning from ten years of running AWS: expect the unexpected. Disks, routers and whole buildings will fail at some point (10 Lessons from 10 Years of AWS). Renting in two neighbourhoods is how you stay open when one fails.

title: 1. What the Cloud Is
text:
The concept, precisely
Cloud computing means renting computing resources (servers, storage, databases, networks) over the internet. You get them on demand and pay for what you use.

A region is a geographic area with several data centres, for example eu-west-2 (London). Regions are independent: what you create in London stays in London. At the time of writing AWS has 39 regions and 123 availability zones (AWS Global Infrastructure).
An availability zone (AZ) is one or more data centres inside a region with separate power, cooling and networking. AZs in a region are linked by fast private connections. Every region has at least three. London’s are eu-west-2a, eu-west-2b and eu-west-2c.
An edge location is a small site close to customers. CloudFront (the content delivery network) uses edge locations to serve files quickly. You do not run servers there.
An account holds your resources and receives one bill. It has a 12-digit account ID.
The shared responsibility model splits the security work. AWS secures the cloud itself: buildings, hardware and the virtualisation layer. You secure what you put in the cloud: your data, who can log in, your firewall rules and the operating system on your servers.
Pay-as-you-go means no upfront payment. On-Demand prices are per hour or per second. You can commit for one or three years for a discount, or use spare capacity (Spot) that AWS can take back at short notice.

Region eu-west-2 (London)
├── AZ eu-west-2a  ── data centre(s), own power and network
├── AZ eu-west-2b  ── data centre(s), own power and network
└── AZ eu-west-2c  ── data centre(s), own power and network
        ▲
        └─ fast private links between the AZs

text:
Worked example: where can the stand live?
List the London availability zones:
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region eu-west-2 \
  --query 'AvailabilityZones[].[ZoneName,ZoneId,State]' --output text
Output (LocalStack):
eu-west-2a  euw2-az2    available
eu-west-2b  euw2-az3    available
eu-west-2c  euw2-az1    available
The output shows three AZs in one region. Notice that eu-west-2a is not euw2-az1: names are a per-account label, IDs are the physical location. The Lemonade plan uses eu-west-2a for web1 and eu-west-2b for web2, so one building can fail without closing the stand.

title: 1. What the Cloud Is
text:
Rules and conventions

Choose one home region and stay in it. The Lemonade Stand uses eu-west-2 everywhere. Set it once with aws configure so you do not have to repeat --region.
Use at least two AZs for anything that must stay up: web servers, load balancers, databases.
Never use the root user for daily work (lesson 2 explains why and what to use instead).
Tag everything with the project name, for example Project=lemonade, so you can find it and see its cost later.
Turn things off. A stopped or deleted resource stops costing compute money; a forgotten one bills every hour.

title: 1. What the Cloud Is
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
The core promise of the cloud is pay only for the hours you use. Every hourly service follows the same rule:
\[
C = r \cdot h
\]
where:

\(C\) is the cost in US dollars;
\(r\) is the hourly rate of the resource, in dollars per hour;
\(h\) is the number of hours the resource runs. AWS uses \(730\) hours for one month, because \(24 \times 365 / 12 = 730\).

Example: web1 is a t3.micro in London at \(r = \$0.0118\) per hour (Linux On-Demand, price at time of writing, November 2026). Running all month gives \(C = 0.0118 \times 730 = \$8.614\). Two web servers cost \(2 \times 8.614 = \$17.228 \approx \$17.23\) a month.
When is buying cheaper than renting? Ignoring electricity, space and repairs, owning a machine that costs \(P\) up front pays off after the break-even number of hours:
\[
h^{\ast} = \frac{P}{r}
\]
where:

\(h^{\ast}\) is the break-even time in hours: below it renting is cheaper, above it buying is cheaper;
\(P\) is the purchase price of a comparable small server, in dollars;
\(r\) is the hourly rental rate, in dollars per hour, as above.

Example: a small $600 server against a t3.micro: \(h^{\ast} = 600 / 0.0118 \approx 50{,}847\) hours, and \(50{,}847 / 730 \approx 69.7\) months, nearly 6 years of running day and night. The extra Saturday server is needed only 8 hours on 52 Saturdays, so \(h = 8 \times 52 = 416\) hours a year. Renting costs \(C = 0.0118 \times 416 \approx \$4.91\) a year. That is far below \(h^{\ast}\), so renting wins easily.
This is a simplified model. Real ownership also pays for power, cooling, networking and people, which makes renting look even better for small, spiky workloads. Large, steady workloads can still be cheaper to own or to reserve.

title: 10. Monitoring and Cost
text: The Lemonade Stand now runs on many AWS services. Two questions remain. Is it healthy right now? And what will this month’s bill be? We want to find out from an email, not from an angry customer or a surprise invoice.

title: 10. Monitoring and Cost
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipA car dashboard and a pocket-money jar



A car has a dashboard. The speedometer shows numbers that change every second (metrics). The trip diary records what happened (logs). A warning light turns on only when the engine has been too hot for a while, not for one hot second (an alarm).
You also have a pocket-money jar with a note: “Tell me when I am about to spend 80% of this month’s money” (a budget).
Werner Vogels’ sixth AWS lesson is know your resource usage: if you do not measure what you use, you cannot control what it costs (2016). The cloud economist Corey Quinn has spent years showing, in his Last Week in AWS newsletter, how the surprise in a bill usually hides in small, forgotten line items, such as a NAT gateway in a test account.

title: 10. Monitoring and Cost
text:
The concept, precisely
Amazon CloudWatch collects numbers and text from your resources.

A metric is a time series of numbers. It is named by a namespace (AWS/EC2), a metric name (CPUUtilization) and dimensions (InstanceId=i-...). EC2 sends basic metrics every 5 minutes, or every minute with detailed monitoring.
A statistic (Average, Maximum, Sum, p99) summarises the values within one period (for example 60 seconds).
CloudWatch Logs stores text: a log group per app (/lemonade/web) contains log streams per source. Set a retention period, or logs are kept, and billed, forever.
Logs Insights queries logs, for example “count errors per 5 minutes”.
An alarm watches one metric. It is in OK, ALARM or INSUFFICIENT_DATA and can send a message to an SNS topic, which emails you, or trigger scaling.
AWS Budgets emails you when actual or forecasted cost passes a threshold. Cost Explorer shows where the money went. Cost allocation tags (Project=lemonade) split the bill by project.
The AWS Pricing Calculator estimates a design before you build it.

What it does

title: 10. Monitoring and Cost
section: Worked example: an alarm, a log group and a budget
text:
Worked example: an alarm, a log group and a budget
Alarm when the web servers’ average CPU is above 80% for 3 one-minute periods in a row:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name lemonade-web-cpu-high \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUUtilization --statistic Average \
  --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 3 \
  --threshold 80 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names lemonade-web-cpu-high \
  --query 'MetricAlarms[].[AlarmName,StateValue,Period,EvaluationPeriods,Threshold]' --output text
Output (LocalStack):
lemonade-web-cpu-high   INSUFFICIENT_DATA   60  3   80.0
INSUFFICIENT_DATA is normal for a new alarm: no data points have arrived yet. Keep the logs for two weeks:
aws logs create-log-group --log-group-name /lemonade/web
aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /lemonade/web --retention-in-days 14
The budget from the Part 4 safety rules: $10 a month, with an email when the forecast passes 80%:
aws budgets create-budget --account-id 123456789012 \
  --budget '{"BudgetName":"lemonade-monthly","BudgetLimit":{"Amount":"10","Unit":"USD"},"TimeUnit":"MONTHLY","BudgetType":"COST"}' \
  --notifications-with-subscribers '[{"Notification":{"NotificationType":"FORECASTED","ComparisonOperator":"GREATER_THAN","Threshold":80,"ThresholdType":"PERCENTAGE"},"Subscribers":[{"SubscriptionType":"EMAIL","Address":"owner@example.com"}]}]'
AWS Budgets is not in LocalStack’s free edition. On a real account this command prints nothing on success.

title: 10. Monitoring and Cost
text:
The Well-Architected pillars
The AWS Well-Architected Framework asks six groups of questions about any design. Here is where this part answered each one for the stand:








Pillar
The question in plain words
Lemonade answer




Operational excellence
Can we change and run it safely?
user data and launch templates; alarms and logs (lessons 4, 6, 10)

Who can do what, and is data protected?
least-privilege IAM, private subnets, no public database (lessons 2, 3, 7)

Does it survive failures?
two AZs, health checks, Multi-AZ, backups (lessons 6, 7)

Is it the right size and type?
burstable instances, target tracking (lessons 4, 6)

Do we pay only for value?

Do we waste as little as possible?
scale in at night; Graviton (t4g) instances use less energy

title: 10. Monitoring and Cost
text:
Rules and conventions

Budget first, everything else second. Create the budget before the first server.
Alarm on symptoms customers feel: errors and slow responses at the load balancer, not only CPU.
“\(M\) out of \(N\)” alarms ignore one-off spikes; page a human only for problems that last.
Every log group gets a retention period.
Tag everything with Project=lemonade and activate the tag for cost allocation.
Review the bill monthly by service and by tag, and delete what nobody can explain.

title: 10. Monitoring and Cost
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
An alarm fires when enough of the recent periods are bad:
\[
\text{ALARM} \iff \Big\lvert \lbrace\, i \in \lbrace 1, \dots, N \rbrace : x_i > \theta \,\rbrace \Big\rvert \ge M
\]
where:

\(x_i\) is the metric statistic in the \(i\)-th most recent period (for example the average CPU in one minute);
\(\theta\) (theta) is the threshold;
\(N\) is --evaluation-periods, how many recent periods are looked at;
\(M\) is --datapoints-to-alarm, how many of them must breach, with \(M \le N\);
\(\lbrace i : x_i > \theta \rbrace\) is the set of breaching periods and \(\lvert \cdot \rvert\) counts them.

Example: with \(\theta = 80\), \(M = 3\), \(N = 5\) and the last five minutes at \(x = (85, 70, 90, 95, 60)\), the breaching values are 85, 90 and 95. That makes 3 periods, and \(3 \ge 3\), so the alarm is ALARM. A single spike \((99, 50, 40, 45, 50)\) gives \(1 < 3\), so it stays OK. Since at least \(M\) periods of length \(p\) must pass, the fastest possible alarm takes \(M \cdot p = 3 \times 60 = 180\) seconds.
The monthly bill is the sum of every line item:
\[
C = \sum_{k=1}^{K} r_k \cdot q_k
\]
where:

\(C\) is the monthly total in dollars;
\(K\) is the number of line items, and \(k\) numbers them;
\(r_k\) is the unit price of item \(k\) (per hour, per GB-month, per alarm…);
\(q_k\) is how many units of item \(k\) were used in the month.

Example: the full Lemonade design running all month in London (\(730\) hours, prices at time of writing, November 2026):









\(k\)
Item
\(r_k \cdot q_k\)
Cost




1
2 × t3.micro (lesson 4)
\(0.0118 \times 730 \times 2\)
$17.23


2
2 × 8 GB gp3 disks
\(0.0928 \times 8 \times 2\)
$1.48


3
ALB hours + about 0.2 LCU (lesson 6)
\(0.02646 \times 730 + 0.0084 \times 0.2 \times 730\)
$20.54


4
3 public IPv4 addresses (ALB in 2 AZs, NAT)
\(0.005 \times 730 \times 3\)
$10.95


5
NAT gateway + 20 GB (lesson 3)
\(0.05 \times 730 + 0.05 \times 20\)
$37.50


6
RDS db.t4g.micro + 20 GB (lesson 7)
\(0.018 \times 730 + 0.133 \times 20\)
$15.80


7
S3, 1 GB (lesson 5)
\(0.024 \times 1\)
$0.02


8
3 CloudWatch alarms
\(0.10 \times 3\)
$0.30



Total
\(\sum_{k=1}^{8}\)
$103.82



The NAT gateway alone is \(37.50 / 103.82 \approx 36\%\) of the bill. Lambda and DynamoDB round to $0 here, and small amounts of data sent to the internet fit in the free 100 GB a month.
Practice costs scale with hours. Building everything, testing for 2 hours and deleting it costs about \(103.82 \times 2 / 730 \approx \$0.28\). That is why the $10 practice budget is safe, if you clean up.
A budget alert compares a forecast with the limit:
\[
\text{alert} \iff F \ge \alpha \cdot B, \qquad F \approx S \cdot \frac{D}{d}
\]
where:

\(B\) is the monthly budget in dollars and \(\alpha\) the alert fraction (0.8 for 80%);
\(F\) is the forecast for the whole month;
\(S\) is the amount spent so far, after \(d\) days of a \(D\)-day month;
\(S \cdot D / d\) is a simple straight-line forecast. AWS uses its own forecasting model, so treat this as an approximation.

Example: \(B = \$10\) and \(\alpha = 0.8\), so the alert line is \(0.8 \times 10 = \$8\). On day \(d = 10\) of a \(D = 30\)-day month you have spent \(S = \$3.10\) because a test server was left running. Then \(F \approx 3.10 \times 30 / 10 = \$9.30 \ge \$8\), so the email arrives on day 10, twenty days before the invoice would have.

title: Part 4: AWS
text:
Parts 1–3 ran the Lemonade Stand on machines we already had. In this part we rent the machines instead. Amazon Web Services (AWS) gives us computers, disks, networks and databases by the hour, in data centres all over the world. We ask for them with one command and give them back when we are done.
Every lesson keeps the same stand, so each new service answers a question the previous lesson raised.

title: Part 4: AWS
text:
Follow along safely
A cloud account is connected to a credit card, so start with these four habits. They cost nothing and prevent nearly every beginner accident.

Use the free plan and credits. New accounts (since 15 July 2025) choose a free plan with up to $200 of credits, valid for 6 months. A free-plan account is not charged at all; when the credits or the 6 months run out, you must upgrade to a paid plan to keep using it. See the AWS Free Tier.
Create a budget alarm first, before anything else (lesson 10 shows the command). The Lemonade budget is $10 a month.
Check who you are before every session:
aws sts get-caller-identity
Clean up. Every lesson ends by deleting what it created. Something you forgot to delete keeps costing money every hour.

You can also practise most commands without an AWS account. The lab runs them against LocalStack, a local AWS emulator in Docker. Outputs marked LocalStack in this part came from that lab (its fake account ID is 000000000000).

title: Part 4: AWS
text:
Lessons

What the cloud is: renting vs owning, regions, availability zones, the shared responsibility model, pay-as-you-go.
IAM and the AWS CLI: who may do what, policies, least privilege, and the command line.
VPC and networking: your private network, CIDR blocks, subnets, routes and firewalls.
EC2: virtual servers, AMIs, instance types, user data, disks.
S3: buckets and objects, durability, a static menu website, presigned links.
Load balancers and auto scaling: one front door, many helpers, health checks.
Databases: RDS and DynamoDB: a managed PostgreSQL and a key-value table.
Containers: ECR and ECS: the Lemonade image on Fargate, compared with k3s.
Serverless: Lambda: code that runs only when called, billed by the millisecond.
Monitoring and cost: CloudWatch alarms, budgets, the monthly bill, Well-Architected.

title: 7. Databases: RDS and DynamoDB

text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipA librarian and a wall of lockers



RDS is like a librarian who looks after your notebook. Every night they make a copy (a backup). With Multi-AZ, they keep a twin notebook in another building and write every new line into both at the same time. If the first building has a fire, the twin takes over within a minute or two. You never touch the shelves: you just ask your questions at the desk (the endpoint).
DynamoDB is like a huge wall of labelled lockers. You open a locker by its exact label (the partition key), and inside, the drawers are sorted (the sort key). Opening a locker is always fast, however big the wall gets. But “which lockers contain a red ball?” means opening every locker (a scan).
Werner Vogels argues that no single database is right for every job, and that each job should use the kind of database built for it (A one size fits all database doesn’t fit anyone, 2018). DynamoDB grew out of the ideas in Amazon’s famous Dynamo paper (DeCandia et al., 2007), written after Amazon’s shopping cart needed to stay writable even while servers failed.

title: 7. Databases: RDS and DynamoDB
text:
The concept, precisely
Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service) runs PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server or Db2 for you.

A DB instance has an instance class (for example db.t4g.micro) and storage (for example 20 GB of gp3).
A DB subnet group lists private subnets in at least two AZs that the database may use.
The endpoint is a DNS name such as lemonade-db.abc123.eu-west-2.rds.amazonaws.com. Apps connect to it, never to an IP address.
Automated backups take a daily snapshot and keep transaction logs, so you can restore to any second in the retention period (1–35 days). RDS uploads the logs every 5 minutes.
Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ. If the primary fails, RDS points the endpoint at the standby. This typically takes 60–120 seconds.
Read replicas are asynchronous copies for extra read traffic. They are not a backup.
A managed master password (--manage-master-user-password) is stored and rotated in AWS Secrets Manager, so it never appears in your scripts.

Amazon DynamoDB is a serverless key-value and document database.

A table holds items (up to 400 KB each) made of attributes.
The primary key is a partition key, optionally plus a sort key. For orders: partition key order_date, sort key order_id.
Query reads all items with one partition key, in sort-key order, which is fast. Scan reads the whole table, which is slow and costly.
Capacity modes: on-demand (pay per request, nothing to plan) or provisioned (you reserve read and write units per second).
Reads are eventually consistent by default (half price), or strongly consistent if you ask.

title: 7. Databases: RDS and DynamoDB
text:
Worked example: the orders database
The PostgreSQL database for the stand:
aws rds create-db-instance --db-instance-identifier lemonade-db \
  --engine postgres --db-instance-class db.t4g.micro --allocated-storage 20 \
  --master-username lemonade --manage-master-user-password \
  --db-subnet-group-name lemonade-db --vpc-security-group-ids "$DB_SG" \
  --backup-retention-period 7 --no-publicly-accessible
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier lemonade-db \
  --query 'DBInstances[].[DBInstanceStatus,Endpoint.Address]' --output text
Illustrative output a few minutes later (RDS is not in LocalStack’s free edition):
available   lemonade-db.c1a2b3c4d5e6.eu-west-2.rds.amazonaws.com
The same orders as a DynamoDB table, one order and one query, from examples/localstack-demo.sh:
aws dynamodb create-table --table-name lemonade-orders --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST \
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=order_date,AttributeType=S AttributeName=order_id,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=order_date,KeyType=HASH AttributeName=order_id,KeyType=RANGE \
  --query TableDescription.TableStatus --output text
aws dynamodb put-item --table-name lemonade-orders \
  --item '{"order_date":{"S":"2026-11-25"},"order_id":{"S":"0001"},"cups":{"N":"2"}}'
aws dynamodb query --table-name lemonade-orders --key-condition-expression "order_date = :d" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":d":{"S":"2026-11-25"}}' --query Count
Output (LocalStack): the table status ACTIVE, then the number of orders on 25 November:
ACTIVE
1

title: 7. Databases: RDS and DynamoDB
text:
Rules and conventions

Databases live in private subnets. Their security group allows port 5432 only from the web servers’ security group.
Turn on backups and test a restore. A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan.
Multi-AZ for anything customers depend on. It doubles the instance price and removes the single point of failure.
Connect by endpoint name, never by IP, so a failover just works.
Design DynamoDB keys from your questions. First write down how you will read the data (“orders of one day”), then choose the keys so that each question is a Query.
Delete practice databases after the lesson, with --skip-final-snapshot only if the data truly does not matter.

Part 3 builds the image lemonade-stand:<git-sha>, and Part 2 ran it on k3s. On AWS we could install Docker on EC2 ourselves, but then we would restart crashed containers, patch servers and spread containers over AZs by hand.

title: 8. Containers: ECR and ECS
text:
Part 3 builds the image lemonade-stand:<git-sha>, and Part 2 ran it on k3s. On AWS we could install Docker on EC2 ourselves, but then we would restart crashed containers, patch servers and spread containers over AZs by hand.
We want a private shelf for our images, and a service that keeps two copies running without us managing any servers.

title: 8. Containers: ECR and ECS
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipLunchboxes and a school canteen



A container image is a lunchbox packed at home. Everything the app needs is inside, so it tastes the same wherever you open it.
ECR is the school’s labelled lunchbox shelf. Each lunchbox has a sticker with its name and a number (the tag).
ECS is the canteen manager. You hand them a card that says “always keep 2 Lemonade lunchboxes open, each needs a small seat” (the task definition and the service). If one lunchbox falls on the floor, the manager opens a new one. With Fargate you do not even bring tables and chairs: the canteen provides the seats and charges per seat-minute.
The lunchbox idea became famous in a five-minute lightning talk. At PyCon in March 2013, Solomon Hykes showed the world a tool called Docker for the first time, in a talk named The Future of Linux Containers (O’Reilly, What is Docker?).

title: 8. Containers: ECR and ECS
text:
The concept, precisely
Amazon ECR (Elastic Container Registry) stores container images.

A repository holds the versions of one image, for example lemonade-stand.
The image URI is <account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/<repository>:<tag>.
A tag (3f2a9c1) is a human label. A digest (sha256:…) is the exact content. Turn on tag immutability so a tag can never be moved to different content.
Lifecycle policies delete old images automatically. Scan on push checks images for known vulnerabilities.

Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) runs containers.

A cluster is a named group where tasks run.
A task definition is the recipe, a JSON document with versions called revisions. It names the image, CPU, memory, ports, environment, logging and two roles. The execution role lets ECS pull the image and write logs. The task role is what the app itself may do (lesson 2).
A task is one running copy of a task definition.
A service keeps desiredCount tasks running, replaces failed ones, registers them in an ALB target group (lesson 6) and rolls out new revisions.
Fargate runs each task on capacity AWS manages: no EC2 instances to patch. You choose CPU and memory per task from a fixed menu.

Amazon EKS runs real Kubernetes with a managed control plane. Your Part 2 manifests would work there almost unchanged. It is the right choice when you want Kubernetes itself. ECS is the simpler AWS-native choice.

title: 8. Containers: ECR and ECS
section: Worked example: two Lemonade tasks on Fargate
text:
Worked example: two Lemonade tasks on Fargate
Push the image built in Part 3:
REGISTRY=123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com
aws ecr create-repository --repository-name lemonade-stand --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE
aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin "$REGISTRY"
docker tag lemonade-stand:3f2a9c1 "$REGISTRY/lemonade-stand:3f2a9c1"
docker push "$REGISTRY/lemonade-stand:3f2a9c1"
The recipe, task-def.json (role ARN shortened):
{
  "family": "lemonade-web",
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "cpu": "256",
  "memory": "512",
  "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ecsTaskExecutionRole",
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "web",
    "image": "123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/lemonade-stand:3f2a9c1",
    "portMappings": [{ "containerPort": 8080 }]
  }]
}
Register it and keep two copies running:
aws ecs register-task-definition --cli-input-json file://task-def.json
aws ecs create-service --cluster lemonade --service-name lemonade-web \
  --task-definition lemonade-web --desired-count 2 --launch-type FARGATE \
  --network-configuration "awsvpcConfiguration={subnets=[$PRIV_A,$PRIV_B],securityGroups=[$SG]}" \
  --load-balancers "targetGroupArn=$TG_ARN,containerName=web,containerPort=8080"
aws ecs describe-services --cluster lemonade --services lemonade-web \
  --query 'services[].[serviceName,runningCount,desiredCount]' --output text
Illustrative output (ECR and ECS are not in LocalStack’s free edition):
lemonade-web    2   2

title: 8. Containers: ECR and ECS
text:
Rules and conventions

Tag images with the git commit SHA and make tags immutable. latest cannot tell you what is running.
Two roles, two jobs: the execution role pulls and logs, the task role is the app’s own permissions. Keep both minimal.
Tasks in private subnets, behind the ALB, in at least two AZs.
Send logs to CloudWatch with the awslogs log driver (lesson 10), because a crashed task’s local logs disappear with it.
Turn on the deployment circuit breaker so a broken revision rolls back by itself.
Pick ECS for simple AWS-only apps and EKS when you need Kubernetes: Part 2’s skills transfer directly to EKS.
