title: 8. Containers: ECR and ECS
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Fargate bills each task for the CPU and memory it asks for, per hour:
\[
C = n \cdot h \cdot \left( v \cdot p_v + g \cdot p_g \right)
\]
where:

\(C\) is the monthly cost in dollars;
\(n\) is the number of tasks and \(h\) the hours they run (730 for a month);
\(v\) is the vCPUs per task and \(p_v\) the price per vCPU-hour ($0.04656 in London);
\(g\) is the memory per task in GB and \(p_g\) the price per GB-hour ($0.00511 in London).

Example: two Lemonade tasks of \(v = 0.25\) vCPU and \(g = 0.5\) GB all month: per task-hour \(0.25 \times 0.04656 + 0.5 \times 0.00511 = 0.01164 + 0.002555 = 0.014195\), so \(C = 2 \times 730 \times 0.014195 \approx \$20.72\). That is close to two t3.micro servers ($17.23), but there is no operating system to patch (prices at time of writing, November 2026).
Not every size is allowed. The memory must come from a menu that depends on the CPU:
\[
g \in G(v), \qquad G(0.25) = \lbrace 0.5, 1, 2 \rbrace, \quad G(0.5) = \lbrace 1, 2, 3, 4 \rbrace, \quad G(1) = \lbrace 2, 3, \dots, 8 \rbrace
\]
where:

\(v\) is the task’s vCPUs;
\(G(v)\) is the set of allowed memory sizes in GB for that CPU;
\(g \in G(v)\) says the chosen memory must be one of them.

Example: \((v, g) = (0.25, 0.5)\) is valid because \(0.5 \in \lbrace 0.5, 1, 2 \rbrace\). \((0.25, 4)\) is rejected because \(4 \notin G(0.25)\). To get 4 GB, raise the CPU to \(v = 0.5\), where \(4 \in G(0.5)\).
During a rolling update, ECS keeps the number of tasks between two limits:
\[
\left\lceil d \cdot \frac{p_{\min}}{100} \right\rceil \;\le\; \text{tasks} \;\le\; \left\lfloor d \cdot \frac{p_{\max}}{100} \right\rfloor
\]
where:

\(d\) is the service’s desired count;
\(p_{\min}\) is minimumHealthyPercent, rounded up (default 100);
\(p_{\max}\) is maximumPercent, rounded down (default 200);
“tasks” counts the tasks running or starting during the deployment.

Example: with \(d = 2\) and the defaults, \(\lceil 2 \times 1 \rceil = 2 \le \text{tasks} \le \lfloor 2 \times 2 \rfloor = 4\). ECS starts two new tasks before stopping the old ones, so the stand never drops below 2. With \(p_{\min} = 50\) the lower limit is \(\lceil 2 \times 0.5 \rceil = 1\), so ECS may stop one old task first. That is the same idea as maxUnavailable and maxSurge in k3s (Part 2).

title: 10. Storage
10. Storage
10. Storage
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipGoldie’s present and the locker room



In The Illustrated Children’s Guide to Kubernetes, Phippy’s friend Goldie gives her a present. Phippy is sad, because she has nowhere to put it. Goldie knows what to do: “Why not put it in a volume?” A volume is a place where containers can keep things, and it appears as part of their own folders.
Think of a school locker room:

A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is the request form: “Class 3B needs one locker, 1 GiB big.”
A PersistentVolume (PV) is the actual locker that gets assigned.
A StorageClass is the locker company. It builds a new locker whenever a form arrives.
The pod is the pupil who uses the locker. If the pupil changes classrooms, the locker and everything inside stay.

In k3s the locker company is the local-path provisioner. Its lockers are folders on the node’s own disk, so they stay in that one building: the pod must always come back to the same node.

title: 10. Storage
text:
The concept, precisely
Volumes are declared in spec.volumes and mounted with volumeMounts. Common types:



Volume type
Lives as long as
Use it for




emptyDir
The pod
Scratch space, or sharing files between containers (sidecar, lesson 4)


configMap / secret
The object
Configuration files (lesson 9)


hostPath
The node’s folder
System agents only; ties the pod to one node and is a security risk


persistentVolumeClaim
The PVC
Application data that must survive the pod



Persistent storage uses three objects:

PersistentVolume (PV): a piece of real storage (a disk, a folder, a network share), with a capacity, access modes and a reclaim policy. PVs are cluster-scoped.
PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC): a request in a namespace: size, access mode, StorageClass. Kubernetes binds each PVC to exactly one PV.
StorageClass: a recipe for dynamic provisioning. When a PVC names a class, the class’s provisioner creates a matching PV automatically.

Binding modes:

Immediate: create and bind the PV as soon as the PVC exists.
WaitForFirstConsumer: wait until a pod that uses the PVC is scheduled, then create the PV on that pod’s node. Local disks need this, otherwise the volume could end up on a node where the pod cannot run.

k3s difference: k3s ships the local-path provisioner and a default StorageClass named local-path, with WaitForFirstConsumer and reclaim policy Delete. Volumes are folders under /var/lib/rancher/k3s/storage/ on the node; change the location with --default-local-storage-path. They are fast and simple, but they live on one node. If that node dies, the data dies with it. For storage that replicates across nodes, the k3s docs describe installing Longhorn.

title: 10. Storage
text:
Every field for this topic









Field
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




pvc.spec.accessModes
How the volume may be mounted
ReadWriteOnce (RWO: one node), ReadOnlyMany (ROX), ReadWriteMany (RWX), ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP: one pod)
accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]


pvc.spec.resources.requests.storage
Requested size
Binary units Ki, Mi, Gi; decimal k, M, G
storage: 1Gi


pvc.spec.storageClassName
Which StorageClass provisions it
Omit it to use the default class; "" means “no dynamic provisioning”
storageClassName: local-path


pvc.spec.volumeName
Bind to one specific existing PV
For static provisioning
volumeName: pv-orders


pv.spec.capacity.storage
PV size
A PVC binds only if its request is ≤ this
storage: 1Gi


pv.spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy
What happens to the PV when the PVC is deleted
Delete (remove the data) or Retain (keep it for manual clean-up)
persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain


storageclass.provisioner
Who creates PVs
In k3s: rancher.io/local-path
provisioner: rancher.io/local-path


storageclass.volumeBindingMode
When to create and bind
Immediate or WaitForFirstConsumer
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer

May PVCs grow later
local-path: false

pod.spec.volumes[].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName
Use a PVC in a pod
Same namespace as the pod
claimName: lemonade-orders

Pod is evicted if it exceeds the limit

Command
What it does
Example

List classes; (default) marks the default
kubectl get sc


kubectl get pvc
Claims and their status (Pending, Bound)
kubectl get pvc -n lemonade

Volumes, reclaim policy and owning claim

Why a claim is still pending
kubectl describe pvc lemonade-orders -n lemonade

title: 10. Storage
text:
Worked example
10-storage.yaml asks for 1 GiB and mounts it at /data. The pod appends one line each time it starts:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: lemonade-orders
  namespace: lemonade
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: local-path
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: order-logger
  namespace: lemonade
spec:
  containers:
    - name: logger
      image: busybox:1.37.0
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo \"order at $(date)\" >> /data/orders.log; sleep 3600"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: orders
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: orders
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: lemonade-orders
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl apply -f 10-storage.yaml
kubectl get pvc -n lemonade              # immediately
kubectl get pvc -n lemonade              # once the pod is scheduled
kubectl get pv
NAME                   PROVISIONER             RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE
local-path (default)   rancher.io/local-path   Delete          WaitForFirstConsumer

NAME              STATUS    VOLUME   CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS
lemonade-orders   Pending                                      local-path

NAME              STATUS   VOLUME                                     CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS
lemonade-orders   Bound    pvc-9ff172f2-077a-463b-a5c5-27f9e977da88   1Gi        RWO            local-path

NAME                                       CAPACITY   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM
pvc-9ff172f2-077a-463b-a5c5-27f9e977da88   1Gi        Delete           Bound    lemonade/lemonade-orders
Pending first is normal here. WaitForFirstConsumer waited until the pod had a node, then the provisioner created the PV there.
Now replace the pod and check that the data survived:
kubectl exec order-logger -n lemonade -- cat /data/orders.log
kubectl delete pod order-logger -n lemonade
kubectl apply -f 10-storage.yaml
kubectl exec order-logger -n lemonade -- cat /data/orders.log
order at Wed Nov 25 14:25:50 UTC 2026

order at Wed Nov 25 14:25:50 UTC 2026
order at Wed Nov 25 14:26:22 UTC 2026
The second pod found the first pod’s line and added its own. On the node, the “locker” is a plain folder:
docker exec k3s-lab ls /var/lib/rancher/k3s/storage/
pvc-9ff172f2-077a-463b-a5c5-27f9e977da88_lemonade_lemonade-orders
The folder name is the PV name, then the namespace, then the claim name. Deleting the PVC would delete this folder too, because the reclaim policy is Delete.

title: 10. Storage
text:
Rules and conventions

Use a PVC for any data you would be sad to lose. Use emptyDir only for scratch data.
Ask for the access mode you really need. local-path supports ReadWriteOnce only; many pods writing the same files at once need an RWX-capable system (NFS, Longhorn RWX, a cloud file share).
Leave storageClassName out to get the cluster default, or name it explicitly in shared manifests.
On clusters with more than one node, remember that local-path data is tied to one node. Back it up, or use Longhorn or network storage for important data.
Use Retain (on a custom StorageClass or by editing the PV) for data that must survive an accidental kubectl delete pvc.
Databases normally belong in a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates, which gives each replica its own PVC (lesson 12).

title: 10. Storage
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Worrying that the PVC is Pending before any pod uses it
It looks stuck
That is WaitForFirstConsumer; create the pod


Asking local-path for ReadWriteMany
PVC stays Pending, with a provisioning error in describe
Use RWO, or a storage system that supports RWX

storage: 1G when you meant 1Gi

title: 10. Storage
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

Binary and decimal sizes
Kubernetes accepts both binary suffixes (Ki, Mi, Gi) and decimal suffixes (k, M, G). They are different numbers:
\[
1\,\texttt{Gi} = 2^{30}\ \text{bytes} = 1{,}073{,}741{,}824\ \text{bytes}, \qquad 1\,\texttt{G} = 10^{9}\ \text{bytes}
\]
where \(2^{30}\) means 2 multiplied by itself 30 times (one gibibyte), and \(10^{9}\) is one billion (one gigabyte).
Example: our claim asked for 1Gi = 1,073,741,824 bytes. Had it said 1G, it would have asked for 1,000,000,000 bytes, which is
\[
\frac{1{,}073{,}741{,}824 - 1{,}000{,}000{,}000}{1{,}073{,}741{,}824} = \frac{73{,}741{,}824}{1{,}073{,}741{,}824} \approx 0.0687
\]
about 6.9% less. The same rule applies to memory (64Mi vs 64M) in lesson 11.


When a claim can bind to a volume
For a statically created PV (no StorageClass doing the work), Kubernetes binds a claim \(c\) to a volume \(v\) only when all of these hold:
\[
\operatorname{bind}(c, v) \iff s_c \le s_v \;\wedge\; M_c \subseteq M_v \;\wedge\; \kappa_c = \kappa_v \;\wedge\; v \text{ is unbound}
\]
where

\(s_c\) is the size the claim requests and \(s_v\) the volume’s capacity, both in bytes.
\(M_c\) is the set of access modes the claim asks for, and \(M_v\) the set the volume offers.
\(\kappa_c\) and \(\kappa_v\) are the StorageClass names of the claim and the volume.
\(\wedge\) means “and”, and \(\iff\) means “exactly when”.

Example: a claim for \(s_c = 1\,\texttt{Gi}\) with \(M_c = \lbrace \text{RWO} \rbrace\) and class manual, and a volume of \(s_v = 5\,\texttt{Gi}\) offering \(M_v = \lbrace \text{RWO}, \text{ROX} \rbrace\) in class manual: \(1 \le 5\), \(\lbrace \text{RWO} \rbrace \subseteq \lbrace \text{RWO}, \text{ROX} \rbrace\), and the classes match, so they bind. The claim then owns the whole 5 Gi volume; the extra 4 Gi cannot be given to anyone else. A claim for \(\lbrace \text{RWX} \rbrace\) would not bind, because \(\text{RWX} \notin M_v\). With dynamic provisioning (our local-path case) the provisioner simply creates a volume with \(s_v = s_c\), so nothing is wasted.

title: 6. Deployments and Rolling Updates
text:
A single pod (lesson 4) is fragile. If it is deleted, or its node dies, nothing brings it back. The Lemonade Stand needs:

Always three copies of the web pod, even after crashes.
Upgrades without closing: move from NGINX 1.30.5 to 1.30.6 while customers are still ordering.
A quick way back when an upgrade is broken.

A Deployment gives us all three.

title: 6. Deployments and Rolling Updates
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipMeerkats, iguanas and a thermostat



In Phippy Goes to the Zoo (Matt Butcher and Karen Chu, illustrated by Bailey Beougher), Phippy shows her niece Zee a row of meerkats at a window. Whenever one tumbles off the ledge, another one hops up in its place, so the row always has the same number. Those are ReplicaSets: they keep a fixed number of identical pods.
Next come iguanas with a giant slingshot. They try to land exactly three iguanas on an island in a pond. When one misses and splashes into the water, they simply launch another until three have made it. Those are Deployments. A Deployment uses ReplicaSets underneath, and adds the clever part: replacing the group with a new version, a few at a time.
The engine inside is a thermostat. You set “21 °C”, and it keeps measuring and switching the heater on or off. You never say “heat for 10 minutes”. Google’s engineers Burns, Grant, Oppenheimer, Brewer and Wilkes describe this in Borg, Omega, and Kubernetes (2016). They call it a reconciliation controller loop: it compares a desired state (how many pods should match a label selector) with the observed state (how many it can find) and takes action to bring the two together. If the controller crashes, it simply starts the comparison again.

title: 6. Deployments and Rolling Updates
text:
The concept, precisely

ReplicaSet: keeps exactly replicas pods that match its selector running. It creates pods from its pod template. You rarely create one yourself.
Deployment: owns ReplicaSets. Each change to the pod template (a new image, a new environment variable) creates a new ReplicaSet. The Deployment then shifts pods from the old ReplicaSet to the new one according to its strategy. Old ReplicaSets are kept, scaled to 0, as revisions you can roll back to.
pod-template-hash: a label that the Deployment adds to each ReplicaSet and its pods, so the old and new generations never select each other’s pods.
Strategy RollingUpdate (the default): replace pods gradually, within two limits:

maxSurge: how many pods may exist above replicas during the update.
maxUnavailable: how many pods may be missing (not ready) during the update.

Strategy Recreate: delete all old pods first, then start the new ones. There is downtime, but two versions never run side by side. Use it only when two versions must not run together.

Deployment lemonade-web
 ├── ReplicaSet lemonade-web-bffff7f7b   (nginx 1.30.5)  replicas: 0   ← old revision
 └── ReplicaSet lemonade-web-848fbbb64c  (nginx 1.30.6)  replicas: 3   ← current
        ├── pod lemonade-web-848fbbb64c-7lrs9
        ├── pod …

What it does
Rule / convention

title: 6. Deployments and Rolling Updates
text:
Worked example
The Deployment (06-deployment.yaml) asks for three NGINX pods, each showing the menu ConfigMap:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: lemonade-web
  namespace: lemonade
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: lemonade
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: lemonade
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.5-alpine
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          volumeMounts:
            - name: menu
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
      volumes:
        - name: menu
          configMap:
            name: lemonade-menu
The menu itself is explained in lesson 9. Apply both:
kubectl apply -f 09-configmap.yaml -f 06-deployment.yaml
kubectl rollout status deploy/lemonade-web -n lemonade
kubectl get rs,pods -n lemonade -l app=lemonade
deployment "lemonade-web" successfully rolled out
NAME                                     DESIRED   CURRENT   READY
replicaset.apps/lemonade-web-bffff7f7b   3         3         3

NAME                               READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
pod/lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-4h9vf   1/1     Running   0
pod/lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-bt5zs   1/1     Running   0
pod/lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-kvnn7   1/1     Running   0

Self-healing
Delete one pod and look again. The meerkat hops up:
kubectl delete pod lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-4h9vf -n lemonade
kubectl get pods -n lemonade -l app=lemonade
NAME                           READY   STATUS    AGE
lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-bt5zs   1/1     Running   7m40s
lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-kvnn7   1/1     Running   7m40s
lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-plxn5   1/1     Running   7m39s
We deleted 4h9vf about one second after the Deployment started, and looked again a few minutes later. There are still three pods. plxn5 is new, and one second younger than its siblings, because the ReplicaSet created it the moment the old one was gone.


Scaling
kubectl scale deploy/lemonade-web -n lemonade --replicas=5
kubectl get deploy lemonade-web -n lemonade
NAME           READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
lemonade-web   5/5     5            5
Scaling back to 3 removes two pods. Scaling does not create a new revision, because the pod template did not change.


A good rolling update
kubectl set image deploy/lemonade-web -n lemonade web=nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.6-alpine
kubectl annotate deploy/lemonade-web -n lemonade kubernetes.io/change-cause="nginx 1.30.6"
kubectl rollout status deploy/lemonade-web -n lemonade
kubectl get rs -n lemonade -l app=lemonade
Waiting for deployment "lemonade-web" rollout to finish: 1 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
Waiting for deployment "lemonade-web" rollout to finish: 2 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
Waiting for deployment "lemonade-web" rollout to finish: 1 old replicas are pending termination...
deployment "lemonade-web" successfully rolled out
NAME                      DESIRED   CURRENT   READY
lemonade-web-848fbbb64c   3         3         3       ← 1.30.6
lemonade-web-bffff7f7b    0         0         0       ← 1.30.5, kept for rollback


A broken update, and the undo
Now someone types a version that does not exist:
kubectl set image deploy/lemonade-web -n lemonade web=nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.99-alpine
kubectl rollout status deploy/lemonade-web -n lemonade --timeout=45s
kubectl get pods,deploy -n lemonade -l app=lemonade
error: timed out waiting for the condition
NAME                            READY   STATUS         RESTARTS
lemonade-web-79cf8988fc-dqq9t   0/1     ErrImagePull   0        ← the one new pod
lemonade-web-848fbbb64c-7lrs9   1/1     Running        0
lemonade-web-848fbbb64c-9vjwb   1/1     Running        0
lemonade-web-848fbbb64c-qbswk   1/1     Running        0

NAME           READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
lemonade-web   3/3     1            3
The stand stayed open. The rolling update created one extra pod (the surge). That pod never became ready, so no old pod was removed. All three 1.30.6 pods kept serving. The Mathematical Abstraction section below explains why it stopped at exactly one extra pod.
kubectl rollout history deploy/lemonade-web -n lemonade
kubectl rollout undo deploy/lemonade-web -n lemonade
kubectl rollout history deploy/lemonade-web -n lemonade
REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
1         <none>
2         nginx 1.30.6
3         typo 1.30.99

Warning: resource deployments/lemonade-web was previously managed with 'kubectl apply'. Rolling back
will not update the kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation …
deployment.apps/lemonade-web rolled back

REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
1         <none>
3         typo 1.30.99
4         nginx 1.30.6
Two things to notice:

Undo did not “go back to revision 2”. It copied revision 2’s template into a new revision 4, and revision 2 disappeared from the list.
kubectl warns you: the Deployment was created with apply, but undo changed it behind the file’s back. In a team, the cleaner undo is to revert the change in Git and kubectl apply the file again. Use rollout undo in an emergency, then fix the file.

title: 6. Deployments and Rolling Updates
text:
Rules and conventions

Always run pods through a Deployment (or another controller), never as bare pods, so they come back after failures.
Keep the selector small and stable (app: lemonade). You cannot change it later without recreating the Deployment.
Trigger rollouts by changing the manifest in Git (the image tag) and applying it. Record why with kubernetes.io/change-cause, or rely on Git history.
Follow every apply in CI with kubectl rollout status --timeout=…, so a broken release fails the pipeline.
Use readiness probes (lesson 11). Without them, “ready” only means “the process started”, and a rolling update can replace good pods with broken ones.
For a small number of replicas, set maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1. Capacity then never drops during an update.

title: 6. Deployments and Rolling Updates
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Template labels do not match the selector
selector does not match template labels
Use the same labels in selector.matchLabels and template.metadata.labels


Changing the selector of an existing Deployment
field is immutable
Delete and recreate it, or create a new Deployment


Reusing the same image tag for new code
apply says unchanged, and old code keeps running
Use a new tag per build (CI/CD part), or kubectl rollout restart


maxSurge: 0 and maxUnavailable: 0
The API rejects it
At least one of them must be above 0


Waiting forever on a broken rollout
Pipeline hangs
rollout status --timeout, and lower progressDeadlineSeconds


Only using rollout undo
The Git file still has the bad version, and the next apply breaks it again
Revert in Git and apply

title: 6. Deployments and Rolling Updates
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

The reconciliation loop
Each pass of the ReplicaSet controller computes
\[
\Delta = r - a, \qquad
\text{action} =
\begin{cases}
\text{create } \Delta \text{ pods} & \text{if } \Delta > 0 \\
\text{delete } |\Delta| \text{ pods} & \text{if } \Delta < 0 \\
\text{do nothing} & \text{if } \Delta = 0
\end{cases}
\]
where

\(r\) is the desired replica count, spec.replicas, a whole number \(\ge 0\).
\(a\) is the number of matching, non-terminating pods the controller observes right now.
\(\Delta\) is the gap it must close.

Example: after we deleted one pod, \(r = 3\) and \(a = 2\), so \(\Delta = 3 - 2 = 1\) and the controller created one pod (plxn5, one second later). After scale --replicas=5: \(\Delta = 5 - 3 = 2\), so two pods were created. After scaling back: \(\Delta = 3 - 5 = -2\), so two pods were deleted.


The rolling-update window
During an update the Deployment must respect
\[
s = \lceil r \cdot \sigma \rceil, \qquad u = \lfloor r \cdot \mu \rfloor, \qquad
N_{\text{total}} \le r + s, \qquad N_{\text{available}} \ge r - u
\]
where

\(r\) is spec.replicas.
\(\sigma\) is maxSurge as a fraction (25% means \(\sigma = 0.25\)). \(\lceil x \rceil\) means round up.
\(\mu\) is maxUnavailable as a fraction. \(\lfloor x \rfloor\) means round down.
\(s\) is the number of extra pods allowed, and \(u\) the number of missing pods allowed.
\(N_{\text{total}}\) is the number of pods that exist (old plus new). \(N_{\text{available}}\) is the number that are ready to serve.

If you write whole numbers instead of percentages (maxSurge: 1), then \(s\) and \(u\) are those numbers directly.
Example with our Deployment: \(r = 3\) and the defaults \(\sigma = \mu = 0.25\).
\[
s = \lceil 3 \times 0.25 \rceil = \lceil 0.75 \rceil = 1, \qquad u = \lfloor 3 \times 0.25 \rfloor = \lfloor 0.75 \rfloor = 0
\]
So \(N_{\text{total}} \le 3 + 1 = 4\) and \(N_{\text{available}} \ge 3 - 0 = 3\). That is exactly what the broken update showed: 4 pods in total (3 old Running plus 1 new ErrImagePull), AVAILABLE 3, and the rollout stuck. It could not add a fifth pod (\(s\) was used up), and it could not remove an old pod (that would make \(N_{\text{available}} = 2 < 3\)).
A bigger example: with \(r = 10\) we get \(s = \lceil 2.5 \rceil = 3\) and \(u = \lfloor 2.5 \rfloor = 2\). So at most 13 pods exist and at least 8 serve during the update. The rounding directions are deliberately cautious: never fewer available pods than you asked for, while still making progress.


Revision numbers
\[
v_{\text{new}} = \max(V) + 1
\]
where \(V\) is the set of revision numbers that currently exist, and \(v_{\text{new}}\) is the number given to the next rollout, including a rollback.
Example: before the undo, \(V = \lbrace 1, 2, 3 \rbrace\). Rolling back to revision 2 created \(v_{\text{new}} = 3 + 1 = 4\) with revision 2’s template, and removed 2. So the history showed \(\lbrace 1, 3, 4 \rbrace\).

title: 5. Labels, Selectors and Namespaces
text:
After a few lessons the lemonade namespace holds web pods, a test pod, a sidecar pod and soon jobs and databases. We need to:

Find groups of objects: “all web pods”, “all pink-lemonade pods”, “everything except the tests”.
Let other objects pick their pods. A Service must know which pods to send customers to, and a Deployment which pods it owns.
Keep the Lemonade Stand apart from a future Cookie Stand on the same cluster, so names do not clash and one team cannot delete the other’s pods by accident.

Labels and selectors solve the first two. Namespaces solve the third.

title: 5. Labels, Selectors and Namespaces
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipName tags and rooms



When Phippy comes aboard Captain Kube’s ship in The Illustrated Children’s Guide to Kubernetes, the captain gives her a name tag. The book explains that Kubernetes uses labels as “nametags” to identify things, and that they are open-ended: you can write whatever helps, such as a role or how stable something is.
A selector is the teacher calling out: “Everyone wearing a yellow sticker, line up!” Nobody needs to know your real name. If you are wearing the sticker, you come.
Later Phippy wants a little privacy, and Captain Kube gives her a namespace: a room of her own on the ship. Things inside the room work together easily, and they are kept a bit apart from the rest of the ship. Two rooms can each have a pupil called “Sam” without any confusion.

title: 5. Labels, Selectors and Namespaces
text:
The concept, precisely

Labels are key: value pairs in metadata.labels. Kubernetes uses them to select objects. They identify things: app, tier, flavor, environment.
Annotations are key: value pairs in metadata.annotations. They are never used for selection. They hold notes and tool settings: a change cause, a Git commit, a Traefik option. Values can be long; the total size of all annotations on one object must stay under 256 KiB.
Selectors come in two kinds:

Equality-based: app=lemonade, flavor!=pink. Several conditions joined by commas must all hold.
Set-based: flavor in (classic,pink), flavor notin (mint), flavor (the key exists), !flavor (the key is missing).

In YAML, matchLabels is the equality form. matchExpressions is the set form, with the operators In, NotIn, Exists and DoesNotExist. Services only support matchLabels-style selectors. Deployments, ReplicaSets, Jobs and DaemonSets support both.
Recommended labels: Kubernetes suggests a shared set so tools can understand your objects:

app.kubernetes.io/name: the app (lemonade)
app.kubernetes.io/instance: this installation (lemonade-prod)
app.kubernetes.io/version: the version (1.30.5)
app.kubernetes.io/component: the part of the app (web)
app.kubernetes.io/part-of: the bigger system (snack-shop)
app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: the tool that manages it (helm)

Helm charts set these for you. This book uses the short app: lemonade to keep examples small.
Namespaces divide one cluster into named groups. Most objects (pods, Services, Deployments, ConfigMaps) are namespaced: their name must be unique only inside their namespace. Some are cluster-scoped: Nodes, Namespaces, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, IngressClasses. Every cluster starts with four namespaces:

default: used when you do not choose one;
kube-system: k3s’s own components, such as Traefik and CoreDNS;
kube-public: readable by everyone;
kube-node-lease: node heartbeats.

Namespaces are not walls. By default, pods in different namespaces can still talk to each other over the network. Namespaces separate names, permissions (RBAC) and quotas. Network isolation needs NetworkPolicies, which k3s enforces with its built-in policy controller.

Same - and --overwrite rules
kubectl annotate deploy/lemonade-web owner=sam -n lemonade


-l key=value
Equality selector
Commas mean AND
kubectl get pods -l app=lemonade,flavor=pink


-l 'key!=value'
Inequality
Also matches objects that lack the key
kubectl get pods -l 'flavor!=pink'


-l 'key in (a,b)'
Set membership
Quote it for the shell
kubectl get pods -l 'flavor in (classic,pink)'


-l 'key notin (a)'
Not in a set
Also matches objects that lack the key
kubectl get pods -l 'flavor notin (mint)'


-l key / -l '!key'
The key exists / is missing

kubectl get pods -l '!flavor'


--show-labels / -L key
Show all labels / one label as a column

kubectl get pods -L flavor


kubectl create namespace
Make a namespace
Or apply a Namespace manifest
kubectl create namespace cookies


kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=
Change your default namespace
Saves typing -n
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=lemonade


kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false
List cluster-scoped kinds

kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false


kubectl delete namespace
Delete a namespace and everything in it
Double-check the name first
kubectl delete namespace cookies



The two selector styles in YAML:
selector:
  matchLabels:
    app: lemonade
  matchExpressions:
    - { key: flavor, operator: In, values: [classic, pink] }

title: 5. Labels, Selectors and Namespaces
text:
Worked example
Give two pods a flavor label. We also gave the stand-alone lemonade-pod from lesson 4 the labels app=lemonade and flavor=mint:
kubectl label pod lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-hwg94 -n lemonade flavor=pink
kubectl label pod lemonade-pod -n lemonade app=lemonade flavor=mint
kubectl get pods -n lemonade -L app,flavor
NAME                           READY   STATUS    APP        FLAVOR
lemonade-pod                   1/1     Running   lemonade   mint
lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-hwg94   1/1     Running   lemonade   pink
lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-lwvx4   1/1     Running   lemonade
lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-ttfs2   1/1     Running   lemonade
till-with-sidecar              2/2     Running
Now ask different questions:
kubectl get pods -n lemonade -l 'app=lemonade,flavor!=pink'
NAME                           READY   STATUS
lemonade-pod                   1/1     Running
lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-lwvx4   1/1     Running     ← has no flavor at all, and still matches
lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-ttfs2   1/1     Running
kubectl get pods -n lemonade -l 'flavor in (classic,pink)'
kubectl get pods -n lemonade -l '!flavor'
NAME                           READY   STATUS
lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-hwg94   1/1     Running

NAME                           READY   STATUS
lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-lwvx4   1/1     Running
lemonade-web-bffff7f7b-ttfs2   1/1     Running
till-with-sidecar              2/2     Running
Notice the trap: flavor!=pink matched pods that have no flavor label at all. Use flavor,flavor!=pink (key exists AND is not pink) if you mean “flavoured, but not pink”.
Labels have power. Giving lemonade-pod the label app=lemonade means the lemonade-web Service (lesson 7) would now send customers to it too, because the Service selects only on app=lemonade. The Deployment’s ReplicaSet does not adopt it, though. The ReplicaSet’s selector also requires pod-template-hash=bffff7f7b, which the bare pod does not have. Remove the label again:
kubectl label pod lemonade-pod -n lemonade app- flavor-
Namespaces and cluster-scoped kinds:
kubectl get namespaces
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false | head -5
NAME              STATUS   AGE

title: 5. Labels, Selectors and Namespaces
text:
Rules and conventions

Put a small, stable set of identifying labels on everything: at least app. On larger systems use the app.kubernetes.io/* set.
Labels are for selecting; annotations are for notes. If no selector will ever use it, make it an annotation.
Keep selectors in Deployments and Services minimal. Never select on something that changes per release, such as a version.
One namespace per app or per team per environment (lemonade, lemonade-staging). Put access rules (RBAC) and ResourceQuota objects on namespaces.
Write metadata.namespace in every manifest of namespaced objects.
Use the DNS label rules (lowercase, -, at most 63 characters) for all names. They are valid everywhere.

title: 5. Labels, Selectors and Namespaces
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Using != or notin and expecting “has the key”
Unlabelled objects appear in the result
Add the bare key: -l 'flavor,flavor!=pink'


Giving an unrelated pod the Service’s label
Customers sometimes reach the wrong app
Use distinct labels per app; check kubectl get endpointslices


Spaces or capitals in a label value
Invalid value … must be no more than 63 characters or similar
Use pink-lemonade


Deleting a namespace to “clean one thing”
Everything in it is gone
Delete specific objects, or use -l


Expecting a namespace to block network traffic
Pods in other namespaces can still connect
Add a NetworkPolicy


Creating a PersistentVolume “in” a namespace
namespace is ignored
PersistentVolumes are cluster-scoped; PVCs are namespaced

title: 5. Labels, Selectors and Namespaces
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
A selector is a condition on a pod’s label set. For an equality-only selector, a pod matches when its labels contain every pair the selector asks for:
\[
\operatorname{match}(\sigma) = \lbrace p \in P \mid \sigma \subseteq L(p) \rbrace
\]
where

\(P\) is the set of pods in the namespace.
\(L(p)\) is the set of key=value pairs on pod \(p\).
\(\sigma\) is the set of pairs in the selector, for example \(\lbrace \texttt{app=lemonade} \rbrace\).
\(\subseteq\) means “every element of the left set is also in the right set”.

Example: with \(\sigma = \lbrace \texttt{app=lemonade} \rbrace\) and the pods above:

hwg94 has \(\lbrace \texttt{app=lemonade}, \texttt{flavor=pink}, \dots \rbrace\), which contains \(\sigma\): it matches.
lwvx4 and ttfs2 have \(\lbrace \texttt{app=lemonade}, \dots \rbrace\): they match.
till-with-sidecar has \(\varnothing\) (no labels): no match.
lemonade-pod (while it had the label) matched too.

So \(|\operatorname{match}(\sigma)| = 4\), and \(\sigma \cup \lbrace \texttt{flavor=pink} \rbrace\) narrows the result to 1 pod. Adding conditions can only shrink the result, never grow it, because a bigger \(\sigma\) is harder to contain.
Set-based conditions test one key at a time. Write \(v_p(k)\) for the value of key \(k\) on pod \(p\), or \(\bot\) (“missing”) if the pod has no such key:
\[
\begin{aligned}
k \;\texttt{in}\; V &:\quad v_p(k) \in V \\
k \;\texttt{notin}\; V &:\quad v_p(k) \notin V \quad (\text{true when } v_p(k) = \bot) \\
k \;\texttt{!=}\; x &:\quad v_p(k) \neq x \quad (\text{true when } v_p(k) = \bot)
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(V\) is a set of allowed values and \(x\) a single value.
Example: for lwvx4, \(v(\texttt{flavor}) = \bot\). Then \(\texttt{flavor in (classic,pink)}\) is false, because \(\bot \notin \lbrace \text{classic}, \text{pink} \rbrace\). But \(\texttt{flavor != pink}\) is true, because \(\bot \neq \text{pink}\). That is exactly why lwvx4 appeared in the != query and not in the in query.

title: 2. k3s Architecture and Installation
text: The Lemonade Stand now has a container image. Next we need a cluster: one or more machines that act as one big computer for containers. Before typing commands we should know which programs make up a cluster, where they run, and where k3s keeps its files. Otherwise every error message will be a mystery.

title: 2. k3s Architecture and Installation
text: The Lemonade Stand now has a container image. Next we need a cluster: one or more machines that act as one big computer for containers. Before typing commands we should know which programs make up a cluster, where they run, and where k3s keeps its files. Otherwise every error message will be a mystery.

title: 2. k3s Architecture and Installation
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipA cluster is a school



Think of the cluster as a school, and every container as a pupil who needs a seat.

The API server is the front office. Every request goes through it: “please enrol three lemonade pupils”. It checks who you are and whether you are allowed to ask.
The datastore is the school notebook. The office writes down every decision. In k3s this notebook is a small SQLite file by default.
The scheduler is the seat assigner. It looks at each new pupil and picks a classroom that has room.
The controller manager is the group of hall monitors. Each monitor keeps checking one thing, like “are there still three lemonade pupils?”, and fixes it when it is wrong. A thermostat works the same way: it keeps checking the temperature and turns the heater on or off.
Each node is a classroom. Its kubelet is the class teacher. It reads the office’s list for that room and makes sure those pupils are really there.
containerd is the teacher’s pair of hands. It actually starts and stops containers.
kube-proxy and Flannel are the corridors and signposts, so messages reach the right room.
CoreDNS is the school phone book. It turns a name like lemonade-web into an address.

In The Illustrated Children’s Guide to Kubernetes, Captain Kube steers a ship made of many rafts lashed together, so from outside it looks like one boat. A cluster is the same: many machines that look like one. In k3s, all the office staff (API server, scheduler and controllers) work in one room, a single k3s process. That is why it is so easy to set up.

title: 2. k3s Architecture and Installation
text:
The concept, precisely
Server and agent. A server runs k3s server. It runs the control plane (API server, scheduler, controller manager), the datastore, and the kubelet and container runtime, so it can run pods too. An agent runs k3s agent. It has only the kubelet, containerd and networking, and it joins a server. One server on its own is already a complete cluster.
The datastore.

SQLite (the default) is for a single server. k3s talks to it through a translation layer called kine, which makes SQLite look like etcd to Kubernetes.
Embedded etcd is for high availability (HA). You start the first server with --cluster-init, and you run an odd number of servers, usually 3.
External MySQL, PostgreSQL or etcd is chosen with --datastore-endpoint.

What k3s bundles. Upstream Kubernetes leaves these choices to you. k3s ships one choice for each, and you can switch any of them off with --disable:








Need
Upstream Kubernetes
k3s default




Container runtime
You install one
containerd (built in)


Pod network (CNI)
You install one
Flannel (VXLAN)


Cluster DNS
You install one
CoreDNS


Ingress controller
None
Traefik v3


LoadBalancer Services
Stay Pending without a cloud
ServiceLB (formerly Klipper LB)


Storage for PVCs
None on bare metal
local-path-provisioner


kubectl top, autoscaling metrics
Install metrics-server
metrics-server


Network policies
Depends on CNI
kube-router’s policy controller


Helm charts as objects
Not available
Helm controller with the HelmChart resource


Gateway API definitions
Install yourself
gateway-api-crd chart



The packaged components are deployed from manifest files that k3s writes into /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests. Each file becomes an AddOn object (lesson 13).
How agents join. An agent opens a connection to a server on port 6443. It proves it is allowed to join with the join token, which is stored on the server at /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token. After that, all kubelet traffic travels through this tunnel, so agents do not need to accept incoming connections from the server.

title: 2. k3s Architecture and Installation
section: Every option and path for this topic
text:
Every option and path for this topic

Install-script environment variables









Variable
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




INSTALL_K3S_VERSION
Install an exact version
Pin it in automation
INSTALL_K3S_VERSION=v1.37.2+k3s1


INSTALL_K3S_CHANNEL
Pick a release channel
stable (default), latest, testing
INSTALL_K3S_CHANNEL=stable


INSTALL_K3S_EXEC
Command and flags for the service
Defaults to server, or agent if K3S_URL is set
INSTALL_K3S_EXEC="server --disable=traefik"


K3S_URL
Server to join
Setting it makes the node an agent
K3S_URL=https://10.0.0.10:6443


K3S_TOKEN
Shared join secret
Copy it from the server’s node-token file
K3S_TOKEN=K10…


K3S_NODE_NAME
Node name
Must be unique in the cluster
K3S_NODE_NAME=stand-2


K3S_KUBECONFIG_MODE
File mode of the kubeconfig
644 lets non-root users read it (lab only)
K3S_KUBECONFIG_MODE=644





Common k3s server flags (also keys in config.yaml)









Flag
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




--disable
Do not deploy a packaged component
Repeat it, or use a comma list
--disable=traefik


--write-kubeconfig-mode
Permissions of k3s.yaml
Keep 600 on real servers
--write-kubeconfig-mode=644


--tls-san
Extra name or IP on the API certificate
Needed to reach the API by a public name
--tls-san=k3s.example.com


--node-label
Label this node at registration
key=value
--node-label=zone=kitchen


--node-taint
Taint this node at registration
key=value:Effect
--node-taint=role=db:NoSchedule


--cluster-init
Start a new embedded-etcd cluster
Only on the first HA server
--cluster-init


--datastore-endpoint
Use an external database
A connection string
--datastore-endpoint="mysql://…"


--default-local-storage-path
Where local-path volumes live
Put it on a big disk
--default-local-storage-path=/data


--secrets-encryption
Encrypt Secrets at rest
Turn it on for real clusters
--secrets-encryption





Files and paths








Path
What it is
Rule / convention




/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml
Admin kubeconfig
Copy it to your laptop; change 127.0.0.1 to the server address


/etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml
Configuration file
Same keys as the CLI flags without --


/etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml.d/*.yaml
Drop-in config files
Loaded in alphabetical order


/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/
Auto-deploy folder
Files here are applied like kubectl apply


/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token
Join token
Keep it secret


/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/db/
SQLite or etcd data
Back it up


/var/lib/rancher/k3s/storage/
local-path volume data
Lost if the node is lost


/usr/local/bin/k3s-uninstall.sh
Removes a server
Deletes cluster data


/usr/local/bin/k3s-agent-uninstall.sh
Removes an agent



/usr/local/bin/k3s-killall.sh
Stops k3s and all its containers
Use before maintenance



A configuration file says the same thing as flags, but you can keep it in Git:
# /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml
write-kubeconfig-mode: "0644"
disable:
  - traefik
node-label:
  - "zone=kitchen"

title: 2. k3s Architecture and Installation
text:
Worked example

Install on Linux
# server
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -
sudo cat /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token

# each agent
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | K3S_URL=https://SERVER_IP:6443 K3S_TOKEN=TOKEN sh -

# remove again (this deletes cluster data)
/usr/local/bin/k3s-uninstall.sh          # on the server
/usr/local/bin/k3s-agent-uninstall.sh    # on an agent
The script installs a systemd (or OpenRC) service. It also installs kubectl, crictl, ctr, k3s-killall.sh and k3s-uninstall.sh.


Look around the lab cluster
These outputs come from the Docker lab cluster described in the part index:
docker exec k3s-lab k3s --version
kubectl get nodes -o wide

kubectl get pods -n kube-system

coredns-577d995dff-hk9ft                  1/1     Running     0
helm-install-traefik-7plmh                0/1     Completed   1
helm-install-traefik-crd-s9fpp            0/1     Completed   0

(We started this lab with --disable=metrics-server to save memory; a default install also shows a metrics-server pod.)
There is no kube-apiserver or etcd pod. They live inside the single k3s process. The auto-deploy folder shows where the add-ons come from:
docker exec k3s-lab ls /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests
kubectl get addons -n kube-system
ccm.yaml  coredns.yaml  gateway-api-crd.yaml  local-storage.yaml  rolebindings.yaml  runtimes.yaml  traefik.yaml

NAME              SOURCE
coredns           /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/coredns.yaml
local-storage     /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/local-storage.yaml
traefik           /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/traefik.yaml
...

title: 2. k3s Architecture and Installation
text:
Rules and conventions

Use one server to learn, and three servers with embedded etcd when the control plane must survive a machine failure.
Give every node a unique host name, or set K3S_NODE_NAME.
Put settings in /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml, not only in install-script variables. Re-running the script without the same variables loses them; the config file stays.
Never edit the packaged manifests (traefik.yaml, coredns.yaml). k3s rewrites them at start-up. Customise with --disable or a HelmChartConfig (lesson 13).
Use the same critical flags (for example --disable and --cluster-cidr) on every server, or the extra servers refuse to join.
Open port 6443/TCP from agents to servers, 8472/UDP between nodes (Flannel VXLAN), 10250/TCP between nodes (metrics) and 2379–2380/TCP between servers (HA etcd).
The documented minimum is 2 cores and 2 GB RAM for a server, and 1 core and 512 MB for an agent.

title: 2. k3s Architecture and Installation
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Copying k3s.yaml to a laptop unchanged
connection refused to 127.0.0.1:6443
Replace 127.0.0.1 with the server’s address


Server reached by a name that is not on its certificate
x509: certificate is valid for …
Add --tls-san=<name> and restart


Two machines with the same host name
The second node never becomes Ready
Set K3S_NODE_NAME or use --with-node-id


Two HA servers instead of three
Losing one server stops the API
Use an odd number: 3 or 5


Editing traefik.yaml in the manifests folder
The change disappears after a restart
Use a HelmChartConfig instead

title: 2. k3s Architecture and Installation
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
With embedded etcd, the servers vote. A change is accepted only when a majority (the quorum) agrees. The k3s documentation states the quorum as \((n/2)+1\), using whole-number division:
\[
q = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor + 1, \qquad f = n - q
\]
where

\(n\) is the number of server nodes in the etcd cluster, a whole number \(\ge 1\).
\(q\) is the quorum: how many servers must be up and agree. \(\lfloor x \rfloor\) means round down.
\(f\) is the number of servers that may fail while the cluster still works.

Example:

\(n = 1\): \(q = \lfloor 0.5 \rfloor + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1\) and \(f = 1 - 1 = 0\). One server cannot lose anything.
\(n = 3\): \(q = \lfloor 1.5 \rfloor + 1 = 2\) and \(f = 3 - 2 = 1\). One server can fail.
\(n = 4\): \(q = \lfloor 2 \rfloor + 1 = 3\) and \(f = 4 - 3 = 1\). Still only one, even though you paid for a fourth machine.
\(n = 5\): \(q = 3\) and \(f = 2\).

This is why HA k3s uses an odd number of servers. Going from 3 to 4 adds a machine but no extra tolerance.
The single-server SQLite set-up has \(n = 1\) in this sense: if that server is down, nobody can change the cluster. Pods that are already running on agents keep running, though, because each kubelet keeps its last instructions.

title: k3s: Kubernetes Made Small
text:
Kubernetes (often written K8s: a K, eight letters, an s) runs containers on many machines and keeps them healthy. The usual way of installing it has many separate parts: an etcd database cluster, several control-plane programs, a network plug-in, a DNS server, an ingress controller, a storage driver. Each part must be installed, configured and upgraded on its own. That is a lot to learn before you can run your first web page.
k3s is a Kubernetes distribution that removes most of that set-up work:

It is one binary of less than 100 MB. All control-plane parts run inside one k3s process.
It ships with the parts a small cluster needs: containerd, Flannel networking, CoreDNS, the Traefik ingress controller, the ServiceLB load balancer, a local-path storage provisioner, metrics-server and a Helm controller.
It stores cluster state in SQLite by default, so you do not need an etcd cluster to start. Embedded etcd is still available when you want high availability.
It is fully conformant. Every kubectl command, manifest and concept in this part also works on any other Kubernetes. You learn the real thing, just with fewer moving parts.

The k3s team explains the name like this. They wanted something about half the size of Kubernetes. “Kubernetes” has 10 letters and is written K8s, so something half as big is a 5-letter word, written K3s. There is no long form and no official pronunciation. Darren Shepherd, chief architect at Rancher Labs, created it. Rancher announced it on 26 February 2019 for edge, IoT, ARM and CI machines. k3s is now a CNCF project.






NoteWhat changes compared with upstream Kubernetes



Only the installation and the bundled add-ons change. Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets, volumes, Jobs and Helm work exactly as the Kubernetes documentation describes. Each lesson has a short “k3s difference” note wherever k3s adds something of its own.

title: k3s: Kubernetes Made Small
section: The running example: a Lemonade Stand
text:
The running example: a Lemonade Stand
Every lesson builds one small thing: a web page that shows a lemonade menu.

Image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.5-alpine. This is a public NGINX image that listens on port 8080 and runs as a non-root user, so you do not have to build anything.
Menu: an HTML page stored in a ConfigMap called lemonade-menu.
Namespace: lemonade.
Label: every web pod carries app: lemonade.
Deployment and Service: both are called lemonade-web.
Address: http://lemonade.localhost, routed by the Traefik ingress controller that k3s ships with.

 browser ──► Traefik (Ingress: lemonade.localhost)
                │
                ▼
         Service lemonade-web  (port 80)
          ┌─────┼─────┐
          ▼     ▼     ▼
        pod   pod   pod        Deployment lemonade-web, 3 replicas
        :8080 :8080 :8080      each mounts ConfigMap lemonade-menu
The CI/CD part later replaces the public image with one it builds and tests itself. The Ansible part shows how to prepare machines like these.

title: k3s: Kubernetes Made Small
text:
Get a lab cluster
On Linux (a VM or a Raspberry Pi is fine), use the official install script:
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -
sudo k3s kubectl get nodes
On macOS or Windows, run k3s inside Docker. Every example in this part was checked this way on k3s v1.37.2+k3s1, the stable channel in November 2026:
docker run -d --name k3s-lab --hostname k3s-lab --privileged \
  -p 6443:6443 -p 8081:80 -p 30080:30080 \
  rancher/k3s:v1.37.2-k3s1 server
docker cp k3s-lab:/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml ./k3s.yaml
export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/k3s.yaml
kubectl get nodes

-p 6443:6443 publishes the Kubernetes API, so kubectl on your laptop can reach it.
-p 8081:80 publishes Traefik’s port 80 as localhost:8081.
-p 30080:30080 publishes the NodePort used in lesson 7.
Docker tags cannot contain +, so the version v1.37.2+k3s1 becomes the tag v1.37.2-k3s1. The latest tag is not maintained.
Give Docker at least 1 GB of free memory. On our test laptop, other containers already used most of Docker’s 8 GB, and the API server kept stalling. We added three memory-saving options there: -e GOMEMLIMIT=350MiB (a smaller Go heap), --tmpfs /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/db (keeps the SQLite file in RAM, so it is lost when the container stops), and --disable=metrics-server after server. A machine with spare memory needs none of them.
Remove the lab with docker rm -f k3s-lab.

Other easy options: k3d (k3d cluster create lemonade), Rancher Desktop, which runs k3s for you, or a Multipass Ubuntu VM with the install script.
The runnable manifests are in examples/. Their file names start with the lesson number.

title: k3s: Kubernetes Made Small
text:
Lessons

Containers and Orchestration: images, containers, registries, and why one machine is not enough.
k3s Architecture and Installation: servers, agents, the control plane as a school, important files.
kubectl and Manifests: how to talk to the cluster and describe what you want.
Pods: the smallest unit that runs a container; phases, restarts and CrashLoopBackOff.
Labels, Selectors and Namespaces: name tags, queries and rooms.
Deployments and Rolling Updates: keep N copies running and upgrade without downtime.
Services and DNS: one stable address for pods that come and go.
Ingress with Traefik: one front door that routes by host name and path.
ConfigMaps and Secrets: settings and passwords outside the image.
Storage: volumes, PersistentVolumeClaims and the local-path provisioner.
Health, Resources and Scheduling: probes, requests and limits, the scheduler, autoscaling.
Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets and StatefulSets: run-to-finish work, timetables, one per node, stable identities.
Helm and Auto-Deploy: charts, releases, and the k3s HelmChart resource.

title: k3s: Kubernetes Made Small
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
The whole part rests on one idea. You write down the desired state, and k3s keeps changing the observed state until the two match.
\[
\Delta(t) = D - O(t)
\]
where

\(D\) is the desired number of something. Here it is the number of lemonade pods you asked for, a whole number \(\ge 0\).
\(O(t)\) is the observed number at time \(t\): the pods that really exist right now.
\(\Delta(t)\) is the gap. A positive \(\Delta\) means “start this many more”. A negative \(\Delta\) means “stop \(|\Delta|\) of them”. \(\Delta = 0\) means “do nothing”.

Example: you ask for \(D = 3\) pods. A machine crashes and takes one pod with it, so \(O(t) = 2\). Then \(\Delta = 3 - 2 = 1\), and k3s starts one new pod. If you then lower the request to \(D = 1\) while \(O = 3\), you get \(\Delta = 1 - 3 = -2\), and k3s stops two pods. Lesson 6 shows this loop running on a real cluster.

title: 8. Ingress with Traefik
text:
The Service from lesson 7 gives the Lemonade Stand a stable address inside the cluster. A NodePort works from outside, but customers would have to type :30080, and every app would need its own odd port.
We want normal web addresses on port 80 (and 443 for HTTPS):

http://lemonade.localhost/ → the lemonade web pods
later, http://cookies.localhost/ → a cookie stand, on the same port 80

Something must look at each HTTP request, read the host name and path, and pass the request to the right Service. That something is an Ingress controller, configured by Ingress objects.

title: 8. Ingress with Traefik
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipThe fish and the reef



In Phippy Goes to the Zoo, Phippy and Zee stop at a big aquarium with a coral reef. Hundreds of tiny fish rush at one single hole in the rock. Moments later they pop out from many small cracks all over the far side of the reef. “Ingresses are beautiful,” sighs Phippy. Traffic arrives at one entrance and is sent on to many destinations inside the cluster.
Or think of the receptionist at a shopping centre. Everyone comes through the same front door. You say “I’m going to the Lemonade Stand”, and the receptionist points you to the right shop. The list of shops on the receptionist’s desk is the Ingress. The receptionist is the Ingress controller. In k3s, the receptionist is called Traefik, and it is already at the desk when the cluster starts.

title: 8. Ingress with Traefik
text:
The concept, precisely

An Ingress is a set of HTTP routing rules: host + path → Service and port. On its own it does nothing.
An Ingress controller is a reverse proxy running in the cluster. It watches Ingress objects and routes real traffic according to them. Upstream Kubernetes ships no controller.
k3s ships Traefik v3. It runs in kube-system behind a LoadBalancer Service on ports 80 and 443. ServiceLB publishes those ports on the node. Traefik registers an IngressClass called traefik, marked as the cluster default.
An Ingress chooses its controller with spec.ingressClassName. If the field is empty, the default class is used.
TLS is done by naming a Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls in spec.tls. Traefik then answers HTTPS for those hosts with that certificate.
Traefik’s own resources. Traefik also has its own IngressRoute resource (traefik.io/v1alpha1) for features that a plain Ingress cannot express, such as middlewares and weighted routing. k3s also installs the Gateway API definitions, the newer, role-oriented successor of Ingress. Plain Ingress is still supported and not deprecated, and it is portable, so this lesson uses it.
Customising Traefik. Write a HelmChartConfig named traefik in kube-system (lesson 13). Never edit k3s’s own traefik.yaml; k3s rewrites it at every start.

curl -H "Host: lemonade.localhost" http://NODE:80/menu
        │
        ▼
 Traefik (kube-system)  ── reads Ingress rules ──►  host lemonade.localhost, path / (Prefix)
        │
        ▼
 Service lemonade-web:80  ──►  pod :8080

title: 8. Ingress with Traefik
text:
Every field for this topic









Field
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




spec.ingressClassName
Which controller handles this Ingress
In k3s: traefik
ingressClassName: traefik


spec.rules[].host
Host name to match
Exact name, or one leading wildcard (*.example.com); omit it to match any host
host: lemonade.localhost


spec.rules[].http.paths[].path
URL path to match
Starts with /
path: /


…paths[].pathType
How path is compared
Prefix (by /-separated segments), Exact, or ImplementationSpecific
pathType: Prefix


…paths[].backend.service.name
Target Service
Same namespace as the Ingress
name: lemonade-web


…paths[].backend.service.port.number / .name
Target Service port
The Service’s port, not the pod’s targetPort
number: 80


spec.defaultBackend
Where unmatched requests go
Optional; otherwise the controller answers 404
defaultBackend: {service: {name: lemonade-web, port: {number: 80}}}


spec.tls[].hosts
Hosts served over HTTPS
Must match rule hosts
hosts: [lemonade.example.com]


spec.tls[].secretName
Secret with tls.crt and tls.key
Type kubernetes.io/tls, same namespace
secretName: lemonade-tls


metadata.annotations
Controller-specific extras
Traefik reads traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/… keys
traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.entrypoints: websecure



Useful commands:








Command
What it does
Example




kubectl get ingress
List rules with host and address
kubectl get ingress -n lemonade


kubectl describe ingress
Show rules and backends
kubectl describe ingress lemonade-web -n lemonade


kubectl get ingressclass
List controllers
kubectl get ingressclass


kubectl create secret tls
Store a certificate for spec.tls
kubectl create secret tls lemonade-tls --cert=c.pem --key=k.pem -n lemonade


curl -H "Host: …"
Test a host rule without DNS
curl -H "Host: lemonade.localhost" http://localhost:8081/

title: 8. Ingress with Traefik
text:
Worked example
The Ingress (08-ingress.yaml):
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: lemonade-web
  namespace: lemonade
spec:
  ingressClassName: traefik
  rules:
    - host: lemonade.localhost
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: lemonade-web
                port:
                  number: 80
kubectl get ingressclass
kubectl apply -f 08-ingress.yaml
kubectl get ingress -n lemonade
NAME                CONTROLLER                      PARAMETERS
traefik (default)   traefik.io/ingress-controller   <none>

ingress.networking.k8s.io/lemonade-web created
NAME           CLASS     HOSTS                ADDRESS      PORTS
lemonade-web   traefik   lemonade.localhost   172.17.0.3   80
ADDRESS is the node IP that ServiceLB uses for Traefik. In the Docker lab, the node’s port 80 is published as localhost:8081:
curl -s -H 'Host: lemonade.localhost' http://localhost:8081/
curl -s http://lemonade.localhost:8081/                     # *.localhost resolves to 127.0.0.1
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H 'Host: cookies.localhost' http://localhost:8081/
<h1>Lemonade Stand</h1>
<p>Classic lemonade: 2.00</p>
<p>Pink lemonade: 2.50</p>
<h1>Lemonade Stand</h1>
…
404
The third request names a host that no rule matches, so Traefik answers 404 itself. Adding the cookie stand later means adding a second rule (or a second Ingress) with host: cookies.localhost. Nothing else changes.
To change Traefik itself, drop a HelmChartConfig into the server’s auto-deploy folder (/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/). This one tells Traefik to keep request logs:
apiVersion: helm.cattle.io/v1
kind: HelmChartConfig
metadata:
  name: traefik
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  valuesContent: |-
    accessLog:
      enabled: true
Value names belong to the Traefik chart version that your k3s ships (here chart 41.6.1, shown by kubectl get helmcharts -n kube-system). Check them with helm show values --repo https://traefik.github.io/charts traefik --version 41.6.1.

title: 8. Ingress with Traefik
text:
Rules and conventions

Use one Ingress per app (per team) rather than one giant shared Ingress. Each team then edits only its own file.
Always set ingressClassName, even though traefik is the default. The manifest then still works on clusters with several controllers.
Point the backend at the Service port (80), not the container port (8080).
Use pathType: Prefix for whole sites, and Exact for single endpoints.
Terminate HTTPS at the Ingress with a TLS Secret. In production, let a tool such as cert-manager renew certificates automatically.
Customise Traefik only through HelmChartConfig. If you do not want Traefik at all, start the k3s servers with --disable=traefik and install another controller.
In Traefik chart v40 and later (shipped with k3s since the June 2026 releases), the Service type moved from service.type to service.spec.type. Old HelmChartConfig files that set service.type are silently ignored.

title: 8. Ingress with Traefik
text:
Common mistakes



Mistake
Symptom
Fix




No Host header (or DNS) matching the rule
Traefik answers 404
Use the exact host name, or curl -H "Host: …"


Backend port set to the container port
404 or 503 from Traefik
Use the Service’s port


Ingress in a different namespace from the Service
Backend not found, 404
Put the Ingress in the Service’s namespace


Service has no ready endpoints
503 Service Unavailable
Fix the pods or the selector (lesson 7)


Another program already uses port 80 on the node
ServiceLB pod stays Pending, Traefik has no address
Free port 80, or move Traefik with a HelmChartConfig


Editing /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/traefik.yaml
Changes vanish after a restart
Use a separate HelmChartConfig file

title: 8. Ingress with Traefik
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
For one host, the controller must pick one rule for each request path. With pathType: Prefix, a rule path \(p\) matches a request path \(x\) when \(p\)’s segments are a prefix of \(x\)’s segments, and the longest matching path wins:
\[
\operatorname{rule}(x) = \underset{p \,\in\, P,\; \operatorname{seg}(p) \,\preceq\, \operatorname{seg}(x)}{\operatorname{arg\,max}} \; |\operatorname{seg}(p)|
\]
where

\(P\) is the set of path values in the rules for the request’s host.
\(\operatorname{seg}(p)\) is the list of path segments: /api/orders becomes \((\texttt{api}, \texttt{orders})\), and / becomes the empty list \(()\).
\(a \preceq b\) means “list \(a\) is a prefix of list \(b\)”, compared segment by segment.
\(|\operatorname{seg}(p)|\) is the number of segments, and \(\operatorname{arg\,max}\) picks the \(p\) with the most segments.

Example: suppose the lemonade host has two rules, \(P = \lbrace \texttt{/}, \texttt{/api} \rbrace\):

Request /api/orders: \(\operatorname{seg} = (\texttt{api}, \texttt{orders})\). Both \(()\) (length 0) and \((\texttt{api})\) (length 1) are prefixes. The maximum is 1, so /api wins.
Request /apix: \(\operatorname{seg} = (\texttt{apix})\). \((\texttt{api})\) is not a segment prefix of \((\texttt{apix})\), because api ≠ apix. Only / matches (length 0), so the request goes to the / rule.
Request /: only / matches.

The same idea decides which host rule applies: an exact host such as lemonade.localhost matches only itself, and a request with any other Host header falls through to the default backend, or to a 404, as we saw with cookies.localhost.

title: 3. kubectl and Manifests
text:
We have a cluster. Now we must tell it, “please run the Lemonade Stand”. Two questions:

How do we talk to the cluster? With the command-line tool kubectl, which sends requests to the API server.
How do we write down what we want, so a teammate can review it, Git can store it, and running it twice does no harm? With a manifest: a YAML file that describes an object.

title: 3. kubectl and Manifests
text:
We have a cluster. Now we must tell it, “please run the Lemonade Stand”. Two questions:

How do we talk to the cluster? With the command-line tool kubectl, which sends requests to the API server.
How do we write down what we want, so a teammate can review it, Git can store it, and running it twice does no harm? With a manifest: a YAML file that describes an object.

title: 3. kubectl and Manifests
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipOrdering at a restaurant



You could shout at the kitchen: “make a lemonade… no wait, two… with ice!” That is imperative: a list of commands, and it is easy to lose track. Or you can fill in an order slip: “Table 4: two lemonades, with ice.” That is declarative. The slip says what you want, not how to make it. The kitchen can read it again at any time to check it got the order right.
A manifest is an order slip with four boxes:

apiVersion + kind: which form you are filling in (“drinks order, version 1”).
metadata: the name tag on the slip (“Table 4”).
spec: what you want (“two lemonades”).
status: the kitchen writes this box, never you (“one lemonade is ready”).

kubectl is the waiter who carries your slip to the front office (the API server). Your kubeconfig file is the waiter’s notebook. It says which restaurant to go to and which membership card to show at the door.

title: 3. kubectl and Manifests
text:
The concept, precisely
kubeconfig. A YAML file (by default ~/.kube/config, or whatever KUBECONFIG points to) with three lists:

clusters: API server URLs and their certificates.
users: credentials.
contexts: pairs of one cluster and one user, plus an optional default namespace.

The current context decides where kubectl sends requests. k3s writes an admin kubeconfig to /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml.
Command grammar.
kubectl <verb> <resource-type> [<name>] [flags]
kubectl get    pods            lemonade-pod  -n lemonade -o wide
Resource types have a singular name, a plural name and short names: pod, pods and po all mean the same type. kubectl api-resources lists them all.
Manifest anatomy.
apiVersion: v1          # API group/version: v1, apps/v1, batch/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1 …
kind: Pod               # object type
metadata:
  name: lemonade-pod    # unique per kind within a namespace
  namespace: lemonade
spec:                   # desired state, written by you
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.5-alpine
# status: …             # observed state, written by the cluster
Imperative vs declarative.

kubectl create, run, scale and set image are imperative: “do this action now”.
kubectl apply -f file.yaml is declarative: “make the cluster look like this file”. You can run apply any number of times. If nothing changed, it reports unchanged. Teams keep manifests in Git and apply them, often from CI/CD.

title: 3. kubectl and Manifests
section: Every command and flag for this topic
text:
Every command and flag for this topic

Commands









Command
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




get
List objects in a table
Add -o wide for more columns
kubectl get pods -n lemonade


describe
Show details and recent events
First stop when something is stuck
kubectl describe pod lemonade-pod -n lemonade


apply
Create or update from a manifest
The normal way to change a cluster
kubectl apply -f 04-pod.yaml


create
Create an object; fails if it exists
Good for one-off objects
kubectl create namespace test


delete
Delete objects
By file, by name, or by label
kubectl delete -f 04-pod.yaml


edit
Open the live object in an editor
Quick fixes only; the file in Git is now out of date
kubectl edit deploy/lemonade-web -n lemonade


logs
Print container output
-f follows, --previous shows the last crashed run
kubectl logs lemonade-pod -n lemonade --tail=20


exec
Run a command inside a container
-- separates kubectl’s flags from the command
kubectl exec -it lemonade-pod -n lemonade -- sh


port-forward
Tunnel a local port to a pod or Service
For debugging, not for customers
kubectl port-forward pod/lemonade-pod 8080:8080 -n lemonade


explain
Documentation of any field
Works offline against your cluster’s API
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.image


diff
Show what apply would change
Run before apply in reviews
kubectl diff -f 06-deployment.yaml


rollout
Status, history and undo of updates
Deployments, DaemonSets, StatefulSets
kubectl rollout status deploy/lemonade-web -n lemonade


scale
Change replicas
Imperative; update the file too
kubectl scale deploy/lemonade-web --replicas=5 -n lemonade


top
CPU and memory use
Needs metrics-server (bundled in k3s)
kubectl top pods -n lemonade


events
Recent events
Same as get events, nicer output
kubectl events -n lemonade


label
Add, change or remove labels
key- removes a label
kubectl label pod lemonade-pod flavor=pink -n lemonade


annotate
Add notes that are not used for selection
--overwrite to change one
kubectl annotate deploy/lemonade-web owner=sam -n lemonade


cp
Copy files to or from a container
Needs tar in the image
kubectl cp lemonade/order-logger:/data/orders.log ./orders.log


wait
Block until a condition is true
Useful in scripts and CI
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/lemonade-pod -n lemonade


config
Read or switch kubeconfig contexts
use-context, get-contexts, set-context
kubectl config get-contexts


api-resources
List all resource types and short names
Shows which types are namespaced
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false





Flags



Flag
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




-n, --namespace
Work in one namespace
Default is the context’s namespace, usually default
-n lemonade


-A, --all-namespaces
List across all namespaces
For get only
kubectl get pods -A


-l, --selector
Filter by labels
See lesson 5
-l app=lemonade


-o wide
Extra columns (IP, node)

kubectl get pods -o wide


-o yaml / -o json
Full object, including status
Good for learning field names
kubectl get pod lemonade-pod -o yaml


-o jsonpath=
Pick single fields
Path starts at the object root
-o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}'


-o name
Print only kind/name
Handy in shell loops
kubectl get pods -o name


-f
File, folder or URL of manifests
Can repeat; - means standard input
-f 00-namespace.yaml -f 04-pod.yaml


-R
Recurse into folders with -f

kubectl apply -R -f examples/


-k
Apply a Kustomize folder
Needs a kustomization.yaml
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod


--dry-run=client
Build the object locally, send nothing
With -o yaml it prints a starter manifest
kubectl create cm demo --from-literal=a=1 --dry-run=client -o yaml


--dry-run=server
Let the API server validate, save nothing
Catches errors that client cannot see
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f pod.yaml


-w, --watch
Keep printing changes
Stop with Ctrl-C
kubectl get pods -w


--context
Use another context for one command
Safer than switching globally
--context staging


--sort-by
Sort by a field

--sort-by=.lastTimestamp


--field-selector
Filter by some built-in fields

--field-selector status.phase=Running

title: 3. kubectl and Manifests
text:
Worked example
Create the namespace twice to see declarative behaviour:
kubectl apply -f 00-namespace.yaml
kubectl apply -f 00-namespace.yaml
namespace/lemonade created
namespace/lemonade unchanged
Let kubectl write a starter manifest for you, without touching the cluster:
kubectl create configmap demo --from-literal=price=2.00 -n lemonade --dry-run=client -o yaml
apiVersion: v1
data:
  price: "2.00"
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: demo
  namespace: lemonade
Run the pod from lesson 4 and read single fields with JSONPath:
kubectl apply -f 04-pod.yaml
kubectl get pod lemonade-pod -n lemonade -o jsonpath='{.status.phase} {.status.podIP}'
pod/lemonade-pod created
Running 10.42.0.9
Ask the cluster itself what a field means:
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.imagePullPolicy
FIELD: imagePullPolicy <string>
ENUM:
    Always
    IfNotPresent
    Never
DESCRIPTION:
    Image pull policy. One of Always, Never, IfNotPresent. Defaults to Always if
    :latest tag is specified, or IfNotPresent otherwise. Cannot be updated.
Preview a change before applying it. Here we bump the image version:
sed 's/1.30.5-alpine/1.30.6-alpine/' 04-pod.yaml | kubectl diff -f -
-  - image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.5-alpine
+  - image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.6-alpine
Let the server catch a mistake that a YAML check would miss. Here, an invalid name:
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f bad-pod.yaml     # metadata.name: Lemonade_Pod
The Pod "Lemonade_Pod" is invalid: metadata.name: Invalid value: "Lemonade_Pod":
a lowercase RFC 1123 subdomain must consist of lower case alphanumeric characters, '-' or '.'

title: 3. kubectl and Manifests
text:
Rules and conventions

Keep manifests in Git and change the cluster with kubectl apply. Treat edit and scale as emergency tools, and copy the change back into the file afterwards.
One file per object, or one file per small group of objects joined with ---. Name the file after what it holds.
Always set metadata.namespace in the file, or always pass -n. Do not rely on whichever namespace the current context happens to have.
Run kubectl diff before apply on shared clusters. Run --dry-run=server in CI to catch invalid fields early.
Learn field names with kubectl explain and kubectl get … -o yaml. Do not guess.
Use --context in scripts so a script never touches the wrong cluster.

title: 3. kubectl and Manifests
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Forgetting -n lemonade
No resources found in default namespace.
Pass -n, or set it once with kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=lemonade


Tabs in YAML
error converting YAML to JSON
Indent with spaces only


Wrong apiVersion for a kind
no matches for kind "Deployment" in version "v1"
Check with kubectl api-resources (Deployments are apps/v1)


Writing a status: section
It is ignored or rejected
Only write spec; the cluster owns status


create in a script that runs twice
AlreadyExists error
Use apply


Forgetting -- before the command in exec
kubectl tries to parse the command’s flags
kubectl exec pod -- ls -l

title: 3. kubectl and Manifests
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
kubectl apply is idempotent: applying the same manifest a second time changes nothing.
\[
\operatorname{apply}\bigl(\operatorname{apply}(S, m), m\bigr) = \operatorname{apply}(S, m)
\]
where

\(S\) is the state of the cluster: the set of all objects stored in the datastore.
\(m\) is a manifest: a set of desired objects, each identified by its kind, namespace and name.
\(\operatorname{apply}(S, m)\) is the new cluster state after applying \(m\) to \(S\). Objects in \(m\) are created or updated to match; objects not in \(m\) are left alone.

Example: start with a cluster that has no lemonade namespace, \(S_0 = \lbrace \text{kube-system}, \text{default} \rbrace\), and take \(m = \lbrace \text{Namespace lemonade} \rbrace\).

The first apply gives \(S_1 = \operatorname{apply}(S_0, m) = \lbrace \text{kube-system}, \text{default}, \text{lemonade} \rbrace\). kubectl prints created.
The second apply gives \(\operatorname{apply}(S_1, m) = S_1\), because “lemonade” is already there. kubectl prints unchanged.

A shell script that runs kubectl create namespace lemonade twice fails the second time. create is not idempotent.
Each object is identified by a key, and two objects in the cluster can never share one:
\[
\operatorname{key}(o) = (g, k, n, x)
\]
where \(g\) is the API group ("" for core, apps, …), \(k\) the kind, \(n\) the namespace (empty for cluster-wide kinds such as Namespace or Node), and \(x\) the name.
Example: ("", Pod, lemonade, lemonade-pod) and (apps, Deployment, lemonade, lemonade-web) are different keys. You may also have a ConfigMap and a Service both called lemonade-web, because their \(k\) differs. A second Pod called lemonade-pod in namespace lemonade would have the same key as the first. apply would update the existing pod, and create would fail with AlreadyExists.
