text: We want the Lemonade Stand’s NGINX container to run inside the cluster, not on a laptop. Kubernetes never runs a bare container. It always wraps one or more containers in a pod. To read any error message later, we need to know what a pod is, which fields it has, and which states it moves through.

title: 4. Pods
text: We want the Lemonade Stand’s NGINX container to run inside the cluster, not on a laptop. Kubernetes never runs a bare container. It always wraps one or more containers in a pod. To read any error message later, we need to know what a pod is, which fields it has, and which states it moves through.

title: 4. Pods
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipSquirrels carrying boxes



At the zoo in Phippy Goes to the Zoo, the first animals Zee sees are small, furry and blue, about the size of squirrels. Each one carries a tiny box and runs back and forth all day. Phippy says they are Pods, and the box each carries is its container. When the container is finished, the pod is finished too.
In the first Phippy book, Captain Kube invites Phippy to move her container “into a pod on board the ship”, and it feels like home. The pod is the cabin: it has a door number (an IP address) and a cupboard (volumes) shared by everyone in it.
A sidecar is exactly like a motorcycle sidecar. The main container drives. A small helper container rides along in the same pod and does one side job, such as reading the log book.

title: 4. Pods
text:
The concept, precisely

A pod is one or more containers that are always placed on the same node and share:

one network identity: one pod IP, and containers reach each other on localhost;
volumes that the pod declares.

Each pod gets its own IP from the cluster’s pod network. In k3s, Flannel hands out addresses from 10.42.0.0/16 by default.
Pods are ephemeral. If one is deleted, or its node dies, it is gone. A new pod gets a new name and a new IP. That is why we normally create pods through a controller such as a Deployment (lesson 6), and reach them through a Service (lesson 7).
The kubelet on the node starts the containers through containerd, and restarts them according to restartPolicy.
Every pod also has a tiny hidden pause container (mirrored-pause in lesson 1). It holds the shared network namespace open.


Pod phases (the status.phase field)







Phase
Meaning




Pending
Accepted, but not all containers are running yet: waiting for a node, pulling images, mounting volumes


Running
Bound to a node, and at least one container is running or restarting


Succeeded
All containers exited with code 0 and will not restart (typical for Jobs)


Failed
All containers have stopped, and at least one exited with an error


Unknown
The node stopped reporting





Container states and common reasons (kubectl get STATUS column)



State
Common reason
What it usually means




Waiting
ContainerCreating
Pulling the image or mounting volumes


Waiting
ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff
Wrong image name or tag, or a private registry without credentials


Waiting
CrashLoopBackOff
The container keeps exiting; the kubelet waits longer before each restart


Running
–
The process is running


Terminated
Completed
Exited with code 0


Terminated
Error
Exited with a non-zero code


Terminated
OOMKilled
Used more memory than its limit (lesson 11)



CrashLoopBackOff is not a phase. It is a reason shown while the kubelet waits between restarts.

title: 4. Pods
text:
Every field for this topic



Field
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




metadata.name
Pod name
Lowercase DNS name; controllers generate it for you
name: lemonade-pod


spec.containers[]
The containers to run
At least one
containers: [{name: web, image: …}]


containers[].name
Container name inside the pod
Unique within the pod
name: web


containers[].image
Image to run
Pin a version tag
image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.5-alpine


containers[].imagePullPolicy
When to pull
IfNotPresent (default for pinned tags), Always (default for :latest), Never
imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent


containers[].ports[].containerPort
The port the process listens on
Informational, but Services and probes can refer to it by name
containerPort: 8080


containers[].env[]
Environment variables
value, or valueFrom a ConfigMap or Secret
env: [{name: SHOP, value: lemonade}]


containers[].command
Replaces the image’s ENTRYPOINT
A list, one item per word
command: ["sh", "-c"]


containers[].args
Replaces the image’s CMD
A list
args: ["echo hello"]


containers[].resources
CPU and memory requests and limits
Lesson 11
requests: {cpu: 50m}


containers[].volumeMounts[]
Where a volume appears inside the container
name must match spec.volumes[].name
{name: menu, mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html}


spec.volumes[]
Volumes the pod provides
Lessons 9 and 10
volumes: [{name: menu, configMap: {name: lemonade-menu}}]


spec.restartPolicy
When the kubelet restarts containers
Always (default), OnFailure, Never
restartPolicy: Never


spec.initContainers[]
Containers that run to completion before the app starts
With restartPolicy: Always they become sidecars
initContainers: [{name: wait-db, …}]


spec.nodeName
Pin the pod to a node and skip the scheduler
Avoid; use scheduling rules instead
nodeName: k3s-lab



command and args follow a simple rule. If you set only args, the image’s own entrypoint runs with your arguments. If you set command, the image’s entrypoint is ignored.

title: 4. Pods
text:
Worked example
The smallest useful pod (04-pod.yaml):
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: lemonade-pod
  namespace: lemonade
spec:
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.5-alpine
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
kubectl apply -f 04-pod.yaml
kubectl get pod lemonade-pod -n lemonade -o wide
NAME           READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP          NODE
lemonade-pod   1/1     Running   0          7s    10.42.0.9   k3s-lab
The events tell the life story of the pod:
kubectl describe pod lemonade-pod -n lemonade      # bottom section
Events:
  Normal  Scheduled  default-scheduler  Successfully assigned lemonade/lemonade-pod to k3s-lab
  Normal  Pulling    kubelet            Pulling image "nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.5-alpine"
  Normal  Pulled     kubelet            Successfully pulled image … in 6.622s. Image size: 25944222 bytes.
  Normal  Created    kubelet            Container created
  Normal  Started    kubelet            Container started
Talk to it through a temporary tunnel, and run a command inside it:
kubectl port-forward -n lemonade pod/lemonade-pod 8080:8080 &
curl -s localhost:8080 | grep '<title>'
kubectl exec -n lemonade lemonade-pod -- nginx -v
<title>Welcome to nginx!</title>
nginx version: nginx/1.30.5

A sidecar
Here a busybox “till” writes sales into a shared emptyDir volume. A sidecar reads them. The single line restartPolicy: Always on an init container turns it into a sidecar that keeps running next to the app:
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: log-reader
      image: busybox:1.37.0
      restartPolicy: Always
      command: ["sh", "-c", "touch /shared/sales.log; tail -f /shared/sales.log"]
      volumeMounts: [{name: shared, mountPath: /shared}]
  containers:
    - name: till
      image: busybox:1.37.0
      command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do echo sold 1 lemonade >> /shared/sales.log; sleep 5; done"]
      volumeMounts: [{name: shared, mountPath: /shared}]
  volumes:
    - name: shared
      emptyDir: {}
kubectl get pod till-with-sidecar -n lemonade
kubectl logs till-with-sidecar -n lemonade -c log-reader --tail=3
NAME                READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
till-with-sidecar   2/2     Running   0          13s
sold 1 lemonade
sold 1 lemonade
sold 1 lemonade
2/2 means two containers, both ready. -c log-reader picks which container’s logs to show.


A crashing pod
kubectl run broken -n lemonade --image=busybox:1.37.0 -- sh -c 'echo out of lemons; exit 1'
kubectl get pod broken -n lemonade -w
NAME     READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
broken   0/1     ContainerCreating  0
broken   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   1
broken   0/1     Error              2
broken   0/1     Error              3
broken   1/1     Running            4
broken   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   4
The gaps between restarts grow each time. The logs show why it dies, and the events show the back-off:
kubectl logs broken -n lemonade
kubectl get events -n lemonade --field-selector involvedObject.name=broken
out of lemons
Warning   BackOff   pod/broken   Back-off restarting failed container broken in pod broken_lemonade(…)
Use kubectl logs --previous to read the output of the run before the latest restart. Clean up with kubectl delete pod broken -n lemonade.

title: 4. Pods
text:
Rules and conventions

One main process per container, and one main container per pod. Add more containers to the same pod only when they must share the same network or files (sidecars, helpers).
Do not create bare pods for apps. Use a Deployment, Job, DaemonSet or StatefulSet, so the pod is replaced after a failure.
Containers in a pod talk over localhost. Pods talk to other pods through Services, never through pod IPs, because pod IPs change.
Write command and args as YAML lists (["sh", "-c", "…"]). That avoids quoting surprises.
Debug in this order: kubectl get (status), kubectl describe (events), kubectl logs (output), kubectl logs --previous (output before the last crash).

title: 4. Pods
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Typo in the image tag
ErrImagePull, then ImagePullBackOff
Fix the tag; check it with docker pull


App exits immediately (a missing setting, a bad command)
CrashLoopBackOff with growing gaps
kubectl logs and kubectl logs --previous


Expecting pods to survive node loss
The pod disappears and nobody recreates it
Use a Deployment


Two containers in one pod on the same port
The second fails with “address already in use”
They share one network namespace; use different ports


Using containerPort to “open” a port
Nothing changes
The process decides which port it listens on; containerPort only documents it


Busybox or alpine pod with no long-running command
Completed, then CrashLoopBackOff under restartPolicy: Always
Give it a long-running command, or use a Job

title: 4. Pods
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
When a container keeps crashing, the kubelet waits longer before each new attempt. The Kubernetes documentation gives the delays as 10 s, 20 s, 40 s and so on, capped at 300 s, and resets them after the container has run for 10 minutes without trouble:
\[
d_k = \min\bigl(10 \cdot 2^{\,k-1},\; 300\bigr)
\]
where

\(k\) is the number of the back-off, counting from \(k = 1\) for the wait after the first repeated crash.
\(d_k\) is the delay in seconds before that restart attempt.
\(\min(a, b)\) picks the smaller of the two numbers. Here it caps the delay at 300 s, which is 5 minutes.

Example:

\(k = 1\): \(d_1 = \min(10 \cdot 2^{0}, 300) = \min(10, 300) = 10\) s.
\(k = 2\): \(d_2 = \min(10 \cdot 2^{1}, 300) = 20\) s.
\(k = 3\): \(d_3 = 40\) s, \(k = 4\): \(d_4 = 80\) s, \(k = 5\): \(d_5 = 160\) s.
\(k = 6\): \(10 \cdot 2^{5} = 320\), so \(d_6 = \min(320, 300) = 300\) s. From now on every wait is 5 minutes.

The total waiting before the seventh attempt is
\[
W_6 = \sum_{k=1}^{6} d_k = 10 + 20 + 40 + 80 + 160 + 300 = 610 \text{ s}
\]
where \(W_n\) is the sum of the first \(n\) delays, in seconds. That is just over 10 minutes. Our broken pod showed exactly this growth: restarts 1, 2, 3 came quickly, and the gap before restart 4 was clearly longer. On a busy laptop the real times drift by a few seconds, because the delay is a minimum wait, not an exact timer.
Why back off at all? If the kubelet restarted a broken container every second, then 100 broken pods would cause 100 restarts per second on one node. With back-off, after six crashes each pod restarts at most once every 300 s. 100 broken pods then cost about \(100 / 300 \approx 0.33\) restarts per second.
Kubernetes has an alpha feature gate, ReduceDefaultCrashLoopBackOffDecay, that would change these defaults to a 1 s start and a 60 s cap. It is off by default in v1.37, so the numbers above are what k3s does.

Kubernetes, “Sidecar Containers”: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/sidecar-containers/.

title: 11. Health, Resources and Scheduling
text:
Three things can still go wrong with the Lemonade Stand:

A frozen pod. NGINX hangs but the process does not exit. Kubernetes thinks everything is fine and keeps sending customers to it.
A greedy pod. One pod uses all the memory on a node and starves its neighbours. Or the cluster accepts more pods than it can really run.
Placement and demand. Some pods must run only on certain machines, and on a hot day three pods are not enough.

Probes answer the first problem, requests and limits the second, and the scheduler and the HorizontalPodAutoscaler the third.

title: 11. Health, Resources and Scheduling
text:
Three things can still go wrong with the Lemonade Stand:

A frozen pod. NGINX hangs but the process does not exit. Kubernetes thinks everything is fine and keeps sending customers to it.
A greedy pod. One pod uses all the memory on a node and starves its neighbours. Or the cluster accepts more pods than it can really run.
Placement and demand. Some pods must run only on certain machines, and on a hot day three pods are not enough.

Probes answer the first problem, requests and limits the second, and the scheduler and the HorizontalPodAutoscaler the third.

title: 11. Health, Resources and Scheduling
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipTetris and the school nurse



Kelsey Hightower, one of the best-known Kubernetes teachers, once explained scheduling at the Container World conference by playing Tetris on stage, as reported by Superuser in 2017. In the first game the blocks just fall wherever they happen to drop, “fully automated” but with no idea of the space they leave behind. Gaps pile up: wasted CPU and memory. In the second game a good player looks at each block’s shape and drops it where it fits best. The Kubernetes scheduler is that good player. A pod’s requests are its shape (“I need 50 millicores and 32 MiB”), and each node is a column with a certain amount of space.
Probes are the school nurse doing rounds:

Readiness: “Are you ready to serve customers?” If not, you sit out for a while, but you stay in school.
Liveness: “Are you even awake?” If you fail several times in a row, you are sent home and a fresh copy of you comes in (the container is restarted).
Startup: “This pupil is slow in the morning; do not check them until they have properly arrived.”

Taints are “Staff only” signs on a door. Only pods carrying the matching pass, a toleration, may go in.

title: 11. Health, Resources and Scheduling
text:
The concept, precisely

Probes
The kubelet runs each probe on every container that defines it. A probe can be:

httpGet: success means an HTTP status from 200 to 399;
tcpSocket: success means a connection opens;
exec: success means the command exits with 0;
grpc: the standard gRPC health check.









Probe
When it fails failureThreshold times in a row
Typical use




readinessProbe
The pod is removed from Service endpoints. No restart.
“Do not send me traffic yet” (warming up, overloaded, dependency down)


livenessProbe
The container is restarted
Recover from deadlocks and hangs


startupProbe
The container is restarted; liveness and readiness wait until startup succeeds
Slow-starting apps, without making liveness slow forever



Readiness also guards rolling updates (lesson 6). A new pod counts as available only once it is ready.


Requests and limits

A request is what the scheduler reserves for a container. Pods are placed only where the requests fit.
A limit is the most a container may use:

going over the CPU limit means the container is throttled (slowed down);
going over the memory limit means it is OOM-killed (OOMKilled) and restarted.

Units:

CPU in cores or millicores: 1 = 1000m, 50m = 0.05 of a core;
memory in bytes with suffixes: 64Mi = \(64 \times 2^{20}\) bytes (lesson 10 explains Mi versus M).

QoS classes follow from these settings and decide who is evicted first when a node runs out of memory:

BestEffort: no requests or limits at all. Evicted first.
Burstable: some requests or limits, but not equal for every resource. Evicted next.
Guaranteed: every container has CPU and memory limits equal to its requests. Evicted last.




The scheduler
For each new pod, the scheduler works in two steps:

Filter: drop every node where the pod cannot run, for example because its requests do not fit, it has no toleration for a taint, or it does not match the pod’s nodeSelector.
Score: rank the remaining nodes (spread, fit, affinity), then bind the pod to the best one.

If no node passes the filter, the pod stays Pending with a FailedScheduling event that says why.

nodeSelector: run only on nodes with these labels.
Node affinity: a richer version, with required and preferred rules.
Pod affinity / anti-affinity: run near, or away from, other pods. For example, “do not put two lemonade pods on the same node”.
Taints and tolerations: a node taint key=value:Effect repels pods that lack a matching toleration. The effects are:

NoSchedule: never place new pods here;
PreferNoSchedule: avoid if possible;
NoExecute: also evict running pods.




Autoscaling
A HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) changes a Deployment’s replicas based on metrics such as average CPU use relative to the request. k3s difference: k3s ships metrics-server, so kubectl top and CPU-based HPAs work on a fresh cluster. Upstream Kubernetes needs it installed separately.

title: 11. Health, Resources and Scheduling
section: Every field and command for this topic
text:
Every field and command for this topic

Probe fields (defaults in brackets)









Field
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




httpGet.path / .port
URL to check
Use a cheap endpoint

Port to connect to
For non-HTTP apps
tcpSocket: {port: 5432}

Command to run

Wait before the first probe [0]
Prefer a startupProbe for slow apps
initialDelaySeconds: 5

Time between probes [10]

periodSeconds: 5

Time to wait for an answer [1]

timeoutSeconds: 2

Failures in a row before acting [3]

failureThreshold: 3


successThreshold
Successes in a row to count as healthy again [1]
Must be 1 for liveness and startup
successThreshold: 1





Resource and placement fields









Field
What it does
Rule / convention
Example

Reserved amount used by the scheduler
Set it on every container

Hard maximum
Memory limit ≥ normal peak use
limits: {cpu: 200m, memory: 64Mi}


spec.nodeSelector

Simple, exact match

Keep pods apart
topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname means “different nodes”
podAntiAffinity: {preferredDuringScheduling…: …}

Must match the taint’s key, value and effect
tolerations: [{key: snack, value: cookies, effect: NoSchedule}]

maxSkew: 1

Field
What it does
Rule / convention
Example

What to scale
A Deployment or StatefulSet
{apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: lemonade-web}

Bounds
minReplicas ≥ 1
minReplicas: 3, maxReplicas: 10

Needs resources.requests set

Commands








Command
What it does
Example

kubectl label nodes
Label a node for nodeSelector

kubectl get hpa
Current and target metric, replica count
kubectl get hpa -n lemonade

kubectl autoscale deploy/lemonade-web --min=3 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70 -n lemonade


kubectl cordon / drain / uncordon
Stop scheduling on a node, evict its pods, allow again
kubectl drain k3s-lab --ignore-daemonsets

title: 11. Health, Resources and Scheduling
text:
Worked example
11-deployment-healthy.yaml is lesson 6’s Deployment with these lines added to the container:
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 50m, memory: 32Mi }
            limits: { cpu: 200m, memory: 64Mi }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
kubectl apply -f 11-deployment-healthy.yaml
kubectl describe pod <one-lemonade-web-pod> -n lemonade
kubectl get pod <one-lemonade-web-pod> -n lemonade -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
    Limits:     cpu: 200m   memory: 64Mi
    Requests:   cpu: 50m    memory: 32Mi
    Liveness:   http-get http://:8080/ delay=0s timeout=1s period=10s successThreshold=1 failureThreshold=3
    Readiness:  http-get http://:8080/ delay=0s timeout=1s period=5s successThreshold=1 failureThreshold=3
  Warning  Unhealthy  kubelet  Readiness probe failed: Get "http://10.42.0.30:8080/": dial tcp 10.42.0.30:8080: connect: connection refused
Burstable
The Unhealthy warning is the readiness probe doing its job. NGINX had not opened port 8080 yet, so the pod was kept out of the Service until a later probe succeeded. The QoS class is Burstable, because the limits are higher than the requests.

What the node has, and what is reserved
kubectl describe node k3s-lab
Allocatable:
  cpu:     16
  memory:  8123676Ki
Allocated resources:
  Resource   Requests     Limits
  cpu        250m (1%)    600m (3%)
  memory     166Mi (2%)   362Mi (4%)
The 250m of CPU requests are CoreDNS’s 100m plus our three web pods at 50m each. The scheduler only looks at these requests, not at live use.


A pod that does not fit
A pod that requests 100 whole CPUs (see the Mathematical Abstraction below):
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "100"
kubectl get pod greedy -n lemonade
kubectl get events -n lemonade --field-selector involvedObject.name=greedy
NAME     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
greedy   0/1     Pending   0          8s
Warning  FailedScheduling  pod/greedy  0/1 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu.
preemption: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.


A taint
kubectl taint nodes k3s-lab snack=cookies:NoSchedule
kubectl run taint-test -n lemonade --image=busybox:1.37.0 -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pod taint-test -n lemonade
kubectl taint nodes k3s-lab snack=cookies:NoSchedule-       # remove it
kubectl get pod taint-test -n lemonade
node/k3s-lab tainted
taint-test   0/1     Pending   0          9s
Warning  FailedScheduling  0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s).
node/k3s-lab untainted
taint-test   1/1     Running   0          19s
The same pod with this toleration would have been scheduled despite the sign:
  tolerations:
    - { key: snack, value: cookies, effect: NoSchedule }


Autoscaling
11-hpa.yaml keeps between 3 and 10 web pods, aiming at 70% of the CPU request:
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: lemonade-web }
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 }
Our lab cluster was started with --disable=metrics-server to save memory. That shows what happens when the HPA has no metrics:
kubectl apply -f 11-hpa.yaml
kubectl get hpa -n lemonade
kubectl describe hpa lemonade-web -n lemonade      # events
NAME           REFERENCE                 TARGETS              MINPODS   MAXPODS   REPLICAS
lemonade-web   Deployment/lemonade-web   cpu: <unknown>/70%   3         10        3
Warning  FailedGetResourceMetric  horizontal-pod-autoscaler  failed to get cpu utilization: unable to get
metrics for resource cpu: unable to fetch metrics from resource metrics API: the server could not find
the requested resource (get pods.metrics.k8s.io)
The HPA keeps the current replica count and waits. We then started a second lab cluster with k3s’s metrics-server, the default, and applied the same files:
kubectl top pods -n lemonade
kubectl get hpa -n lemonade
NAME                            CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
lemonade-web-66587fd89c-9jkvk   1m           12Mi
lemonade-web-66587fd89c-gdtc4   1m           12Mi
lemonade-web-66587fd89c-hwwv7   1m           12Mi

NAME           REFERENCE                 TARGETS       MINPODS   MAXPODS   REPLICAS
lemonade-web   Deployment/lemonade-web   cpu: 2%/70%   3         10        3
Each idle pod uses 1m of its 50m request, which is \(1/50 = 2\%\). The Mathematical Abstraction section below shows why the HPA still keeps 3 replicas.

title: 11. Health, Resources and Scheduling
text:
Rules and conventions

Give every long-running container a readiness probe. Add a liveness probe only if the app can hang without exiting, and make it check the process itself, not its dependencies, or one database outage restarts everything.
Use a startupProbe for slow starters instead of a large initialDelaySeconds on liveness.
Set CPU and memory requests on every container. Without them the scheduler is playing Tetris blindfolded, and the HPA cannot compute utilisation.
Set a memory limit close to the real peak. Be careful with CPU limits: throttling can make latency spiky, and many teams set CPU requests only.
Use labels plus nodeSelector or affinity to choose nodes, and taints to keep ordinary pods off special nodes.
Keep minReplicas ≥ 2 for anything customer-facing, so one pod can fail while the HPA reacts.

title: 11. Health, Resources and Scheduling
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Liveness probe that checks the database
All pods restart together when the database blips
Check only the app; put dependency checks in readiness


Liveness probe too strict for a slow start
CrashLoopBackOff with Liveness probe failed
Add a startupProbe, or raise failureThreshold


No requests
Pods pile onto one node; HPA shows <unknown>
Set resources.requests


Memory limit below real use
OOMKilled, then restarts
Raise the limit; measure with kubectl top


Requests larger than any node
Pending, Insufficient cpu or Insufficient memory
Lower the requests, or add a bigger node


Taint without a matching toleration
Pending, untolerated taint
Add a toleration, or remove the taint


HPA while metrics-server is disabled
TARGETS <unknown>/70%, FailedGetResourceMetric
Keep k3s’s metrics-server enabled

title: 11. Health, Resources and Scheduling
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

How fast a failure is noticed
A probe acts after failureThreshold failures in a row, spaced periodSeconds apart. The worst case, from the moment the app breaks until Kubernetes acts, is about
\[
t_{\text{detect}} \le T \cdot F + \tau
\]
where

\(T\) is periodSeconds, the time between probes, in seconds.
\(F\) is failureThreshold, the number of failures in a row needed.
\(\tau\) is timeoutSeconds, how long the last probe may wait for an answer.
\(t_{\text{detect}}\) is the time until the pod is marked unready (readiness) or restarted (liveness).

Example: the readiness probe has \(T = 5\), \(F = 3\), \(\tau = 1\), so \(t \le 5 \times 3 + 1 = 16\) s before customers stop being sent to a frozen pod. The liveness probe has \(T = 10\), \(F = 3\), \(\tau = 1\), so \(t \le 10 \times 3 + 1 = 31\) s before it is restarted. Readiness is deliberately quicker: stopping traffic is cheap, a restart is not.


CPU units
\[
c_{\text{cores}} = \frac{c_{\text{milli}}}{1000}
\]
where \(c_{\text{milli}}\) is a CPU amount in millicores (the m suffix), and \(c_{\text{cores}}\) is the same amount in whole cores.
Example: a request of 50m is \(50 / 1000 = 0.05\) cores, one twentieth of one core. The limit 200m is \(0.2\) cores. Three web pods request \(3 \times 0.05 = 0.15\) cores in total.


Does a pod fit on a node?
The scheduler’s resource filter keeps node \(n\) only if
\[
\sum_{q \in Q_n} r_q + r_{\text{new}} \le A_n
\]
where

\(Q_n\) is the set of pods already on node \(n\).
\(r_q\) is the request of pod \(q\) for one resource (CPU or memory). Each resource is checked separately.
\(r_{\text{new}}\) is the new pod’s request for the same resource.
\(A_n\) is the node’s allocatable amount of that resource.

Example (CPU): the lab node has \(A = 16\) cores \(= 16{,}000\)m, and \(\sum r_q = 250\)m is already requested. Another web pod: \(250 + 50 = 300 \le 16{,}000\), so it fits. The greedy pod: \(250 + 100{,}000 = 100{,}250 > 16{,}000\), so it does not fit. That is exactly the Insufficient cpu event.
Example (memory): \(A = 8{,}123{,}676\) Ki, and \(166\) Mi \(= 166 \times 1024 = 169{,}984\) Ki is requested. The node could accept about \(\lfloor (8{,}123{,}676 - 169{,}984) / (32 \times 1024) \rfloor = \lfloor 7{,}953{,}692 / 32{,}768 \rfloor = 242\) more web pods by memory requests. Requests are a promise, not a measurement. Live use can be lower or higher.


How the HPA chooses a replica count
\[
d = \left\lceil c \cdot \frac{m}{g} \right\rceil, \qquad \text{scale only if } \left| \frac{m}{g} - 1 \right| > 0.1
\]
where

\(c\) is the current number of replicas.
\(m\) is the current metric: average CPU use as a percentage of the request, across the pods.
\(g\) is the target, averageUtilization.
\(d\) is the desired number of replicas, which is then clamped between minReplicas and maxReplicas.
\(0.1\) is the default tolerance. Changes within ±10% of the target are ignored, so the HPA does not flap.

Example (measured): the idle stand above had \(c = 3\), \(m = 2\%\) and \(g = 70\%\). The ratio is \(2 / 70 \approx 0.029\), and \(|0.029 - 1| = 0.971 > 0.1\), so the HPA computes \(d = \lceil 3 \times 0.029 \rceil = \lceil 0.086 \rceil = 1\). That is below minReplicas, so it is clamped up to 3, exactly the REPLICAS 3 shown.
Example: a hot afternoon. \(c = 3\), \(m = 140\%\) (each pod uses 70m of its 50m request) and \(g = 70\%\). The ratio is \(140 / 70 = 2\), and \(|2 - 1| = 1 > 0.1\), so it scales: \(d = \lceil 3 \times 2 \rceil = 6\) pods. On a cool morning, \(m = 75\%\) gives a ratio of \(75 / 70 \approx 1.07\), and \(|1.07 - 1| = 0.07 \le 0.1\), so it stays at 3. On a very hot day, \(m = 300\%\) gives \(d = \lceil 3 \times 300/70 \rceil = \lceil 12.86 \rceil = 13\), which is clamped to maxReplicas = 10.

title: 13. Helm and Auto-Deploy
text:
By now the Lemonade Stand is a folder of YAML files. Three new wishes appear:

Staging and production differ only a little: two replicas in staging, five in production, another image tag. Copying every file per environment invites mistakes.
Installing someone else’s software, such as a monitoring tool or a database, should be one command, not forty files.
The cluster should set itself up. When a new k3s server starts, it should install the things it always needs without anyone typing commands.

Helm solves the first two. The k3s Helm controller and auto-deploy folder solve the third.

title: 13. Helm and Auto-Deploy
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipA recipe card with blanks



A Helm chart is a recipe card with blanks: “Make ___ cups of lemonade with ___ spoons of sugar.” The values fill in the blanks: cups: 3, sugar: 2. You can use the same card for a small party and a big one, with different values.
When you actually make a batch, that batch is a release. Helm writes each batch in its notebook as revision 1, 2, 3…. If today’s batch tastes bad, you say “make it the way we did in revision 1” (a rollback).
A chart repository is the library where people share recipe cards.
Fun fact: Helm was born at a company called Deis in 2015. One of its co-creators is Matt Butcher, the same person who wrote The Illustrated Children’s Guide to Kubernetes with Phippy the giraffe.
The k3s auto-deploy folder is a letterbox in the school office. Drop a note in the box, and the office does what it says, every morning, even after the holidays. A HelmChart note in that box says: “please cook this recipe with these values.”

title: 13. Helm and Auto-Deploy
text:
The concept, precisely

Chart: a folder with

Chart.yaml (name, version, appVersion);
values.yaml (the default values);
templates/ (manifests with Go-template placeholders such as { .Values.replicas } and { .Release.Name }).

Values: the settings that fill the templates. Later sources override earlier ones: the chart’s values.yaml, then files passed with -f, then --set.
Release: one installation of a chart, under a name, in a namespace. Helm stores each revision as a Secret in that namespace. That is how history and rollback work.
Repository: an HTTP index of charts (helm repo add, or --repo URL), or an OCI registry (oci://ghcr.io/...).
Helm 4 is the current major version (the lab used v4.3.2). Its everyday commands are the same as Helm 3. One renamed flag: --atomic is now --rollback-on-failure.

k3s difference: the Helm controller. k3s runs a controller that watches HelmChart objects (helm.cattle.io/v1). For each one it runs a short-lived Job called helm-install-<name>, which runs helm install or helm upgrade inside the cluster. Deleting the object uninstalls the chart. Traefik itself is installed this way.
HelmChartConfig objects add values to a chart that k3s installs, for example to customise Traefik (lesson 8). Its name and namespace must match the HelmChart.
k3s difference: the auto-deploy folder. Any manifest file placed in /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/ on a server is applied automatically, like kubectl apply, at start-up and whenever the file changes. Each file becomes an AddOn object in kube-system. Three things to know:

Deleting the file does not delete what it created.
A .skip file next to it (traefik.yaml.skip) makes k3s ignore that manifest.
k3s does not copy these files between servers. With several servers, keep them identical yourself.

title: 13. Helm and Auto-Deploy
section: Every command and field for this topic
text:
Every command and field for this topic

Helm commands









Command
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




helm create
Generate a starter chart
Delete what you do not need
helm create lemonade


helm lint
Check a chart for problems
Run it in CI
helm lint ./13-lemonade-chart


helm template
Render the manifests locally, install nothing
Review what would be applied
helm template lemonade ./13-lemonade-chart --set replicas=3


helm install
Create a release
--create-namespace creates the namespace
helm install lemonade ./13-lemonade-chart -n lemonade-helm --create-namespace


helm upgrade
New revision with a new chart or new values
--install creates it if missing (good for CI)
helm upgrade --install lemonade ./13-lemonade-chart -n lemonade-helm --set replicas=3


helm rollback
Go back to an earlier revision
Creates a new revision
helm rollback lemonade 1 -n lemonade-helm


helm history
List revisions

helm history lemonade -n lemonade-helm


helm list
List releases
-A for all namespaces
helm list -n lemonade-helm


helm get values
Values a release was installed with
--all includes the defaults
helm get values lemonade -n lemonade-helm


helm uninstall
Remove a release

helm uninstall lemonade -n lemonade-helm


helm show values
Default values of a chart
Read before overriding
helm show values --repo https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo podinfo


helm repo add / update
Register or refresh a repository
Or pass --repo per command
helm repo add podinfo https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo











Flag
What it does
Example




--set key=value
Override one value
--set replicas=3


-f file.yaml
Override many values from a file
-f values-prod.yaml


-n / --create-namespace
Target namespace, and create it if missing
-n lemonade-helm --create-namespace


--version
Pin the chart version
--version 6.17.0


--wait / --timeout
Wait until the resources are ready
--wait --timeout 5m


--rollback-on-failure
Roll back automatically if the upgrade fails (Helm 4)
--rollback-on-failure


--dry-run
Simulate an install or upgrade
--dry-run=server





HelmChart fields (k3s)









Field
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




metadata.namespace
Where the HelmChart object lives
Usually kube-system
namespace: kube-system


spec.repo
Chart repository URL

repo: https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo


spec.chart
Chart name, or a URL to a .tgz

chart: podinfo


spec.version
Chart version
Pin it
version: 6.17.0


spec.targetNamespace
Where the chart’s resources go
Default default
targetNamespace: lemonade


spec.createNamespace
Create the target namespace
Default false
createNamespace: true


spec.valuesContent
Values as an inline YAML block
Like a -f file
see the worked example below


spec.set
Simple value overrides
Wins over valuesContent
set: {replicaCount: "2"}


spec.timeout / spec.failurePolicy
Helm timeout; reinstall (default) or abort on failure

failurePolicy: abort

title: 13. Helm and Auto-Deploy
text:
Worked example

A tiny chart
13-lemonade-chart/ has three files. The template uses two placeholders from the release and the values:
# Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: lemonade
version: 0.1.0
appVersion: "1.30.5"
# values.yaml
replicas: 2
image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.5-alpine
# templates/deployment.yaml (excerpt)
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-web
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicas }}
  # …
        - name: web
          image: {{ .Values.image }}
Render it without a cluster:
helm lint ./13-lemonade-chart
helm template lemonade ./13-lemonade-chart --set replicas=3 | grep -E 'name: lemonade-web|replicas'
1 chart(s) linted, 0 chart(s) failed
  name: lemonade-web
  replicas: 3


Install, upgrade, roll back
helm install lemonade ./13-lemonade-chart -n lemonade-helm --create-namespace --wait
helm upgrade lemonade ./13-lemonade-chart -n lemonade-helm --set replicas=3 --wait
kubectl get deploy -n lemonade-helm
helm get values lemonade -n lemonade-helm
STATUS: deployed
REVISION: 1
Release "lemonade" has been upgraded. Happy Helming!
REVISION: 2
NAME           READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
lemonade-web   3/3     3            3
USER-SUPPLIED VALUES:
replicas: 3
helm rollback lemonade 1 -n lemonade-helm --wait
helm history lemonade -n lemonade-helm
kubectl get deploy -n lemonade-helm
Rollback was a success! Happy Helming!
REVISION   STATUS       CHART            DESCRIPTION
1          superseded   lemonade-0.1.0   Install complete
2          superseded   lemonade-0.1.0   Upgrade complete
3          deployed     lemonade-0.1.0   Rollback to 1
NAME           READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
lemonade-web   2/2     2            2
Like kubectl rollout undo in lesson 6, a rollback creates a new revision (3) that copies an old one (1). Replicas went back to the chart’s default of 2.


Let k3s install a chart: the HelmChart resource
13-helmchart.yaml asks k3s to install the public podinfo demo chart (by Stefan Prodan) into the lemonade namespace:
apiVersion: helm.cattle.io/v1
kind: HelmChart
metadata:
  name: podinfo
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  repo: https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo
  chart: podinfo
  version: 6.17.0
  targetNamespace: lemonade
  valuesContent: |-
    replicaCount: 1
kubectl apply -f 13-helmchart.yaml
kubectl get helmchart podinfo -n kube-system
kubectl get job helm-install-podinfo -n kube-system
kubectl get pods -n lemonade -l app.kubernetes.io/name=podinfo
helm list -n lemonade
helmchart.helm.cattle.io/podinfo created
NAME      REPO                                     CHART     VERSION   TARGETNAMESPACE   FAILED
podinfo   https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo   podinfo   6.17.0    lemonade          False

NAME                   STATUS     COMPLETIONS   DURATION
helm-install-podinfo   Complete   1/1           10s

NAME                      READY   STATUS              RESTARTS   AGE
podinfo-c6497595d-dsmkf   0/1     ContainerCreating   0          3s

NAME      NAMESPACE   REVISION   STATUS     CHART            APP VERSION
podinfo   lemonade    1          deployed   podinfo-6.17.0   6.17.0
We never ran helm install. The Helm controller started the Job helm-install-podinfo, which ran Helm inside the cluster in 10 seconds, and the podinfo pod started right after. The last command shows that it is an ordinary Helm release, which the helm CLI can see too. To change the values, edit the HelmChart and apply it again. To uninstall, delete the HelmChart.


The auto-deploy folder
Copy any manifest into the server’s manifests folder. Here it is a tiny ConfigMap with the opening hours (13-opening-hours.yaml):
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: opening-hours
  namespace: lemonade
data:
  hours: "10:00-18:00"
docker cp 13-opening-hours.yaml k3s-lab:/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/opening-hours.yaml
# on a Linux server: sudo cp 13-opening-hours.yaml /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/opening-hours.yaml
kubectl get addon opening-hours -n kube-system
kubectl get configmap opening-hours -n lemonade -o jsonpath='{.data.hours}'
NAME            SOURCE                                                     CHECKSUM
opening-hours   /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/opening-hours.yaml   28db14dd18a3…
10:00-18:00
The file became an AddOn called opening-hours (named after the file), and k3s applied the ConfigMap within seconds, without kubectl apply. The checksum lets k3s notice when the file changes, and it applies the file again on the next change and on every restart.
Combine the two ideas, a HelmChart file in the manifests folder, and a brand-new k3s server installs your charts on its first boot. The Ansible part shows how to place such files on many servers at once.

title: 13. Helm and Auto-Deploy
text:
Rules and conventions

Use plain manifests while an app is small. Move to a chart when you really need the same app with different values in several places.
Pin chart versions (--version, spec.version) exactly as you pin image tags.
Keep per-environment values in files (values-staging.yaml, values-prod.yaml) in Git. Use --set only for one-off values such as an image tag from CI.
In CI, run helm lint and helm template, then helm upgrade --install --wait --rollback-on-failure.
Do not manage the same release with both the helm CLI and a k3s HelmChart object. Pick one owner.
Never edit k3s’s own packaged manifests. Add your own files, and use HelmChartConfig to change packaged charts.
Remember that removing a file from the auto-deploy folder does not uninstall anything. Delete the objects (or the HelmChart) explicitly.

title: 13. Helm and Auto-Deploy
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




--set replicas=3 on install, forgotten on upgrade
Upgrade resets replicas to the default
Keep values in a file, or use --reuse-values carefully


Installing a release twice
cannot re-use a name that is still in use
helm upgrade --install


Wrong value name (replica instead of replicas)
Nothing changes, and Helm gives no error
Check with helm template and helm show values


Underscore in an auto-deploy file name
AddOn … is invalid: metadata.name
File names become object names: use lowercase and -


HelmChart object in the wrong namespace
Nothing gets installed
Put it in kube-system (or where the Helm controller watches) and set targetNamespace


Different manifests on different servers
Objects flip between versions
Keep the auto-deploy folders identical on all servers

title: 13. Helm and Auto-Deploy
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

Which value wins
A value is looked up in an ordered list of sources, and the last source that defines it wins:
\[
v(k) = s_j(k), \qquad j = \max \lbrace i \mid k \in \operatorname{dom}(s_i) \rbrace
\]
where

\(k\) is a value key, such as replicas.
\(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_m\) are the value sources in increasing precedence. For the helm CLI: \(s_1\) is the chart’s values.yaml, then the -f files in the order given, then --set.
\(\operatorname{dom}(s_i)\) is the set of keys that source \(s_i\) defines, and \(s_i(k)\) is its value for \(k\).
\(j\) is the index of the highest-precedence source that defines \(k\), and \(v(k)\) is the value that ends up in the templates.

Example: the chart says replicas: 2 (\(s_1\)), values-prod.yaml says replicas: 4 (\(s_2\)), and the command adds --set replicas=5 (\(s_3\)). All three define replicas, so \(j = \max \lbrace 1, 2, 3 \rbrace = 3\) and \(v = 5\). Drop the --set, and \(j = 2\), so \(v = 4\). The key image is defined only in \(s_1\), so \(j = 1\) and the default image is used. In our upgrade, --set replicas=3 gave \(v = 3\). The rollback restored revision 1’s values, where only \(s_1\) applied, so \(v = 2\).
k3s’s HelmChart uses the same rule with its own documented order: chart defaults, then HelmChart.spec.valuesContent, then valuesSecrets, then HelmChartConfig.spec.valuesContent, then its valuesSecrets, and finally HelmChart.spec.set, which wins.


Release revisions
\[
r_{\text{new}} = \max(R) + 1
\]
where \(R\) is the set of revision numbers stored for the release, and \(r_{\text{new}}\) is the number given to the next install, upgrade or rollback.
Example: after the upgrade, \(R = \lbrace 1, 2 \rbrace\), so helm rollback lemonade 1 created \(r_{\text{new}} = 2 + 1 = 3\), with revision 1’s contents. Unlike kubectl rollout undo, Helm keeps the copied revision (1) in its history and marks it superseded.

title: 1. Containers and Orchestration
text:
Sam built the Lemonade Stand web page on a laptop. It works there. On the shop’s server it fails: the server has a different NGINX version, a missing configuration file, and another program already using the same port.
Once that is fixed, a second problem appears. The page runs on one server. If that server reboots for an update, the stand is closed. If a school trip arrives and 200 children open the menu at once, one server is too slow.
We need two things:

A way to package the app together with everything it needs, so it runs the same way everywhere. That is a container.
Something that runs many copies of that package on several machines, restarts them when they die, and sends customers to the healthy ones. That is an orchestrator. Kubernetes is one, and k3s is a small Kubernetes.

title: 1. Containers and Orchestration
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipPhippy finds a home



In The Illustrated Children’s Guide to Kubernetes, written by Matt Butcher, illustrated by Bailey Beougher and designed by Karen Chu, there is a little app called Phippy. She is a one-page PHP app. She lives at a crowded hosting company next to strange apps she does not know. She wishes for a place of her own.
A friendly whale (a nod to Docker’s logo) tells her to move into a container. It is a tidy little room with everything she needs. But a container on its own is “like a fancy living room floating in the middle of the ocean”: nobody connects it to the network, restarts it, or gives it company. Then Captain Kube sails up on a huge ship made of many rafts tied together, and Phippy finds a real home on board. Kubernetes is the Greek word for a ship’s captain or helmsman.
Cookies. An image is a cookie cutter. A container is a cookie made with it. You can make 100 identical cookies from one cutter. Eating a cookie does not damage the cutter. A registry is the shop shelf where everyone keeps and shares their cookie cutters.
Pets and cattle. Randy Bias tells the story this way, building on a talk about scaling SQL Server by Microsoft’s Bill Baker. A pet server has a name, like “Bob the mail server”. When Bob is sick, everyone stops working to nurse him. Cattle servers are numbered (www001 to www100). When one gets sick, you replace it and the herd carries on. Kubernetes treats containers as cattle. That is why we never name a pod “Bob”.

title: 1. Containers and Orchestration
text:
The concept, precisely

Container image: a read-only package of files, made of stacked layers: an operating-system userland, libraries, your app, and metadata such as which command to run. It is identified by a name and a tag, for example nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.5-alpine. It can also be pinned to a digest (@sha256:…), which is a fingerprint of the exact bytes.
Container: a normal Linux process started from an image. The kernel isolates it with namespaces, so it has its own view of files, network and process IDs. cgroups limit how much CPU and memory it can use. It shares the host’s kernel.
Registry: a server that stores images, for example Docker Hub (docker.io) or GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io). Machines pull images from it.
Container runtime: the program on each machine that pulls images and starts containers. k3s ships with containerd. You do not need Docker on a k3s node.
Orchestrator: software that decides where containers run and keeps them in the state you asked for. It restarts them, scales them, connects them, and updates them gradually.


Container vs virtual machine









Virtual machine
Container




What is inside
A whole guest operating system, including its own kernel
Only the app and its files; uses the host kernel


Start-up time
Tens of seconds to minutes
Usually under a second to a few seconds


Typical size
Gigabytes
Megabytes (our NGINX image is a 26 MB download, 90 MB unpacked)


Isolation
Very strong (hardware virtualisation)
Strong, but containers share one kernel


Good for
Running different operating systems, strong tenant separation
Packaging and shipping apps many times a day





What an orchestrator does for the Lemonade Stand








Need
Without an orchestrator
With Kubernetes / k3s




Run 3 copies
Log in to 3 servers by hand
Write replicas: 3


A copy crashes
Someone notices and restarts it
Restarted automatically


A server dies
Its copies are gone
Copies are recreated on other servers


Customers need one address
Configure a load balancer by hand
A Service gives one stable address


New version
Stop, copy, start, and hope
A rolling update replaces copies one by one

title: 1. Containers and Orchestration
text:
Worked example
Start the Lemonade Stand image as a plain container on your laptop. This shows what an image is before Kubernetes is involved:
docker run --rm -d --name lemonade -p 8080:8080 nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30.5-alpine
curl -s localhost:8080 | grep '<title>'
docker rm -f lemonade
<title>Welcome to nginx!</title>
The same image is just as easy to start a hundred times. Deciding where those hundred copies should run is the hard part, and the orchestrator does it.
Now look inside the lab k3s node. It has no Docker. containerd holds the images that k3s itself uses:
docker exec k3s-lab crictl images
IMAGE                                        TAG                     SIZE
docker.io/rancher/klipper-lb                 v0.4.17                 5.79MB
docker.io/rancher/local-path-provisioner     v0.0.37                 13.4MB
docker.io/rancher/mirrored-coredns-coredns   1.14.7                  21.7MB
docker.io/rancher/mirrored-library-traefik   3.7.15                  50.2MB
docker.io/rancher/mirrored-pause             3.10.2                  268kB
These are the bundled add-ons: the ServiceLB load balancer (klipper-lb), storage, DNS and the Traefik ingress controller. Lesson 2 explains each one.

title: 1. Containers and Orchestration
text:
Rules and conventions

Build one image per app and run it everywhere: laptop, CI and cluster. Configure it with settings (lesson 9), not by rebuilding.
Pin image tags to a real version (1.30.5-alpine). latest changes under your feet, so two nodes can run different code with the same name.
Keep images small. The image travels to every node, and a smaller one starts faster.
Treat containers as cattle. Never fix a running container by hand; change the image or the manifest and replace the container.
Do not store data inside a container’s own filesystem. It disappears when the container is replaced. Use volumes (lesson 10).

Mistake
Symptom

The fix disappears after a restart

Expecting Docker on a k3s node
docker: command not found
Use k3s crictl and k3s ctr, or just kubectl


Image only exists on your laptop
Pod shows ErrImagePull
Push it to a registry, or import it with k3s ctr images import

title: 1. Containers and Orchestration
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Why run copies at all? Suppose each copy of the stand is unavailable some fraction of the time, and the copies fail independently of each other. Then the stand is closed only when all copies are down at the same moment:
\[
P_{\text{closed}} = p^{\,n}
\]
where

\(p\) is the probability that one copy is down at a random moment. It is a number between 0 and 1, for example \(0.05\) means “down 5% of the time”.
\(n\) is the number of copies (replicas), a whole number \(\ge 1\).
\(P_{\text{closed}}\) is the probability that the whole stand is closed, also between 0 and 1.

Example: with one copy, \(p = 0.05\) and \(n = 1\) give \(P_{\text{closed}} = 0.05^{1} = 0.05\), which is 5% of the time. With three copies:
\[
0.05^{3} = 0.05 \times 0.05 \times 0.05 = 0.000125
\]
That is \(0.0125\%\) of the time, about 66 minutes a year instead of about 18 days a year.
Assumption: the formula only holds if the copies fail independently. If all three run on the same machine and that machine dies, they fail together and the real \(P_{\text{closed}}\) is close to the machine’s own failure rate. This is why the scheduler spreads pods across nodes (lesson 11).
A second, illustrative calculation shows why containers make many copies cheap. If a machine has \(M\) MiB of memory and each copy needs \(m\) MiB, the number of copies that fit is
\[
k = \left\lfloor \frac{M}{m} \right\rfloor
\]
where \(M\) and \(m\) are in mebibytes (MiB), and \(\lfloor x \rfloor\) means “round down to a whole number”, because you cannot run 0.4 of a copy.
Example (illustrative numbers): take \(M = 4096\) MiB. A small VM that needs \(m = 512\) MiB for its own operating system plus 16 MiB for NGINX gives \(\lfloor 4096 / 528 \rfloor = \lfloor 7.76 \rfloor = 7\) copies. A container that needs only \(m = 16\) MiB gives \(\lfloor 4096 / 16 \rfloor = 256\) copies. Real numbers depend on the app, but the gap explains why containers became the unit that clusters schedule.

title: 9. ConfigMaps and Secrets
text:
The menu prices live inside the web page. If they were baked into the image, changing “Pink lemonade 2.50” to 2.75 would need a new image, a new build and a new rollout. Also, the cash register needs a payment API key. That key must not be in the image or in Git, where anyone who can pull or read them would see it.
We want:

Settings (the menu, opening hours) stored next to the app, and changeable without rebuilding. That is a ConfigMap.
Secrets (keys, passwords, certificates) stored separately, with tighter access. That is a Secret.

title: 9. ConfigMaps and Secrets
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipThe chalkboard and the secret burrows



A ConfigMap is the chalkboard menu outside the stand. When lemons get more expensive, you rub out “2.50” and write “2.75”. You do not rebuild the stand.
In Phippy Goes to the Zoo, Zee walks past burrows where clearly something lives, but she cannot see anything. “The Secrets are in here,” says Phippy, “but you can’t see them without these decoder glasses.” That is a Secret: it is kept out of plain sight, and only someone with the right glasses (permission) can look.
But here is the grown-up warning. The “glasses” Kubernetes uses by default are very simple. Secret values are written in base64, which is like writing a message in Pig Latin. It hides the text from a quick glance, but anyone who knows the trick can read it. The real protection is who is allowed to open the burrow (access rules) and whether the cluster’s notebook is locked (encryption at rest).

title: 9. ConfigMaps and Secrets

title: 9. ConfigMaps and Secrets
text:
Worked example
The menu ConfigMap (09-configmap.yaml) holds one file. The Deployment from lesson 6 mounts it as NGINX’s HTML folder:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: lemonade-menu
  namespace: lemonade
data:
  index.html: |
    <h1>Lemonade Stand</h1>
    <p>Classic lemonade: 2.00</p>
    <p>Pink lemonade: 2.50</p>

Change a price without a new image
Apply an edited copy, then poll the live site through the Ingress until the new price appears:
sed 's/2.50/2.75/' 09-configmap.yaml | kubectl apply -f -
# poll every 3 s
curl -s -H 'Host: lemonade.localhost' http://localhost:8081/ | grep Pink
configmap/lemonade-menu configured
new price after 19s
<p>Pink lemonade: 2.75</p>
There was no rollout and no restart. The kubelet rewrote the mounted file after 19 seconds, and NGINX simply served the new file.


A Secret as an environment variable
09-secret.yaml creates the Secret with stringData, and a cashier pod that reads it:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: lemonade-payment
  namespace: lemonade
type: Opaque
stringData:
  PAYMENT_API_KEY: demo-key-123
---
# … in the cashier pod's container:
      env:
        - name: PAYMENT_API_KEY
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: lemonade-payment
              key: PAYMENT_API_KEY
kubectl apply -f 09-secret.yaml
kubectl get secret lemonade-payment -n lemonade -o jsonpath='{.data.PAYMENT_API_KEY}'; echo
kubectl get secret lemonade-payment -n lemonade -o jsonpath='{.data.PAYMENT_API_KEY}' | base64 -d; echo
kubectl logs cashier -n lemonade
ZGVtby1rZXktMTIz
demo-key-123
key length: 12
The second command is the “decoder glasses”. Anyone who may get the Secret can read it, which is why access to Secrets must be restricted.


Updating a Secret does not update env vars
kubectl create secret generic lemonade-payment -n lemonade \
  --from-literal=PAYMENT_API_KEY=new-key-4567890 --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl exec cashier -n lemonade -- sh -c 'echo ${#PAYMENT_API_KEY} $PAYMENT_API_KEY'
secret/lemonade-payment configured
12 demo-key-123
The running pod still has the old 12-character key. Environment variables were fixed when the container started. Restart the workload (kubectl rollout restart) to pick up a new key, or mount the Secret as a volume if the app can re-read files.
Finally, the k3s-specific check:
docker exec k3s-lab k3s secrets-encrypt status
Encryption Status: Disabled, no configuration file found
The lab cluster was started without --secrets-encryption, so Secrets sit in SQLite base64-encoded only. Turn it on for any real cluster.

title: 9. ConfigMaps and Secrets
text:
Rules and conventions

Anything that differs between environments (prices, URLs, feature switches) goes into a ConfigMap. Anything that would hurt if leaked goes into a Secret. The image stays the same everywhere.
Never commit real Secret values to Git. Create them from a secret store or a CI secret (CI/CD part), or use an encrypting tool such as Sealed Secrets or SOPS.
Enable --secrets-encryption on k3s servers, and limit who may get or list Secrets with RBAC.
Prefer volumes for data that should update live, and env vars for values read at start-up. After changing env-var sources, run kubectl rollout restart.
A common pattern for safe rollouts: put a version in the name (lemonade-menu-v2), mark it immutable: true, and point the Deployment at the new name. The change then goes through a normal, reversible rolling update.

title: 9. ConfigMaps and Secrets
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Thinking base64 is encryption
The key leaks through kubectl get secret -o yaml or a backup
Restrict access with RBAC; enable --secrets-encryption


echo 'key' \| base64 for data
The value contains a hidden newline, and authentication fails
echo -n 'key' \| base64, or use stringData


Expecting env vars to change after an update
The app still uses the old value
kubectl rollout restart deploy/…


Mounting with subPath and expecting live updates
The file never changes
Mount the whole directory, or restart the pods


ConfigMap or Secret missing when the pod starts
CreateContainerConfigError
Create it first, or mark the reference optional: true


A volume mounted over an existing folder
The image’s own files in that folder disappear
Mount to a dedicated path, or use items

title: 9. ConfigMaps and Secrets
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

How much bigger base64 makes a value
Base64 turns every 3 bytes into 4 printable characters, padding the last group:
\[
b = 4 \left\lceil \frac{n}{3} \right\rceil
\]
where

\(n\) is the length of the original value in bytes.
\(\lceil x \rceil\) means round up to a whole number, because a partial group still produces 4 characters.
\(b\) is the length of the base64 text in characters (bytes).

Example: demo-key-123 has \(n = 12\) bytes, so \(b = 4 \lceil 12/3 \rceil = 4 \times 4 = 16\). The real value ZGVtby1rZXktMTIz has exactly 16 characters. For the rotated key new-key-4567890, \(n = 15\) gives \(b = 4 \times 5 = 20\). For a 1,000,000-byte file, \(b = 4 \lceil 333{,}333.3 \rceil = 4 \times 333{,}334 = 1{,}333{,}336\) bytes. So a file of about 1 MB no longer fits in a 1 MiB (\(1{,}048{,}576\)-byte) Secret once it is encoded. Encoding costs about 33% extra space, and it buys no secrecy: decoding needs no key.


How long a volume update can take
The Kubernetes documentation bounds the delay before a changed ConfigMap appears in a mounted volume:
\[
t_{\text{update}} \le T_{\text{sync}} + T_{\text{cache}}
\]
where

\(t_{\text{update}}\) is the time, in seconds, from kubectl apply until the new file is visible in the pod.
\(T_{\text{sync}}\) is the kubelet’s periodic sync interval. Its default (syncFrequency) is 60 s.
\(T_{\text{cache}}\) is the delay of the kubelet’s ConfigMap cache. With the default watch-based cache it is the watch propagation delay, usually well under a second.

Example: with \(T_{\text{sync}} = 60\) s and \(T_{\text{cache}} \approx 0\) s, the bound is about \(60 + 0 = 60\) s. Our measurement of \(t_{\text{update}} = 19\) s fits inside it. The pod’s next sync simply came 19 s after our change. Another try could take anywhere from about 0 to 60 s. If you need the change now, kubectl rollout restart replaces the pods, and new pods always mount the current version.

title: 12. Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets and StatefulSets
text:
A Deployment keeps identical web pods running forever. The Lemonade Stand has four jobs that do not fit that shape:

Squeeze six batches of lemons, two at a time, then stop. Work that finishes.
Print the sales report every day at 18:00. Work on a timetable.
Check the fridge thermometer on every machine. One pod per node, including nodes added later.
Keep a ledger where copy 0 and copy 1 each keep their own book under a stable name, even after restarts.

Kubernetes has one controller for each: Job, CronJob, DaemonSet and StatefulSet.

text:
A Deployment keeps identical web pods running forever. The Lemonade Stand has four jobs that do not fit that shape:

Squeeze six batches of lemons, two at a time, then stop. Work that finishes.
Print the sales report every day at 18:00. Work on a timetable.

Kubernetes has one controller for each: Job, CronJob, DaemonSet and StatefulSet.

title: 12. Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets and StatefulSets
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipMore animals at the zoo



Phippy Goes to the Zoo has an animal for almost every one of these:

Raccoons are CronJobs. They lie asleep in their enclosure. Every now and then one jumps up, sweeps the whole place with a broom, and goes back to sleep. Zee wants to take one home to clean her room.
Vultures are DaemonSets. Stone pillars rise from a hill, and one vulture sits on top of every pillar. When a bird flies away, another takes its place. Phippy jokes that if you built a new pillar, a bird would land on it before you could say “cube cuddle”. New node, new pod.

And two more pictures:

A Job is a chore list on the fridge: “Squeeze 6 batches. Two children may squeeze at the same time.” When all 6 are ticked off, the chore is done. Nobody squeezes forever.
A StatefulSet is a row of numbered desks. Child number 0 always sits at desk 0, with notebook 0. If child 0 goes home sick, the new child 0 sits at desk 0 and finds the same notebook, with yesterday’s notes still in it.

title: 12. Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets and StatefulSets
text:
The concept, precisely

Job: creates pods until a number of them have succeeded (completions), running at most parallelism at once. Failed pods are retried, with an increasing delay, up to backoffLimit (default 6). The pod template must use restartPolicy: Never or OnFailure.
CronJob: creates a Job according to a cron schedule. concurrencyPolicy decides what happens if the previous run is still busy. Without timeZone, the schedule is read in the controller manager’s local time zone.
DaemonSet: runs exactly one copy of a pod on every node that matches, now and in the future. Use it for node agents: log collectors, monitoring, network helpers. k3s difference: ServiceLB is itself built from DaemonSets (the svclb-… pods in lesson 7).
StatefulSet: like a Deployment, but each pod has a stable identity:

a fixed name <name>-0, <name>-1, …;
a fixed DNS name <pod>.<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, through a headless Service;
its own PVC, created from volumeClaimTemplates and named <template>-<pod>. The PVC is kept when the pod is replaced.

By default, pods start in order (0, then 1, …) and stop in reverse order (podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady).

title: 12. Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets and StatefulSets
text:
Worked example

A Job: 6 batches, 2 at a time
12-job.yaml:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: squeeze-lemons
  namespace: lemonade
spec:
  completions: 6
  parallelism: 2
  backoffLimit: 3
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: squeeze
          image: busybox:1.37.0
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo squeezing a batch; sleep 5"]
kubectl apply -f 12-job.yaml
kubectl wait -n lemonade --for=condition=Complete job/squeeze-lemons
kubectl get job squeeze-lemons -n lemonade
kubectl get pods -n lemonade -l job-name=squeeze-lemons
job.batch/squeeze-lemons condition met
NAME             STATUS     COMPLETIONS   DURATION
squeeze-lemons   Complete   6/6           24s

NAME                   READY   STATUS      AGE
squeeze-lemons-ffc6w   0/1     Completed   24s    ← wave 1
squeeze-lemons-zsw9l   0/1     Completed   24s
squeeze-lemons-546td   0/1     Completed   16s    ← wave 2
squeeze-lemons-bmg86   0/1     Completed   16s
squeeze-lemons-g7crc   0/1     Completed   8s     ← wave 3
squeeze-lemons-mdvrl   0/1     Completed   8s
The pod ages show three waves of two pods, about 8 seconds apart. The Mathematical Abstraction section below explains the 24 s.


A CronJob, and running it by hand
12-cronjob.yaml runs at 18:00 London time and never overlaps itself:
spec:
  schedule: "0 18 * * *"
  timeZone: Europe/London
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: report
              image: busybox:1.37.0
              command: ["sh", "-c", "echo sales report for $(date +%F)"]
kubectl apply -f 12-cronjob.yaml
kubectl get cronjob -n lemonade
kubectl create job manual-report --from=cronjob/daily-sales-report -n lemonade
kubectl logs -n lemonade job/manual-report
NAME                 SCHEDULE     TIMEZONE        SUSPEND   ACTIVE   LAST SCHEDULE
daily-sales-report   0 18 * * *   Europe/London   False     0        <none>
job.batch/manual-report created
sales report for 2026-11-25
Testing a CronJob by creating a Job from it is the normal way to check it, without waiting until 18:00.


A DaemonSet
12-daemonset.yaml puts one “thermometer” pod on each node. It learns its node’s name from the downward API (fieldRef: spec.nodeName):
kubectl apply -f 12-daemonset.yaml
kubectl get ds -n lemonade
kubectl logs -n lemonade ds/node-thermometer --tail=1
NAME               DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   NODE SELECTOR
node-thermometer   1         1         1       1            1           <none>
checking k3s-lab
DESIRED 1, because the lab has one node. Join an agent (lesson 2) and DESIRED becomes 2 without any change to the manifest.


A StatefulSet with its own books
12-statefulset.yaml contains a headless Service and two ledger pods, each with its own 100 Mi volume:
spec:
  serviceName: ledger
  replicas: 2
  # … pod template writes "I am $HOSTNAME" into /books/owner.txt …
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: books
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 100Mi
kubectl apply -f 12-statefulset.yaml
kubectl get pods,pvc -n lemonade -l app=ledger
kubectl get pvc -n lemonade
kubectl exec ledger-0 -n lemonade -- cat /books/owner.txt
NAME           READY   STATUS    AGE
pod/ledger-0   1/1     Running   8s
pod/ledger-1   1/1     Running   5s       ← started after ledger-0 (OrderedReady)

NAME              STATUS   VOLUME                                     CAPACITY
books-ledger-0    Bound    pvc-c2e4e722-b2a2-4851-ac6f-d31990832b0d   100Mi
books-ledger-1    Bound    pvc-376e9fa5-88a7-40f3-afdc-c3217bbb4c0a   100Mi
I am ledger-0
Now delete ledger-0 and look again:
kubectl delete pod ledger-0 -n lemonade
kubectl get pods -n lemonade -l app=ledger
kubectl exec ledger-0 -n lemonade -- cat /books/owner.txt
kubectl run dns-sts -n lemonade --image=busybox:1.37.0 --restart=Never --rm -i -- \
  nslookup ledger-0.ledger.lemonade.svc.cluster.local
NAME       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
ledger-0   1/1     Running   0          5s      ← a new pod, with the same name
ledger-1   1/1     Running   0          41s
I am ledger-0
I am ledger-0                                    ← the old line is still there
Name:   ledger-0.ledger.lemonade.svc.cluster.local
Address: 10.42.0.46
The replacement pod got the same name, the same volume (so the file now has two lines) and the same DNS name. Its IP address may differ, which is why clients use the DNS name. A Deployment pod would have come back with a random name and an empty emptyDir.

title: 12. Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets and StatefulSets
text:
Rules and conventions

Use a Job for anything that must finish (migrations, imports, batch work). Make each pod’s work idempotent: a retry may repeat work that half-succeeded.
Always set backoffLimit and activeDeadlineSeconds, so a broken Job stops instead of retrying for hours. Set ttlSecondsAfterFinished so finished Jobs are cleaned up.
For CronJobs, always set timeZone and concurrencyPolicy (usually Forbid). Test them with kubectl create job --from=cronjob/….
Use a DaemonSet only for node-level agents. Ordinary apps use Deployments.
Use a StatefulSet when each replica needs its own identity or data (databases, queues). A StatefulSet does not make an app replicated by itself: the app must know how to work as primary and replica.
Back up StatefulSet volumes. With k3s’s local-path, each PVC lives on one node.

title: 12. Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets and StatefulSets
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




restartPolicy: Always in a Job
The API rejects the Job
Use Never or OnFailure


Cron schedule written in local time without timeZone
Runs at the “wrong” hour
Set timeZone


Long CronJob runs that overlap
Two reports at once, double work
concurrencyPolicy: Forbid


StatefulSet without its headless Service
Pods have no stable DNS names
Create a Service with clusterIP: None and set serviceName


Expecting PVCs to vanish with the StatefulSet
Old data is still there after redeploying
That is the default (Retain); delete the PVCs on purpose, or set the retention policy


A DaemonSet that skips the server node
DESIRED is lower than the number of nodes
Add tolerations for the node’s taints

title: 12. Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets and StatefulSets
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

How long the Job takes
With \(C\) completions, \(P\) in parallel, and each pod working for \(t\) seconds plus a start-and-stop overhead of \(o\) seconds:
\[
T_{\text{job}} \approx \left\lceil \frac{C}{P} \right\rceil \cdot (t + o)
\]
where

\(C\) is completions and \(P\) is parallelism, both whole numbers \(\ge 1\).
\(\lceil C/P \rceil\) is the number of waves, rounded up because a half-full wave still takes a full wave’s time.
\(t\) is the work time of one pod (our sleep 5), and \(o\) is the time to create, start and clean up a pod. Both are in seconds.
\(T_{\text{job}}\) is the expected wall-clock time of the Job.

Example: \(C = 6\), \(P = 2\), so \(\lceil 6/2 \rceil = 3\) waves. With \(t = 5\) s and no overhead we would expect \(3 \times 5 = 15\) s. We measured 24 s, with waves 8 s apart, so \(t + o = 8\) and \(o = 3\) s per wave on this busy laptop: \(3 \times (5 + 3) = 24\) s, as measured. With \(P = 3\) the same work needs \(\lceil 6/3 \rceil = 2\) waves, about \(2 \times 8 = 16\) s. With \(P = 4\) it still needs \(\lceil 6/4 \rceil = \lceil 1.5 \rceil = 2\) waves: the extra parallel slot is wasted in the second wave.


Retry delays for failed Job pods
The Job controller recreates failed pods after a growing delay, 10 s, 20 s, 40 s and so on, capped at ten minutes:
\[
d_k = \min\bigl(10 \cdot 2^{\,k-1},\; 600\bigr)
\]
where \(k = 1, 2, \dots\) counts the failures so far, and \(d_k\) is the delay in seconds before the next attempt.
Example: with backoffLimit: 3, a pod that always fails is retried after \(d_1 = 10\), \(d_2 = 20\) and \(d_3 = 40\) s. Then the Job is marked Failed. That is about \(10 + 20 + 40 = 70\) s of waiting, plus the run times. With the default backoffLimit: 6, the waits are \(10 + 20 + 40 + 80 + 160 + 320 = 630\) s, over ten minutes, which is why setting a smaller limit matters.


How often a CronJob runs
A cron schedule is five sets, one per field. The job runs at every combination:
\[
N_{\text{week}} = |M| \cdot |H| \cdot |W| \qquad (\text{when day-of-month and month are } *)
\]
where

\(M\) is the set of minutes (0–59), \(H\) the set of hours (0–23), and \(W\) the set of weekdays (0–6, with 0 = Sunday) allowed by the schedule.
\(|X|\) is the number of elements in a set.
\(N_{\text{week}}\) is the number of runs per week.

Example:

0 18 * * * gives \(M = \lbrace 0 \rbrace\), \(H = \lbrace 18 \rbrace\) and \(W = \lbrace 0, \dots, 6 \rbrace\). So \(N = 1 \times 1 \times 7 = 7\) runs a week, one each evening.
A “check the lemons every 15 minutes during opening hours on weekdays” schedule */15 9-17 * * 1-5 gives \(M = \lbrace 0, 15, 30, 45 \rbrace\) (\(|M| = 4\)), \(H = \lbrace 9, \dots, 17 \rbrace\) (\(|H| = 9\), both ends included) and \(W = \lbrace 1, \dots, 5 \rbrace\) (\(|W| = 5\)). So \(N = 4 \times 9 \times 5 = 180\) runs a week. The last run each day is at 17:45, not 18:00.



StatefulSet names
\[
\operatorname{pods}(s, n) = \lbrace s\text{-}i \mid i \in \lbrace 0, 1, \dots, n-1 \rbrace \rbrace, \qquad \operatorname{pvc}(v, s\text{-}i) = v\text{-}s\text{-}i
\]
where \(s\) is the StatefulSet name, \(n\) its replicas, \(i\) the ordinal number, and \(v\) the name of the volume claim template.
Example: \(s = \texttt{ledger}\), \(n = 2\) and \(v = \texttt{books}\) give the pods \(\lbrace \texttt{ledger-0}, \texttt{ledger-1} \rbrace\) and the PVCs books-ledger-0 and books-ledger-1, exactly as listed above. Scaling to \(n = 3\) adds ledger-2 and books-ledger-2. Scaling back to \(n = 2\) removes the highest ordinal, ledger-2, but keeps its PVC for next time.

title: 12. Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets and StatefulSets
text:
References

Kubernetes, “Jobs”: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/ (completions, parallelism, back-off 10 s doubling, capped at ten minutes, backoffLimit default 6).
Kubernetes, “CronJob”: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs/.
Kubernetes, “DaemonSet”: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/daemonset/, and “StatefulSets”: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset/.
Matt Butcher and Karen Chu, Phippy Goes to the Zoo: https://www.cncf.io/phippy/phippy-goes-to-the-zoo-book/.

title: 7. Services and DNS
text:
The three lemonade pods have addresses like 10.42.0.21, 10.42.0.22 and 10.42.0.23. Each rolling update (lesson 6) replaces them with new pods and new IPs. If the cash register had to remember pod IPs, it would break after every release.
We need:

One stable address and name inside the cluster that always reaches whichever lemonade pods are ready.
Load spreading across those pods.
A way for customers outside the cluster to get in.

A Service does all three.

title: 7. Services and DNS
text:
The three lemonade pods have addresses like 10.42.0.21, 10.42.0.22 and 10.42.0.23. Each rolling update (lesson 6) replaces them with new pods and new IPs. If the cash register had to remember pod IPs, it would break after every release.
We need:

One stable address and name inside the cluster that always reaches whichever lemonade pods are ready.
Load spreading across those pods.
A way for customers outside the cluster to get in.

A Service does all three.

title: 7. Services and DNS
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipA tunnel and a phone number



In The Illustrated Children’s Guide to Kubernetes, Phippy has made many clones of herself, and they come and go. Captain Kube opens a tunnel between Phippy’s group and the rest of the ship. “Even when your clones come and go, this tunnel will stay here,” he says, “so you can discover other pods, and they can discover you!” That tunnel is a Service.
Or think of the shop’s phone number. Customers call one number, “Lemonade Stand”. Whoever is working today answers. Staff change shifts, and each person has their own mobile number (the pod IP), but the shop number (the Service) stays the same. The phone book that turns the name “lemonade-web” into that number is CoreDNS.
To reach the shop from the street:

NodePort is a numbered side door, such as door 30080, in every building of the cluster.
LoadBalancer is the big front gate. In k3s, a helper called ServiceLB opens that gate on the nodes themselves, so you do not need a cloud provider.

title: 7. Services and DNS
text:
The concept, precisely

A Service has a selector (for example app: lemonade). Every ready pod whose labels match becomes an endpoint. The endpoints are stored in EndpointSlice objects, which the control plane updates as pods come and go.
ClusterIP (the default type): a virtual IP from the service range (10.43.0.0/16 in k3s) that works only inside the cluster. kube-proxy, built into k3s, programs the node’s packet rules so that traffic to ClusterIP:port reaches one of the endpoints on targetPort.
NodePort: a ClusterIP plus the same port opened on every node, from the range 30000–32767.
LoadBalancer: a NodePort plus an external address. Upstream Kubernetes needs a cloud or a tool such as MetalLB for this, otherwise the address stays <pending>. k3s ServiceLB creates a small svclb-… pod on each node, which uses a host port to forward traffic, and reports the node’s IP as the external address. Traefik itself is exposed this way.
Headless (clusterIP: None): no virtual IP. DNS returns the pod IPs directly. StatefulSets use this (lesson 12).
ExternalName: a DNS alias to a name outside the cluster, such as a managed database. It has no proxying at all.
DNS: CoreDNS answers for <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Inside the same namespace the short name lemonade-web is enough. From another namespace use lemonade-web.lemonade.

              Service lemonade-web  10.43.86.108:80
                 selector app=lemonade
        ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
        ▼              ▼              ▼
 10.42.0.21:8080  10.42.0.22:8080  10.42.0.23:8080     (EndpointSlice)

Commands:








Command

Example

kubectl get endpointslices

kubectl get endpointslices -n lemonade -l kubernetes.io/service-name=lemonade-web
