title: 7. Services and DNS
text:
Worked example
The ClusterIP Service (07-service.yaml) and a NodePort Service (07-service-nodeport.yaml) differ only in type and nodePort:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: lemonade-web
  namespace: lemonade
spec:
  selector:
    app: lemonade
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: lemonade
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
      nodePort: 30080
kubectl apply -f 07-service.yaml -f 07-service-nodeport.yaml
kubectl get svc -n lemonade
kubectl get endpointslices -n lemonade -l kubernetes.io/service-name=lemonade-web
NAME                    TYPE        CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)
lemonade-web            ClusterIP   10.43.86.108   <none>        80/TCP
lemonade-web-nodeport   NodePort    10.43.115.30   <none>        80:30080/TCP

NAME                 ADDRESSTYPE   PORTS   ENDPOINTS
lemonade-web-db6kn   IPv4          8080    10.42.0.21,10.42.0.23,10.42.0.22
The EndpointSlice lists exactly the three web pods on port 8080. Now call the Service by name from a throw-away pod in the same namespace:
kubectl run dns-test -n lemonade --image=busybox:1.37.0 --restart=Never --rm -i -- \
  wget -qO- http://lemonade-web
<h1>Lemonade Stand</h1>
<p>Classic lemonade: 2.00</p>
From outside, through the NodePort. The Docker lab publishes node port 30080 as localhost:30080:
curl -s http://localhost:30080/
<h1>Lemonade Stand</h1>
<p>Classic lemonade: 2.00</p>
<p>Pink lemonade: 2.50</p>
And a LoadBalancer Service in k3s. Traefik is one, and ServiceLB gave it the node’s IP as its external address:
kubectl get svc traefik -n kube-system
NAME      TYPE           CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)
traefik   LoadBalancer   10.43.174.216   172.17.0.3    80:30940/TCP,443:30664/TCP
On a cloud cluster without a load-balancer controller, EXTERNAL-IP would stay <pending>. In k3s it works out of the box.

title: 7. Services and DNS
text:
Rules and conventions

Name the Service after the app (lemonade-web). The name becomes its DNS name.
Call other apps by Service name, never by pod IP. Use the short name inside a namespace, and name.namespace across namespaces.
Keep port stable for clients (80), and map it to whatever the container uses with targetPort (8080).
Use ClusterIP for internal traffic, Ingress (lesson 8) for HTTP from outside, and NodePort or LoadBalancer for non-HTTP traffic such as TCP games or MQTT.
Let Kubernetes pick nodePort unless a firewall rule needs a fixed number.
Only ready pods receive traffic. Readiness probes (lesson 11) are what make a Service safe during rollouts.

title: 7. Services and DNS
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Selector does not match the pod labels
EndpointSlice is empty, so connections are refused or time out
Compare kubectl get pods --show-labels with the Service’s selector


targetPort is the Service port instead of the container port
Connection refused
targetPort: 8080 (what the container listens on)


Calling lemonade-web from another namespace
DNS name not found
Use lemonade-web.lemonade


nodePort: 8080
The API rejects it: not in the valid range
Use 30000–32767


Two LoadBalancer Services on the same port in k3s
The second one’s svclb pods stay Pending
ServiceLB uses host ports; pick another port or another node pool


Pinging a ClusterIP
No reply, although HTTP works
A ClusterIP is virtual and only forwards the declared ports; test with HTTP, not ping

title: 7. Services and DNS
text:
Mathematical Abstraction

Who is behind the Service
\[
E = \lbrace (\operatorname{ip}(p), t) \mid p \in P,\; \sigma \subseteq L(p),\; \operatorname{ready}(p) \rbrace
\]
where

\(P\) is the set of pods in the Service’s namespace.
\(L(p)\) is the set of labels of pod \(p\), written as key=value pairs.
\(\sigma\) is the Service’s selector, also a set of key=value pairs. \(\sigma \subseteq L(p)\) means “the pod has every label the selector asks for”.
\(\operatorname{ready}(p)\) is true when the pod passes its readiness checks.
\(t\) is the targetPort, and \(E\) is the resulting set of endpoints (IP, port).

Example: \(\sigma = \lbrace \texttt{app=lemonade} \rbrace\). The three web pods have \(L = \lbrace \texttt{app=lemonade}, \texttt{pod-template-hash=bffff7f7b} \rbrace\), which contains \(\sigma\), and they are ready. So \(E = \lbrace (10.42.0.21, 8080), (10.42.0.22, 8080), (10.42.0.23, 8080) \rbrace\), exactly the EndpointSlice shown above. The bare lemonade-pod from lesson 4 has no labels, so \(\sigma \not\subseteq \varnothing\) and it receives no traffic.


How load spreads
In its default mode, kube-proxy picks an endpoint at random for each new connection. With \(n\) ready endpoints, each one is chosen with probability \(1/n\), so on average
\[
R_{\text{pod}} = \frac{R}{n}
\]
where \(R\) is the number of new connections per second arriving at the Service, \(n = |E|\) is the number of ready endpoints, and \(R_{\text{pod}}\) is the expected number of connections per second for each pod.
Example: a school trip opens the menu \(R = 90\) times per second, and \(n = 3\), so each pod gets \(90 / 3 = 30\) per second on average. If one pod fails its readiness check, \(n\) becomes 2 and each remaining pod gets \(90 / 2 = 45\). This is why you size replicas for \(n - 1\) pods, so the stand survives losing one. Note that this spreads connections, not requests: one browser that keeps a connection open stays on one pod.


How many NodePorts exist
\[
N = 32767 - 30000 + 1 = 2768
\]
where \(N\) is the number of different NodePort values available in the default range. The \(+1\) is there because both ends of the range are allowed. Each NodePort Service port uses one of them on every node, so a cluster can have at most 2768 NodePort ports in total. That is plenty for a lemonade stand, and a reason to put HTTP apps behind one Ingress instead.

title: Providers, Resources and Data Sources
text:
The Lemonade Stand now needs things from three places: a container image from Docker, a web server from AWS, and a Cloud Run service from Google Cloud. Terraform itself knows nothing about any of them. Something has to translate resource "aws_instance" "web" into real AWS API calls.
There is a second problem. The containers need the image to exist before they start, and the web server needs its firewall rule first. Who decides the order?

title: Providers, Resources and Data Sources
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipTranslators and a chain of friends



Terraform speaks only one language: HCL. The cloud companies all speak different languages. So Terraform hires a translator for each one: a Docker translator, an AWS translator, a Google translator. Each translator is a provider. You tell Terraform which translators to bring, and exactly which version, so that your friends’ computers bring the same ones.
The order works like a chain of friends passing a ball. Lily cannot pass the ball to Sam until Max has passed it to her. You never write “Max first, then Lily”. You only write “Lily gets the ball from Max”, and the order follows by itself. In Terraform, whenever one resource mentions another (image = docker_image.nginx.image_id), that mention is the “gets the ball from” link.

title: Providers, Resources and Data Sources
text:
The concept, precisely

A provider is a plugin, downloaded by terraform init, that knows one API: Docker, AWS, Google Cloud, GitHub, even “write a local file”.
A resource is an object the provider creates, updates and deletes for you. Terraform owns it.
A data source is an object the provider only reads. Somebody else owns it: an Amazon machine image, an existing network, today’s date.
A reference such as docker_image.nginx.image_id reads an attribute of another object. Every reference adds an edge to the dependency graph. Terraform walks that graph to decide the order.


Choosing providers: required_providers
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.10"
  required_providers {
    docker = { source = "kreuzwerker/docker", version = "~> 4.7" }
  }
}









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




required_version
the Terraform versions allowed to run this code
a lower bound is usually enough
required_version = ">= 1.10"


required_providers
which providers to install
one entry per provider, in versions.tf
see above


source
registry address [host/]namespace/type
host defaults to registry.terraform.io
"hashicorp/aws", "kreuzwerker/docker"


version
a constraint on provider versions
always set one
"~> 6.0"


local name
the key, such as docker
must match the resource prefix (docker_container)
docker = { ... }





Version constraints









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




= (or no operator)
exactly this version
too strict for providers; fine for modules
"= 4.7.0"


!=
anything except this version
to skip one known-bad release
"!= 6.12.0"


>, >=
newer than / at least
lower bounds
">= 1.10"


<, <=
older than / at most
upper bounds
"< 7.0"


~>
“pessimistic”: only the rightmost number may grow
the usual choice for providers
"~> 6.0"


,
combines constraints (all must hold)

">= 6.10, < 7.0"





The lock file
terraform init records the exact versions it chose, plus checksums, in .terraform.lock.hcl. This is the real file from examples/01-local/:
provider "registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/local" {
  version     = "2.9.1"
  constraints = "~> 2.9"
  hashes = [
    "h1:bek0XHcE8X713/1PR+sMKZFwLnamznJdYbORghbFRn0=",
    "zh:25606c7a5e308144fb627f6e31611bb52ff72bb9ae2d27af39673ab1a6b3c1bf",
    ...
Commit it. Your teammates and CI then install the same 2.9.1, and the checksums prove the plugin was not tampered with. terraform init -upgrade moves to newer versions inside the constraint and rewrites the file.


Configuring a provider, and alias
provider "aws" { region = "eu-west-2" }

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "ireland"
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "menu_backup" {
  provider = aws.ireland
  bucket   = "lemonade-menu-backup"
}
The first block is the default aws provider, in London like the rest of the book. The second is a copy in Ireland, so the menu backup survives a London outage. It is picked per resource with provider = aws.ireland. Never put access keys in a provider block. Credentials come from the environment (lesson 10).


Resources and their addresses









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




resource "TYPE" "NAME"
declares an object Terraform owns
TYPE comes from the provider; NAME is yours
resource "docker_image" "nginx"


address TYPE.NAME
how state, plans and references name it
unique in a module
docker_image.nginx


attribute TYPE.NAME.ATTR
reads a value of the object
many are (known after apply)
docker_image.nginx.image_id


instance key
one copy when using for_each / count
["key"] or [0]
docker_container.stand["web1"]


depends_on
an extra edge Terraform cannot see from references
rare; explain it in a comment
depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.read_menu]


provider
choose a non-default provider copy
used with alias
provider = aws.ireland





Data sources
data "aws_ami" "al2023" {
  most_recent = true
  owners      = ["amazon"]
  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["al2023-ami-2023.*-x86_64"]
  }
}
From examples/aws/main.tf. It finds the newest Amazon Linux image, so the server uses ami = data.aws_ami.al2023.id instead of a hard-coded ID that differs per region and goes stale. The address starts with data., and Terraform never creates or deletes it.

title: Providers, Resources and Data Sources
section: Worked example: the graph decides the order
text:
Worked example: the graph decides the order
examples/02-docker/main.tf has one image and two containers, and each container references the image. Real output:
$ terraform graph | grep -- "->"
  "docker_container.stand" -> "docker_image.nginx";

$ terraform apply -auto-approve
docker_image.nginx: Creating...
docker_image.nginx: Creation complete after 6s
docker_container.stand["web2"]: Creating...
docker_container.stand["web1"]: Creating...
docker_container.stand["web1"]: Creation complete after 0s
docker_container.stand["web2"]: Creation complete after 0s

$ terraform destroy -auto-approve
docker_container.stand["web2"]: Destroying...
docker_container.stand["web1"]: Destroying...
docker_image.nginx: Destroying...
Three things to notice:

The arrow means “depends on”: containers depend on the image.
The image was created first, then both containers started at the same time. They do not depend on each other, so Terraform runs them in parallel.
Destroy runs in the reverse order: containers first, image last. An image still used by a running container cannot be removed.

init showed the version constraint at work:
- Finding hashicorp/local versions matching "~> 2.9"...
- Installed hashicorp/local v2.9.1 (signed by HashiCorp)

title: Providers, Resources and Data Sources
text:
Rules and conventions

Every provider gets a source and a version constraint, and the lock file is committed.
Use ~> on the minor version for providers (~> 6.0) to get bug fixes and features but never a breaking major release.
Let references create the order. Add depends_on only for a dependency Terraform cannot see, such as “the server reads this permission at boot”, and say why in a comment.
Prefer data sources over hard-coded IDs (AMI IDs, project numbers, network IDs).
No credentials in .tf files, ever.

title: Providers, Resources and Data Sources
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




No version constraint
a new major provider release breaks a plan months later
add version = "~> X.Y" and commit the lock file


Not committing .terraform.lock.hcl
teammates get different provider versions
commit it; update it with init -upgrade on purpose


Two provider "aws" blocks, neither with alias
Error: Duplicate provider configuration
give every extra copy an alias and pick it with provider = aws.<alias>


depends_on everywhere “to be safe”
slower plans and needless replacements
remove it; use references


Hard-coded AMI ID
InvalidAMIID.NotFound in another region
use data "aws_ami"


Wrong source for a third-party provider
Failed to query available provider packages ... hashicorp/docker
set source = "kreuzwerker/docker"; it is not a HashiCorp provider

title: Providers, Resources and Data Sources
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
A ~> constraint is an interval. Write \(\operatorname{allow}(x)\) for the set of versions that the constraint ~> x accepts:
\[
\operatorname{allow}(a.b) = \lbrace v : a.b \le v < (a+1).0 \rbrace, \qquad
\operatorname{allow}(a.b.c) = \lbrace v : a.b.c \le v < a.(b+1).0 \rbrace
\]
where:

\(v\) is a candidate provider version;
\(a\), \(b\), \(c\) are the major, minor and patch numbers you wrote after ~>;
\(\le\) and \(<\) compare versions number by number from the left (so \(2.10 > 2.9\));
\(\lbrace v : \dots \rbrace\) is “the set of all versions \(v\) for which the condition holds”.

Example: ~> 2.9 has \(a = 2\), \(b = 9\), so it allows \(2.9 \le v < 3.0\). The installed local provider \(v = 2.9.1\) satisfies it, and 3.0.0 would not. For AWS, ~> 6.0 allows \(6.0 \le v < 7.0\), which is why init installed 6.74.0. With three numbers, ~> 2.9.1 gives \(a.(b+1).0 = 2.10.0\), so it allows only \(2.9.1 \le v < 2.10.0\): patch releases only.
References turn the configuration into a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Apply visits it in a topological order, and destroy in the reverse order:
\[
u \to v \;\Rightarrow\; \operatorname{pos}_{\text{apply}}(v) < \operatorname{pos}_{\text{apply}}(u)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{pos}_{\text{destroy}}(u) < \operatorname{pos}_{\text{destroy}}(v)
\]
where:

\(u \to v\) is an edge: resource \(u\) references (depends on) resource \(v\);
\(\operatorname{pos}(x)\) is the moment resource \(x\) is handled, so smaller means earlier;
“acyclic” means no chain of arrows leads back to its start; a cycle is an error (Error: Cycle).

Example: let \(c\) be docker_container.stand and \(i\) be docker_image.nginx. The real graph has \(c \to i\), so apply must handle \(i\) before \(c\) (the image completed after 6 s, then the containers started), and destroy must handle \(c\) before \(i\) (containers destroyed first). Both match the real output.
How long can an apply take, at the very least? Count rounds in which each operation takes one step:
\[
T \ge \max\left(L, \left\lceil \frac{n}{p} \right\rceil\right)
\]
where:

\(T\) is the number of rounds;
\(L\) is the number of resources on the longest dependency chain (a chain cannot be parallelised);
\(n\) is the total number of resource instances to change;
\(p\) is -parallelism, the maximum number of operations at once (default 10);
\(\lceil \cdot \rceil\) rounds up.

Example: the Docker example has \(n = 3\) (one image, two containers) and its longest chain is image → container, so \(L = 2\). With \(p = 10\): \(T \ge \max(2, \lceil 3/10 \rceil) = \max(2, 1) = 2\) rounds, which is what happened: image, then both containers together. With -parallelism=1: \(T \ge \max(2, \lceil 3/1 \rceil) = 3\) rounds, one resource at a time. This is a simplified model. Real operations take different times, and Terraform starts each one as soon as its dependencies finish rather than in fixed rounds.

title: Expressions, Loops and Functions
text:
The Lemonade Stand grows from one web server to two, then three. Copying the docker_container block three times works, but every fix must then be made three times. You want to say “one container for each stand in this list”.
You also need small calculations: build a URL from a port, give each stand its own network range, write the menu from a list of drinks. Terraform has a little expression language for exactly this.

title: Expressions, Loops and Functions
text:
The Lemonade Stand grows from one web server to two, then three. Copying the docker_container block three times works, but every fix must then be made three times. You want to say “one container for each stand in this list”.
You also need small calculations: build a URL from a port, give each stand its own network range, write the menu from a list of drinks. Terraform has a little expression language for exactly this.

title: Expressions, Loops and Functions
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipName tags versus seat numbers



Your class lines up for a photo. The teacher can label each child in two ways.

Seat numbers (count): “child 0, child 1, child 2”. If the child in seat 0 goes home, everybody shuffles along. Now the child who was number 1 is number 0, and the photographer thinks every child changed.
Name tags (for_each): “Ana, Ben, Cleo”. If Ana goes home, Ben is still Ben and Cleo is still Cleo. Only Ana’s spot is empty.

Terraform remembers each copy by its number or its name. Use name tags whenever the copies are different things, like different stands.

title: Expressions, Loops and Functions
text:
The concept, precisely

Expressions









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




reference
reads a value
var., local., data., module., or TYPE.NAME
docker_image.nginx.image_id


"${ }"
puts a value into a string
the only special use of $
"lemonade-${each.key}"


cond ? a : b
conditional: a when true, else b
both sides should have the same type
var.env == "prod" ? 3 : 1


arithmetic
+ - * / %
numbers only
40 * var.price


comparison and logic
== != < <= > >=, && \|\| !
result is bool
var.price > 0 && var.price < 10


index
list[i], map["key"]
lists count from 0
var.stands[0]


splat [*]
takes one attribute from every element of a list
short for a for expression
local.boxes[*].port


for (list)
[for x in coll : f(x)] builds a list
add if to filter
[for s in var.stands : upper(s)]


for (map)
{for k, v in coll : key => value} builds a map
keys must be unique
{for n, p in var.stands : n => "http://localhost:${p}"}





Repetition: count and for_each









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




count = N
makes N copies, addressed [0] … [N-1]
for identical copies, or 0/1 to switch a resource off and on
count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0


count.index
the current copy’s number
only inside a count block
"menu-${count.index}.txt"


for_each = MAP or SET
one copy per key, addressed ["key"]
the default choice for distinct things
for_each = var.stands


each.key
the current key
with a set, key and value are equal
"lemonade-${each.key}"


each.value
the current value
the map’s value
external = each.value


dynamic "NAME"
repeats a nested block
use sparingly; it hurts readability
see below



for_each accepts a map or a set of strings, never a plain list, because a list may contain duplicates and has no stable names. Convert with toset(...).
resource "aws_security_group" "web" {
  name = "lemonade-web"

  dynamic "ingress" {
    for_each = [80, 443]
    content {
      from_port   = ingress.value
      to_port     = ingress.value
      protocol    = "tcp"
      cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
    }
  }
}
Inside a dynamic block, the loop variable is named after the block: ingress.value.


The functions you will use every day
Real terraform console results:









Command
What it does
Rule / convention
Example → real result




length(x)
number of elements or characters
works on lists, maps, strings
length(var.stands) → 3


merge(a, b)
combines maps; later keys win
for default tags
merge({ a = 1 }, { b = 2, a = 3 }) → { a = 3, b = 2 }


lookup(m, k, d)
m[k], or d if k is missing
the default is required
lookup({ web1 = 8088 }, "web2", 8080) → 8080


toset(list)
removes duplicates and order
to feed for_each
toset(["web1", "web2", "web1"]) → toset(["web1", "web2"])


format(spec, ...)
printf-style text
%s text, %d integer, %.2f two decimals
format("Lemonade: $%.2f", 2.5) → "Lemonade: $2.50"


join(sep, list)
glues a list into one string

join(", ", ["web1", "web2"]) → "web1, web2"


upper(s), lower(s)
changes letter case

upper("web1") → "WEB1"


file(path)
reads a file as a string
path relative to path.module
file("${path.module}/menu.html")


templatefile(path, vars)
reads a file and fills in ${...} and %{...}
name templates *.tftpl
see below


cidrsubnet(prefix, newbits, netnum)
carves a smaller network out of a bigger one
see the maths below
cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 1) → "10.0.1.0/24"



A template file menu.html.tftpl:
<h1>Lemonade Stand ${stand}</h1>
%{ for drink, price in drinks ~}
<p>${drink}: ${format("$%.2f", price)}</p>
%{ endfor ~}
called as templatefile("${path.module}/menu.html.tftpl", { stand = "web1", drinks = { lemonade = 2.5, iced_tea = 3 } }) gives
<h1>Lemonade Stand web1</h1>
<p>iced_tea: $3.00</p>
<p>lemonade: $2.50</p>
Map keys are visited in alphabetical order, so iced_tea comes first. The ~ trims the newline after each directive.

title: Expressions, Loops and Functions
section: Worked example: count reshuffles, for_each does not
text:
Worked example: count reshuffles, for_each does not
A scratch configuration makes one menu file per stand with count:
variable "stands" {
  type    = list(string)
  default = ["web1", "web2", "web3"]
}

resource "local_file" "menu" {
  count    = length(var.stands)
  filename = "${path.module}/menu-${var.stands[count.index]}.txt"
  content  = "Stand ${var.stands[count.index]}\n"
}
After applying it, remove web1 from the list (real output, trimmed):
$ terraform plan -var 'stands=["web2","web3"]'
  # local_file.menu[0] must be replaced
      ~ filename = "./menu-web1.txt" -> "./menu-web2.txt" # forces replacement
  # local_file.menu[1] must be replaced
      ~ filename = "./menu-web2.txt" -> "./menu-web3.txt" # forces replacement
  # local_file.menu[2] will be destroyed
  # (because index [2] is out of range for count)
Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 3 to destroy.
You removed one stand, and Terraform wants to touch three files. Everyone shuffled seats.
The Lemonade Docker example uses for_each over a map instead. Removing web2 (real output):
$ terraform plan -var 'stands={web1=8088}'
  # docker_container.stand["web2"] will be destroyed
  # (because key ["web2"] is not in for_each map)
Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
One stand removed, one container destroyed, and web1 is untouched.

title: Expressions, Loops and Functions
text:
Rules and conventions

Use for_each for things with an identity (stands, users, buckets). Use count only for identical copies or a 0/1 on/off switch.
Keys of for_each must be known at plan time. Use names from variables, not IDs that the cloud invents.
Put long expressions in a local with a good name instead of repeating them inline.
Try every new function in terraform console before using it in a resource.
Keep dynamic blocks for truly variable nested blocks. A short repeated block is often clearer.
Keep templates in *.tftpl files next to the code, and pass every value they use explicitly.

title: Expressions, Loops and Functions
text:
Common mistakes



Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Removing an item from a count list
plan replaces every item after it
switch to for_each; move existing state with moved blocks (lesson 7)


for_each = ["web1", "web2"]
The given "for_each" argument value is unsuitable (a list)
for_each = toset([...]) or a map


for_each over values known only after apply
Invalid for_each argument ... cannot be determined until apply
use names from variables as keys


Using count and for_each together
Invalid combination of "count" and "for_each"
choose one


cidrsubnet with too large a netnum
prefix extension of 8 does not accommodate a subnet numbered 256
netnum must be below \(2^{k}\), where \(k\) is newbits

title: Terraform
text:
In Parts 4 and 5 you built the Lemonade Stand on AWS and Google Cloud by hand. You clicked through consoles and typed aws and gcloud commands. It worked, but three questions stay hard:

Can you do it again? A new region, a staging copy, a rebuild after an accident means doing every step again, in the right order, without forgetting one.
What exactly is running? After a month of small fixes, nobody remembers which settings were changed, or why.
What will this change break? A click takes effect at once. There is no preview.

Terraform answers all three. You write down what you want, such as “one web server, one firewall rule, one menu bucket”, in small text files. Terraform compares that wish list with what really exists, shows you the difference as a plan, and then makes reality match. The files live in Git, so every change can be reviewed, repeated and undone.

title: Terraform
text:
The Lemonade Stand as code
   you write                    Terraform                      real world
 ┌─────────────┐   plan    ┌──────────────────┐   apply   ┌──────────────────────┐
 │ main.tf     │ ───────▶  │ wish list  vs    │ ───────▶  │ Docker containers    │
 │ variables.tf│           │ state notebook   │           │ AWS EC2 + firewall   │
 │ outputs.tf  │ ◀──────── │ = list of changes│ ◀──────── │ Google Cloud Run     │
 └─────────────┘  outputs  └──────────────────┘  records  └──────────────────────┘
                                   │
                           terraform.tfstate (what Terraform built last time)
The same three steps repeat in every lesson: write → plan → apply.

title: Terraform
section: Run the lab with nothing but Docker
text:
Run the lab with nothing but Docker
You do not need to install Terraform or create a cloud account. The official hashicorp/terraform image contains the whole tool. Define this helper once in your shell:
tf() {
  docker run --rm -it -e CHECKPOINT_DISABLE=1 \
    -v "$PWD":/work -w /work \
    -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
    hashicorp/terraform:1.17.2 "$@"
}

-v "$PWD":/work -w /work shares the current folder with Terraform.
-v /var/run/docker.sock:... lets Terraform start containers on your laptop. Only the Docker example needs it.
CHECKPOINT_DISABLE=1 turns off Terraform’s “is there a newer version?” check, which can make commands hang inside a container.

Then cd devops/terraform/examples/01-local and run tf init, tf plan and tf apply. The lab README lists every example.








Folder
What it shows
Needs




examples/01-local/
the first plan and apply: a menu file and a random stand name
Docker

two real Lemonade web servers on localhost:8088 and :8089
Docker

one module used twice
Docker


examples/aws/
an EC2 web server and a firewall rule on AWS
AWS account to apply; validate-only here


examples/gcp/
a public Cloud Run service
Google Cloud project to apply; validate-only here

title: The Core Workflow
text:
You change the Lemonade price from $2.50 to $3.00 and run terraform apply. The plan says 2 to add, 0 to change, 2 to destroy. Destroy? You only changed a price!
To use Terraform safely you need to read a plan the way a pilot reads a checklist: every symbol, every count. This lesson walks through the commands in the order you run them and teaches you to predict a plan before Terraform prints it.

title: The Core Workflow
text:
You change the Lemonade price from $2.50 to $3.00 and run terraform apply. The plan says 2 to add, 0 to change, 2 to destroy. Destroy? You only changed a price!
To use Terraform safely you need to read a plan the way a pilot reads a checklist: every symbol, every count. This lesson walks through the commands in the order you run them and teaches you to predict a plan before Terraform prints it.

title: The Core Workflow
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipWrite the shopping list before you shop



Before going to the shop, you look in the fridge and write a list: “buy lemons (we have none), buy one more bag of sugar, throw away the old milk”. Your parent reads the list and says “yes” or “no”. Only then do you go shopping.
terraform plan is writing the list. The fridge is the real world, and the recipe is your .tf files. terraform apply is going shopping after someone said “yes”. A saved plan (-out) is a list your parent signed: at the shop you buy exactly what is on it, nothing more.
Some things cannot be fixed in place. If the recipe now needs a blue lunchbox and you own a red one, you cannot repaint it. You throw away the red one and buy a blue one. That is a replacement.

title: The Core Workflow
text:
The concept, precisely
The everyday loop is:
init  →  fmt  →  validate  →  plan  →  apply  →  (later) destroy








Step
Touches the real world?
Needs credentials?




init
no (downloads plugins, sets up the backend)
only for a remote backend


fmt, validate
no
no


plan
reads real resources to compare
yes


apply, destroy
changes real resources
yes




Every core command









Command
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




init
installs providers and modules, configures the backend, writes .terraform.lock.hcl
safe to run any time; rerun after adding providers or modules
terraform init


init -upgrade
picks the newest provider versions the constraints allow
commit the updated lock file afterwards
terraform init -upgrade


fmt
rewrites files in the standard style
-check for CI, -recursive for subfolders
terraform fmt -recursive


validate
checks syntax, references and types offline
run after init; no credentials needed
terraform validate


plan
compares files with reality and prints the changes
read every line before applying
terraform plan


apply
plans, asks for yes, then makes the changes
with a saved plan it applies without asking
terraform apply


destroy
deletes everything in the state
same as apply -destroy
terraform destroy


show
prints the state, or a saved plan, in readable form
-json for scripts
terraform show


output
prints output values
-raw for one string, -json for maps
terraform output -json urls


console
interactive calculator for expressions
try functions here first
echo 'cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 1)' \| terraform console


graph
prints the dependency graph in DOT format
pipe to Graphviz to draw it
terraform graph \| dot -Tsvg > graph.svg


providers
lists the providers the configuration and state need
debugging “which version?”
terraform providers


version
Terraform and provider versions
paste it into bug reports
terraform version





The flags that matter



Flag
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




-out=FILE
saves the plan to a file
apply that file later for “exactly this, nothing else”
terraform plan -out=tfplan


-var 'k=v'
sets one variable
overrides every other source (lesson 5)
-var 'price=3'


-var-file=FILE
loads variables from a file
one file per environment
-var-file=staging.tfvars


-target=ADDR
plans only one resource and its dependencies
emergency use only: it prints a warning for a reason
-target=random_pet.stand


-replace=ADDR
forces one resource to be destroyed and recreated
replaces the old terraform taint
-replace=random_pet.stand


-auto-approve
skips the yes question
only in pipelines or throwaway labs
terraform apply -auto-approve


-refresh-only
updates the state to match reality, changes nothing real
use to accept drift
terraform apply -refresh-only


-destroy
plans the deletion of everything
preview before destroy
terraform plan -destroy


-parallelism=N
at most N operations at once (default 10)
lower it if an API rate-limits you
-parallelism=2


-lock=false
does not take the state lock
dangerous: two people could write at once
avoid


-input=false
never prompts; fails if a variable is missing
always set it in CI
terraform plan -input=false


-detailed-exitcode
exit code 2 when the plan has changes
lets scripts detect drift
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode


-no-color
plain text output
for logs and CI
terraform plan -no-color





Plan symbols



Symbol
What it means
Lemonade example




+
create
first apply of local_file.menu


-
destroy
destroy, or a stand removed from the map


~
update in place, the object survives
changing a tag on an EC2 instance


-/+
destroy, then create a replacement
changing the menu text of local_file.menu


+/-
create the replacement first, then destroy
the same, with create_before_destroy (lesson 7)


<=
read a data source
looking up the newest Amazon Linux image



Inside a resource, # forces replacement marks the argument that made Terraform choose -/+, and (known after apply) marks values the cloud will invent, such as IDs.

title: The Core Workflow
section: Worked example: plan, save, apply, drift
text:
Worked example: plan, save, apply, drift
All output below is real, from examples/01-local/, trimmed.
1. Save a plan, then apply exactly that plan.
$ terraform plan -out=lemonade.tfplan
Saved the plan to: lemonade.tfplan

$ terraform apply lemonade.tfplan
Apply complete! Resources: 2 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
No yes question: the saved plan is the approval.
2. Change the price and read the plan. Edit $2.50 to $3.00 in main.tf:
$ terraform plan
  # local_file.menu must be replaced
-/+ resource "local_file" "menu" {
      ~ content              = <<-EOT # forces replacement
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
A local file cannot be edited in place by this provider, so a new file replaces the old one. “1 to add, 1 to destroy” is one replacement, not two separate actions. The Docker example in lesson 5 gives 2 to add, 2 to destroy for the same reason: two containers, each replaced.
3. Detect drift with an exit code. Delete menu.txt by hand, then:
$ terraform plan -detailed-exitcode
  # local_file.menu will be created
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
$ echo $?
2
4. Accept drift instead of fixing it. Sometimes the hand-made change is the one you want to keep:
$ terraform apply -refresh-only -auto-approve
Note: Objects have changed outside of Terraform
  # local_file.menu has been deleted
This only updated the state. The file is still missing, so the next plan still says 1 to add. Refresh-only changes what Terraform believes, never what exists. To really keep a deletion, remove the resource from the code too.
5. Preview a destroy.
$ terraform plan -destroy
  # random_pet.stand will be destroyed
Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
Only one resource, because the state no longer contains the deleted file.

title: The Core Workflow
text:
Rules and conventions

Run fmt and validate before every commit. They are free and need no credentials.
In shared environments, use plan -out and then apply <planfile>. The thing you reviewed is then the thing that runs.
Read the summary line first, then search the plan for -/+ and -. Those are the lines that can lose data.
Use -target and -replace only to recover from problems, and write down why in the commit or ticket.
In CI always add -input=false -no-color, and use -detailed-exitcode for scheduled drift checks.
Never use -lock=false on shared state.

title: The Core Workflow
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Skimming the plan
a database is replaced (-/+) and its data is gone
search for -/+ and # forces replacement; protect it with prevent_destroy


Treating -target as normal workflow
the state slowly stops matching the code
plan without -target afterwards and fix the differences


Applying a saved plan after the state changed
Error: Saved plan is stale
plan again; this protection is the reason to save plans


Expecting -refresh-only to repair drift
the next plan still shows changes
refresh-only updates belief, not reality; run a normal apply


terraform fmt -check passing locally, failing in CI
different Terraform versions
pin the version in CI and in required_version

The price is written inside the menu text, and the ports are written inside each container. To open a staging stand with a different price, you would have to copy the files and edit them by hand, and the copies would drift apart.
What you want is one configuration with a few knobs on the outside: price, which stands, which ports. You also want the configuration to tell you useful things when it finishes, such as “your stands are at these URLs”.

title: Variables, Outputs and Locals
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipA vending machine



A vending machine has buttons on the outside, a window where your snack drops out, and gears inside that you never touch.

The buttons are variables: inputs you choose each time (“price = 3”).
The drop window is an output: what the machine gives back (“your stand is at http://localhost:8088”).
The gears are locals: helper values the machine works out for itself (“40 cups × price = today’s sales”).

A good vending machine also refuses silly buttons. Press “price = 0” and a sign lights up: “A cup of lemonade cannot be free.” That sign is a validation rule.

title: Variables, Outputs and Locals
text:
The concept, precisely

Variables
examples/02-docker/variables.tf:
variable "price" {
  description = "Price of one cup, in dollars"
  type        = number
  default     = 2.5

  validation {
    condition     = var.price > 0
    error_message = "A cup of lemonade cannot be free or cost less than nothing."
  }
}
You read it anywhere as var.price.









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




type
the allowed type; values are converted or rejected
always set it
type = map(number)


default
value used when nobody sets one
omit it to make the variable required
default = 2.5


description
text shown in docs and prompts
always write one
description = "Price of one cup"


validation
a rule checked before planning
condition must mention the variable
condition = var.price > 0


error_message
text shown when validation fails
a full sentence ending with a full stop
see above


sensitive
hides the value in plan and apply output
still stored in plain text in state
sensitive = true


nullable
whether null is an allowed value
false makes null fall back to the default
nullable = false


ephemeral
value available during the run but never saved in state or plan files
for short-lived secrets such as tokens
ephemeral = true





Every way to set a variable









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




default in the block
the fallback
lowest priority
default = 2.5


TF_VAR_<name>
environment variable
handy in CI and for secrets
export TF_VAR_price=2.75


terraform.tfvars
loaded automatically
the project’s normal values
price = 3


terraform.tfvars.json
same, JSON format
for generated values
{"price": 3}


*.auto.tfvars
loaded automatically, in alphabetical order
per-topic files
lemonade.auto.tfvars


-var-file=FILE
loads a file you name
one per environment
-var-file=staging.tfvars


-var 'name=value'
one value on the command line
quick overrides
-var 'price=4'


interactive prompt
asks if a required variable is still unset
disable with -input=false in CI
var.price  Enter a value:





Outputs
examples/02-docker/outputs.tf:
output "urls" {
  description = "Open these in a browser"
  value       = { for name, port in var.stands : name => "http://localhost:${port}" }
}









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




value
what to print and store
any expression
value = aws_instance.web.public_ip


description
documentation
always write one in modules
description = "Open these in a browser"


sensitive
shows <sensitive> in the output list
required when the value comes from a sensitive variable
sensitive = true


terraform output
prints every output
-json for scripts
terraform output -json urls


terraform output -raw NAME
prints one string with no quotes
strings, numbers and booleans only
terraform output -raw url



Outputs are also how a module hands values back to its caller (lesson 8).


Locals
locals {
  cups_per_day = 40
  daily_sales  = local.cups_per_day * var.price
}









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




locals { }
defines named values; several blocks allowed
for values used more than once, or long expressions
locals { cups_per_day = 40 }


local.<name>
reads one
note: local, singular
local.daily_sales



A local is not an input: nobody can override it from outside. If people need to change it, make it a variable.

title: Variables, Outputs and Locals
text:
Worked example
Validation stops bad input before anything is planned (real output):
$ terraform plan -var price=0
Error: Invalid value for variable

  on variables.tf line 7:
   7: variable "price" {
    │ var.price is 0

A cup of lemonade cannot be free or cost less than nothing.
Outputs after apply (real):
$ terraform apply -auto-approve
Outputs:
urls = {
  "web1" = "http://localhost:8088"
  "web2" = "http://localhost:8089"
}

$ terraform output -json urls
{"web1":"http://localhost:8088","web2":"http://localhost:8089"}

$ terraform output -raw urls
Error: Unsupported value for raw output
-raw refused because urls is a map, not a string.
Locals and a sensitive output (real, from a scratch folder):
Outputs:
daily_sales = 100
till_pin = <sensitive>

$ terraform output till_pin
"4321"
$ grep -c '"4321"' terraform.tfstate
1
sensitive only hides the value in the summary. Anyone who can run terraform output or read the state can see it. That is why state must be protected (lesson 7).
Who wins? The same price variable, set in more and more places, each time read back with terraform console:
default only:                     2.5
+ TF_VAR_price=2.75:              2.75
+ terraform.tfvars (3):           3
+ lemonade.auto.tfvars (3.5):     3.5
+ -var-file=summer.tfvars (3.75): 3.75
+ -var price=4 after it:          4
  -var price=4 BEFORE -var-file:  3.75

title: Variables, Outputs and Locals
text:
Rules and conventions

Every variable has a type and a description; add validation for anything a person types.
Required inputs have no default. Then Terraform stops if they are missing instead of guessing.
Use one *.tfvars file per environment (staging.tfvars, prod.tfvars) and pass it with -var-file.
Keep secrets out of .tfvars files in Git. Pass them as TF_VAR_* from a secret store, and mark them sensitive (or ephemeral when the provider supports it).
Name variables after what they mean (price, stands), not where they are used (container_content_price).
Output what a human or another tool needs next: URLs, IP addresses, IDs.

title: Variables, Outputs and Locals
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




No type, then -var 'stands=["web2"]'
Terraform treats the value as one string; Invalid index errors
declare type = list(string)


Writing var.local_name for a local
Reference to undeclared input variable
locals are local.<name>


Expecting sensitive to encrypt
the secret is readable in terraform.tfstate
encrypt and restrict the state backend; prefer ephemeral for secrets


An output built from a sensitive variable without sensitive = true
Error: Output refers to sensitive values
add sensitive = true to the output


A CI job hangs
Terraform is waiting at an interactive prompt for a missing variable
add -input=false so it fails fast

title: Variables, Outputs and Locals
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Terraform collects every value that was set for a variable and keeps the one from the highest-precedence source:
\[
\operatorname{value}(x) = s_k(x), \qquad k = \max \lbrace\, i : \text{source } s_i \text{ sets } x \,\rbrace
\]
where:

\(x\) is one variable, such as price;
the sources are numbered from lowest to highest precedence: \(s_0\) = default, \(s_1\) = TF_VAR_* environment variable, \(s_2\) = terraform.tfvars, \(s_3\) = terraform.tfvars.json, \(s_4\) = *.auto.tfvars files, \(s_5\) = -var and -var-file on the command line;
\(s_i(x)\) is the value that source \(s_i\) gives to \(x\);
\(\max\) picks the largest index \(i\) among the sources that set \(x\), the most important one;
inside \(s_4\), files are read alphabetically, and inside \(s_5\), flags are read left to right; in both cases the later one wins.

Example: in the run above the price was set by \(s_0 = 2.5\), \(s_1 = 2.75\), \(s_2 = 3\), \(s_4 = 3.5\), and in \(s_5\) by -var-file (3.75) followed by -var (4). The set of sources that set it is \(\lbrace 0, 1, 2, 4, 5 \rbrace\), so \(k = 5\). Inside \(s_5\) the last flag was -var price=4, so \(\operatorname{value}(\texttt{price}) = 4\). Swap the two flags and the last one is the file, giving 3.75, exactly as the real output shows.
A validation rule is a test that must hold before Terraform plans anything:
\[
\operatorname{accept}(x) \iff c(x) = \text{true}
\]
where:

\(c\) is the condition expression;
\(\operatorname{accept}(x)\) means planning continues with value \(x\);
\(\iff\) means “exactly when”.

Example: \(c(\texttt{price}) = (\texttt{price} > 0)\). For \(\texttt{price} = 2.5\): \(2.5 > 0\) is true, so it is accepted. For \(\texttt{price} = 0\): \(0 > 0\) is false, so it is rejected with the error message, as in the real run.
The local daily_sales is an ordinary formula:
\[
\text{sales} = n \times p
\]
where \(n\) is cups_per_day (cups) and \(p\) is price (dollars per cup), so sales are in dollars per day.
Example: \(n = 40\) and \(p = 2.5\) give sales \(= 40 \times 2.5 = 100\), the real output daily_sales = 100. With -var price=3 the same local becomes \(40 \times 3 = 120\), without editing any file.

title: Infrastructure as Code
text:
In Part 4 you set up the Lemonade Stand on AWS by hand: a network, a firewall rule, a web server and a menu bucket, about fifteen steps in the console. Now the owner asks for a staging copy to test new drinks before customers see them.
You open your notes and find that step 9 says “change the security group (forgot which rule)”. Nobody knows exactly what production looks like any more. Doing it again will take an afternoon and will not come out quite the same.
Infrastructure as Code fixes this. You write the setup down once, in files, and a tool builds it from the files, identically, every time.

title: Infrastructure as Code
text:
In Part 4 you set up the Lemonade Stand on AWS by hand: a network, a firewall rule, a web server and a menu bucket, about fifteen steps in the console. Now the owner asks for a staging copy to test new drinks before customers see them.
You open your notes and find that step 9 says “change the security group (forgot which rule)”. Nobody knows exactly what production looks like any more. Doing it again will take an afternoon and will not come out quite the same.
Infrastructure as Code fixes this. You write the setup down once, in files, and a tool builds it from the files, identically, every time.

title: Infrastructure as Code
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipThe LEGO instruction booklet



A LEGO booklet does not say “pick up a brick, now pick up another brick”. It shows pictures of the finished castle. You look at the picture, look at your table, and add whatever is missing.
Terraform files are that picture. You draw the finished Lemonade Stand: two web servers, one firewall rule, one menu. Terraform looks at the picture, looks at what is really there, and adds only what is missing. If a tower falls off, you look at the picture again and rebuild just the tower.
Martin Fowler tells the same story with weather. A server set up by hand is a snowflake server (2012): beautiful, unique, and impossible to make again. Better is a phoenix server, named after the bird that burns up and is reborn from its ashes. Because the booklet exists, you can throw the server away and rebuild it any time, and it comes back exactly the same.

title: Infrastructure as Code
text:
The concept, precisely
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means defining servers, networks and cloud services in text files, keeping those files in version control, and letting a tool create the real thing from them. Fowler’s definition (2016) stresses that the files are the lasting source of truth. A change made by hand on a server is temporary and should be copied back into the code. Kief Morris’s book Infrastructure as Code (O’Reilly, 3rd edition 2025) is the standard long read on the topic.
Three words carry the whole idea:

Declarative. You describe the result (“there is one menu file with this text”), not the steps. Compare:
# imperative: steps, and running it twice does something twice
echo "Lemonade: \$2.50" >> menu.txt
# declarative: the result; running it twice changes nothing the second time
resource "local_file" "menu" {
  filename = "menu.txt"
  content  = "Lemonade: $2.50\n"
}
Desired state. The files describe how the world should look. Terraform’s job is to close the gap between “should” and “is”.
Plan before apply. Terraform always shows the gap as a list of changes before it touches anything.


Terraform and OpenTofu
Mitchell Hashimoto described the idea behind Terraform in a 2011 blog post. As he tells it in “The Story of HashiCorp Terraform”, the 2014 release was exactly that idea. Version 0.1 came out in July 2014 and supported only AWS and DigitalOcean. Today thousands of providers exist.
On 10 August 2023 HashiCorp changed the licence of future Terraform releases from the open-source MPL 2.0 to the Business Source License (BSL 1.1). The community forked the last open version. The fork was renamed OpenTofu and joined the Linux Foundation on 20 September 2023, reached general availability in January 2024, and became a CNCF sandbox project in April 2025. IBM completed its acquisition of HashiCorp on 27 February 2025.
For everything in this book the two tools behave the same: replace terraform with tofu. This part uses Terraform 1.17.

run it first, and again after adding providers or modules
terraform init

title: Infrastructure as Code
text:
Worked example: your first apply
The file examples/01-local/main.tf needs no cloud at all. It creates a random stand name and writes a menu file:
terraform {
  required_providers {
    local  = { source = "hashicorp/local", version = "~> 2.9" }
    random = { source = "hashicorp/random", version = "~> 3.9" }
  }
}

resource "random_pet" "stand" {}

resource "local_file" "menu" {
  filename = "${path.module}/menu.txt"
  content  = "Welcome to the ${random_pet.stand.id} lemonade stand!\nLemonade: $2.50\n"
}
Two resources: a random two-word name, and a file whose text uses that name. Run the four steps (real output, trimmed):
$ terraform init
- Installed hashicorp/random v3.9.1 (signed by HashiCorp)
- Installed hashicorp/local v2.9.1 (signed by HashiCorp)
Terraform has been successfully initialized!

$ terraform plan
  # local_file.menu will be created
  # random_pet.stand will be created
Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

$ terraform apply -auto-approve
random_pet.stand: Creation complete after 0s [id=perfect-moccasin]
local_file.menu: Creation complete after 0s [id=83faada0...]
Apply complete! Resources: 2 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.

$ cat menu.txt
Welcome to the perfect-moccasin lemonade stand!
Lemonade: $2.50

$ terraform plan
No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
The last line is the point of the whole lesson. Running Terraform a second time does nothing, because reality already matches the picture.
Now break something on purpose. Delete menu.txt and plan again:
$ rm menu.txt
$ terraform plan
  # local_file.menu will be created
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
Terraform noticed that one tower fell off and plans to rebuild only that tower. The random name stays. Finally, clean up:
$ terraform destroy -auto-approve
local_file.menu: Destroying...
random_pet.stand: Destroying...
Destroy complete! Resources: 2 destroyed.
Destroy removed the file before the name, the reverse of creation order, because the file depends on the name. Lesson 4 explains this ordering.

title: Infrastructure as Code
text:
Rules and conventions

The files are the truth. If you fix something by hand in a console, copy the fix into the code the same day, or the next apply will undo it.
Keep every Terraform folder in Git, but never commit terraform.tfstate or the .terraform/ folder (lesson 7).
Do commit .terraform.lock.hcl. Terraform’s own init message says so: it pins exact provider versions for everyone.
Always read the plan. The summary line Plan: X to add, Y to change, Z to destroy is the first thing to check.
Use -auto-approve only in examples like this one or in a pipeline that already reviewed a saved plan (lesson 10).
Prefer rebuilding (phoenix) over patching by hand (snowflake).

title: Infrastructure as Code
text:
Common mistakes



Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Running plan before init
Error: Inconsistent dependency lock file or “provider not installed”
run terraform init in that folder


Changing the real resource by hand
the next plan wants to “change” or “create” it back
put the change in the code, or accept the plan that restores it


Treating Terraform like a script (“run it to add one more server”)
confusion about why a second run does nothing
edit the files to describe two servers; then apply


Deleting terraform.tfstate
Terraform tries to create everything again, and duplicates or name clashes appear
never delete state; store it remotely (lesson 7)


Mixing terraform and tofu on one folder
state written by a newer tool version cannot be read by an older one
pick one tool and one version per project

title: Infrastructure as Code
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Treat the world as a set of resources. Terraform computes the gap between your picture and reality, then closes it:
\[
\Delta = \operatorname{plan}(D, R), \qquad \operatorname{plan}\big(D, \operatorname{apply}(D, R)\big) = \emptyset
\]
where:

\(D\) is the desired set: every resource described in your .tf files;
\(R\) is the real set: what actually exists right now (as Terraform last recorded and refreshed it);
\(\operatorname{plan}(D, R)\) is the list of changes \(\Delta\) that would turn \(R\) into \(D\);
\(\operatorname{apply}(D, R)\) performs \(\Delta\) and returns the new reality;
\(\emptyset\) is the empty set: “no changes”;
the right-hand equation says that after one apply, a second plan is empty. This property is called idempotency: doing it twice is the same as doing it once.

Example, with the run above. Let \(p\) stand for random_pet.stand and \(m\) for local_file.menu.

Before the first apply: \(D = \lbrace p, m \rbrace\) and \(R = \emptyset\). So \(\Delta\) creates both: \(\lvert \Delta \rvert = 2\), which is the real line Plan: 2 to add.
After apply: \(R = D\), so \(\operatorname{plan}(D, R) = \emptyset\), the real line No changes.
After rm menu.txt: \(R = \lbrace p \rbrace\). The gap is \(D \setminus R = \lbrace m \rbrace\), so \(\lvert \Delta \rvert = 1\): Plan: 1 to add.
For destroy, the desired set becomes \(D = \emptyset\), so every member of \(R\) is removed: \(\lvert \Delta \rvert = \lvert R \rvert = 2\), matching 2 destroyed.

This is a model, not the full algorithm. Terraform also compares the attributes of resources that exist in both sets (lesson 3), but the set picture is enough to predict most plans.

title: Terraform in CI/CD
text:
So far terraform apply runs on someone’s laptop. That raises the questions from Part 3 again. Which version of the code was applied? Did anyone review the plan? Whose cloud keys sit on that laptop, and for how long?
The Lemonade team wants the same rules for infrastructure as for the app. Every change arrives as a pull request. A robot shows the plan. A person approves it. The robot applies exactly what was approved, using credentials that expire within the hour.

title: Terraform in CI/CD
text:
So far terraform apply runs on someone’s laptop. That raises the questions from Part 3 again. Which version of the code was applied? Did anyone review the plan? Whose cloud keys sit on that laptop, and for how long?
The Lemonade team wants the same rules for infrastructure as for the app. Every change arrives as a pull request. A robot shows the plan. A person approves it. The robot applies exactly what was approved, using credentials that expire within the hour.

title: Terraform in CI/CD
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipThe signed permission slip



For a school trip, the teacher writes a slip: “We will visit the zoo, the lemonade stand and the park.” Your parent reads it and signs it. On the day, the class visits exactly those three places. If the teacher wants to add the toy shop, a new slip must be signed.
In a pipeline the saved plan is the slip, the reviewer’s approval is the signature, and terraform apply tfplan is the trip. If anything changed after the slip was signed, Terraform refuses to go. It says the plan is stale and asks for a new one.
The bus driver gets a day pass instead of a key to the whole bus depot. That is OIDC: the pipeline gets a pass that works for about an hour and then stops working.

title: Terraform in CI/CD
text:
The concept, precisely
The shape of a Terraform pipeline, building on the deployment-pipeline idea from Part 3:
pull request ──▶ fmt -check ─▶ init ─▶ validate ─▶ plan -out=tfplan ─▶ show plan to reviewers
merge to main ─▶ (wait for approval on the "production" environment) ─▶ apply tfplan
every night  ──▶ plan -detailed-exitcode ─▶ exit 2? alert: someone changed things by hand

The plan job
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write

jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v4
        with:
          terraform_version: 1.17.2
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/lemonade-terraform
          aws-region: eu-west-2
      - run: terraform fmt -check
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform validate
      - run: terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: tfplan
          retention-days: 1


The apply job
  apply:
    needs: plan
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    environment: production
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v4
        with:
          terraform_version: 1.17.2
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/lemonade-terraform
          aws-region: eu-west-2
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: tfplan
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform apply -input=false tfplan
environment: production is where the approval happens. In the repository settings, the production environment gets required reviewers, so the job waits until one of them clicks Approve.


Every piece, explained



Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




hashicorp/setup-terraform@v4
installs Terraform on the runner
pin terraform_version to the same version as required_version
terraform_version: 1.17.2


terraform fmt -check
fails if any file is unformatted
first, because it is fastest
exit code 3 on a messy file (lesson 2)


-input=false
never wait for typed input
on every command in CI
terraform plan -input=false


plan -out=tfplan
saves the exact plan
the artifact that gets approved
terraform plan -out=tfplan


upload-artifact / download-artifact
carries the plan file from job to job
short retention-days: plans can contain secrets
retention-days: 1


apply tfplan
applies the saved plan, no questions
refuses if the state changed since
terraform apply -input=false tfplan


environment:
ties the job to a GitHub environment
add required reviewers to production
environment: production


concurrency:
only one run per group at a time
one group per state, so runs queue
concurrency: terraform-prod


permissions: id-token: write
lets the job request an OIDC token
without it, cloud login fails
see above


aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
exchanges the OIDC token for temporary AWS credentials
trust only this repository and branch in the IAM role
role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::...


google-github-actions/auth@v3
the same for Google Cloud (Workload Identity Federation)
no service-account key files
workload_identity_provider: projects/.../providers/github


schedule: + -detailed-exitcode
nightly drift check
exit code 2 means drift (lesson 3)
cron: "0 3 * * *"





Staging and production: folders, not tricks









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




one folder per environment
envs/staging/ and envs/prod/, each with its own backend key and tfvars
recommended: separate state, separate credentials, obvious in reviews
envs/prod/main.tf calls module "stand"


terraform workspace new NAME
creates another state for the same folder
fine for short-lived copies (a test per pull request)
terraform workspace new pr-42


terraform workspace select NAME
switches which state the folder uses
easy to forget which one is selected
terraform workspace select staging


terraform.workspace
the current workspace’s name inside the code
for naming, such as "lemonade-${terraform.workspace}"
"lemonade-pr-42"



HashiCorp’s own documentation says CLI workspaces are not a good fit when environments need separate credentials and access controls. Production almost always does, so give it its own folder.

title: Terraform in CI/CD
section: Worked example: the stale plan protection
text:
Worked example: the stale plan protection
This is the guarantee the whole pipeline rests on, run for real on a laptop. A plan is saved for review, then someone else applies a different change first:
$ terraform plan -var price=3.00 -out=reviewed.tfplan
Saved the plan to: reviewed.tfplan
$ grep serial terraform.tfstate
  "serial": 1,

# meanwhile, another run applies price=2.75
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 1 destroyed.
$ grep serial terraform.tfstate
  "serial": 4,

$ terraform apply reviewed.tfplan
Error: Saved plan is stale
The given plan file can no longer be applied because the state was changed by
another operation after the plan was created.
The reviewer approved “change the price to 3.00 starting from state 1”. The world is no longer state 1, so applying that plan could do something nobody reviewed. Terraform refuses, and the pipeline must plan again.

title: Terraform in CI/CD
text:
Rules and conventions

Every change goes through a pull request. Nobody runs apply from a laptop against shared environments.
The plan that was reviewed is the plan that is applied: plan -out, then apply <file>.
Production applies wait for a human approval in a protected environment.
Use OIDC (AWS IAM roles, Google Workload Identity Federation). Never store long-lived cloud keys as repository secrets.
Give the pipeline’s role only the permissions this configuration needs. Use a read-only role for plan on pull requests from forks.
Add concurrency per state, as well as the backend lock, so runs queue instead of failing.
Run a scheduled drift check and treat exit code 2 as an alert.

title: Terraform in CI/CD
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Running apply without a saved plan in CI
the applied changes differ from what reviewers saw
plan -out=tfplan in one job, apply tfplan in the next


Missing id-token: write
Could not load credentials from any providers or “unable to get ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL”
add the permission to the workflow or job


Long-lived AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID secret
a leaked key works until someone notices
switch to OIDC; delete the key


Plan artifact kept for 90 days
secrets from the plan sit in old artifacts
retention-days: 1


One workspace-switched folder for staging and prod
someone applies the staging change to prod
separate folders, states and roles


Different Terraform versions locally and in CI
fmt -check or the state format disagree
pin the same version in setup-terraform and required_version

title: State and Backends
text:
Two people look after the Lemonade Stand. Ana runs terraform apply on her laptop and creates the web server. The next day Ben runs terraform apply on his laptop, and Terraform tries to create a second web server.
Terraform did not forget the server. Ben’s laptop simply never had the file in which Ana’s Terraform wrote down what it built. That file is the state. Where it lives, who may write it, and what is inside it decide whether a team can use Terraform safely.

title: State and Backends
text:
Two people look after the Lemonade Stand. Ana runs terraform apply on her laptop and creates the web server. The next day Ben runs terraform apply on his laptop, and Terraform tries to create a second web server.
Terraform did not forget the server. Ben’s laptop simply never had the file in which Ana’s Terraform wrote down what it built. That file is the state. Where it lives, who may write it, and what is inside it decide whether a team can use Terraform safely.

title: State and Backends
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipThe notebook and the bathroom key



Terraform keeps a notebook. Every time it builds something, it writes a line: “I built the red tower, and its secret number is 7Q3”. Next time, it reads the notebook to know which towers are its towers. If the notebook is lost, Terraform thinks it never built anything and builds everything again.
So the class keeps one notebook in a shared cupboard, not one per child. That cupboard is the backend. The cupboard also has a rule, like the single key for a petrol-station bathroom: only the child holding the key may write in the notebook. Everyone else waits. That key is the lock.
And because the notebook lists everything, including the secret number of the till, the cupboard must be locked against strangers too.

title: State and Backends
text:
The concept, precisely
State is a JSON file (terraform.tfstate) that maps every resource address in your code to the real object it manages, plus the attributes Terraform last saw. It is how Terraform knows that docker_container.stand["web1"] is container 68d3dc46....
State is needed because:

the cloud has no idea which objects “belong” to your configuration;
many attributes, such as IDs and IP addresses, exist only after creation;
deleting a block from the code must mean “destroy that object”, which requires remembering it.

Drift is any difference between the state and reality caused outside Terraform: a file deleted by hand, a firewall rule clicked in the console. plan refreshes the state first, so drift shows up as planned changes (lesson 3).
State can contain secrets in plain text. Lesson 5 showed a sensitive value sitting readable in terraform.tfstate. Treat the state like a password file.

Backends: where state lives









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




local (default)
terraform.tfstate in the current folder
fine for one person and labs; never commit it
no backend block


s3
state in an S3 bucket
use_lockfile = true for locking; encrypt = true
see below


gcs
state in a Google Cloud Storage bucket
locks automatically
see below


cloud block
HCP Terraform (HashiCorp’s service)
state, locking and runs in one place
cloud { organization = "lemonade" }


key / prefix
the path of this state inside the bucket
one per environment and component
key = "prod/web/terraform.tfstate"


terraform init -migrate-state
copies state to a new backend
run after changing the backend block
terraform init -migrate-state


terraform init -reconfigure
uses the new backend without copying
when the old state should be left behind
terraform init -reconfigure



The AWS version, for the bucket from Part 4:
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "lemonade-tf-state"
    key          = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-2"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}
The S3 backend can lock with a small lock file next to the state (use_lockfile). Terraform 1.10 introduced it, and 1.11 made it generally available. 1.11 also deprecated the older DynamoDB table lock (dynamodb_table), which will be removed in a future version. The Google Cloud version, for Part 5:
terraform {
  backend "gcs" {
    bucket = "lemonade-tf-state"
    prefix = "prod"
  }
}
Turn on versioning for the state bucket, so a bad write can be rolled back. Allow only the people and pipelines that run Terraform to read it.


State commands









Command
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




state list
lists every tracked address
the first command when debugging
terraform state list


state show ADDR
prints one resource’s recorded attributes

terraform state show random_pet.stand


state mv A B
renames an address in the state
prefer a moved block (reviewable)
terraform state mv random_integer.price_cents random_integer.cents


state rm ADDR
forgets a resource, leaves the real object
prefer a removed block
terraform state rm random_integer.cents


state pull
prints the raw state JSON
read-only inspection
terraform state pull \| jq .serial


state push
overwrites remote state
dangerous; only for disaster recovery
avoid


force-unlock ID
removes a stuck lock
only when you are sure no run is active
terraform force-unlock 21876308-...


-lock-timeout=60s
waits for the lock instead of failing
useful in CI
terraform plan -lock-timeout=60s





Refactoring blocks: moved, import, removed









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




moved
“the object at address A is now at address B”
keep it in the code until every environment has applied it
from = local_file.menu, to = local_file.price_list


import
adopt an existing real object into the state
to is an address, id is the provider’s ID format
to = random_integer.price_cents, id = "250,100,500"


-generate-config-out=FILE
with import blocks, writes the matching resource code for you
review and tidy the generated file
terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf


removed
stop managing a resource
add lifecycle { destroy = false } to keep the real object; without it, the object is destroyed
see below





lifecycle: changing how a resource is replaced or protected









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




create_before_destroy
builds the replacement first, then deletes the old one (+/-)
for things customers use, such as web servers
create_before_destroy = true


prevent_destroy
any plan that would destroy it fails
for databases and state buckets
prevent_destroy = true


ignore_changes
ignores drift in the listed arguments
when another system legitimately changes them
ignore_changes = [tags]


replace_triggered_by
replaces this resource when another one changes
e.g. restart containers when the image changes
replace_triggered_by = [docker_image.nginx]


precondition / postcondition
assertions checked before or after the change
fail early with a clear message
condition = self.public_ip != ""

title: State and Backends
text:
Worked example
All output below is real, from scratch folders, and trimmed.
Rename without moved. Change resource "local_file" "menu" to "price_list":
  # local_file.menu will be destroyed
  # (because local_file.menu is not in configuration)
  # local_file.price_list will be created
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
Terraform does not know it is the same file. For a database, this plan would delete your data.
Rename with moved:
moved {
  from = local_file.menu
  to   = local_file.price_list
}
  # local_file.menu has moved to local_file.price_list
Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
Protect it. With lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }, a destroy plan stops:
Error: Instance cannot be destroyed
Resource local_file.price_list has lifecycle.prevent_destroy set, ...
Release it without deleting it:
removed {
  from = local_file.price_list

  lifecycle {
    destroy = false
  }
}
 # local_file.price_list will no longer be managed by Terraform, but will not be destroyed
Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
$ ls menu.txt
menu.txt
Adopt an existing object with an import block. The random provider’s ID format for an integer is result,min,max:
resource "random_integer" "price_cents" {
  min = 100
  max = 500
}

import {
  to = random_integer.price_cents
  id = "250,100,500"
}
  # random_integer.price_cents will be imported
Plan: 1 to import, 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
Apply complete! Resources: 1 imported, 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
This is how you turn a hand-made snowflake server (lesson 1) into code: write or generate the resource block, import it, then let Terraform manage it.
Two runs at once. One terminal applies a slow change. Five seconds later a second terminal runs plan:
Error: Error acquiring the state lock
Lock Info:
  ID:        21876308-45f5-cf2e-01f3-ac1110af3861
  Operation: OperationTypeApply
  Who:       root@8e030cbc3912
The same plan with -lock-timeout=60s waited instead:
Acquiring state lock. This may take a few moments...
No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.

title: State and Backends
text:
Rules and conventions

One state per environment and component (prod/web, staging/web). Small states mean faster plans and smaller blast radius.
Shared state always lives in a remote backend with locking, encryption, versioning and tight access.
Never edit terraform.tfstate by hand, and never commit it. The .gitignore in examples/ excludes it.
Refactor with moved, import and removed blocks rather than state mv, import or state rm commands. Blocks appear in the plan and in code review.
Use prevent_destroy on anything that holds data.
If you see a lock error, find out who holds it before you even think about force-unlock.

title: State and Backends
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




State on a laptop, team of two
duplicate servers, or “already exists” errors
move to an s3 or gcs backend with init -migrate-state


Committing terraform.tfstate to Git
secrets in the repository; merge conflicts in JSON
add it to .gitignore, rotate exposed secrets, use a backend


Renaming a resource or module call
plan destroys and recreates it
add a moved block


removed without destroy = false
the real object is destroyed
add lifecycle { destroy = false }


force-unlock while a run is active
two writers corrupt the state
only unlock a lock whose run you know has died


ignore_changes = all to silence drift
Terraform silently stops managing the resource
list only the specific arguments another system owns

title: State and Backends
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
The state is a function from addresses to real objects:
\[
\sigma : A \to I
\]
where:

\(A\) is the set of resource addresses Terraform manages, such as random_integer.price_cents;
\(I\) is the set of real object IDs at the provider;
\(\sigma(a)\) is the ID recorded for address \(a\).

Example: let \(q\) stand for random_integer.price_cents. After the import, terraform state show printed id = "250", so \(\sigma(q) = 250\), and \(A = \lbrace q \rbrace\) gives \(\lvert A \rvert = 1\). After state rm, \(A = \emptyset\), and terraform state list | wc -l printed 0.
A moved block relabels an address without touching the object:
\[
\sigma'(b) = \sigma(a), \qquad a \notin \operatorname{dom}(\sigma'), \qquad \Delta = \emptyset
\]
where:

\(a\) is the from address and \(b\) the to address;
\(\sigma'\) is the state after the move;
\(\operatorname{dom}(\sigma')\), the domain, is the set of addresses the new state knows;
\(\Delta\) is the plan’s list of real changes.

Example: with \(a\) = local_file.menu and \(b\) = local_file.price_list, the real plan printed has moved to and Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy, so \(\Delta = \emptyset\). Without the block, Terraform instead sees \(a \in S \setminus D\) (destroy) and \(b \in D \setminus S\) (create), so \(\lvert \Delta \rvert = 2\): the real 1 to add, 1 to destroy.
Locking guarantees that at most one run writes the state at any moment:
\[
\forall t: \ \lvert W(t) \rvert \le 1
\]
where:

\(t\) is a moment in time;
\(W(t)\) is the set of Terraform runs holding the state lock at time \(t\);
\(\forall t\) reads “for every moment \(t\)”.

Example: the slow apply took the lock at \(t = 0\) s and held it for about 20 s. The second run at \(t = 5\) s would have made \(\lvert W(5) \rvert = 2\), so it was refused (Error acquiring the state lock). With -lock-timeout=60s it waited until about \(t = 20\) s, when \(\lvert W \rvert\) dropped back to 0, and then took the lock: \(\lvert W \rvert = 1\) again, never 2.
