title: HCL Syntax
text:
You open the Lemonade Stand’s examples/02-docker/ folder and see resource "docker_container" "stand" { ... }. Which word is a keyword, which is a name you chose, and which is a value? Where do curly braces go, and why are some values in quotes and some in square brackets?
Terraform files are written in HCL, the HashiCorp Configuration Language. HCL is small: a few shapes, repeated everywhere. Learn the shapes once and you can read any Terraform file.

title: HCL Syntax
text:
You open the Lemonade Stand’s examples/02-docker/ folder and see resource "docker_container" "stand" { ... }. Which word is a keyword, which is a name you chose, and which is a value? Where do curly braces go, and why are some values in quotes and some in square brackets?
Terraform files are written in HCL, the HashiCorp Configuration Language. HCL is small: a few shapes, repeated everywhere. Learn the shapes once and you can read any Terraform file.

title: HCL Syntax
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipLabelled boxes with stickers



Think of a storage shelf full of boxes. Each box has a label on the front, “Toy cars: red ones”. Inside the box, every toy has a sticker saying what it is: colour = "red", wheels = 4.
In HCL a block is a box, its labels are the words written on the front, and its arguments are the stickers inside, always name = value. A box can hold a smaller box, a nested block. That is the whole language. The rest is just which boxes exist and which stickers they accept.

title: HCL Syntax
text:
The concept, precisely

Anatomy of a block
resource "docker_container" "stand" {   # block type, then two labels
  name  = "lemonade-web1"               # argument: name = expression
  image = docker_image.nginx.image_id   # expression that references another resource

  ports {                               # nested block (no "=")
    internal = 80
    external = 8088
  }
}

Block type (resource): a keyword that Terraform knows.
Labels ("docker_container", "stand"): for a resource, the first label is the resource type (defined by the provider) and the second is the local name you choose. Together they form the address docker_container.stand.
Argument (name = "lemonade-web1"): an input you set. One argument per line.
Nested block (ports { ... }): no equals sign. It can usually be repeated.
Attribute: a value you can read from a resource, often only known after creation, such as docker_image.nginx.image_id.



Every top-level block type



Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




terraform
settings for Terraform itself: versions, providers, backend
one per root module, usually in versions.tf
terraform { required_version = ">= 1.10" }


provider
configures a plugin that talks to an API
one per provider (plus aliases)
provider "docker" {}


resource
something Terraform creates and owns
two labels: type and local name
resource "local_file" "menu" { ... }


data
something Terraform only reads
address starts with data.
data "aws_ami" "al2023" { ... }


variable
an input to the configuration
in variables.tf
variable "price" { type = number }


output
a value printed after apply and readable by others
in outputs.tf
output "urls" { value = ... }


locals
named helper values
referenced as local.<name> (singular!)
locals { cup = 2.5 }


module
uses another folder of Terraform code
lesson 8
module "web1" { source = "./modules/stand" }


moved
records a rename so nothing is destroyed
lesson 7
arguments from and to, two addresses


import
adopts an existing real object
lesson 7
arguments to (an address) and id (the cloud’s ID)


removed
stops managing a resource; with lifecycle { destroy = false } the real object is kept
lesson 7
from (an address) plus a lifecycle block


check
a health assertion reported on each plan and apply
warnings, not errors
check "menu_up" { assert { ... } }





Values and types









Keyword
What it is
Rule / convention
Example




string
text
double quotes only
"lemonade-web1"


number
whole or decimal number
no quotes
2.5, 8088


bool
true or false
lowercase, no quotes
true


list(T)
ordered values of one type, may repeat
square brackets, index from 0
["web1", "web2"]


set(T)
unordered values, no duplicates
made with toset(...)
toset(["web1", "web2"])


map(T)
key => value pairs, keys are strings
curly braces
{ web1 = 8088, web2 = 8089 }


object({...})
a fixed shape with named fields of different types
describe the shape in a type
object({ name = string, port = number })


tuple([...])
a fixed-length list with a type per position
rare in hand-written code
tuple([string, number])


null
“not set”: the argument falls back to its default
no quotes
default = null


any
“accept whatever type is given”
use sparingly; prefer real types
type = any





Strings, in detail



Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




"${...}"
interpolation: put a value inside text
the only use of $ that HCL treats specially
"lemonade-${each.key}"


doubled dollar before {
a literal dollar-brace in the text
needed for shell variables inside strings
see the block below the table


%{ if } / %{ for }
template directives inside strings
keep them short; use templatefile for big ones
"%{ if var.open }Open%{ else }Closed%{ endif }"


<<-EOT ... EOT
heredoc: multi-line text, indentation stripped
the - lets you indent the body
see user_data in examples/aws/main.tf


\n, \", \\
escapes inside double quotes

"Lemonade: $2.50\n"



command = "echo $${HOME}"   # Terraform passes on: echo ${HOME}
A $ followed by anything other than { is plain text, which is why "Lemonade: $2.50" needs no escape.


Comments









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




#
comment to end of line
the convention; fmt leaves it alone
# one stand per laptop port


//
same as #
allowed, less common
// old style


/* ... */
multi-line comment
for temporarily disabling a block while testing
/* resource ... */





The file layout convention
Terraform reads every .tf file in the folder as one configuration. File names and order do not matter to Terraform, but they matter to people, so everyone uses the same names. The Lemonade Docker example follows the convention exactly:
examples/02-docker/
├── versions.tf    # terraform { required_version, required_providers }
├── main.tf        # provider, resources, data sources
├── variables.tf   # variable blocks
└── outputs.tf     # output blocks
Bigger projects add providers.tf, locals.tf or one file per area (network.tf, web.tf). Small projects can keep everything in main.tf, as examples/01-local/ does.

title: HCL Syntax
section: Worked example: let fmt fix the style
text:
Worked example: let fmt fix the style
A messy file:
resource "local_file" "menu" {
filename="menu.txt"
    content = "Lemonade: $2.50"
  file_permission="0644"
}
terraform fmt -check -diff reports the problem without changing the file (real output):
$ terraform fmt -check -diff
main.tf
--- old/main.tf
+++ new/main.tf
-filename="menu.txt"
-    content = "Lemonade: $2.50"
-  file_permission="0644"
+  filename        = "menu.txt"
+  content         = "Lemonade: $2.50"
+  file_permission = "0644"
$ echo $?
3
The non-zero exit code is what lets a CI pipeline fail on unformatted code. Plain terraform fmt rewrites the file in place. The rules it applies:

two spaces of indentation per level;
the = signs of consecutive arguments are lined up;
one argument per line;
a blank line separates groups (fmt keeps your blank lines and aligns within each group).

title: HCL Syntax
text:
Rules and conventions

Names are snake_case: resource "docker_container" "stand", never "Stand" or "stand-web".
Do not repeat the type in the name: aws_instance.web, not aws_instance.web_instance.
Singular names: stand, not stands. With for_each the keys (["web1"], ["web2"]) make the instances plural.
Meta-arguments first: put count, for_each and provider at the top of a block, then a blank line, then normal arguments, then nested blocks, then lifecycle last.
Quote strings, not numbers or booleans: port = 8088, enabled = true.
Give every variable a type and a description. The type catches mistakes early (lesson 5).
Run terraform fmt -recursive before every commit.

title: HCL Syntax
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Single quotes: name = 'web1'
Error: Invalid character
HCL strings use double quotes only


= before a nested block: ports = { ... }
Unsupported argument; An argument named "ports" is not expected here. Did you mean to define a block of type "ports"?
write ports { ... }


Two arguments on one line in a multi-line block
Error: Missing newline after argument
one argument per line (single-line blocks may hold only one argument)


locals.cup
Error: Reference to undeclared resource
the block is locals, the reference is local.cup


Indexing a set: toset(x)[0]
Error: Invalid index
sets have no order; convert with tolist() or use a list


Putting the same resource address in two files
Error: Duplicate resource configuration
all files in a folder are one configuration; rename one

title: HCL Syntax
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Three of the types are best understood as small pieces of maths. First, a set keeps each distinct value once:
\[
\operatorname{toset}(L) = \lbrace x : x \in L \rbrace, \qquad \lvert \operatorname{toset}(L) \rvert \le \lvert L \rvert
\]
where:

\(L\) is a list, such as ["web1", "web2", "web1"];
\(\operatorname{toset}(L)\) is the set of values that appear in \(L\), without order and without repeats;
\(x \in L\) means “\(x\) appears somewhere in \(L\)”;
\(\lvert \cdot \rvert\) means “how many elements”.

Example: \(L = [\texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2}, \texttt{web1}]\) has \(\lvert L \rvert = 3\). Real terraform console output for toset(["web1", "web2", "web1"]) is toset(["web1", "web2"]), so \(\lvert \operatorname{toset}(L) \rvert = 2 \le 3\). The duplicate disappeared, which is exactly why for_each accepts sets but not lists.
Second, a list is indexed from zero, and an index is only valid inside the list:
\[
L[i] \text{ is defined} \iff 0 \le i < \lvert L \rvert
\]
where:

\(i\) is a whole number, the position you ask for;
\(L[i]\) is the element at that position, counting from \(0\);
\(\iff\) means “exactly when”.

Example: for stands = ["web1", "web2", "web3"], \(\lvert L \rvert = 3\), so the valid indices are \(0, 1, 2\). var.stands[0] is "web1" (real console output). var.stands[3] fails, because \(3 < 3\) is false.
Third, a map is a function from keys to values:
\[
m : K \to V, \qquad m(k) = v
\]
where:

\(K\) is the set of keys (always strings in HCL);
\(V\) is the set of possible values (all of one type, such as numbers);
\(m(k) = v\) means “looking up key \(k\) gives value \(v\)”; each key has exactly one value.

Example: the Docker example’s stands = { web1 = 8088, web2 = 8089 } has \(K = \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2} \rbrace\), \(V\) = numbers, \(m(\texttt{web1}) = 8088\) and \(m(\texttt{web2}) = 8089\). Because each key maps to one value, two stands can never accidentally share a key, but two stands could share a port. That is a rule Terraform does not check for you.

text:
References

HashiCorp, “Configuration Syntax”: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/syntax/configuration
HashiCorp, “Types and Values”: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/expressions/types
HashiCorp, “Strings and Templates”: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/expressions/strings
HashiCorp, “Style Guide”: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/style

title: Modules
text:
The Lemonade Stand now has a staging copy and a production copy, and each has two stands. Every stand needs the same few resources: a container, a menu, a port. Copying those blocks four times means four places to fix every bug.
You want to write “how to build one stand” once, then say “build one called web1 at $2.50 and one called web2 at $3.00”. That reusable piece is a module.

title: Modules
text:
The Lemonade Stand now has a staging copy and a production copy, and each has two stands. Every stand needs the same few resources: a container, a menu, a port. Copying those blocks four times means four places to fix every bug.
You want to write “how to build one stand” once, then say “build one called web1 at $2.50 and one called web2 at $3.00”. That reusable piece is a module.

title: Modules
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






Tip‘Build this wheel four times’



Big LEGO booklets have a small boxed page that says “build this wheel, ×4”. You learn to build one wheel, build it four times, and clip the four wheels onto the car. The wheel page is a module. The car’s booklet calls it four times.
Each call can be a little different, a red wheel or a blue wheel. Those differences are the module’s inputs. Once a wheel is built, the car needs to know where it is, “the wheel’s axle is here”. That is the module’s output.
But nobody prints a boxed page for a single brick. “Put one brick here, ×1” would only make the booklet longer. A module must be worth the page it takes.

title: Modules
text:
The concept, precisely

Every Terraform folder is a module. The folder where you run terraform is the root module.
A child module is a folder that another module calls with a module block.
The child’s variable blocks are its inputs, and its output blocks are its outputs. Everything else inside is private.
The caller reads an output as module.<NAME>.<OUTPUT>.

examples/03-module/ calls one tiny module twice:
module "web1" {
  source = "./modules/stand"
  name   = "web1"
  price  = 2.5
}

module "web2" {
  source = "./modules/stand"
  name   = "web2"
  price  = 3
}

output "menus" {
  value = [module.web1.menu_file, module.web2.menu_file]
}
The module itself, modules/stand/main.tf, has two inputs, one resource and one output:
variable "name" { type = string }
variable "price" { type = number }

resource "local_file" "menu" {
  filename = "${path.root}/menu-${var.name}.txt"
  content  = "Stand ${var.name}: lemonade ${format("$%.2f", var.price)}\n"
}

output "menu_file" {
  value = local_file.menu.filename
}

The module block









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




source
where the module’s code lives
required; a literal string, no variables
"./modules/stand"


version
which release, for registry modules
always pin registry modules
version = "~> 6.8"


inputs
every other argument sets one of the child’s variables
names must match the child’s variable blocks
price = 2.5


count / for_each
many copies of the whole module
addresses become module.stand["web1"]
for_each = var.stands


providers
passes a specific provider copy (alias) in
needed for multi-region
providers = { aws = aws.london }


depends_on
an extra dependency on the whole module
rare
depends_on = [module.network]


module.NAME.OUTPUT
reads an output of the child
only outputs are visible
module.web1.menu_file





Kinds of source









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




local path
a folder in the same repository
must start with ./ or ../
"./modules/stand"


registry
NAMESPACE/NAME/PROVIDER on the Terraform Registry
use with version
"terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"


Git
a Git repository, pinned to a tag
?ref= a tag, not a branch
"git::https://github.com/acme/tf-stand.git?ref=v1.2.0"



After adding or changing a source, run terraform init again: it downloads modules as well as providers.


The standard module structure
modules/stand/
├── README.md       # what it does, an example call
├── main.tf         # resources
├── variables.tf    # inputs, each with type and description
├── outputs.tf      # outputs, each with description
└── versions.tf     # required_providers (no provider blocks!)
A reusable module declares which providers it needs, but it never configures them (no region, no credentials). The caller does that. Our teaching module keeps everything in one main.tf because it is only 15 lines long.


Using a famous registry module
The community module terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws builds a whole AWS network, the one from Part 4, in one block:
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "~> 6.8"

  name           = "lemonade"
  cidr           = "10.0.0.0/16"
  azs            = ["eu-west-2a", "eu-west-2b"]
  public_subnets = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24"]
}
Read a registry module’s inputs and outputs on its registry page, and read its code before trusting it in production.

title: Modules
text:
Worked example
Real output from examples/03-module/:
$ terraform init
Initializing modules...
- web1 in modules/stand
- web2 in modules/stand
- Installed hashicorp/local v2.9.1 (signed by HashiCorp)

$ terraform apply -auto-approve
  # module.web1.local_file.menu will be created
  # module.web2.local_file.menu will be created
Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
Apply complete! Resources: 2 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
Outputs:
menus = [
  "./menu-web1.txt",
  "./menu-web2.txt",
]

$ cat menu-web1.txt menu-web2.txt
Stand web1: lemonade $2.50
Stand web2: lemonade $3.00

$ terraform state list
module.web1.local_file.menu
module.web2.local_file.menu
The addresses show the nesting: module.web1.local_file.menu is “the local_file.menu inside the module call named web1”.

title: Modules
section: When not to make a module

title: Modules
text:
Rules and conventions

One module, one purpose, named after what it builds (stand, network), not after the tool (terraform-module-1).
Every input has a type and description. Every output has a description.
Pin registry modules with version and Git modules with ?ref=<tag>.
Child modules never contain provider blocks, only required_providers.
Keep the root module thin: it calls modules and passes values between them.
Use path.module for files that ship with the module and path.root for files that belong to the caller. The teaching module writes the menus at path.root so they appear next to main.tf.

title: Modules
text:
Common mistakes



Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Forgetting terraform init after adding a module
Module not installed
run terraform init


Passing an input the module does not declare
Unsupported argument; An argument named "colour" is not expected here
add a variable "colour" to the module, or remove the argument


Reading a module’s resource directly: module.web1.local_file.menu.filename
Unsupported attribute
expose it with an output and read module.web1.menu_file


A variable in source
Variables not allowed
source must be a literal string


An unpinned registry module
a new major version changes resources on the next init -upgrade
add version = "~> X.Y"


Renaming a module call
everything inside is destroyed and recreated
add a moved { from = module.old  to = module.new } block (lesson 7)

title: Modules
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
A module call behaves like a function. It takes inputs, creates resources and returns outputs:
\[
M : (x_1, \dots, x_k) \mapsto (o_1, \dots, o_m)
\]
where:

\(M\) is the module, here modules/stand;
\(x_1, \dots, x_k\) are its \(k\) input variables, here \(k = 2\): name and price;
\(o_1, \dots, o_m\) are its \(m\) outputs, here \(m = 1\): menu_file;
\(\mapsto\) reads “maps to”: given these inputs, the module produces these outputs (and, unlike a pure function, it also creates real resources).

Example: \(M(\texttt{web1}, 2.5) = \texttt{./menu-web1.txt}\) and \(M(\texttt{web2}, 3) = \texttt{./menu-web2.txt}\), exactly the two values in the real menus output. The text inside the files, “lemonade $2.50” and “lemonade $3.00”, is the side effect.
The number of resources a configuration manages is the sum over all module calls:
\[
R = r_0 + \sum_{c=1}^{N} r_c
\]
where:

\(R\) is the total number of resource instances in the state;
\(r_0\) is the number of resources written directly in the root module;
\(N\) is the number of module calls (each for_each key counts as one call);
\(r_c\) is the number of resources created by call \(c\).

Example: examples/03-module/ has \(r_0 = 0\) (the root only calls modules), \(N = 2\) calls, and each creates \(r_c = 1\) file. So \(R = 0 + (1 + 1) = 2\), matching Plan: 2 to add and the two lines of terraform state list. With a production copy that adds two more calls, \(R = 0 + 4 \times 1 = 4\), still without writing a new resource block.
When is a module worth it? As a heuristic, not a law, extract when the same group of blocks is needed at least three times:
\[
\text{make a module} \iff n_{\text{uses}} \ge 3 \ \land\ n_{\text{resources}} \ge 2
\]
where:

\(n_{\text{uses}}\) is how many places need the same group of resources;
\(n_{\text{resources}}\) is how many resources the group contains (one would be a thin wrapper);
\(\land\) means “and”, and \(\iff\) “exactly when”.

Example: a Lemonade stand (container + menu + firewall rule) is needed for web1 and web2 in staging and production, so \(n_{\text{uses}} = 4 \ge 3\) and \(n_{\text{resources}} = 3 \ge 2\): make a module. A single S3 bucket used once has \(n_{\text{uses}} = 1\): write the resource directly. Our teaching module breaks the rule on purpose (\(n_{\text{resources}} = 1\)) so the mechanics stay visible.

title: The Lemonade Stand on AWS and Google Cloud
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipSame drawing, different brick brands



You drew a lemonade stand and want to build it twice: once with LEGO and once with a different brick brand. The drawing is the same: a counter, a roof, a sign. But the bricks do not fit each other. A LEGO roof piece is not a roof piece from the other brand.
Terraform is the same. HCL, plan and apply work the same for every cloud. The bricks, the resource types, belong to one cloud: aws_instance is an AWS brick and google_cloud_run_v2_service is a Google brick. Yevgeniy Brikman makes the same point in his famous Gruntwork article “Why we use Terraform and not Chef, Puppet, Ansible, Pulumi, or CloudFormation”. Terraform gives you one tool and one language for every cloud, not one file that runs on any cloud.

title: The Lemonade Stand on AWS and Google Cloud
text:
The concept, precisely

From hand-built services to Terraform resources









Keyword
AWS resource (Part 4)
Google Cloud resource (Part 5)
Lemonade use




virtual machine
aws_instance
google_compute_instance
web1


firewall rule
aws_security_group
google_compute_firewall
allow port 80


network
aws_vpc, aws_subnet
google_compute_network, google_compute_subnetwork
10.0.0.0/16


container service
aws_ecs_service (Fargate)
google_cloud_run_v2_service
the Lemonade image


object storage
aws_s3_bucket
google_storage_bucket
the menu, the Terraform state


permission
aws_iam_role_policy and friends
google_cloud_run_v2_service_iam_member and friends
who may call or change it


look up an image
data "aws_ami"
data "google_compute_image"
newest operating system





The AWS version: one web server and its firewall
From examples/aws/main.tf, the firewall and the server:
resource "aws_security_group" "web" {
  name = "lemonade-web"

  ingress {
    from_port   = 80
    to_port     = 80
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }

  egress {
    from_port   = 0
    to_port     = 0
    protocol    = "-1"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }
}

resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami                    = data.aws_ami.al2023.id
  instance_type          = "t3.micro"
  vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.web.id]

  user_data = <<-EOF
    #!/bin/bash
    dnf install -y nginx
    echo '<h1>Lemonade: $2.50</h1>' > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
    systemctl enable --now nginx
  EOF

  tags = { Name = "lemonade-web1" }
}
The image comes from the data "aws_ami" lookup in lesson 4. user_data is a script the server runs at its first boot. In a real project, Ansible (Part 1) or a pre-built image would replace it.


The Google Cloud version: a public Cloud Run service
From examples/gcp/main.tf:
resource "google_cloud_run_v2_service" "web" {
  name                = "lemonade-web"
  location            = var.region
  deletion_protection = false

  template {
    containers {
      image = var.image
    }
  }
}

resource "google_cloud_run_v2_service_iam_member" "public" {
  name     = google_cloud_run_v2_service.web.name
  location = google_cloud_run_v2_service.web.location
  role     = "roles/run.invoker"
  member   = "allUsers"
}
There is no server, firewall or operating system to describe. Cloud Run runs the container and gives it an HTTPS URL. The second resource lets anyone on the internet call it. Replace the default sample image with the Lemonade image that the CI/CD part builds.


The arguments that matter









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




region (AWS provider)
which AWS region to build in
a variable, never hard-coded in many places
region = var.region


project (Google provider)
which Google Cloud project to build in
the Part 5 project
project = "lemonade-stand-dev"


ingress / egress
inbound / outbound firewall rules
open only the ports you serve
from_port = 80, to_port = 80


cidr_blocks
which source addresses a rule allows
0.0.0.0/0 means “everyone”
["0.0.0.0/0"]


instance_type
the size of the VM, and therefore its price
start small
"t3.micro"


user_data
first-boot script
keep it short; prefer images or Ansible
<<-EOF ... EOF


deletion_protection
Cloud Run refuses to be destroyed while true (the provider default)
set false for labs, keep true in production
deletion_protection = false


member = "allUsers"
grants a role to the whole internet
only for public websites
role = "roles/run.invoker"


uri
the Cloud Run service’s HTTPS address
expose it as an output
google_cloud_run_v2_service.web.uri





Credentials come from outside the code



Command
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




aws sso login / AWS_PROFILE
gives Terraform AWS credentials
the AWS provider reads the same settings as the aws CLI
AWS_PROFILE=lemonade terraform plan


gcloud auth application-default login
gives Terraform Google credentials
never download service-account key files for a laptop
gcloud auth application-default login


OIDC in CI
short-lived credentials for pipelines
lesson 10
aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials

title: The Lemonade Stand on AWS and Google Cloud
text:
Worked example
These two folders are checked with init -backend=false and validate. That proves the code is correct for the current providers, without an account and without spending money. Real output:
$ cd examples/aws && terraform init -backend=false
- Installed hashicorp/aws v6.74.0 (signed by HashiCorp)
$ terraform validate
Success! The configuration is valid.

$ cd ../gcp && terraform init -backend=false
- Installed hashicorp/google v8.12.0 (signed by HashiCorp)
$ terraform validate
Success! The configuration is valid.
With your own account from Part 4 or Part 5, the full cycle is:
terraform init
terraform apply                         # read the plan: AWS shows 2 to add, Google Cloud 2 to add
curl "$(terraform output -raw url)"     # the Lemonade page (AWS: wait a minute for the first boot)
terraform destroy                       # stop paying
The AWS provider is large. If validate fails inside a small Docker VM with Plugin did not respond, give Docker more memory or add -e GOMEMLIMIT=450MiB -e GOGC=20 to the docker run command. That is how this book’s check was run.

title: The Lemonade Stand on AWS and Google Cloud
text:
Rules and conventions

One folder (and one state) per cloud and per environment. Do not mix AWS and Google resources in one configuration unless they truly depend on each other.
Credentials never appear in .tf files or in variables with defaults.
Look up images and zones with data sources instead of copying IDs from a console.
Open firewalls only as wide as needed: port 80 to the world for a public site, never port 22.
Keep deletion_protection and prevent_destroy on anything holding data in production.
Always destroy lab resources when you finish. The cost formula below shows why.
crumbs: The Lemonade Stand on AWS and Google Cloud

title: The Lemonade Stand on AWS and Google Cloud
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




No credentials configured
AWS: No valid credential sources found; Google: could not find default credentials
aws sso login / gcloud auth application-default login


Cloud Run API not enabled in the project
Cloud Run Admin API has not been used in project ... or it is disabled
gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com (or a google_project_service resource)


destroy fails on Cloud Run
cannot destroy service without setting deletion_protection=false
set it to false, apply, then destroy


Website unreachable on AWS
the security group has no egress rule or the wrong port
allow inbound 80; Terraform removes AWS’s default egress rule, so declare it


Expecting the AWS file to run on Google Cloud
resource types are unknown to the other provider
write one configuration per cloud; share only ideas and variables
